Foreword

It is my privilege to write a foreword for this book entitled “Maxillofacial
Trauma: A Clinical Guide” having 24 chapters on different aspects of maxillofacial trauma including basic as well as clinical topics.
In the last two decades, there have been tremendous advancements in the
management of maxillofacial trauma and facial injuries. The approach and
treatment scenario in the field of maxillofacial trauma is changing very fast.
This book covers each and every aspect of maxillofacial trauma which
includes diagnostic approach, treatment planning, patient concerns, and
recent advancements.
I wish all the best to the authors of this book and recommend this to all
readers and wish that they all will be benefitted.

Preface

The book entitled “Maxillofacial Trauma: A Clinical Guide” has been
designed in such a way that it amalgamates the basic concepts in understanding the science of maxillofacial skeleton as well as the clinical skills required
in managing the complex facial fractures. The book has two sections: First
one deals with the introduction of maxillofacial trauma, biomechanics of
maxillofacial skeleton, principles of osteosynthesis and internal fixation,
medicolegal aspects of maxillofacial trauma, and preoperative workup which
provides a brief outline of basic concepts in understanding the anatomy and
physiology of facial skeleton. The other section is oriented clinically with
case-based discussion that starts from the emergency management of facial
trauma including the recent protocols of basic life support and advanced
trauma life support, emergency airway management followed by definitive
management guidelines in stabilizing and fixing the fractured facial bones.
The clinical cases have been discussed in a way to provide practical knowledge and skills to the postgraduate students and clinicians which will enhance
their knowledge and facilitate the decision-making process.
Previously, students had to go through various textbooks to procure the
information regarding anatomy, physiology, biomechanics, anesthetic perspectives, clinical protocol required but this one book will provide all necessary details in one place. We have also included the current evidences and
existing controversies in deciding treatment of complex clinical conditions
like panfacial trauma and condylar fractures. The chapters include various
clinical pictures, schematic diagram, classifications, flow chart including
treatment algorithms which will make the subject easy to understand.
This book is a collaborative effort of contributors from premier institutions
of the country which makes it unique. We express our sincere gratitude to all
the authors for their valuable contribution.
We acknowledge our editing team members Dr Madan Mishra, Dr Richik
Tripathi, Dr Arun Pandey, and Dr Janani Anand Kumar for their valuable
inputs. We are also thankful to Mr Rajesh Kumar, Mr Chandan Kumar, and
Mr Lalit Vishwakarma, our photography and art team, for their tremendous
efforts.
We also wish to thank Mr. Gaurav Singh and Mr Ejaz Ahmad from
Springer Nature for their valuable support.

Introduction
to Craniomaxillofacial Trauma
Akhilesh Kumar Singh and Janani Anand Kumar

‘Face is Considered as Mirror of the Soul’

1.1

Introduction

Face is a unique component of the human body,
which plays a very important role in identification of an individual. Every individual has a
unique facial pattern; no two individuals have an
exactly similar face, except for the identical
twins. Face is a structural unit which consists of
multiple compartments that is responsible for
various vital functions. It is covered by the skin
externally, while the deep layers include fat, muscles, nerves, blood vessels and bones. Facial skeleton is anatomically divided into three parts: the
upper third, the middle third and the lower third
(Fig. 1.1). The upper third is formed prominently
by the frontal bone, followed by the middle third
which commences from just below the frontal
bone and terminates at the level of the upper
teeth. The mandible dictates the lower third [1].
The upper third consists of the sturdy cranial
bones encasing the brain and protects it from any

A. K. Singh (*) · J. Anand Kumar
Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery Unit,
Faculty of Dental Sciences, Institute of Medical
Sciences, Banaras Hindu University, Varanasi,
Uttar Pradesh, India
e-mail: aksingh.dent@bhu.ac.in

external injury. The middle third includes two
orbital cavities, which accommodates the eyeballs for visual sensation. Anteriorly, it contains
the nasal passage, which is the entry portal of air
for breathing and is also responsible for the sense
of smell. Located on the lateral aspect are the ears
which have two important functions of hearing
and maintaining body balance. The lower portion
comprises the oral cavity which is responsible for
three major functions such as speech, mastication
and deglutition. Therefore, face acts as a reservoir of different special sensory organs. Due to
the prominent and superior position of the face in
the body, it is easily prone to various types of
insults.
Craniomaxillofacial (CMF) trauma includes
any external injury to the hard and soft tissues of
the head, face and neck region. Trauma to these
regions may be in the form of abrasion, laceration, contusion, hematoma, avulsion, burn, bone
fractures, etc. CMF trauma can be associated
with significant morbidity and mortality since the
head and neck region houses numerous vital
structures such as brain, orbital cavity and its
contents, nasal passage, oral cavity, pharynx, etc.
It may involve life-threatening situations such as
brain injury, airway obstruction, excessive bleed-

patient becomes morbid both physically and

protect the brain from any direct injury.

ing from major vessels and shock. Therefore,
management of a CMF trauma case always commences with stabilization of the patient and providing basic life support, if required. The primary
management of the patient is then followed by
definitive treatment such as fracture reduction
and fixation, soft tissue repair or reconstruction
of any defect, which varies according to individual case scenario. In some cases, it is wise to
defer the diagnosis and definitive treatment until
the swelling subsides or other associated severe
injuries are resolved. Treatment planning is a step
of prime importance that precedes the actual
treatment phase, which includes a detailed systematic evaluation of the patient and all the
required investigations such as X-rays, CT scan
and blood reports. The treatment varies according to the type and severity of the injury. A definitive treatment in CMF trauma is inevitable for
several reasons such as:

Historical Perspective

Review of literature reveals that the first writings appeared as early as 1600 BC; however, it
was Hippocrates in 400 BC who first developed
a clear concept of re-approximation of fracture
and immobilization [2]. The importance of
occlusion was first seen to be mentioned in
1180 [3]. In the pre-antibiotic era, closed reduction was strongly recommended for any type of
fracture due to the high risk of infections which
lead to osteomyelitis and bone necrosis; therefore, external pin fixators gained popularity
during this time. After the development of antibiotics and techniques of anaesthesia, open
treatment of fractures gained popularity. A
Belgian surgeon named Albin Lambotte
improved the techniques of Hansmann and
coined the term internal fixation [4].
In 1958, Maurice Edmond Müller, Martin
Allgöwer, H. Willenegger, Robert Schneider and
Walter Bandi along with few other general and
orthopaedic surgeons conducted a meeting at
Biel/Bienne, Switzerland, which later developed
into the group called ASIF (Association for the
Study of Internal Fixation) or AO (Arbeitsgemein-­
Schaftfur Osteosynthesefragen). They formulated a ‘working hypotheses’ that included four
principles for obtaining optimal results. They
were:
1. Anatomical reduction
2. Rigid internal fixation
3. Atraumatic technique on soft tissue as well as
on the bone
4. Early pain-free active mobilization during the
first 10 postoperative days [5].

1

Introduction to Craniomaxillofacial Trauma

It was Christiansen in 1945 who introduced
bone plates to maxillofacial surgery [6]. In the
late 1960s and early 1970s, several investigators
began to identify the difference between the long
bone fracture and maxillofacial fractures. New
armamentarium was developed specially
designed for maxillofacial fractures. This period
came to be widely known as the ‘modern era’ of
internal fixation for maxillofacial fractures [5]. In
the mid-1960s, Luhr introduced the concept of
compression plating to maxillofacial surgery. He
designed a Vitallium mandibular compression
bone plate using the gliding screw principle [7].
Spiessl was the first one to apply the AO/ASIF
principles to the treatment of mandibular fractures [8]. In the early 1970s, Spiessl started using
and modifying the AO/ASIF instruments for the
mandible [9]. In 1970, Brons and Boering introduced lag screws to maxillofacial surgery [10].
Schmoker and Niederdellmann in 1973 developed eccentric dynamic compression plate,
which obviated the need for a tension band [11].
In 1973, Michelet and co-workers reported a
plating system which was small, easily adaptable
and of non-compression type that could be fixed
trans-orally with monocortical screws [12]. In
1978, Champy et al. introduced the concept of
miniplate and the ideal lines of osteosynthesis. It
was a modification of the plating system originally described by Michelet et al. [13]. In 1992,
Farmand and Dupoirieux developed the concept
of 3D miniplates whose shape is based on the
principle of the quadrangle as a geometrically
stable configuration for support [14]. Locking
plate system was introduced in 2003 by Raveh
et al. in collaboration with AO/ASIF Institute
(Davos, Switzerland) [15].

1.2.1

Evolution of Diagnostic
Imaging

Radiographic imaging was developed by Wilhelm
Conrad Roentgen in 1895. Following this, the
first dental radiographs were made in 1896 with
the use of glass photographic plates/roll to capture the images. In 1921, production of regular
dental films started as machine-made packets.

5

The bite-wing technique was introduced by
Raper in 1925, followed by the development of
paralleling technique by McCormack in 1937.
Dr. Yrjo Veli Paatero in 1948 first introduced the
panoramic radiography technique and also the
extraoral film; hence, he is known as the father of
panoramic radiography [16, 17]. There are various views of extraoral imaging that can be utilized in maxillofacial imaging such as
posteroanterior projection, lateral oblique projection, Caldwell projection, Waters’ view,
submental-­
vertex projection/jug handle view,
reverse Towne’s projection, etc. From the time of
its invention, plain radiography has always continued to be the mainstay of diagnosis till date.
However, it was associated with some drawbacks
such as overlapping of structures, most of the
projections being impractical in patients with
cervical injury, etc., which led to the development of computed tomography (CT) by Godfrey
Hounsfield in 1972, which gives more detailed
information than plain radiography. It was the
first technology to allow the visualization of both
hard and soft tissues by image processing
enhancement [18]. The image contrast of soft tissues that contain good vascularity can be
enhanced by injecting intravenous contrast
agents. In 1997, cone-beam CT (CBCT) was first
introduced in imaging of maxillofacial region.
CBCT produces images of high diagnostic quality with sub-millimetre resolution. It can provide
three-dimensional representation of the maxillofacial skeleton with minimal distortion. Spiral
and multislice CT are recent advancements that
can produce nine times larger image and have
high-quality reconstruction. CT has become the
preferred modality of imaging after its advent,
since it has more sensitivity for fracture detection, provides multiple views in various sections
and has the ability to provide three-dimensional
view of the structure [17]. Even after the advent
of CT scan, conventional radiographs are considered invaluable in certain scenarios such as in
gunshot injury cases to clearly visualize the bullet and in fracture involving teeth to determine
the exact position and status of the teeth.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) refers to
the technique by which images of the body are

6

created using magnetic field and radio waves. It
was the combined efforts of Paul Lauterbur and
Peter Mansfield who invented MRI in the early
1970s and received Nobel Prize in 2003. In 1977,
Raymond Damadian developed a full-body MRI
machine for medical use. It is commonly recommended for evaluating soft tissue abnormalities.
Although it has a wide range of application in
maxillofacial diagnosis such as TMJ pathologies,
benign and malignant tumours of the soft tissue,
etc., it has minimal application in maxillofacial
trauma and is limited to soft tissue injuries and
CSF leak. The main advantage of MRI over other
imaging modalities is that there is zero radiation
exposure [17].
In recent years, surgeons have gradually
started progressing towards computer-aided
CMF surgery. Computer-aided CMF surgery can
be divided into computer-aided presurgical planning, intraoperative navigation and intraoperative
CT/MRI imaging. In 1987, Brix and Lambrecht
applied the technique of computer-aided manufacturing (CAM) in oral and maxillofacial surgery, which led to fabrication of three-dimensional
models by stereolithography (STL). This technology was a major breakthrough in diagnostic
imaging, since producing life-sized resin model
of skeletal and soft tissue anatomy could influence planning and implementation of CMF surgeries to a great level. CAD/CAM software can
also be used for fabricating custom-milled titanium plates or patient-specific implants for
reconstruction [19]. Endoscopic approach to
maxillofacial trauma is a topic of recent interest,
which finds its use in the treatment of zygomatic
arch fracture, orbital trauma, frontal sinus wall
and sub-condylar fractures [20]. The peak of evolution is the robotic surgery, which is practised in
a very few centres across the world. In spite of
these advancements in diagnostics, developing
countries like India face a major difficulty due to
the unavailability of these important diagnostic
aids at every level of health-care centre. Due to
its high cost, CT and MRI machines are provided
only in tertiary and a very few secondary health-­
care centres. Therefore, most of the trauma
patients in critical condition from primary and
some secondary health-care centres are referred

A. K. Singh and J. Anand Kumar

to higher centres. A study by Bergeron et al. in
2017 showed that 84% of the patients are being
referred to higher centres for CT scan [21]. This
could lead to significant delay in diagnosis and
increased expenses. It also poses a great threat to
the patients’ life.

1.3

Epidemiology

Maxillofacial trauma is one of the frequently
reported cases in any emergency set-up. The aetiology and pattern of injury varies according to
the region of study. According to Global Burden
of Disease Study (2017) estimates, highest incidence of cases was reported in Central Europe,
Eastern Europe and Central Asia with a regional
incidence of 254 cases per 100,000 population.
In 2017, there has been a whopping 7,538,663
new facial fracture cases across the world. The
global incidence was 98 cases per 100,000 population, which has not changed significantly in the
past three to four decades. The geographic distribution of prevalence was similar to incidence
[22]. In most regions, incidence rises from age 5
to 20 and rise again over 70 years (Fig. 1.2). In
most of the epidemiologic studies, men are more
commonly injured than women [24]. Aetiology
of facial fracture across the world are motor vehicle accidents (MVAs), fall from height, physical
assault, exposure to mechanical forces, firearm
injuries due to warfare and terrorism, sports-­
related injuries and other injuries like animal
bite, etc. Globally, falls were the predominant
cause of facial fractures, whereas in developing
Southeast Asian countries like India, Pakistan,
Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, etc. MVAs are found to

A 9-year retrospective study conducted in
India (2015) revealed that road traffic accidents
(RTA) had a high tendency towards mandible
fractures (43.8%), followed by midface fractures
(39.3%) and frontal bone fractures (16.9%). In
mandible, condyle region was the most susceptible, followed by para-symphysis and symphysis
region. Interestingly, it was seen that, in case of
heavy vehicle accidents, midface fractures
(49.41%) were seen more commonly when compared to mandible fractures (27.05%). Similar to
RTA, assault also resulted in a higher number of
mandible fractures (49.33%), followed by midface fractures (30.67%) and upper face fractures
(20%). Fall, in turn, resulted in a greater number
of frontal bone fractures [25].
According to the National Trauma Data Bank
(USA), the head is the most commonly affected
region in paediatric trauma cases, with the face
being the fourth. Paediatric facial fractures
account for 15% of all facial fractures; however,
most of the paediatric trauma cases are limited to
dentoalveolar fractures and soft tissue injury.
Green stick and oblique fractures are the commonly seen entity in paediatric population.
Children between 12 and 18 years have the highest facial fracture incidence, with common aetiology being interpersonal violence, followed by
sports injury. Children of 6–11 years have the
second highest incidence with common aetiologies being RTA and play. Facial fractures are
reported the least in children aged 0–5 years with
aetiology likely being fall [26, 27]. Fracture pattern in paediatric trauma cases varies according
to the region where the study is based. A study
conducted by Gassner et al. [27] in Austria
recorded the facial fracture pattern in children
below 15 years as Le Fort I 0.2%, Le Fort II
0.8%, Le Fort III 0.5%, zygoma 12.7%, zygomatic arch 2.2%, orbital floor 17.3%, frontal
bone 5.2%, maxilla 19.2%, nasal bone 5.9%,
mandibular symphysis 1.6%, mandibular body
11.8%, collum 12.9%, mandibular processes 4%
and caput 5.2% [27]. Paediatric trauma requires
prompt attention, as it could hamper the growth
of the associated structures and result in significant morbidity.

Maxillofacial fracture injuries caused by
MVAs and fall from height have a high tendency
to be associated with concomitant injuries of
other parts of the body, whereas assault and gunshot injury cases are less likely to have concomitant injuries. They are most commonly serious
life-threatening injuries that require immediate
attention, which often delays facial fracture
management leading to complications such as
malunion, fibrosis, scarring, etc. (Fig. 1.5) [23].

of Injury

been developed for serving various purposes
such as determining the status of the patient,
communication and record purpose, predicting
the treatment outcome and prioritizing the

1

Introduction to Craniomaxillofacial Trauma

1.3.2

Prevention

Although the advancements in diagnostic aids,
surgical techniques and treatment modalities
could assure the patient an appreciable treatment outcome, it is inevitable for the healthcare systems around the world to develop
awareness programmes for injury prevention
and to make sure that every individual has adequate access to immediate emergency care and
definitive treatment.

1.3.3

Road Traffic Accidents

• Enforcement of strict laws such as mandatory
use of helmets for two-wheeler riders and seat
belt for four-wheeler riders
• Prohibiting the use of mobile phones and
headsets while driving
• Conducting public awareness programmes to
obey traffic rules
• Speed limit restriction and speed breakers
• Strict prohibition on road racing and driving
under alcohol influence
• Installing adequate streetlights and traffic signals

1.3.5

• Resolving conflict between countries through
arbitration, conciliation, mediation, negotiation, collaborative law, etc.

1.3.6

Sports Injury

• Use of protective headgear, mouth guard, protective pads, etc
• Avoiding violent sports
• Obeying rules of the game
• Proper nutrition and adequate hydration
• Proper rest and recovery

Falls

Since globally fall has been reported widely to be
the cause for maxillofacial trauma, awareness
programmes must be conducted addressing every
factor that leads to fall. Aetiology of fall varies
with different age groups. In young age, the aetiology may be built environment, socio-economic
status, type of furniture, etc., whereas in adults, it
is most commonly due to alcohol consumption.
In elderly population, there are numerous factors
that might lead to fall such as weakness, poor
visual acuity, medication related, alcohol/drug
abuse and other factors [22].

1.3.4

9

Warfare and Terrorism

• Arms control and diplomacy
• Law enforcement and military efforts against
terrorism

1.4

Conclusion

Craniomaxillofacial trauma is a significant cause
of morbidity and mortality across the world. It
requires prompt attention, since it can handicap
the patient by various means. Sooner the treatment, better are the results. Management of a
CMF trauma case requires an experienced surgeon with deep knowledge of the anatomy, treatment protocol and possible complications. In the
last few decades, advancements in science have
helped to produce improved outcomes in
­maxillofacial trauma management. Health-care
systems need to be improvised so that every individual receives immediate medical attention at
affordable cost and feasible distance, without any
need for inter-centre transportation. More focus
by the health-care bodies and common people is
required on various possible ways to prevent and
mitigate the occurrence of trauma.

2.1

Introduction

Orofacial and scalp injuries present to the maxillofacial surgeons, but the seriousness varies from
a small laceration to major pan-facial trauma.
Signs and symptoms of head and neck trauma are
determined by the anatomical arrangement of
various structures and are helpful to elucidate the
underlying injuries clinically and target the
investigations.
The human skull is comprised of 28 bones.
Out of which, eight are cranial bones, 14 are
facial bones, and the remaining six are ear ossicles. Cranium consists of paired parietal and temporal and unpaired frontal, occipital, sphenoid
and ethmoid bones. The facial bones consist of
two unpaired bones, the mandible and the vomer,
and six paired which include maxilla, zygomatic
bone, lacrimal, nasal, palatine and inferior nasal
conchae. The three ear ossicles are paired and are
malleus, incus and stapes (Table 2.1).
The trainee surgeon should be aware of the
relation of the various bones. However, they
should be familiar with the skull as a whole unit.
So, we divided the skull into six zones and tried
to correlate these zones with basic principles of
maxillofacial trauma. This chapter discusses the
clinically relevant anatomy of facial skeleton and

The anatomy of the face for trauma is best
divided into zones that are predominantly involved
and are treated by maxillofacial surgeons. We have
divided the facial zones/facial skeleton roughly
into six zones (Fig. 2.1). This an arbitrary zonal
division for ease of classification of the structures
that are usually grouped for treatment.
The zones are:
• Zone I: All structures above the line joining
the supraorbital ridge frontonasal junction to
the lateral border of the zygomatic process of
the frontal bone.
• Zone II: Central area below the frontonasal
suture up to the bony anterior nasal spine.

2.2

Zone I

This area includes the frontal bone and the frontal sinuses and the scalp. The scalp is a five-layered structure, extending from the forehead in
the front to the superior nuchal line at the back
of the neck and root of the external ear helix and
zygomatic arch laterally. From superficial to
deep, it consists of the skin, subcutaneous tissue, musculoaponeurotic layer, loose areolar
connective tissue and periosteum. The first three
layers are adherent, and the scalp moves easily
over the fourth layer, which is the plane of dis-

section utilised for surgeries in this region.
Traumatic lacerations of this region more often
result in separation in this loose areolar layer.
The muscle of importance from surgical point
of view in this region is the occipito-frontalis,
which consists of two frontal bellies anteriorly
and two occipital bellies posteriorly, which are
joined by the galea aponeurotica in between, in
the region of the vertex of the skull.
The frontalis muscle originates from the galea
and inserts into the skin at the superior margin of
the orbits, root of the nose, and into other muscles of the region—the orbicularis oculi, corrugator supercilii and procerus. The temporal branch
of facial nerve is responsible for raising the eyebrows, which causes the horizontal wrinkles
across the forehead.
This relation is important for coronal
approach, for fractures of frontal sinus and zygomatic arch.
The occipitalis muscle originates from the
superior nuchal line of occipital bone and mastoid process of temporal bone and inserts into the
galea. It is responsible for moving the scalp
backwards.

2.2.1

Frontal Sinus

The frontal sinus is asymmetrical, with multiple
incomplete septations. The frontal sinus is absent
in 4% of the population. The sinus cavity lies
between the anterior and posterior tables. The
thicker anterior table has cancellous bone
between its cortical plates. The thinner posterior
table lies in direct contact with the dura. Whereas
the posterior table is only 0.1–4.8 mm thick,
offering little protection to the anterior cranial
fossa and its contents, the anterior table requires
a force of 800–2200 pounds of force for a fracture to occur. Of all the facial bones, the anterior
table can resist the greatest force, and therefore, a
fracture is likely to be associated with orbital and
naso-ethmoidal complex fractures. The floor of
the frontal sinus is the roof of the orbit laterally,
and the naso-frontal outflow tract lies medially.
The frontal recess, which is the outflow tract
pathway of the frontal sinus, is bounded posteri-

2

Surgical Anatomy of the Face

orly by the skull base, anteriorly by the anterior
wall of the agger nasi or middle meatus, laterally
by the lamina papyracea/superior medial orbital
wall and medially by the vertical attachment of
the middle turbinate to the skull base.
Anterior scalp is supplied by the internal
carotid artery through its supratrochlear and
supraorbital branches. Lateral scalp is supplied
by the branches of the external carotid artery
through superficial temporal, occipital and posterior auricular branches.
The supraorbital and supratrochlear veins join
to form the facial vein. Facial vein joins the anterior tributary of the retromandibular vein and
drains into the internal jugular vein. The lateral
scalp is drained through the posterior auricular
and posterior tributary of the retromandibular
vein. This will drain into the external jugular
vein. The occipital vein drains the posterior scalp
and joins the internal jugular vein.
The sensory nerve supply to this zone is through
the C2/3 cervical plexus and trigeminal nerve,
whilst the motor nerve is facial nerve. As the
supratrochlear and supraorbital nerves emerge
from their respective foramina, the supraorbital
nerve bundle is superficial to the corrugator supercilii, whilst the supratrochlear traverses through it.

aspect by the angular branch, superior labial and
branches of the maxillary artery. The facial vein
drains the nose and communicates to the cavernous sinus through the superior ophthalmic vein.
The ethmoid bones and the nasomaxillary
complex are involved in facial trauma. Medial
canthal ligament reattachment is an important
aspect in trauma management besides achieving
the projection of the radix of the nose. The medial
canthal ligament is a complex three-dimensional
structure and is attached to the anterior and posterior lacrimal crest. Repositioning after canthal
detatchment to the posterior lacrimal crest will
prevent post traumatic epiphora. It is important to
understand that the cribriform plate is around
1/2 –1 cm below the fronto-ethmoid suture.

2.4

Zone III

The orbits are conical in shape. The height of the
orbit is usually 35 mm, whereas the width is
around 40 mm. The total volume of the orbit and
globe is 30 cc and 7 cc, respectively. These can
vary in different races and ages. The child’s orbit
is rounder, but with age, the width increases. At
the age of 5 years, 85% of orbital growth is
achieved, and by 7 years of age, it is complete.
The length from the medial orbital rim to apex is

and the frontal process of the maxilla. The distance from the anterior lacrimal crest to the anterior ethmoidal foramen is 24 mm, the distance

The roof of the orbit is derived from the sphenoid and the frontal bones. In general, the thickest bone is at the apex and thins as the walls
diverge anteriorly and then thickens again at the
rims on the surface of the face. Although the bone
of the medial wall is the thinnest followed by the
floor of the orbit, in reality the medial wall is supported by perpendicular septa of the ethmoid
sinuses. Therefore, the floor of the orbit is most
vulnerable to fracture. Due to early CT scan protocols for head injury, more medial wall fractures
are now diagnosed and may confound the established norm above.
The inferior orbital fissure, superior orbital
fissure, anterior and posterior ethmoidal foramen
and optic canal are important landmarks, and one
has to be cognizant of their contents. The inferior
orbital fissure contents can be sacrificed without
much consequence during orbital floor exploration. The infraorbital groove which lies 1 cm pos-

A. Kusanale

terior to the orbital rim contains the infraorbital
nerve. It is 5 mm below the rim and may be
closely apposed to the periosteum. Sometimes
there are branches of the infraorbital artery that
penetrate the floor and can bleed during the
exploration.
Superior orbital fissure is located near the
apex of the orbit. This fissure serves as the conduit for the III (oculomotor), IV (trochlear), first
division of the V (ophthalmic branch) and VI
(abducens). In addition, the ophthalmic vein
courses through this structure. Medial to the
superior orbital fissure at the orbital apex lies the
optic canal separated by the optical strut. Through
this canal run the optic nerve and the ophthalmic
artery.
The infraorbital foramen can be easily palpated about 1 cm below the infraorbital rim. The
nerve lies beneath the SMAS.
The lamellar structure of the lower lid is
important to understand for access. This sandwiched structure is composed of the tarsal plate
in the middle with the conjunctiva on the posterior aspect and the orbicularis muscle and skin
on the outside. Traditionally the skin and muscle are considered as the outer lamella, and the
tarsal plate and conjunctiva are called the inner
lamella. They meet at the grey line of the lid
margin. The orbicularis muscle is a concentric
muscle surrounding the palpebral fissure with
pre-tarsal, pre-septal and orbital fibres. Orbital
septum is attached to the arcus marginale at the
edges of the orbital rim and serves as an important barrier for intraocular and cutaneous infections or bleeding.
The four rectus muscles and the oblique muscles move the eye and work synchronously. The
movements are important to help understand the
Hess charts and its documentation.
It is important to know that the internal and
external carotid arterial branches form a network through the angular, ciliary, supratrochlear and ethmoidal arteries. And the veins
through the superior and inferior ophthalmic
veins communicate to the cavernous sinus,
facial vein and ­pterygoid venous plexus. The
lymphatic drainage is to the level I neck nodes
and facial nodes.

Zone IV

The areas of the zygomatic bones and the parotid
gland with the facial nerve are considered as a
composite here. The zygoma has four projections, which create a quadrangular shape: the
frontal, temporal, maxillary and infraorbital rim.
The zygoma articulates with four bones: the frontal, temporal, maxilla and sphenoid. A zygomatic
complex fracture includes disruption of the four
articulating sutures: zygomaticofrontal, zygomaticotemporal, zygomaticomaxillary and zygomaticosphenoid sutures (Fig. 2.3).
The zygomatic arch includes the temporal
process of the zygoma and the zygomatic process
of the temporal bone. The glenoid fossa and articular eminence are located at the posterior aspect
of the zygomatic process of the temporal bone.
The facial nerve, which has five branches, lies
within the substance of muscles of the facial
expression. It is deep to the SMAS (the superficial musculo-aponeurotic system).
An important area where one encounters the
facial nerve is the area over the main body of the
zygoma in the area where one sees the zygomatic
cutaneous retaining ligaments. The nerve lies
above the buccal fat pad and is devoid of the protective covering of the parotid fascia. The parotid
duct lies caudal to this. The temporal branch is
parallel to the Pitanguy’s line (Fig. 2.4).

zygomatic bone. (2) Temporal process of the zygomatic
bone. (3) Maxillary process of the zygoma. (4) Zygomatic
buttress

Fig. 2.4 Pitanguy’s line. This is line 0.5 cm below the
tragus and 1.5 cm above the lateral brow. The frontal
branch is seen as a white linear structure just below the
fascia. Also note the superficial nature of the superficial
temporal artery

When raising the coronal flap, the layer above
the deep temporal fascia and the superficial temporal fascia is to be borne in mind for this branch.
An incision through the deep temporal fascia at
45 degrees from the external auditory canal and
parallel to the Pitanguy’s line will protect the
nerve. The frontal branch is just above the periosteum over the arch and crosses the arch at the
anterior-middle third junction (Fig. 2.5).
The marginal mandibular nerve crosses the
body of mandible, about 2 cm posterior to the
oral commissure. It supplies the depressor muscles of the lip and may have more than one
branch, which may anastomose with the cervical
branch of facial nerve. Dingman and Grabb [1]
have described the course and relation of the
nerve to the inferior border of mandible and the
facial artery, which can be used as a marker to
locate the nerve. Posterior to the artery, the nerve
was above the inferior border in 81% cases,
whilst in the rest 19%, it formed an arc below the
mandible, maximum 1 cm inferiorly. Anterior to
the artery, the nerve always lay above the mandibular border. In majority of cases, it is superficial to the facial artery and vein. The nerve also
lies in the fascia below the platysma. The submandibular incision should therefore always be
2 cm below the inferior border of mandible to
avoid injuring this branch.

The area between the malar eminence, angle
of mandible and the angle of mouth, where the

2.5.1

Parotid Duct

The parotid gland and the parotid duct are often
involved in penetrating soft tissue injuries of the
face. Management of ductal injuries depends

upon the location of the injury. Van Sickels and
Alexander [2] have classified these injuries into
three types anatomically: those occurring within
the glandular tissue, those occurring over the
masseter muscle and injuries anterior to the masseter. The course of the parotid duct can be
described along an imaginary line drawn from
the tragus to the mid-portion of the upper lip. The
duct emerges from the anterior border of the
gland and lies on the surface of the masseter muscle. At the anterior border of masseter, it passes
deep to pierce the buccinator and exits the oral
mucosa at the level of the second upper molar.
Any trauma in this plane should arouse suspicion
of ductal injury. The duct is also intimately
related to the buccal branches of facial nerve
(which travels along with the duct on the masseter muscle) and the transverse facial artery in this
region.
The facial artery and the superficial temporal
artery are relevant in this region. Superficial temporal artery is a branch of external carotid artery,
posterior to neck of mandible within the parotid
gland. It runs lateral to the posterior root of zygomatic process. It divides into frontal and parietal
branches, 5 cm superior to zygomatic process.
This vessel lies just beneath the subcutaneous tissue and is likely to be damaged. The middle temporal artery supplies the temporal muscle and
fascia. It originates above zygomatic process and
pierces the temporo-parietal fascia and runs over
the squamous temporal bone. The anterior auricular artery supplies the anterior portion of tragus,
lobe and external auditory canal.
Other important structures are the buccal fat
pad which is evident immediately after fenestration of the periosteum in the zygomatic buttress
region. It lies lateral and can hinder the visibility
especially when suction is used. It can be used to
repair defects in the maxilla and sinus fenestrations as pedicled tissue. Pterygoid venous plexus
can produce bothersome bleeding and requires
meticulous pressure, cautery and fibrin glue to
arrest it. It drains the pterygoid muscle region and
communicates to the middle cranial fossa, orbit
and facial vein. It is drained by the maxillary vein
which then joins the superficial temporal vein to
form the retromandibular vein. The pterygopala-

2

Surgical Anatomy of the Face

tine fossa which is wedged between the pterygoid process of the sphenoid and the posterior
aspect of the maxilla is a passage for neurovascular bundles.

2.6

Zone V

This is a transverse zone that constitutes the
paired maxillae, palate and dentoalveolar segments. The two maxillae are connected by a midline suture; the bones together compose a
five-sided pyramid. The anterior surface slopes
downwards from its superior contact with the
frontal and nasal bones at an angle of approximately 15°. The most prominent point at the
anterior surface is the anterior nasal spine.
The lateral surface of the maxillae forms the
infratemporal fossae and buccal vestibule and
attaches to the zygoma. Most of the superior surface forms the majority of the orbital floor. The
medial surface of each maxilla forms the midline
suture and lateral nasal walls. This includes the
nasal concha and sinus ostia. The inferior border
is comprised of the palatal vault and alveolus,
which bears the teeth. The posterior border abuts
the sphenoid bone and the pterygomaxillary
suture. Within the maxilla is the maxillary sinus.
The strong buttresses of the maxilla are the lateral piriform buttress, the zygomatic buttress, the
greater palatine buttress and the floor of the nose.
The palatine bone is L shaped and abuts the posterior maxilla as a paired structure. These bones
assist the maxilla in forming the posterior sinus,
the posterior lateral nasal wall and the pterygomaxillary suture.
The maxillary artery which is the branch of
the external carotid artery lies very close to the
neck of the condyle. It is divided into mandibular,
pterygopalatine and pterygoid parts. Posterior
superior alveolar artery may cause bleeding when
the tuberosity is fractured. Another place that
may cause bleeding is when the pterygoid muscles are traumatised.
The angular artery is a terminal segment of the
facial artery. It anastomoses with the dorsal nasal
branch of ophthalmic artery on the medial aspect
of the orbit. Labial artery may be ligated on one

17

side due to the collateral supply. The sphenopalatine artery is another branch that is implicated in
epistaxis and may need ligating at the sphenopalatine foramen usually through an endoscopic
approach. Greater palatine artery and its branches
supply the soft palate and hard palate and may be
utilised for coverage and can cause bleeding in
trauma.
The dentition and developing tooth buds will
present challenges for management of paediatric
patients.

2.7

Zone VI

This comprises the mandible and oral tissues.
This is standard topic in maxillofacial curriculum. The important things are the different
changes in the mandible according to age. The
vascularity decreases in older edentulous mandible, and one has to be aware of excessive periosteal stripping. The neurovascular bundle may be
more superficial especially in relation to the mental foramen, whereas in a growing mandible, the
tooth buds and deciduous teeth will pose problems in fixation.
The body of the mandible has protuberances
on the lingual symphysis region called the genial
tubercles where the genioglossus and the geniohyoid muscles are attached. In a multi-­fragmented
mandibular fracture, this can be a difficult region
to achieve reduction. Any avulsion of the tongue
muscle attachments here can potentially create an
airway issue. The sublingual artery, a branch of
lingual artery, and submental artery, a branch of
the facial artery, perforate the lingual cortex after
having supplied the genioglossus, geniohyoid
and anterior belly of digastric. This is important
as it can cause significant bleeding.
The condylar region is accessed via a transcutaneous incision. The relation of the facial nerve
and parotid gland has to be borne in mind. Blunt
dissection through the parotid tissue with retraction avoids transection of the nerve but may cause
stretch injury.
The mucosa of the floor of the mouth is easily
torn, and the Wharton’s duct and lingual nerve
are prone to injury. The lingual nerve will cross

18

A. Kusanale

the duct roughly in the premolar-molar region.
The duct orifice should be left unsutured in any
laceration, or a stent should be placed to prevent
narrowing. The lingual nerve is in a close relation
to the mandible in the region of the third molar.
The inferior alveolar neurovascular bundle enters
the mandibular ramus via the mandibular foramen. The nerve tends to be 4–5 mm below the
lingula, a bony strut. An area on the lateral aspect
of the ramus that corresponds to the lingula on
the medial aspect is called anti-lingula. The foramen lies roughly midway between the anterior
and posterior borders of the ramus. The inferior
alveolar nerve travels posterior to anterior in the
mandibular canal and exits via the mental foramen. The terminal branch supplies the incisor
teeth. The mental nerve loops on itself for
2–3 mm anterior to the mental foramen and then
exits the mandible.
The maxillary artery lies medial to the condyle and can cause brisk bleeding during inadvertent damage. The inferior alveolar artery is the
main supply as well as the periosteal supply
through branches of lingual and facial artery.

2.8

Neck

The mandible can be accessed through the neck
in certain situations. The incision takes one
through the skin, subcutaneous fat, platysma
and deep cervical fascia. The deep cervical fascia extends from the superior nuchal line mastoid and lower border of the mandible cranially.
The caudal attachment is to the clavicleacromial-­sternal girdle. It is divided into superficial, middle and deep. Subplatysmal dissection
will protect the facial nerve so long as the dissection stays hugging it. Another way to protect
the marginal mandibular branch of the facial
nerve is to stay below the submandibular gland
capsule. The nerve is anterior to this plane. The
facial nerve lies superficial to the facial vein,
and ligating and retracting the vein is entirely a
safe procedure.

Fig. 2.7 Black arrow is demonstrating the hypoglossal
nerve and the yellow arrow the ansa cervicalis. The white
arrow is pointing to the posterior belly of the digastric
muscle

The hypoglossal nerve lies over the hyoglossus and below the submandibular gland as one
retracts the mylohyoid muscle. Lingual nerve
loops cranial to the submandibular gland and is
attached to the gland through the submandibular
ganglion. The submental artery lies close to the
anterior belly of the digastric, and this can bleed
when incisions are off midline. Between the
hyoid bone and the chin is a safe zone for incision
for submental intubation, provided the dissection
hugs the mandible as one enters the floor of the
mouth.
The external carotid artery lies medial to the
internal jugular vein and occasionally needs to be
ligated. One ascertains if the artery being ligated
or clamped has branches which are the giveaway
for it being external rather than internal carotid
artery. The hypoglossal nerve loops at the carotid
bifurcation, and the ansa cervicalis will help
identify it correctly (Fig. 2.7).
The accessory nerve is roughly 1 cm above the
so-called Erb’s point in the posterior triangle
(where the great auricular nerve curves and
ascends over the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle). This will help to asses
any injury in the posterior triangle of the neck.
The nerve descends obliquely from this point to
enter the trapezius muscle four finger breadths
above the clavicle (Fig. 2.8).

Biomechanics of the Maxillofacial
Skeleton
Kuldeep Vishwakarma and Bharat Shukla

3.1

Introduction

The biomechanics of maxillofacial region is a
dynamic phenomenon. It is ruled by the interplay
between anatomical structures, muscle attachment, force acting over bones, and other mechanical factors. The knowledge of bony structure,
composition, and mechanical properties is vital
for a better understanding of biomechanics and
healing and repair of the maxillofacial skeleton.

3.2

3.2.1

 ones (Origin, Structure,
B
Composition,
and Mechanical Properties)
 rigin of Bones of Facial
O
Skeleton

During embryogenesis, bones of facial skeleton
are formed by two different mechanisms:
1. Membranous bone formation, where mineralization occurs directly in the organic matrix
formed by the mesenchymal connective tissue, for example, frontal, parietal, nasal, maxilla, zygomatic, and mandible [1].

K. Vishwakarma (*) · B. Shukla
Specialty of Oral & Maxillofacial Surgery, Apex
Trauma Center, SGPGIMS,
Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh, India

2. Endochondral bone formation, where mineralization occurs in a cartilaginous framework
leading to bone formation, for example, bones
of the skull base, occipital bone, nasal septum,
and nasal conchae [1].
Regardless of the origin of the bone, any further growth or repair occurs by membranous
mechanism.

3.2.2

Structure

Facial skeleton is composed of two types of bone
tissue, a lighter weight and less densely packed
cancellous bone and a more densely packed compact or lamellar bone. These two types of tissues
are arranged in different patterns in different
bones of the facial skeleton depending upon the
functional demand.
Bones of cranial vault have an outer and
inner table of compact bone and a middle layer
of cancellous bone, providing a protection to
the brain against direct impact. Bones of the
midface have a thin layer of compact bone and
a framework of cancellous bone acting as a
shock-absorbing structure, while the mandible
is mostly composed of cortical bone with cancellous bone in the body, angle, and condyle
region [2].
The bone is a metabolically dynamic organ,
and it undergoes continuous modeling and

© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2021
A. K. Singh, N. K. Sharma (eds.), Maxillofacial Trauma,
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-33-6338-0_3

21

22

K. Vishwakarma and B. Shukla

remodeling. Three types of cells are responsible
for maintaining the bone homeostasis. Osteoblasts
are bone-forming cells, osteoclasts are responsible for bone resorption, and osteocytes are mature
bone cells.
Osteoblasts are responsible for bone collagen
matrix formation. They are derived from mesenchymal cells of bone marrow. Osteoblasts synthesize a collagen-rich matrix, called as osteoid,
which mineralizes gradually and transforms into
calcified bone. The microscopic appearance is
different for woven and lamellar bone. As the
name suggests, woven bone has collagen fibrils
that are randomly oriented. In lamellar bone, collagen fibers are arranged in parallel bundles and
layers. In fracture healing, woven bone ultimately
gets transformed into lamellar bone through a
process of Haversian remodeling [2].
Osteoclasts are derived from mononuclear
macrophages. They are multinucleated cells with
ruffled borders. They are primary cells for bone
resorption. This activity is limited to Howship’s
lacunae, which are small subcellular chambers
with a low pH [2].
Osteocytes are the most abundant cell type in
the bone, derived from osteoblasts. They are
placed regularly inside the bone matrix. They are
morphologically stellate in shape, connected to
each other by long slender cell processes. They
pass through bone matrix through small canals or
canaliculi [2].

3.2.3

Composition

collagenous proteins (osteocalcin, osteonectin,
sialoprotein, phosphoproteins, α2-glycoproteins,
etc.) [3].

3.2.4

Mechanical Properties

Mechanical properties of a material are determined by their microstructure. Technically, the
bone can be considered as a fiber-reinforced
polymer (composite). The collagen fibers (mainly
type 1) are responsible for providing tensile
strength, whereas the mineral matrix provides the
compressive strength. The length and orientation
of these fiber bundles vary in different parts of the
bone as per the specific loading conditions.
Hence, the mechanical properties of the bone differ in different directions, making it an anisotropic material [3].
The bone is a brittle material and can withstand elongation of 2% before it breaks. The bone
is strong against the compressive forces and the
ultimate strength is about 1 MPa, whereas the
tensile strength is only 1/3 of the compressive
strength. This is the reason why bone breaks first
on the tension side when subjected to bending
forces [3].

3.3.2

Biomechanics of Mandible

A bone experiences different types of loads,
namely, linear and angular loads. Linear loads

24

K. Vishwakarma and B. Shukla

include shear and tension/compression, whereas
angular loads include torsion and bending [3].
The mandible is subjected to forces derived by
muscles of mastication. Earlier the biomechanics
of mandible was described by simple beam
mechanism, which stated that on application of
load there will be tensile stress on upper border
and compressive stress on lower border (Fig. 3.2).
The intermediate zone lying between tension and
compression zone was called as neutral zone
which passes approximately at the level of inferior alveolar canal [5].
This method was oversimplification of the
complex forces acting over the mandible during
function. This method does not include the role
of musculature, bite forces, and bending of mandible under functional stress. Later on studies
were carried out involving free body diagram,

photoelastic resin, strain gauge, and finite element analysis [6–8].
Out of these, finite element analysis is believed
to be the most accurate assessment, which demonstrated that if occlusal force is applied anterior
to fracture site, then principle of simple beam
mechanism will be employed, and if occlusal
force is applied posterior to fracture site, then
effects of contralateral muscle action come into
play [9–14]. Therefore, if the loading force is
applied anterior to the fracture line, it will produce tension zone at upper border and compression zone at the lower border, and if it is applied
posterior to the fracture line, it will result in compression at upper border and tension zone at
lower border (Fig. 3.3a, b).
The mandible is also subjected to torsional
forces especially in the symphysis and parasymphysis region. The elevator muscles exert forces
lateral to the long axis of mandible, while the
occlusal forces are applied medial to this axis
producing torsional forces. These torsional
forces acting on both halves of the mandible
result in compressive stress at the superior margin and tensile stress at the inferior margin in the
symphysis region (Fig. 3.4) [15]. Powerful
clenching also results in lateral bending of the
body of mandible, producing compressive stress
at buccal surface and tensile stress over lingual
cortex [16].

margin and tensile stress at inferior margin

Fig. 3.4 Torsional forces acting on the mandible result in

The tension and compression zones don’t
remain in constant location and change continuously according to the location of external load
during mastication especially in the body region
of the mandible [17]. Therefore, placement of
osteosynthesis material in the juxta-alveolar
region is very effective in providing functionally
stable fixation in the body region of the
mandible.
In the symphysis region, all possible scenarios
of loading conditions result in compression at the
upper margin and tension at the lower margin
[17]. And as the effect of torsional force is maximum in the symphysis and parasymphysis region,
two miniplates (one at the inferior border and the
other at the upper margin using monocortical
screws) should be used to counter the torsional
stress in this region.
The angle fracture in most functional situations tends to develop tensile stress at the superior margin and compressive stress at the lower
margin (Fig. 3.5). Therefore, placement of osteosynthesis material at the superior border more
effectively neutralizes the functional forces and
provides functionally stable fixation.
In sub-condylar fracture, the forces acting on
the fractured fragment produce tensile strain
along the sigmoid notch and compressive stress
along the posterior border. Besides, the condylar
fragment is also subjected to rotational forces
[18]. Therefore, to counter both the compressive
and tensile forces, at least two miniplates should
be applied in nonparallel fashion, one along the

and the occlusal load result in tensile stress at superior

posterior border and the other parallel to the sigmoid notch.

3.3.3

Biomechanics of Midface

The biomechanics of midface is less understood
owing to its complex geometry. The medial
(nasomaxillary) and lateral (zygomaticomaxillary) vertical buttresses absorb most of the occlusal loads. The goal of management of midface
fracture is aimed at stabilization and reconstruction of these pre traumatic load pathways
(Fig. 3.6) [17].
Following fixation and stabilization of the
fracture, the osteosynthesis materials (plates)
become the new force flow pathway. If the fixation materials are placed in an abnormal pattern,
then these may be subjected to abnormal stress
concentration, leading to screw loosening and
implant failure (Fig. 3.7a, b) [17].
Unlike mandible, the vector of muscle forces
in the midface region always tends to displace the
fractured fragments. Maximum muscle pull is
experienced by zygomatic bone, thus making it
vulnerable to maximum displacement on fracture. The frontozygomatic suture region experiences the highest amount of stress and is the
principal area for fixation. On the other hand,
muscle pull of masseter can be dealt effectively
by fixation of fracture at zygomaticomaxillary
buttress region [1].

K. Vishwakarma and B. Shukla

Fig. 3.6 Black arrows depicting midface force flow
pattern

3.4

Fracture Healing

The bone is peculiar in the fact that it heals by
regeneration rather than by repair as compared
with healing of other tissues of the body which
usually leads to scar formation. Fracture healing
involves a complex biological process and is
affected by many local and systemic factors
[19].
Depending upon the accuracy of reduction of
fractured fragment, degree of interfragmentary
movement, and other biomechanical and biological factors, two forms of fracture healing are
observed:
1. Indirect/secondary bone healing
2. Direct/primary bone healing

3.4.1

Indirect/Secondary Bone
Healing

Indirect bone healing is most commonly observed
when the fractured fragments are not in perfect

Fig. 3.7 (a) Placement of implants along the normal
force flow pathway. (b) Placement of plate at abnormal
location reroutes force distribution leading to stress concentration and implant failure

anatomical alignment and are subjected to micromotion and loading conditions.
This type of healing typically occurs in cases
of closed reduction, for example, maxillomandibular fixation, suspension wiring, and external fixation, which lacks anatomical reduction
and involves micromotion between the
fragments.
Indirect fracture healing involves a cascade of tissue differentiation stages (Fig. 3.8).
Following trauma, a hematoma is formed
between the fractured fragment and in the
surrounding area. This hematoma is replaced
by the granulation tissue, which transforms
into interfragmentary fibrous connective tissue. Then interfragmentary fibrous connective tissue is converted into fibrocartilage.
Later this fibrocartilage undergoes mineralization, followed by vascular ingrowth of
fibrocartilage leading to formation of calcified cartilage.

3

Biomechanics of the Maxillofacial Skeleton

27

Fig. 3.8 Cascade of events: indirect/secondary bone healing

This mineralization of fibrous cartilage starts
from the fractured bony ends and proceeds
toward the center of the fracture gap until the
entire cartilage gets mineralized. Then calcified
fibrocartilage is resorbed and woven bone is laid
by osteoblasts. The function of the bone is
restored at this stage. Later on, this woven bone
undergoes Haversian remodeling and is transformed into lamellar bone.

• Fibrocartilage formation and its
mineralization

• Woven bone formation and Haversian

3.4.2

Direct/Primary Bone Healing

Direct bone healing is observed in cases of absolute stability (rigid internal fixation) and correct
anatomical reduction of the fractured fragments.
In this type of healing, lamellar bone is formed
directly; it skips the callus formation stage.
Contact
Healing Mechanical
continuity
between the fracture fragments with gap of less
than 0.01 mm and strain less than 2% is prerequisite for contact healing to occur [19]. The osteoclasts get activated at the end of osteon near the
fractured end, resulting in formation of cutting
cones. These cutting cones move at a rate of
50–100 μ/day and are able to propagate across
the fracture line. At the rear end of these cutting
cones, osteoblasts becomes activated and lay
down the lamellar bone forming the closing cone.
This results in formation of new lamellar bone in
the axial direction and simultaneous reestablishment of the Haversian system (Fig. 3.9a).
Gap Healing Gap healing eventuates if the gap
between the fracture fragments is less than

K. Vishwakarma and B. Shukla

800 μ–1 mm and fixation is rigid enough to keep
the interfragmentary strain less than 2% [19].
Here osteoblasts lay down the lamellar bone in
the direction perpendicular to the long axis of the
bone. This orientation of the lamellar bone is
mechanically weak and undergoes secondary
remodeling ultimately resulting in orientation
along the long axis of the bone and restoration of
Haversian system. Here the bony union and reestablishment of Haversian system don’t occur
simultaneously (Fig. 3.9b).

3.5

Delayed Union It occurs when the bone fails to
unite within the predicted time. It may be due to
inadequate blood supply, irradiation, or inadequate stability of fractured segments.
Nonunion It is termination of bone healing process before bony union of fractured segments. It
may be due to compromised blood supply, severe
damage to adjacent periosteum, and inadequate
fixation of fractured ends leading to mobility and
infection.

Conclusion

A better understanding of anatomical structures,
their origin, and forces acting on them leads to
finer management of fractured segments. Facial
buttresses function as natural intrinsic strong pillars and need to be restored for optimum function. Knowledge of biomechanics of the
maxillofacial skeleton enables the maxillofacial
surgeons for proper selection of implants and
precise placement to negate the functional
stresses. Fracture healing is a complex biological
process; one must be in acquaintance with the
various stages and types of healing. These cumulative efforts will lead to effectual fracture management and patient care.

Principles of Osteosynthesis
Arun Pandey and Janani Anand Kumar

4.1

Introduction

Osteosynthesis refers to the procedure in which the
fracture ends are joined and stabilized by means of
mechanical devices such as metal plates, pins, rods,
wires or screws. Fracture reduction and stabilization
is an inevitable procedure especially after a maxillofacial trauma in order to restore patient’s pre-injury
form and function of facial structures. The principle
of fixation/osteosynthesis has seen a wide range of
evolution in the past three decades. It has evolved
from a mere wire fixation of fracture segments up to
locking plates and screws, microplates and screws
specially designed for maxillofacial region, etc.

4.3.2

Rigid Fixation

• Definition: Rigid fixation can be defined as a
type of fixation that prevents/allows minimal
interfragmentary movement between the fracture segments during active loading [3].
• Type of bone healing: Primary bone healing—
osteoclasts invade the minimal gap present
between the fracture segments, followed by
angiogenesis and deposition of osteoid by
osteoblasts, which eventually gets remodelled
to become mature bone.
• Usually demands a two-point fixation, such as a
bone plate fixation at the inferior border of the
fracture along with a tension band fixation at the
superior border with a miniplate or an arch bar.
• Reconstruction plate and eccentric dynamic
compression plate (EDCP) are exceptions
from this two-point fixation principle [1].
Rigid fixation techniques include:
• Two miniplates across a fracture
• Two lag screws across a fracture
• Reconstruction plate fixation with at least three
screws on each side of the fracture (four screws
on either side in case of segmental defects)
• Large compression plate across a fracture
with/without a tension band

4.4

Compression Osteosynthesis

Definition: Compression osteosynthesis was first
described by R. Danis as the plating system that
can produce compression of the fracture fragments
resulting in maximum frictional interlocking and
preload between them, producing an absolute stable fixation with zero mobility [4] (Fig. 4.2).
Principles:
1. Preload/compression prevents distraction at
the tension zone.
2. Friction stabilizes the fracture fragments against
torsion until it is greater than the external load.

Fig. 4.2 Fracture stabilized by a compression device

3. Linear compression between the fracture
segments prevents interfragmentary motion
by counteracting the torsional, bending and
shearing forces produced during function.
4. The distribution of inter-fragmental pressure
should be as uniform as possible.
Indications:
• Linear fractures of the mandible
• Oblique surface fractures of the mandible (lag
screws)
• Fracture at zygomaticofrontal suture
• Fracture at the root of the zygomatic arch
Advantages:
• An ideal condition for primary bone healing.
• It allows the sharing of load between the bone
and the implants (plates and/or screws).
• Absolute rigid and stable osteosynthesis.
Disadvantages:
• It is extremely technique sensitive and highly
prone to error during application.
• Compression osteosynthesis tends to fail by
screw loosening if micromotion occurs
between the fracture segments.
• It requires strong bony buttress on either side of
the fracture to apply the compression device.
• If the plates/screws are not applied properly,
unfavourable dynamic forces are created that
could result in plate failure.
In order to achieve compression, either bone
plates or screws or both together may be used. There
are two types of compression that can be applied:
static compression and dynamic compression.

4.4.1

Static Compression

Principle: Static compression refers to a phenomenon in which the compression unit solely pro-

34

A. Pandey and J. A. Kumar

duces interfragmentary friction adequate enough
to enable a rigid fixation that could withstand/
neutralize the forces (bending, torsion and shear)
imposed on the mandible during physiologic
functions [5].

a

b

4.4.2

Dynamic Compression
(Pauwells, 1935, 1965)

The advent of tension band principle led to the
evolution of dynamic compression technique
since the methods of static compression alone
were found to be insufficient to counteract all the
functional forces due to the complex biomechanics of the mandible. The tension band neutralizes
the tensile stresses, which eventually reduces the
total stress on the compression unit. In this
method, there is combined action of the compression device and physiological forces in preventing interfragmentary motion [5].
Principle: In this method, the tensile forces
that act on the superior border of the mandible
are absorbed by the tension band and are transformed into compression by the action of reduction forceps and the masticatory apparatus, as a
result of which, the fracture fragments are pressed
against each other [Fig. 4.3].
Ideal situation:
1. Bony buttress on both the sides of the fracture
(transverse fractures)
2. Sufficient space to apply the tension band
(supra-angular and ramus of the mandible)

4.4.3

The Tension Band Principle

• The activation of masticatory musculature
produces tension on the alveolar side of the
mandible and compression at its base, which
causes the fracture to gape superiorly.
• This gaping or distraction increases by a factor of 10 to 65 when a DCP is applied at the
inferior border of the mandible.
• Therefore, if a DCP is applied along the inferior border, then a tension band, either in the
form of a plate or an arch bar, is required on
the alveolar side, depending upon the dental
status and the fracture location (Fig. 4.4a, b).

c

d

Fig. 4.3 Technique of DCP application. (a) The plate is
slightly overbent to counter for lingual splaying. (b) At
first, the left screw is inserted and tightened sufficient
enough that the screw, plate and bone become a single
unit. (c) The right screw is inserted and tightened to its
eccentric position, which causes the plate to move along
with the left bone fragment pulling it towards the left fragment causing compression. Therefore, tightening of the
right screw causes compression from the left side, as
depicted by the arrows. This produces compression from
a single side. If compression from both the sides is
required, then the left screw is also tightened to its eccentric position. (d) Both the outer screws are inserted and
tightened in their centric position

• The tension band absorbs the bending forces,
neutralizes it and also converts it into compression, to add on to the compression produced by the implant.
Application of tension band:
• The farther the tension band is placed from the
centre of rotation of the fragments, the lower
are the stresses to which it will be subjected
(up to 100 times lower).
• The tension band need not to be very strong or
large in intact alveolar process and dentulous
mandible, where the distance between the inferior border and the splint or plate is sufficient.

• Tension band plate: Applied in the retromolar
region—two-hole plate is sufficient.
• Tension band splint: Applied in the dentulous
region as the presence of tooth roots prohibits
the proper placement of tension band plate.
There should be a minimum of two sound
teeth on each side of fracture.
Contraindications for using the plate and tension band system [5]:
• Lack of space
• Absence of teeth
• Lack of need
Indications for fixation with EDCP or reconstruction plate without a tension band [5]:
• Angle fractures
• Edentulous fractures
• Isolated transverse fractures

4.4.4

Compression with a Plate

A compression plate is a bone plate with specially designed oval-shaped holes, which on fas-

tening with screws produces compression
between the fracture fragments.
General technique:
• For producing uniform compression throughout the fracture, it is essential to achieve
proper approximation of the fracture ends,
either manually or with the help of reduction
forceps, before the implants are placed.
• Compression plates in general must be fixed
perpendicular to the fracture line.
• Compression plates are usually stronger and
more rigid than adaptation plates as compression
is only possible as long as the plate does not
deform under the forces applied. Because of the
resulting forces, bicortical screw insertion is
mandatory in compression plate osteosynthesis.
Special considerations:
• When compression is applied on one side of a
fracture, the opposite sides tend to open up. In
the case of the mandible, these are the lingual
side and the superior border (Fig. 4.5a, b).

4.4.6

Eccentric Dynamic
Compression Plate (EDCP)

• Eccentric dynamic compression is a method
which can provide compression both at alveolar border and the base of the mandible [4].
• The EDCP (eccentric dynamic compression
plate) has longitudinal inner holes for producing inter-fragmental compression on the basal
side and oblique outer holes for compression
on the alveolar side (Fig. 4.7).
• The eccentric action of the plate obviates
the need for a tension band, especially when
a reduction forceps with pressure rollers is
used initially to reduce and compress the
fragments.
• Indicated in transverse fracture of the mandible (especially the edentulous mandible).
• Contraindicated in central fractures of the
mandibular angle, as there is not enough space
to insert the necessary number of screws.

Fig. 4.7 Eccentric dynamic compression plate

37

4.4.7

Compression with Lag Screws

• Principle: A screw that glides through the cortex of the near fragment and engages the cortex
of the remote fragment with its threads, when
tightened, drawing the fragments together and
compressing their surfaces (Fig. 4.8).
• Indications:
–– Oblique and oblique surface fractures
–– Mandibular
symphyseal
transverse
fractures
–– Angle fracture
–– Condylar fracture
–– Midface (periorbital, zygomatic arch, sub-­
nasal) fracture
–– Ridge augmentation
–– Fixation of bone grafts
–– Sagittal split osteotomies
• Technique of lag screw fixation:
–– As a first step, the cortex of the proximal
bone fragment is drilled to a diameter as
wide or wider than the width of the outer
thread diameter of the lag screw. This is
called as a gliding hole because the screw
will glide through it without gripping the
bone [6].
–– Through the gliding hole, a special drill
guide of diameter lesser than that of the lag
screw (preferably the core diameter of the
lag screw) is inserted, and the cortex of the
remote bone fragment is drilled centrally.
This is called the thread hole, since the lag
screw will grip as it is inserted into this hole.
–– The gliding hole and thread hole must be
coaxial.
–– When a cortex screw is used, the gliding hole
should match the outer diameter of the thread
(2.7 mm), while the thread hole matches the
diameter of the shank (2 mm). If not, the
screw will transfix the fragments instead of
approximating and compressing them.

Fig. 4.8 Fracture stabilized with a lag screw

38

A. Pandey and J. A. Kumar

–– The screw should be placed in such a way
that its long axis bisects the angle formed
by line perpendicular to the fracture line
and to the long axis of the bone [4].
• Lag screw fixation is preferred particularly in
cases where two broad and flat surfaces need to
be approximated and fixed in position. It also
requires that the length of the fracture surface be
equal or more than the height of the mandible
and twice the height in atrophic mandible cases.
Therefore, lag screw fixation is most appropriate for ‘oblique surface’ fractures that exhibit a
more sagittal than frontal orientation. Lag
screws could produce a rigid fixation of the
mandible only if the fracture surfaces are large
enough to accommodate a minimum of two and
preferably three screws. If only one screw can
be inserted (as in fracture at the root of the zygomatic arch), then an additional form of fixation
is recommended (e.g. a bone plate).
• Advantages:
–– Reduction in operating time
–– Good interfragmentary compression
–– Minimal implant use
–– Low complications
• Disadvantages:
–– Potential risk of damage to the mental/
alveolar nerve and to the tooth roots
–– Technique sensitive

4.4.8

Position Screws

• Both the fragments drilled with a pilot hole.
• Gliding hole not used (Fig. 4.9)
• For repositioning small fragments, i.e. in comminuted fracture
• For fixation of bone grafts
• In sagittal split osteotomies to prevent the
mispositioning of the condyles

in Combination with a Lag

4.5

Non-rigid Fixation

• Definition: Non-rigid fixation refers to the
type of fixation that allows movement between
the fractured segments [6].
• Type of bone healing: Secondary bone healing – involves formation of hematoma, bone
callus, hyaline cartilage, woven bone and
finally lamellar bone.
• High risk of malunion and non-union of fracture, since it cannot provide stability against
the torsional and shear forces that the mandible is subjected to.
• Requires other additional fixation measures
such as maxillomandibular fixation (MMF).
• Examples: Interosseous wiring and interdental
bridal wiring.
• No more used for the fixation of craniofacial
fractures due to its poor technique and high
failure rate.
• A more evolved version of this technique is
widely used in the modern era of internal fixation of craniofacial fractures known as ‘functionally stable fixation’.

4.6

Functionally Stable Fixation

• Definition: Functionally stable fixation refers
to the type of fixation that allows normal
active movements of the skeletal unit during
the process of bone healing, with the presence of interfragmentary motion at the fracture site.
• Type of bone healing: Indirect or secondary
bone healing. In such circumstances, there is
deposition of periosteal callus, resorption of the
fragment ends and tissue differentiation through
various stages from fibrous to osseous.

39

• Commonly used based on Champy’s principles of mandibular osteosynthesis [7].
• Example: Single miniplate technique of treating mandibular angle or body fractures.
• Advantages:
–– Successful combination of interfragmentary motion, active skeletal movements and
secondary bone healing
–– Smaller exposure required
–– Feasible through intra-oral approach
–– Early mobilization
• Disadvantages:
–– Chances of non-union/malunion present
–– Cannot be used in case of segmental defect
and severe comminution

4.7

Miniplate Osteosynthesis

4.7.1

Historical Background

Miniplate osteosynthesis is a concept developed
by Champy et al. in 1977 based on the experiments performed by them on 13 fresh mandibles.
Champy et al. noted that when the mandibles
were loaded with increasing forces, it led to the
fracture of the bone or chipping of the cortex, but
the plate remained undamaged. In 1978, a second
set of experiment was performed on strain
gauges, both in vivo and in vitro. They concluded
that the force required to fracture a jaw was
higher than the maximum masticatory forces
which miniplates can sustain easily [7].
It is a modification of the technique of mono-­
cortical osteosynthesis proposed by Michelet
et al. in 1967 [8], where miniature plates were
placed in the juxta-alveolar region. The rationality of the Michelet’s principles was validated
through a series of experiments carried out in
Strasbourg, France, from 1971 to 1974.

4.7.2

Introduction

It is a method in which mono-cortical small-plate
osteosynthesis is done commonly through an intraoral approach. The concept was primarily developed for mandibular fractures and is well
documented in literature. Physiological movements

40

of jaw produce forces of tension along the alveolar
border and forces of compression along the lower
border of the mandible. These forces produce flexion of the body of the mandible, which is maximum
at the angle region and minimum at the premolar
region. The forces also produce torsion at the mandibular symphysis region, which is strongest at the
midline region [9]. Champy et al. studied these
forces in detail with regard to a mathematic model
of the mandible and determined the ideal line of
osteosynthesis along which the mono-cortical
plates can be fixed to overcome the displacing
forces [10] (Fig. 4.11). The plates are thus placed in
a biomechanically favourable zone, known as the
tension zone, which lies just below the apices of the
teeth roots. Champy et al. disproved the concept of
compression osteosynthesis, since compression is
naturally produced at the lower border of the mandible. Therefore, they advocated the placement of
mono-cortical miniplates only at the tension zone.
By this way, the plate thickness was reduced which
leads to another advantage of increasing the malleability of the plate. These miniplates produce adequate stability, which renders the IMF unnecessary.
Various clinical studies have proven the efficacy of
miniplate osteosynthesis and also its advantages
over the other modalities of treatment [11, 12].
Biomechanical principles: Based on the
experiments performed in Strasbourg, France, by
Groupe d’Etude en Biomécanique OstéoArticulaire de Strasbourg (GEBOAS) [4].
• Plates and screws must be strong enough to
withstand all the functional stresses.
• Adequate malleability for better adaptation.
• Smaller in dimension.

A. Pandey and J. A. Kumar

4.7.3

I deal Lines of Osteosynthesis
of the Mandible (Fig. 4.11)

• Tension zone at the base of the alveolar process, just below the root apices.
• Two lines in the inter-foraminal span—one
line just below the root apices and the other
one at the inferior border of the mandible,
4–5 mm below the sub-apical line.
• Mono-cortical plate fixation below the root
apices results in neutralization of stresses at
the tension zone while restoring the physiological compressive forces, which is the
dynamic compression.

4.7.4

Technical and Anatomical
Considerations of Miniplate
Application

• Inter-foraminal span: One plate near the inferior border and one below the root apices,
maintaining a gap of minimum 4–5 mm
between both the plates (Fig. 4.12).
• Behind mental foramen: Single plate applied
just below the root apices and above the mandibular canal.
• At the angle: Single plate along the external
oblique ridge (Fig. 4.13).
• Body of the mandible: Screw length to be used
is approximately 4 mm, as the thickness of the
outer cortex in this region is 3.3 mm at an
average.
• Root apices: Screws should be placed at a distance at least twice the length of the crown of
the tooth, from the alveolar process (Fig. 4.14).

Fig. 4.11 Champy’s ideal line of osteosynthesis in mandible
