• Mental foramen lies at the middle of the alveolar crest and inferior border of the mandible,
on a vertical line related to the first or second
molar and also at a higher level to the canine
root apex. Thus, the plate should be fixed very
cautiously due to the increased risk of injury
to the root.
• Plate recommended: Four holes with gap or
six holes with gap.
• Inter-plate distance: 4.5 mm.
• Drilling of hole need not be perpendicular
(angle up to 30° to the surface of plate is permissible) but should be monoaxial.
• Fixation of screw needs a minimum of three
screw heads.
• Drilling should be stopped when a decrease in
the resistance is felt (after 3–4 mm), which
indicates cancellous bone or canal is reached.
• Minimum of two screws must be fixed on each
side of the fracture.
• Appropriate length of screw: 7 mm (at an
average).
• Avoid excessive tightening of the screw, since
it leads to microfracture within the bone.
• Edentulous mandible: Avoid superior aspect
for plate application.
• Children (<13 years): Plate must be fixed at
the inferior border. Till 6 years of age, fixation

• Frontal bone: Thickness is 4–9 mm; thus,
5 mm screws can be placed safely.

Miniplate Specifications

• Thickness: 0.5–1 mm (AO/ASIF) (4 holes
with gap, 6 holes with gap and 8–16 holes

• Shape of the plate: Straight, orbital, L, T, X, Y,

• Screw length: 5, 6, 7, 9, 11, 13 and 15 mm

4.7.6

Single and Multiple Fractures

• Treatment plan differs for isolated and multiple fractures.
• Application of a single 2.0 mm system miniplate along the ideal line of osteosynthesis is
adequate in isolated fractures along with arch
bar application.
• When two or more fractures are present, there
is increased tendency for displacement due to
bilateral loss of support.
• In a case of more than one linear fracture,
rigid fixation is recommended for at least one
of the fractures [2].
• For example, in a case of mandibular angle
fracture along with a fracture on contralateral
body region, it is recommended to fix the body
region with two 2.0 mm miniplates or any
stronger plate, along with arch bar fixation
and one 2.0 mm miniplate fixation at the superior border at the angle region.
• Stronger rigid fixation is preferably done at the
fracture involving dentate segment. Exception
to this statement is the condyle fracture, which
always requires a rigid fixation.

Functional Advantages

• Patient safety—reduced airway risk
• Patient comfort
–– Immediate mouth opening
–– Ease of nutrition
–– Improved communication

4.7.9

Disadvantages of Miniplating
Osteosynthesis

• Malocclusion—Previously, it was reported
that there is a slightly increased incidence
of malocclusion in patients with mandibular fractures treated by miniplate osteosynthesis when compared to patients treated
by IMF alone [8]. Therefore, many surgeons today use 2.0 mm titanium miniplates for ORIF of mandibular fractures
supplemented with 1 or 2 weeks of
MMF. However, surprisingly recent studies
have shown that there is no significant differences in treating isolated mandible fractures with open reduction and internal
fixation and immediate release versus open
reduction and internal fixation with
5–7 days of MMF [13, 14].
• Sensory disturbance—Sensory disturbance
does not usually occur with mono-cortical
miniplating. However, when the fracture is
near the mental foramen region, there are
chances of mental nerve damage during
entire procedure, especially during miniplate
insertion [9].
• Cannot be used in the areas of excessive strain
such as bone defects or comminuted fractures
which are not in adequate contact.
• Should not be used for the management of
delayed fracture due to higher rate of
malocclusion.
• Plate cannot be adjusted after screw fixation.

4.7.10 Miniplate Osteosynthesis
for Edentulous Jaw Fracture
• The principle of miniplate osteosynthesis for
an edentulous jaw is the same as that for the
dentulous jaw.
• Ideal osteosynthesis line is usually situated on
the edentulous ridge due to the loss of the
alveolar bone.
• In a severely atrophic mandible, the inferior
alveolar nerve runs along the superior border,
sometimes on its upper surface of the mandible.
• The place for the plate is determined depending on the location of the alveolar nerve, either
below the nerve or on the superior border of
the mandible.
• Smallest possible plate must be used.
• In the absence of the stabilizing effect of the
teeth, the mandibular body acts as a fulcrum
for the action of the suprahyoid muscles and
the elevators of the mandible.
• The use of two miniplates is recommended in
severely atrophied cases, since studies have
proven that a single miniplate cannot provide
sufficient stabilization of the atrophic mandible [15].
• However, since there is lack of height for two
miniplate fixations, surgeons usually opt for
reconstruction plate fixation in edentulous
cases.

4.7.11 Miniplate Osteosynthesis
for Mandibular Condyle
Fracture
Fracture of the mandibular condyle is often seen
to be associated with other mandibular fractures.
Conservative treatment with appropriate
exercises is sufficient for most condylar frac­
tures. Miniplate fixation of the associated mandibular fractures with avoidance of intermaxillary
fixation permits such conservative therapy.
According to recent AO/ASIF guidelines, two
2.0 mm miniplates should be fixed with a minimum of two screws on each side of the fracture
line for a stable osteosynthesis [16]. A rigid fixation is essential in any surgically reduced subcondylar fracture, since it is a region that

Fig. 4.15 Miniplate fixation at the mandibular condyle
region

undergoes constant motion due to multidirectional stresses (Fig. 4.15). A bicortical screw fixation along the posterior border of the ascending
mandibular ramus is recommended, in order to
engage into the strong cortical bone. A single
anatomically shaped condylar plates can be also
used as an alternative to two miniplates.

4.7.12 Miniplate Osteosynthesis
in the Upper and Midface
Region
Miniplate osteosynthesis also finds its application in the upper and midface fracture cases and it
is proven to be efficacious [9]. There are various
approaches that allow the use of miniplates at all
levels for the fixation of reduced upper and midface fractures such as intra-oral, para-orbital,
bitemporal, coronal, pre-auricular and other local
incisions. In the midface, the vertical and horizontal buttresses that transmit biomechanical

A. Pandey and J. A. Kumar

a

b

c

d

Fig. 4.16 Miniplate fixation of the midface region

forces are the regions that are suitable for miniplate fixation.
Regions recommended for miniplate fixation
on the midface (Fig. 4.16) [4]:
Vertical buttresses:
• Medial maxillary—piriform rim
• Lateral maxillary—malar buttress
• Posterior maxillary—pterygomaxillary column
Horizontal buttresses
• Superior transverse—frontal bar
• Middle transverse—infraorbital rim and zygomatic arch
• Inferior transverse—maxillary alveolus
In any degree of midfacial fracture, the height,
width and anteroposterior dimensions can be recon-

structed by miniplate osteosynthesis. This can be
done at these sites alone or with the use of primary
bone grafting as required [17]. Zygomatic complex
fractures which are unstable after elevation can
readily be treated by miniplate osteosynthesis.
Champy et al. reported that the application of a fourhole miniplate to the zygomaticofrontal suture provides stability in the three spatial planes [18].

4.7.13 Microplates
The forces acting on the midface region are far
lesser when compared to the mandible; this allows
the use of microplates in this region. Microplates
are thinner and more malleable than miniplates
resulting in easier manipulation and insertion, at
the same time restoring structural integrity. A

4

Principles of Osteosynthesis

45

major advantage of the microplates is that they are
less readily palpable when plated on bony prominences such as infraorbital margin and frontozygomatic suture region. However, it is not
suitable for fixation of comminuted fractures [19].

–– Stress shielding effect
It refers to the reduction in bone density
(osteopenia) as a result of the removal of
normal stress from the bone by an
implant (for instance, the femoral component of a hip prosthesis). This is
because by Wolff’s law, the bone in a
healthy person or animal will remodel in
response to the loads it is placed under.
Therefore, if the loading on a bone
decreases, the bone will become less
dense and weaker because there is no
stimulus for continued remodelling that
is required to maintain bone mass [20].

Reconstruction Plate

• The built-in locking mechanism can obviate

4.10

Load-Sharing
Osteosynthesis

• Principle: Stability at the fracture site is created by the frictional resistance between the
bone ends and the hardware used for fixation.
• Requirement: Adequate bony buttressing at
the fracture site.
• Examples: Lag screw fixation technique, compression plating and miniplate fixation.
• Advantages: Smaller device, minimal exposure and avoidance of stress shielding
effect.
• Disadvantage: Cannot be used in fractures
with defects or comminuted fractures due
to the lack of bony buttressing at the fracture site.

4.11

External Fixation

4.11.1 External Fixator Devices
• Definition: External fixation is a type of fixation in which the fracture segments are fixed
with metallic pins connected to an external
fixator device which is placed outside the skin
(Fig. 4.18) [21].
• Type: Closed reduction technique which provides semi-rigid fixation.
• Device components: Rods and pins along with
an external fixator device.
• Examples:
–– Uniphasic and biphasic acrylic splints,
external bed traction, plaster head caps and
metal headframes
–– Modified Roger Anderson device—uniphasic system
–– Joe Hall Morris appliance—biphasic system
• Indications for external fixation:
–– In case of severe trauma to the face, the facial
skeleton tends to collapse inwards; these cases
in addition to stabilization and fixation require
an external traction force in different planes

4

Principles of Osteosynthesis

47

and directions, which can be accomplished
with the use of external fixation devices [22].
–– Infected open comminuted fractures.
–– Fractures with bone loss.
–– Gunshot fractures.
–– Cases in which surgical exposure of fracture sites may interrupt blood supply.
–– Open fractures in multiple injured patients.
–– Pathologic fractures.
–– Osteomyelitis in the presence of unstable
internaI fixation.
–– Preliminary fixation after a mandibular
resection.
–– In some orthognathic cases.
• Advantages:
–– Biologically oriented method since it does
not involve stripping of the periosteum and
hardly disrupts the nutritive pathway of the
fractured bone.
–– Involves minimal soft tissue disruption.
–– Allows immediate mouth opening.
• Drawbacks of external fixation devices:
–– Poor patient compliance—interference
with head movements and disturbance during rest or sleep
–– Postoperative infections, cellulitis around
the pins
–– Pin loosening
–– Non-union
–– Necrosis of bone surrounding the pins
–– Chances of injury to the inferior alveolar
nerve
–– Chances of damage to the parotid gland
This technique is employed only in cases where
internal fixation has failed or is not feasible.

4.12

Maxillomandibular Fixation

It is important to realize that establishment of
occlusion is imperative for the successful treatment of mandibular fractures.
Indications:
• For maintaining the normal occlusion that is
achieved after reduction of fracture.
• Following accurate reduction of a fracture, to
immobilize mandible for a recommended
period of time, for bone healing to occur.
• As a closed reduction process in which occlusion is taken as a guide for the alignment.
• It is also used along with any plating system to
act as a tension band or a means of maintaining occlusion and immobilization.
The period of immobilization varies with the
type and location of fracture, age of the patient
and presence of retained tooth in fracture line
(Tables 4.1 and 4.2).

4.14

Dental Wiring

4.14.1 Direct Interdental Wiring [23]
4.14.1.1 Gilmer’s Wiring
• Indication: First aid method for achieving temporary immobilization of fractured fragments
• Procedure:
–– Pre-stretched and cut 24- or 26-gauge
stainless steel wire is passed around the
teeth (not necessarily every teeth) through
the interdental space and twisted to produce a 3 cm tail.
–– After anatomic reduction of fracture, intermaxillary fixation is done by twisting the
corresponding upper and lower tails together
to obtain a criss-cross bracing (Fig. 4.19).

Fig. 4.19 Gilmer’s wiring

–– Twist ends are cut and tugged to avoid any
trauma to the soft tissue.
• Advantages: Immediate immobilization
• Disadvantages:
–– If one wire breaks, then all the wires should
be released to repair and re-fix
–– In case of emergency conditions, patient
cannot release MMF by himself

4.14.1.2 Risdon’s Wiring
• Indication:
–– Primary and early mixed dentition—when
anatomy of the teeth does not allow for
maxillomandibular fixation with arch bar.
• Types:
–– Type I—continuous cable used on the
entire arch
–– Type II—two separate cables joined at the
midline of the arch
• Procedure:
–– A pre-stretched and cut 26-gauge wire is
twisted around the distal most strong tooth
on both the sides in such a way that the
twisted cable ends are on the buccal side.
–– Now both the ends are twisted together at
the midline to form an arch bar like cable
at the cervical ends of the teeth
(Fig. 4.20a).
–– Circumdental wires are passed around
every tooth and are twisted individually.
These cables from each side are twisted
together to form two separate cables which
in turn are twisted at the midline to make a
huge rosette (Fig. 4.20b, c).
–– Alternatively, each circumdental wire can
be twisted, cut and tugged in its position to
form many small rosettes, over which elastics are applied to produce intermaxillary
fixation (Fig. 4.20d).
• Disadvantages:
–– Soft tissue trauma by the rosette
–– Laborious procedure
4.14.1.3 Essig’s Wiring
• Indication:
–– To stabilize dento-alveolar fracture
–– As anchoring device for MMF
–– Sufficient number of teeth on either side of
the fracture line

• Procedure:

4.14.2 Indirect Dental Wiring
4.14.2.1 Ivy Eyelet Wiring (Fig. 4.22)
• Indication:
• Primary and early mixed dentition—when
dental status does not allow for maxillomandibular fixation with arch bar fixation
• Preparation of eyelets:
–– 26-gauge soft stainless steel wires are used.
–– Wire should be stretched to about 10% of
its original length in order to prevent wire
loosening after fixation.
–– Eyelet wires are made by twisting the middle of the cut wire around the shaft of a rod
of 3 mm diameter (preferably around the
shaft of a 1.5 mm drill bit).
–– Three to four twists are recommended.
–– Ends are cut to equalize the length, after
leaving sufficient material for convenient
twisting around the teeth.
• Procedure:
–– The constructed loop is passed interproximally between two stable teeth (preferably between two molars/premolars/
central incisors).

a

A. Pandey and J. A. Kumar

–– The ends of the wire are brought to the buccal side by again passing interdentally
around the mesial surface of one tooth and
distal surfaces of another tooth on either
side of the loop.
–– The distal wire is then passed through the
loop to the mesial side and tightened to the
mesial wire in an apical direction
(Fig. 4.22a).
–– The loop is then tightened and adapted into
the interproximal space.
–– This procedure is repeated on the corresponding side of the opposite jaw and also
in multiple locations (Fig. 4.22b).
–– MMF between Ivy loops can be achieved
by different methods.
–– Commonly, a smaller gauge wire is passed
through the corresponding upper and lower
loops, twisted, cut and tugged (Fig. 4.22c).
–– Disadvantages:
–– Time-consuming intraoperatively.
–– Insufficient strength to maintain occlusion
during heavy manipulation in severely displaced fracture cases.
–– Wire breaks easily.

4.15.1 Clove Hitch Method (Fig. 4.24)
4.15.1.1 Arch Bars
Arch bars are the most favoured method maxillomandibular fixation. They can be prefabricated
or custom-made. There are a variety of prefabricated arch bars such as Erich, Jelenco, Krupps,
etc. Erich arch bar is the most commonly used
type. It is a prefabricated malleable stainless steel
arch bar with hooks incorporated to aid in MMF.
• Indications:
–– For temporary stabilization of fracture in
emergency cases before the definitive
treatment
–– For fixation of avulsed or mobile teeth and
dento-alveolar fractures
–– As a tension band in combination with
internal fixation of fractures
–– As an integral part of skeletal suspension
wiring
–– Preoperatively and postoperatively, to
maintain/guide occlusion or to restrict
mandibular movements for a recommended
period of time
–– Intraoperatively, to maintain teeth in proper
occlusion during fracture fixation
–– Long-term fixation in conservative
management
• Procedure [6]:
–– The procedure can be performed under
local anaesthesia/IV sedation/general
anaesthesia.
–– Adjust the shape and length of the arch bar
for both the arches.

Fig. 4.23 Hallam modification of Ivy eyelet wiring

51

–– The arch bar is usually placed from distal
to the first molar on one side to the corresponding point on the other side. It can be
modified according to the dental status and
requirement.
–– 24-gauge wire is pre-stretched and cut into
pieces of sufficient length.
–– A circumdental wire is placed either around
the first molar or second premolar of one
side (preferably fractured side).
–– The measured arch bar is then placed along
dento-gingival junction in such a way that
one end of the wire is above the arch bar
and the other end is below it. Now both the
ends are held together at the end by a wire
twister, and the arch bar is secured to the
teeth by twisting the wire in a clockwise
direction.
–– Care must be taken to position the arch bar
properly in such a way that the curvature of
the hooks faces away from the occlusal surface, so as to aid in elastic or wire application for MMF.
–– Now, circumdental wires are secured
around every tooth in a similar way starting
from molar teeth of one side to the midline
and from midline to posterior teeth on the
other side. Any excess arch bar is cut at the
other end. Excess circumdental wires are
cut and twisted to form rosettes, which are
tugged interdentally, facing away from the
gingiva.
–– Same procedure is repeated for the opposite arch. It must be ensured that the hooks
are positioned symmetrically in the upper

Brackets
• Indication:
–– Easily reduced, nondisplaced or immobile

–– Younger patients
–– Patients previously undergoing orthodontic

• Procedure:

• Advantages:
–– No risk of contaminated wire stick

–– Local anaesthesia may not be needed.

• Disadvantages:
–– Loss of brackets during the postoperative
period.
–– Ease of removing the wires/elastics by the
patient.
–– Adequate stabilization is difficult to
achieve.

4.15.1.4 Hybrid Arch Bars (Fig. 4.29)
• Hybrid arch bar system functions in a manner
similar to traditional EABs but is retained by
bone-borne self-drilling locking screws in the
maxilla and mandible rather than circumdental wires.
• A minimum of five screws are required in
each arch.
• Lugs are easily bent to ensure that screws are
placed between the roots of adjacent teeth.

Disadvantages:

4.17

Splinting

A splint is a rigid or flexible device/aid used to
support, protect and immobilize teeth that have
been weakened (endodontically or ­periodontally),
avulsed, traumatized, replanted or fractured.
Splinting is known as the process of application
of splint as a means of immobilization in the
above-mentioned scenarios. Splinting is not usually recommended for primary dentition. In permanent dentition, splinting is recommended in
various cases such as subluxation, luxation, avulsion, class IV root fracture and dento-alveolar
fractures (Table 4.4).

(2012) [16]
• Extrusion injuries: semi-rigid fixation for

4.17.2 Desired Characteristics
of a Splint
• It is simple to create and put in place.
• It prevents further traumatization of the
injured tooth.
• It enables physiological movement and therefore healing.
• It does not obstruct occlusion.
• It makes maintenance of oral hygiene
possible.
• It makes it possible to monitor vitality.
• It does not obstruct endodontic treatment
when necessary.
• It is aesthetic.
• It is easily removed.
There are various types of splints that can be
utilized according to the individual case and surgeons’ expertise.

4.17.3.2 Semi-Rigid/Flexible Splints/
Non-rigid Splints
• Orthodontic brackets and arches
• Wire and composite splints
• Fibre splints
• Titanium trauma splints (TTS)

4.17.4.2

 ire Ligature Splints
W
(Fig. 4.34)
Wire ligature splints are sometimes used by oral
surgeons in clinics where dental splinting materials may not be available. These splint types are
generally rigid and impinge on the gingival tissues with resulting inflammation.
4.17.4.3 Arch Bar Splints
Arch bars are readily available metal bars which
can be fixed onto the dentition with the help of
wires. Arch bars are discussed in detail in the following text.
4.17.4.4 Acrylic Splints
As their name suggests, these splints are made
from acrylic material. They are not used for isolated dental traumas. They are indicated in cases
of luxation of a tooth in combination with a fracture of the alveolar bone. The best-known splint
of this type is the Pfeiffer splint.
This splint may be made in two ways:
• The direct method is performed directly in the
patient’s mouth, and for that reason, it is very
uncomfortable because the acrylic sets in the
mouth are creating an unpleasant warm reaction.
• The indirect method is prepared in laboratory
with the help of cast models.

4.17.4 Rigid Splints
4.17.4.1 Suture Splints
In this method, either a soft wire or a surgical
suture is used for splinting. A soft wire splinting
is commonly indicated in deciduous dentition.
The wire is woven around the traumatized teeth,
along with a minimum of two healthy teeth on
either side for stabilization. In case if the traumatized tooth is isolated, with no neighbouring
teeth, then it is fixed tightly to the surrounding
gingiva with a surgical suture. The drawback of
this method is that the soft wire or suture tends to
break easily during mastication, and also it hampers oral hygiene maintenance.

Fig. 4.34 Wire ligature splint

58

A. Pandey and J. A. Kumar

4.17.5 Flexible/Non-rigid Splint
4.17.5.1 Composite and Wire Splints
Composite and wire splints are the most commonly used in clinical practice and are flexible
splints when the wire has a diameter of
0.3–0.4 mm.
4.17.5.2 Orthodontic Wire
and Bracket Splints (Fig. 4.35)
This splint involves orthodontic brackets bonded
to the teeth with resin-based orthodontic cement
and connected with a light 0.014 NiTi flexible
wire. Care must be taken that orthodontic forces
do not develop stress that disturbs the healing
phase of an injured tooth. The drawback of this
type of splint was found to be irritation to the lips
when compared to composite and wire splints
and titanium trauma splints.
4.17.5.3 Fibre Splints
These types of splint include:
•
•
•
•

Fishing line
Glass-ionomer fibre
Ribbond splint
Kevlar fibre

Fishing line and glass-ionomer fibre are used
in the same way as in a wire-composite splint.
Fibre splints are attached either with an
unfilled resin or with composite resin.

4.17.5.4 Titanium Trauma Splint (TTS)
TTS is a rhomboid mesh type splint made of
pure titanium. It is 0.2 mm in thickness and is
available in different lengths from 52 to 100 mm.
Its rhomboid form and minimal thickness aids in
better adaptation and fixation. The size of the
rhomboid opening is a meagre of 1.8 Å ~ 2.8 mm
which requires a mere quantity of composite for
fixation and also makes it easier during splint
removal.

4.18

Conclusion

The success of any surgery lies largely on the
knowledge of the surgeon. It is ineluctable for a
surgeon to have knowledge of all the available
treatment modalities at that particular period and
the principle behind each of them, in order to
choose the appropriate treatment required for the
patient without any delay. Through this chapter,
effort has been made to give a wide view of all
the fixation mechanisms that have been used in
the past and are being used at present. A combined analysis of the pros and cons of every technique, along with patient particulars, is essential
to choose the appropriate treatment in any CMF
trauma case.

5.1

Introduction

Monopoly and regionalism were prominent
aspects of ancient human civilization which
gave rise to many military wars and civil wars.
Complex wounds and fractures of skeletal system
are the consequences of these wars. Earlier, non-­
rigid materials were used by different surgeons
to stabilize the fracture segments. Soon thereafter
following discovery of metals and construction
of rigid materials, rigid fixation of fracture was
started. These metallic materials were fixed over
fracture segments, and they were splinted to the
body part using wires or bandages. Development
of metal bone pins made it possible to insert the
pins in the bone fragments and stabilize them
“externally.” Recurrent infections due to poor
biocompatibility and corrosion behavior of metals pushed the medicine professionals to search
for a more inert and biocompatible material.
Introduction of stainless steel and later on titanium to the medical field made it possible to fix
the fractures “internally.” Today internal fixation
has gained much advancement and popularity in
the medical field.

R. Tripathi (*) · Shweta
Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery Unit, Faculty of
Dental Sciences, Institute of Medical Sciences,
Banaras Hindu University,
Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh, India

5.2

History

For centuries, maxillofacial fractures have been
treated using various conservative techniques
like immobilization, splinting techniques, and
maxillomandibular fixation. Immobilization
and splinting of facial bones is supposed to be
the oldest method of facial fracture management. During the fifth century BC, Hippocrates
advocated the use of bandaging for immobilization and wires for splinting teeth to reduce facial
fracture [1]. Similar treatment method was used
by Sushruta in 600 BC. He used face bandaging
for immobilization and bamboo sticks for splinting the fractured facial bones [1, 2]. The barber
surgeons (twelfth to early eighteenth century)
did many modifications in bandaging techniques
and tooth splinting methods in such a way that
the immobilization of the jaw was made more
effective and occlusion was restored satisfactorily (Fig. 5.1). Pierre Fauchard took a scientific
approach for managing dental disorders, and he
published a book in 1728 in which he described
oral anatomy and function. He stated various
methods of restoration of tooth and fabrication of
artificial dentures. Inspired from his description
of oral anatomy and artificial dentures, modifications were made thereafter to fabricate intraoral
splints for treating maxillomandibular fractures.
Although these methods of treating facial fractures aptly reduced the fractured bones, they
greatly compromised the jaw function [3, 4].

A. K. Singh, N. K. Sharma (eds.), Maxillofacial Trauma,
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-33-6338-0_5

Fig. 5.1 Bandaging of facial bone

a

Notable contribution was made by Thomas
Gunning (1866), Gurnell Hammond (1871), and
Thomas Gilmer (1887) in devising intraoral splints
and wiring methods. Works of Martin Kirschner
(1909), Dr. Varaztad H. Kazanjian (1916), and
Robert H. Ivy (1922) were a breakthrough in management of facial fractures. Sir Kazanjian during
World War I used wires to reduce small fragmented
bones, and he devised external splints to support
comminuted fractures [2, 3]. Ivy method of wiring
and intermaxillary fixation became the most popular method of wiring and IMF, and it is still in practice. Dr. Kirschner introduction of K wires made it
easy to pass wires through fractured facial bones.
Works of Lambotte (1902) and Roger Anderson
(1934) popularized the use of external pins for
fixation of fractures (Fig. 5.2). This technique was
named as “external fixation” as the fixator device
was present outside the body. During World War
II, external fixators were used prominently for
reducing various fractures of the body. Major disadvantages of external fixation were injury to vital
structures through the pins and infections [2].
Icart (1770), a French surgeon in Castres, used
brass wire as ligature fixation on a young man with

b

Fig. 5.2 Reduction of mandibular fracture using external pin fixation device

c

5

Basic Introduction to Internal Fixation Devices and Armamentarium

a humeral fracture. In 1886, Hansmann of Hamburg
published the use of metal bone plates with transcutaneous screws. Arbuthnot Lane (1892) and
Albin Lambotte (1905) modified the technique and
gave the term “internal fixation” [2–4].
In the twentieth century, Sherman improved
Lambotte’s designs and created fine-pitched,
threaded, parallel, self-tapping screws which
were made of corrosion-resistant vanadium
steel, which was better than silver and ivory
materials in terms of strength [2, 3]. These
alloys had several drawbacks as they were
inflammatory and were replaced by titanium
in the late 1970s. All of these osteosynthesis
devices had a common situation; the fracture
segments remain apart by a noticeable distance
from each other. To overcome this situation,
Collins (1920) and Eggers and Roosth (1959)
developed plates having slot-like or sliding
holes. When screws are tightened, they slide
toward the slot and closely approximate the
fracture segments together. Inspired from this
development, Danis (1949) developed the compression plates, in which slots are designed in
such a way that they cause compression at the
fracture line when screws are tightened [4]. Luhr
(1968, 1969) initiated compression osteosynthesis of mandible using vitallium plates. This
was further modified by Spiessl (1969, 1975);
he suggested the plates applied to the mandible
must not be bulky or oversized and plate size
must conform to the dimension of mandible
and must be of enough thickness to withstand
masticatory forces or muscle pull. According to
Michelet (1973) and Champy (1975), the mandible is in a state of dynamic compression and
the plates have to bear the tensile stress created
by dynamic compression. They kept the size of
plate very small and of enough size to neutralize the tensile stress and applied it to the line
of maximum tension. Their concept of dynamic
compression was a breakthrough in the field
of internal fixation, and based on their theory,
more sophisticated system developed afterward
what we’ve today known as “miniplate osteosynthesis” [5] (Table 5.1).

5.3

Bone Plates

Bone plate refers to any plate that is used to stabilize or immobilize bone fragments [6, 7]. It can
be made of metal or any rigid material. Bone plate
comes in various designs and shapes. Depending
upon its design and shape, the plate serves the
following mechanical functions:
•
•
•
•
•

Compression.
Neutralization.
Tension band.
Buttressing.
Bridging.

Compression function of bone plate can be
accomplished either by incorporating inclined
plane or eccentric holes in it. When screws are
tightened in the holes, they glide toward each
other; in this way, they bring the bone segments
close together which compress against each other
(Fig. 5.3).
Neutralization function of bone plate is the
plate potential to prevent the bone from torsional
and bending forces. In other words, it helps to
neutralize forces which a compromised bone
cannot withstand of its own. The thickness and
rigidity of plate material is the deciding factor for
neutralization function (Fig. 5.4).
Tension banding of plate is fixing the plate
in a region where the bone encounters maximum tension during the function. The plate is of
adequate strength to neutralize tensional forces;
however, it may not prevent the bone from bend-

64

R. Tripathi and Shweta

Fig. 5.3 Compression bone plate

The buttress function of plate is the ability of
plate to resist axial and vertical forces. In vertical fractures of the bone, bone strength is compromised, such that it cannot withstand axial and
vertical forces. Buttress plating in simple words
provides “buttressing” support to weakened bony
architecture (Fig. 5.6a–e).
The bridge function of plate is seen whenever there is a continuity defect of the bone. The
bone plate bridges the defect and transmits loads
from one bony surface to another. Reconstruction
plates applied after segmental resection are fine
example of bridge function of plates (Fig. 5.7).

5.3.1

Fig. 5.4 Neutralization function of bone plate

ing or torsional forces. Young’s module of the
plate material defines its ability to resist tension
(Fig. 5.5a–d).

Miniplates and Microplates

All the plates used in maxillofacial surgery having plate thickness 1.3 m or less can be considered as miniplates. It is based on Michelet and
Champy’s principles, which advocate the use of
small malleable plates and monocortical screws
for fixation of various fractures of maxillofacial
regions [8]. According to them, a plate must be of
enough thickness and tensile strength to neutralize the force of tension created at the fracture line
[8, 9]. They opposed the use of bulky compression plates and highlighted its stress shielding
effect. They popularized the concept of “functional fixation” [10]. According to AO, small and

Delta Plate

It is used for rigid fixation of condylar neck and
sub-condylar fractures of mandible. This plate
has a longitudinal arm containing two holes and
two holes at the corner of the plate. This shape of
the plate allows the plate to receive the load and
to resist tensile strain and compressive strain at
anterior and posterior surface, respectively. The
tensile and compressive stress runs parallel to
both sides of plate as the base of the plate is oriented toward the angle of mandible (Fig. 5.11).

System

The locking plate and screw is unique in design.
It has locking screw head which gets locked into
the plate during screw tightening (Fig. 5.15a, b).
It was developed to overcome two major drawbacks of conventional plating system, which
are frequent loosening of screw leading to loss
of reduction and movement of bone fragments
toward plate upon screw tightening [15, 16]. It is
not always possible to contour the plate perfectly
along the bony surface. In such a case when plate
is applied and screws are tightened, the bone
fragments tend to move toward the plate leading
to either widening of fracture gap or formation of
step defect at the fracture line. In locking plates,
due to locking nature of screw migration of bony
fragments toward plate is minimal and proper

5.3.8

Reconstruction Plate

Reconstruction plates are non-compression plates
which are mainly designed to bridge a bony
defect. These are commonly used in comminuted
fractures or severely displaced angle. These are
the only load-bearing plates available. Therefore,
they are designed to be thicker and stouter than
all other plates, so that they can absorb all the
functional loads that the mandible is subjected
to. While using reconstruction plate, the posterior
most screw should be at least 1 cm away from the
fracture site. Reconstruction plates are available
in various sizes ranging from 2.7 mm to 3.5 mm
(Fig. 5.16). They may or may not use locking

Bone Screws

Screw is a mechanism which is used to convert
rotational motion or torque into a linear motion.
The main function of a screw is to fix a bone plate
onto the bone and make it a single unit. They also
serve other purposes as follows:
Functions of Screws
1. To stabilize the bone.
2. To secure fixation plate to the bone.
3. To compress fractured bone fragments.
4. To fix appliances to the bone.

Outer diameter

Root diameter
Thread angle
Pitch

The original function of the screw is not to
interfere with the healing function, but to provide adequate stiffness, to resist excess motion/
movement, and to remain in equilibrium during
function.

Two types of screws are used in oral and

the cancellous screws. The cancellous screws
have long shaft, whereas the cortical screws
have no shaft at all. Lag screw is a modified
cancellous screw characterized by presence of
a long shaft.

bone or into the plate, it creates compression

is greater when compared to cortical screws.

5.4.1

Pullout Strength of Screw

The pullout strength of screw is the capability of
the screw to resist pulling out. To increase pullout
strength, the following steps can be undertaken:
1. Increase the outer diameter.
2. Decrease the inner diameter.
3. Increase the thread density.
4. Apply in the area of maximum cortical/cancellous density.

(a) Non-self-tapping—The thread of the screw
extends up to the whole length. At first the
pilot hole is made. The thread must be precut in the pilot hole with the help of a tap of
same diameter as that of the screw before
the actual screw insertion (Fig. 5.21a). This
technique has the advantage that the debris
formed while drilling the pilot hole is
removed by the tap and there is a chance for
irrigation after tapping, which also aids in
removal of debris and cooling down the
bone.

(b) self-tapping screw,
(c) self-drilling and
self-tapping screw

cortical bone directly without tapping, since
the screw itself acts as a tap. Since this
method requires putting in a lot pressure

Disadvantages of Self-Tapping Screws
1. Excessive torque required during insertion.
2. Screw fracture due to fatigue.
3. Poor control of operator over direction of
tapping.
4. High incidence of loosening as the cutting
flutes have fewer threads at the tip which may
not be enough to engage the far cortex of the
bone.

5.4.2

 oncept of Stress Shielding
C
and Its Effect on Screw
Loosening

In a healthy bone, much of the load is sustained by cortical part of the bone and is transferred through bone trajectories to the adjacent
bones. The haversian system is well developed
in healthy bone, and there is good presence of
capillary network. When the bone fractures,
this haversian system is disturbed and circulation is compromised, and if a screw or a metal
plate is applied, much of the load is sustained
by the metal plate and screw, and a part of the
bone which is in contact with the plate undergoes
disuse atrophy compromising the strength of the
bone [7]. Presence of screw in cancellous bone
further disturbs microcirculation leading to poor
bone growth around screw and poor mechanical
interlocking of screw. All of these factors collectively contribute to screw loosening and failure
of hardware. Other reasons of screw loosening
are listed in Table 5.2. This concept of protection
of stress concentration over fractured bone sur-

Table 5.2 Causes of screw loosening
Causes of screw loosening:
• Excessive heat during drilling (heat necrosis of
bone)
• Improper drilling angle
• Damaged drill
• Small pilot hole and excessive compression
(Pressure necrosis of bone)

face by metal plate or screw is known as stress
shielding effect. To prevent stress shielding, thin
plates are used nowadays as it would allow partial functioning of the bone after metal plate has
been applied.

5.4.3

Lag Screws

Lag screw fixation is a technique of fracture compression which is highly efficient and effective. It
eliminates the use of plates and provides a rigid
fixation only with the help of screws. It was introduced by Brons and Boering in 1970. Lag screw
can be applied in linear or oblique fractures. It is
not suitable when there is comminution or bone
loss. Lag screws are mainly used in fractures of
mandible symphysis, parasymphysis, and angle
region and to less extent in the body region of
mandible. Presence of inferior alveolar nerve
interferes with placement of lag screws, so its use
in body region is limited. Lag screws can also be
used along with other internal fixation devices to
provide additional stability. For proper application of lag screw, a perpendicular hole is drilled
across the fracture line and screw is inserted.
When screw is tightened, the terminal thread of
screw engages the opposite cortex and brings into
close approximation (Fig. 5.22).
It must be kept in mind the hole just below
the head of screw must be of the same size as
the screw head to permit its proper movement
across the fracture line; otherwise, a small hole
will hinder the gliding movement of lag screw.
When compared to miniplates, lag screw fixation is comparatively less time-consuming and
requires less instrumentation, but good surgeon
skill is needed to drill the holes properly.

5.4.4

Emergency Screws

When the threads created in the bone get stripped
away or the hole becomes too large for the screw,
by errors in handling, then the next larger sized
screw is used, which is commonly referred to as
emergency/salvage screw. The emergency screws
for 1.5 mm, 2.0 mm, and 2.5 mm systems would
be 2.0 mm, 2.4 mm and 2.7 mm screws, respectively (Fig. 5.23).

5.5

 lloy Constituents of Metal
A
Bone Plates and Screws

Metal bone plates used in oral and maxillofacial
surgery can be broadly divided into two categories based on its composition:
• Stainless steel plates.
• Titanium plates.
Stainless steel has been discontinued in developed countries due to its high corrosion susceptibility and low malleability. Another drawback
of stainless steel is that it interferes with modern radio diagnosis devices such as magnetic

resonance imaging and computed tomography.
Titanium is widely recommended since it produces minimum artifacts in radio-diagnostic
images and is more resistant to corrosion.
Depending upon crystal structure, titanium
can be classified into α and β types. α-Titanium
has hexagonal close packed structure, while β has
body-centered cubic structure. To improve the
mechanical and chemical properties of titanium,
few more elements are added. These elements
stabilize either α- or β-phase of the titanium
(Table 5.3).
Following addition of the stabilizers, the titanium alloy can be broadly classified into three
types:
1. α-Type alloy (having predominance of alpha
titanium),
2. α- plus β-type alloy (presence of both alpha
and beta titanium),
3. β-Type alloy (predominance of beta
titanium).
α- plus β-type alloy and β-type alloy are most
commonly used to make plates and screws used
in oral and maxillofacial surgery owing to their
superior properties over alpha-type alloy.

5.6

R. Tripathi and Shweta

Bioresorbable Plate
and Screw

In pediatric growing patients, a second surgery is
often required to remove the metal plates as they
interfere with the growth of facial bones. Few
other drawbacks of metal hardware are infections, stress shielding, and interferences with
modern radio-diagnostic devices. Bioresorbable
plates and screws were developed to overcome
the shortcomings of metallic fixation devices.
These are semirigid materials which when
applied over the bone start degrading itself within
a certain time period. It retains enough strength
to hold fracture segments together until the bony
union is completed [18].
The plate thickness of current bioresorbable
plates ranges from 1.5 mm to 0.5 mm, while
screw diameter ranges from 2.2 mm to 1.5 mm
(Fig. 5.24).
The following chemicals are the main constituents of bioresorbable plates and screws:

talline and hydrolyzed completely within 1 to
2 years. Current hardware which are made from
PDLA resorb within 12–30 months. PLLA is
slightly inferior to PDLA in terms of biocompatibility and hydrolysis capability, and it also takes
a longer time to resorb completely when compared to PDLA. Copolymers of PGA, PDLA,
and PLLA are considered as the second-generation bioresorbable materials. The composition
of different constituents can be altered to get the
desired biological and mechanical properties of
the hardware. The composition is altered in such
a way that the final material will retain enough
strength for 6–8 weeks, and it will take around
12–18 months for complete degradation. Coating
with hydroxyapatite is the innovative method to
induce osteoconduction at the application site
and to improve biocompatibility of the hardware
[18–20] (Table 5.4).

of screw being placed, direction of fracture
line, and proximity to vital structures (e.g.,
presence of mental foramen close to parasymphysis fracture).
• Self-tapping screws perform poorly in this

tion of placement which is quite easier with

There are three main parts of a drill bit: cutting
edge, flutes, and land (Fig. 5.41a, b).
The cutting edge is the actual part responsible
for bone cutting, the flutes work to guide the
bone chips away from the hole being drilled,
and the land is the surface between two adjacent flutes.
The reaming edge helps to remove the bone
debris, and it runs along whole length of the
drill bit.
An angle is formed between leading age of
land and central axis of drill bit which is
known as rake or helical angle. For efficient
cutting, rake angle must be kept small (25–30
degrees).
During drilling, there is generation of excessive heat which can injure the osteocytes and
causes heat necrosis of the bone.

• It has been found that rise in bone temperature
beyond 47 degree Celsius for more than
1 minute can cause thermal damage to the
bone. To prevent this injury, use of copious
irrigation is recommended during drilling.
Drill Guides
• Drill guide is used to drill the far cortex to the
inner diameter of screw.
• Drill guide has an extension on its tip that has
exactly the same diameter as the external
diameter of screw.
• It is important that prior to drilling fracture
segments should be properly reduced.
• Neutral drill guides are designed to place the
screw centrally.
• Locking plate and screw system are used with
threaded drill guides.
• The disadvantage includes that it is difficult to
irrigate the tip of the drill. Therefore, repeatedly removal of drill bit is necessary to wash
off the debris as well as cool down the tip.

Aluminum Templates
• Aluminum template in maxillofacial surgery
is used to avoid repeated bending of plates.
• They are bendable in three dimensions by following the complex contours of the craniofacial region.
• The plates are contoured with the help of this
guide.
• These templates can be reused after sterilizing.

Plate Cutters
• For titanium plates, three different types of
cutters are available for cutting plates.
• The first plate cutter works effectively for
mesh and craniofacial plates.
• The second is for cutting mandibular reconstruction or universal fracture plates.
• The third is having additional mechanical efficiency to cut large plates (Fig. 5.43).

Bending Pliers and Plate Benders
• The bending of plates is done by three basic
instruments.
• The first is bending irons that are single-unit
instruments with handle and a receptacle to
receive a plate for bending and contouring the
required three-dimensional shape.
• Bending plier has two basic forms; the first is
single hinge which is useful for bending
microplates and miniplates.
• The second type of plier has additional
mechanical advantage that allows contouring
of plates in more gentle curves for better adaptation to the bone. It uses the mechanical
advantage of fulcrum.
• The plates are bent by these pliers either in
plane, out of plane, or last segment of the
plate.
• Plate benders are required to bend the reconstruction plate into the required mandibular
arch form (Fig. 5.42).

6.1

Introduction

The word “medicolegal” is derived from the
Latin word medicus meaning medical and legalis meaning legal. The Merriam-Webster
Dictionary defines it as “of or relating to both
medicine and law” [1]. In context to the maxillofacial trauma, road traffic accidents are of
special medicolegal implications as most
patients with these injuries have multisystem
trauma that requires coordinated management
between physicians and surgeons of various
specialities dealing with emergency medicine.
Maxillofacial surgeon, otolaryngologist, plastic
surgeon, anaesthetist and general surgeon need
to work as trauma team. These patients require
careful and regular assessment communications
with the surgeon.
Trauma to the maxillofacial region involves
important functional systems such as vision,

hearing, olfaction, somatic sensation, mastication
and deglutition. A special consideration is
required towards vital structures in the head and
neck region. The disfigurement as a result of
these fractures can be devastating with huge psychological impact. It is important for facial
trauma surgeons to not only understand the standard of care but also the pitfalls that can expose
them to litigation. The entire trauma team should
be well versed with the essential principles of
good communication and appropriate documentation. Informed consent and proper surgical
management by following the recommended
clinical guidelines may protect the clinician from
litigation.

6.2

Historical Background

Ancient Indian literature has various descriptions
of medicolegal practice. Kautilya’s Arthashastra
describes the causes of death. They stated that the
death can be caused by either stopping the breathing (four ways—strangling, hanging, asphyxiation, drowning), physical injury (two ways:
beating and throwing from height) or poisoning
(by snake, insects or drugs). It also gives list of
forensic evidences and also describes the necessity of autopsy for establishing the cause of death.
Charaka Samhita gives detailed description of
various poisons, symptoms, signs and its treatment. The first book on forensic medicine was

© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2021
A. K. Singh, N. K. Sharma (eds.), Maxillofacial Trauma,
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-33-6338-0_6

87

88

G. Paul et al.

published by an Italian physician “Fortunato
Fedele” in 1602. Paulus Zacchias is considered
as the father of forensic/legal medicine. He published the famous book on legal medicine known
as Quaestiones medico-legales. In 1678 during
British rule, John Waldo and Bezaliel Sherman
inspected a death in custody and issued the first
death certificate in India. The first medicolegal
autopsy was performed in India by Dr. Edward
Bulkley on 28 August 1693. The first wound certificate was also issued by Dr. Bulkley on 9
August 1695 [2]. Medical jurisprudence is
defined as the branch of science and medicine
which deals with the study and application of
knowledge of medicine to legal problems, such
as inquests and in the field of law [3]. In 1807,
Andrew Duncan, professor of medicine at the
University of Edinburgh, was credited first to
establish forensic medicine in Britain and was
first to occupy the chair founded. Dr. J P Modi is
considered as the father of Indian forensic
medicine.

6.3

Medicolegal Case (MLC)

It is defined as “any case of injury or ailment
where, the attending doctor after history taking
and clinical examination considers that investigations by law enforcement agencies are warranted
to ascertain circumstances and fix responsibility
regarding the said injury or ailment according to
the law”. An emergency medical officer (EMO)
who is attending to the case may label it as a
MLC. All government doctors are duty-bound to
attend a MLC. A private practitioner cannot
refuse to examine a MLC by citing a jurisdiction
problem. Table 6.1 depicts some examples of
MLC.
Injury Indian Penal Code (IPC) Section 44
defines injury as any harm, whatever illegally,
caused to any person in the body, mind, reputation or property (Table 6.2).
Hurt IPC Sect. 319 defines hurt as bodily pain,
disease or infirmity caused to any person.

6.4

Manner of Infliction

It can be:
1. Natural.
2. Unnatural (accidental/homicidal/suicidal).
Both investigating officer and the forensic
physician come together to ascertain the manner
of infliction, after going through the circumstantial evidences submitted. In case of trauma, the
role of doctor usually comprises assessing
whether trauma is due to unnatural manner or due
to disease. After examination if the nature of the
injury is mechanical, i.e. injury to the tooth, sockets, gums, cheeks, lips, etc., then the manner of
infliction should be documented as unnatural.
Detailed clinical examination should be done in
diagnosing the dental disease from which he is
suffering.

6.8

Medicolegal Examination

First of all, assess the mental status and record
the vitals. Perform the clinical examination
methodically and thoroughly; one should be gentle and humble while evaluating the patient. You
should explain the procedure and every move to
the patient. Examine the injuries adequately;
observe the movements carefully especially in
suspicion of cervical bone fractures. You should
respect the privacy of the individual while
undressing.
From medicolegal point of view, a series of
questions should include:

6

Medicolegal Aspects in Maxillofacial Trauma

1. How did the injury occur? The answer will
indicate the location of possible injury zones.
2. By whom the injuries are caused? (name and
number of accused involved).
3. The motive behind assault.
4. Weapon used to inflict the injuries.
5. Place where the injury occurred.
6. Date and time especially in case of avulsed
or displaced teeth. Any inconsistency
between the appearance of the wounds in a
child and history supplied should raise
suspicion.
7. What he did after being assaulted? (i.e.
whether he visited the police station or came
back home or took treatment from any other
hospital).
8. Was the patient unconsciousness? If yes, for
how long? Is there headache/amnesia/nausea/vomiting? These are all signs of head
injury and require medical attention.
9. History of past dental injury.
10. Is there any derangement in occlusion? An
affirmative answer can imply one of the following conditions: tooth luxation, alveolar
fracture, jaw fracture or luxation or fracture
of the temporomandibular joint.
11. Attendant’s explanation may or may not be
compatible with the mode of causation of
injury. For dental injuries resulting from a
fall, for example, one would expect to also
find bruised or abraded knees, hands or
elbows. When these additional injuries are
not present, further inquiry is required.
Before examining the oral cavity and facial
regions, note the general physical findings
that are consistent with assault/scuffle.

6.8.1

Documentation of Clinical
Findings

Look for bruises or abrasions on the chest, abdomen and back and extremities reflecting the shape
of the offending object, e.g. belt buckle, strap and
hand. Bite marks and bald patches may be present. Both oral and facial injuries of assault may
occur alone or in conjunction with injuries to
other parts of the body. Intraoral examination

91

should include evaluation of laceration of soft tissues, missing teeth and step deformity in mandibular and maxillary arches. All missing teeth
should be accounted for which may require
radiographic evaluation of the chest. Lack of
proper occlusion is often reported by the patient.
A step deformity in the occlusal plane with a ruptured gingiva at the site or a sublingual haematoma is a strong indicator of mandibular fracture.
Assessment of other part injuries should be documented for medicolegal purpose. Multiple interdisciplinary consultation like neurosurgery,
ophthalmology, otorhinolaryngology, plastic surgery, orthopaedics, trauma and emergency should
be done to rule out associated injuries.

6.9

Importance of Wound
Pattern Characteristics [4]

Recording of the appearance and dimensions of
wound may be a very important factor in identifying the cause of injury and type of weapon
used. The documentation of the location of the
injury, exact measurement in all dimensions,
other characteristics of bruises, abrasions, cuts,
lacerations, stab wounds and entry/exit wounds.
Diagrams, body maps and photography are helpful in recording the prima facie and reproducing
the injury patterns in subsequent investigations
while appearing in court or at autopsy.
Abrasion is defined as destruction of the skin,
which usually involves the superficial layers of
the epidermis only. Age of abrasion can be
roughly estimated on the basis of its appearance:
•
•
•
•

Fresh—bright red in colour.
12–24 h—bright scab.
2–3 days—reddish-brown scab.
4–7 days—epithelial covering the defect
under the scab.
• After 7 days—scab dies and falls.
Contusion or bruise is defined as an effusion
of blood into the tissues, due to the rupture of
blood vessels, caused by blunt trauma. It is seen
as reddish-purple swelling of the skin that does
not blanch when pressed upon. Fresh contusion is

G. Paul et al.

usually tender and slightly raised. When a contusion fades, its colour changes over time as the
body metabolises the blood cells in the skin:
•
•
•
•
•
•

Fresh—red.
Few hours to 3 days—blue.
4 days—bluish black to brown
5–6 days—greenish
7–12 days—yellow
2 weeks—normal.

Incised wound—It is a clean cut through the
tissue, which is longer than its depth. Age of an
uncomplicated incised wound can be estimated
from its healing pattern:
• Fresh—haematoma formation.
• 12 h—red swollen and adherent edges
• 24 h—continuous layer of endothelium covered by scab of dry clot
• 36 h—capillary network complete
• 48–72 h—connective tissue
• 3–5 days—vessel thickening and obliteration
• 1–2 weeks—scar formation.
Stab or punctured wound—it is usually caused
by a sharp-pointed object, penetrating the skin
and underlying tissues, which is deeper than its
length and width on the skin. The wound of entry
is larger with inverted edges and the exit wound
is smaller with everted edges.

6.10

Admission and Discharge
of MLC

When a MLC is admitted, the same should be
documented on admission papers, case sheets,
investigations, X-rays and all related hospital
records. On discharge of a MLC, it should be
intimated to the police authorities of the hospital. Even in case of leave against medical
advice (LAMA) or absconding state, police
authorities should be informed immediately. At
the time of discharge, detailed instructions to
the patient regarding treatment, follow-up,
general care, diet and exercise should be given
in writing.

In case of death of MLC, do not issue death
certificate or hand over the dead body to the relatives of the deceased. Inform the police immediately, send the body to the hospital mortuary for
preservation, and request for medicolegal autopsy
by an authorised doctor. After the legal formalities are completed, the dead body is released to
the lawful relatives by the police.

6.11

Informed Consent
for Trauma

Consent to medical treatment as an ethical and
moral principle is probably as old as medical science. It is inconceivable that a medical practitioner
at any point in history would have treated or operated on a patient without his or her permission.
However, consent to treat as a legally binding
entity is of recent origin. Today, it is validated by
multiple principles drawn from social and behavioural sciences, moral philosophy, human rights,
ethics and laws of a particular country. One of the
principle guiding tenets of informed consent
involves the rights of patients to make clear assertions of what can or cannot be done to their bodies
based on unbiased and full disclosure of the benefits and risks that will ensue from treatment. While
most diagnostic treatment procedures are today
performed only with a clear informed consent,
there are some which attract particular attention in
the matter of informed consent.
The necessity for informed consent in trauma
is guided by the nature of injury. Maxillofacial
injuries often have concomitant head, thoracic
and other injuries where the exception to
informed consent can be invoked to perform surgery under the provisions of law that permits procedures done “in good faith” where life is
endangered. Other indications for waiving
informed consent include, but are not restricted
to:
1. Airway compromise.
2. Excessive bleeding.
3. Urgency in reimplantation of teeth.
4. Retrobulbar haematoma requiring decompression, etc.

6

Medicolegal Aspects in Maxillofacial Trauma

Definition Farlex’s free online dictionary has a
simple definition of informed consent. It is
“Consent by a patient to a surgical or medical
procedure or participation in a clinical study after
achieving an understanding of the relevant medical facts and the risks involved” [5].
A more descriptive definition is sometimes
employed to capture the nuances of informed
consent. It may thus be defined as “Consent given
by a patient after understanding his/her condition, procedure, risks and alternatives based on
unbiased information by the medical professional
in a language and manner which is unambiguous,
lucid”.

6.11.1 History and Theory
of Informed Consent
The key historical signposts in the evolution of
the informed consent as a valid legal document
can be traced to cases from the US judicial system, though the basic principles find their roots
in English common law. While consent has been
a well-known moral requirement before treatment, it gained legal sanctity only in 1914 with
the case of Schloendorff vs Society of New York
Hospital. It set the tone for a legally acceptable
premise of self-determination [6]. Justice
Benjamin Cardoza summarised the basic philosophy in his judgement: “Every human being
of adult years and sound mind has a right to
determine what shall be done with his own body
and a surgeon who performs an operation without his patients consent commits an assault for
which he is liable”. However, it was with a series
of case in the 1960s and 1970s that self-determination came to be legally binding as a legal principle, and more importantly, the importance of
full divulgence by the doctor based on which a
consent can be made became a dictum. Important
cases include the Salgo vs Leland Stanford Jr.
case (1972) and the Canterbury vs Spence case
(1972) [7]. Informed consent thereafter became
a legal remedy equivalent to “battery” if it was
not obtained. Informed consent (IC) in research
largely evolved due to the World War II atrocities

93

in Nazi concentration camps. The IC documents
in research have been formulated and reviewed
by the Nuremberg conference and the Helsinki
declaration. They are closely monitored for content by organisations such as the WHO, FDA and
ICMR in India.
Types of Informed Consent [8].
1. Implied.
2. Oral or written consent.
Implied Consent It is given by the behaviour of
the patient such as entering the clinic or emergency room and permitting examination.
Oral Consent Verbal consent is acceptable for
inconsequential procedures such as examination,
taking of impressions or even routine low exposure X-rays, etc.
Written Consent While oral consent is an
acceptable consent, it can often be challenged
and the giving of consent cannot often be proved
or validated. It is more binding to give a consent
that is reduced to writing and duly signed by the
consenting parties or their legal guardians in the
case of under-aged children. In the case of illiterates, the consent should be read out to the consenting party in a language known to them in the
presence of an independent witness who should
attest to the fact by affixing their signature.
Video Consenting In several countries,
informed consent documentation (ICD) is captured on video for greater authenticity. This is
particularly so in case of high-risk cases that have
potential for mortality and/or morbid outcomes.
Digital technology and ability to store large data
have made this a practical solution to conflicts in
the process of obtaining consent.

6.11.2 Valid Consent: Ethical Duty
This follows the Supreme Court judgement in
Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2016
UKSC 11], which ruled that when discussing the
benefits and risks of various treatment options
with patients, clinicians must:

94

• Provide information about all material risks.
• Disclose any risk to which a reasonable person in the patient’s position would attach
significance.
Before Montgomery, a dental professional’s
duty to warn patients of risks was based on whether
they had acted in line with a responsible body of
dental opinion; this was known as the Bolam test.
The Bolam test, or Hunter v Hanley in
Scotland, still applies to assessing standards of
care in wider negligence cases.
The GDC’s standards for the dental team set
out as one of its key principles the need for dental
professionals to share information with patients
so those patients can make a decision.
As a dental professional, you also have an
ethical duty to discuss material risks with patients
when obtaining consent for treatment.

6.11.3 Informed Consent in Oral
and Maxillofacial Surgery
Informed consent for oral and maxillofacial surgery is particularly relevant because several procedures are elective cosmetic surgeries with a
high degree of risks, subjective dissatisfaction
with outcomes and complications or sequelae
that cause disutility to the patient.
Minor Oral Surgery Many procedures ranging
from extractions to dento-alveolar surgeries are
commonly referred to as minor surgery, although
such a classification is not accurate. Every surgical procedure, whether done under local or general anaesthesia, carries some elements of risk or
possibility of unwanted sequelae.
The question often asked is how one decides
on what risks are material or relevant for the sake
of an informed consent. This is decided by the
“the prudent patient test” which determines what
a reasonable patient in the position of a plaintiff
(complainant) would attach significance to, in
coming to a decision on the treatment advice
given. The surgeon must foresee what side effect
or complication a patient may consider to be sig-

G. Paul et al.

nificant. For example, a patient may not place
significance on some mild pain and swelling following surgery. It is therefore not necessary to
obtain informed consent for the same. However,
a patient may be upset over a prolonged or permanent paraesthesia or neurological sequelae,
and any such possibility must be communicated.
Other consents of significance must include:
1. Temporary or permanent neurosensory disturbance or motor function.
2. Necessity for maxillomandibular fixation and
liquid diet.
3. Non- or malunion in case it is anticipated and
necessity for bone grafting.
4. Transient or permanent scars.
5. Anticipated functional problems like restricted
mouth opening or occlusal discrepancy.
6. Limitation in restoring deformity especially in
major midface fractures.
7. CSF rhinorrhoea and transient or permanent
loss of smell.
8. Any other anticipated deficit or deformity.
The ability to discern that which the patient
might perceive as worth knowing about before a
procedure is called the prudent patient test.

6.11.4 Major Surgery Under General
Anaesthesia
Major surgical procedures involving more than
one medical professional need multiple consent
forms. For example, all procedures being done
under general anaesthesia require separate
informed consent form for surgery and anaesthesia. In the case of more than one surgical specialist being involved in a surgery, every specialist
must obtain a relevant informed consent to cover
risks in their own fields of work. In the case of
polytrauma involving ophthalmologists, neurosurgeons, orthopaedic surgeons or plastic surgeons in a single patient, every specialist must
obtain a separate informed consent document
before surgery. All informed consents must be
specific to procedures and custom-tailored to the
risks in a particular patient [8].

6

Medicolegal Aspects in Maxillofacial Trauma

Secondary surgery and appearance altering
procedures (AAP) have special needs. In addition
to the regular risks encountered in maxillofacial
surgery like neurosensory deficits, bleeding, nonor malunion, avascular necrosis, occlusal discrepancies, etc., there is also an issue of results falling
below expectations, which is largely subjective. It
is pertinent that some psychiatric disorders like
body dysmorphic disorders (BDD) have an important role in subjective dissatisfaction. Surgeons
involved in appearance altering procedures during
reconstruction must take great care to refer patients
with obsessive concerns about small imperfections
and should include psychological evaluation as
part of the consenting process [9].
The informed consent document should
include:
1. The purpose of the proposed procedure.
2. A summary of the surgical approach.
3. Expected benefits and limitations.
4. A description of postoperative recovery; possible complications and known side effects,
including those that are rare.
5. Risks associated with anaesthetics, analgesics
and antibiotics; appropriate alternatives,
including the option of no treatment or surgery at all.
The informed consent document may need to
take into consideration the following principles,
and the surgeon and his team can make appropriate changes to accommodate them. These have
been enunciated by Lord Scarman in the case of
Sidaway v Board of Governors of the Bethlem
Royal Hospital [10]:
1. The individual should be of adult years
(18 years in India) and sound mind and should
have the legal mental capacity to choose what
happens to his body.
2. It should offer a choice that entails an opportunity to evaluate knowledgeably the options
available and the risks attendant on each
(including no surgery option).
3. The doctor should therefore disclose all material risks. The material risks are determined by
the “prudent patient test” which determines

95

what a “reasonable” patient in a position of a
plaintiff (complainant) would attach significance to, in coming to a decision on the treatment given.
In addition to this in the Indian context:
4. All informed consent must be in a language
understood by the patient (vernacular like
Hindi, Tamil, Malayalam, Bhojpuri,
Kannada, etc.) known as expressed consent
(tacit consent).
5. In case of illiterates, the informed consent
must be read to them in the presence of an
independent witness who must sign on the
space provided.
6. In children below 18, a parent or guardian can
sign on behalf of the child (loco parentis).
Recent concerns have suggested that informed
consent should also cover diagnostic tests. It is a
common practice in some countries, including
India, to do a routine HIV testing. These can be
undertaken only with an informed consent including pretesting counselling. Many countries also
insist on informed consent for multiple high-dose
radiation especially with the use of CT scan.

6.11.5 Informed Consent
and Negligence in Oral
and Maxillofacial Surgery
Informed consent regulations today are largely
governed by the principles of medical negligence
rather than the tort of battery as in the early days.
Any injury, even expected, may be considered a
negligent act if there is no informed consent. The
situation can be defended if it is an emergency
and no relative or next of kin is available. The
civil liability for the same will be similar to the
liability for medical negligence.
Similarly, informed consent does not absolve
the surgeon from liability for negligence if it is
proved that it could have been avoided if the surgeon had exercised reasonable care.
In short, liability for negligence can be mitigated by an informed consent, but informed consent cannot totally absolve a surgeon for an
obvious negligent act.

1. Loss of teeth.

4. Non-vitality of teeth.
5. Fracture of any facial bone.
6. Loss of soft tissue and severe scarring.
7. Neurological deficit (motor or sensory).

• Class 1—(0–5%) Disorder of cutaneous structure, e.g. visible scars.
• Class 2—(5–10%) Loss of supporting structure with or without cutaneous disorder, e.g.

it precludes social acceptance.

The American Association of Oral and
Maxillofacial Surgery (AAOMS) guidelines
award percentages for the complete masticatory
apparatus. It awards 24% for a person who is
restricted to liquid diet (40–60% if tube feeding
is necessary) and 5–19% if person is restricted to
semisolids (includes those with ability to wear
dentures). We have taken the liberty of awarding
points for individual teeth. However, if the whole
masticatory apparatus is to be evaluated, one
may separately evaluate absence of teeth, occlusal disharmony, TMJ movement (craniomandibular articulation), muscle power, etc. and arrive
at a figure by using Kessler’s formula:
A + B (100 - A ) 100
Further, the AAOMS guidelines classify the
percentiles into two categories: (1) percentage of
normal and (2) percentage impairment of whole
person. The dichotomy does not seem reasonable
and is likely to cause further confusion. Finer
details such as lateral excursion, etc. which have
been dealt with in the AAOMS guidelines have
been ignored.
Similarly, the concept of deformity and disfigurement has been dealt with differently in the
AAOMS and the AMA guidelines. The matter
of disfigurement is complicated by issues such
as personality crisis and the impact of social
acceptance. As suggested earlier, this criterion
can be incorporated into Kessler’s formula, thus
resolving the issue of multiple disabilities and
deformities.

Finally, the question of who can give a disability certificate. The Indian sources are silent in the
matter of maxillofacial injuries. However, the
law in many American states clearly provides for
the role of a board qualified oral surgeon or maxillofacial surgeon to issue disability certification
for the maxillofacial region.
Contrary to general perception, it is not necessary that these criteria need to be made by
­statutory bodies. General usage can give legal
legitimacy. It would of course be in the best interest of the surgeon, patient and public if these suggestions can be scrutinised, amended and
enlarged to accommodate a larger spectrum of
disabilities and deformities.

6.11.11 C
 an a Dental Surgeon/
Maxillofacial Surgeon Issue
a Death Certificate?
Previously, if a death occurs in a dental set-up, a
medical doctor was called upon to issue a death
certificate. In June 2014, code of ethics under
dental act were revised; the regulations state that
now dentist can issue death certificate in any case
of an injury in oral and maxillofacial region, a
natural death or death related to trauma occurring
under the care of a dentist.

6.11.12 Indemnity/Insurance:
General Dental Council
(GDC)
This is not a new requirement dental professionals
have always been required to have appropriate
indemnity arrangement in place so that patients
can claim any compensation to which they may
be entitled. This requirement is part of the standards. In November 2015, registration rules have
changed: the dental care professionals applying
for registration and those renewing their registration will need to show that they have indemnity
cover in place. If you are under your employer’s
policy, then make sure that you have an access to
the details of the policy.

G. Paul et al.

6.11.13 C
 onsumer Protection Act
(CPA)
The CPA was passed by the Indian parliament to
safeguard and protect the interest of consumers.
CPA aims at simplification of procedures for
seeking redressal of the grievances of the patient
or their relatives. It was on 13 November 1995
that the Supreme Court of India delivered the
judgement on the application of CPA to medical
profession, hospitals, dispensaries, nursing
homes and related services. The potential for
criminal liability of dentists is relatively low—in
the event of death occurring during the course of
dental treatment, proof of gross negligence alone
will hold against the dental practitioner.
Nevertheless, even in the absence of such proof,
the dentist can still be held accountable in civil
law under the CPA and is liable to pay compensation [12].
Thus, there is a need to raise the awareness of
the health professionals and dentist in particular
to make their practice dedicated to welfare of
patient and to serve the humanity.

6.12

Conclusion

Dentofacial trauma is common in day-to-day
practice. Meticulous medicolegal examination
and documentation is of utmost importance at the
initial stage. The medicolegal examination should
be done jointly by the team of forensic experts
including a forensic odontologist. Informed consent documentation is an important and critical
part of all treatment plans and often includes
invasive or potentially harmful investigations. A
proper informed consent that is realistic and
involves full disclosure if the patient is exposed
to a chance of injury for which he has no utility is

a necessary part of all treatment protocols.
Informed consent documents respect the right of
patients to take a decision on how their body is
treated based on all available information. It is a
moral, ethical and legal obligation to obtain a
consent based on credible information. It also
provides a safety net for the surgeon when unexpected adverse complications occur. Trauma surgery, unlike elective procedures, has some
relaxation particularly if it is life-saving and it is
done in good faith as per the Supreme Court and
legislated lives, even in the absence of a bystander
or relative.

7.1

Introduction

The patients of faciomaxillary trauma present
in emergency resuscitation area with frightening facial appearances and threatened difficult
airway which can be complicated further by
deformed facial anatomy head and cervical spine
injury. They all are full stomach, having blood or
blood mixed secretions, vomitus, foreign bodies,
and facial and laryngeal tracheal injuries with
edema. Management of acute airway obstruction is prime as per ATLS guidelines to prevent
hypoxic brain injury [1]. Emergency surgery is
not routinely required in each and every patient;
it is only needed when the airway is compromised
due to tracheó bronchial injuries or severe hemorrhagic shock due to polytrauma [2]. Definitive
or reconstructive surgery is generally planned in
a hemodynamically stable patient after the primary and secondary ATLS surveys and management of ABCDE.

S. Sahu

Postgraduate Institute of Medical Sciences,
Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh, India
N. Verma (*)
Department of Anesthesiology, IMS, BHU,
Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh, India
D. Jain
Department of Anesthesiology, AIIMS,
New Delhi, India

The probability of encountering a difficult
airway is high in maxillofacial trauma because
of distorted anatomy (Fig. 7.1). The American
Society of Anesthesiologists has defined the difficult airway as “the clinical situation in which
a trained anesthesiologist experiences difficulty
with facemask ventilation of the upper airway,
difficulty with tracheal intubation, or both.” Both
the surgeon and the anesthesiologist have to work
in tandem and be on the same page with respect
to the management of airway as well as the whole
patient in such situations. The airway and anesthetic management in a trauma patient with maxillofacial injury can be divided into emergency
airway management and anesthetic management
for elective correction surgery. Preanesthetic
evaluation mandates a brief history regarding
the events that lead to injury, the mechanism of
injury, and the preexisting comorbidities.

7.2

Emergency Management
of Maxillofacial Injuries

The initial management of maxillofacial trauma
is similar to any trauma patient and should be
based on the Advanced Trauma Life Support
(ATLS) protocol—ABCDE [1]. We should
identify immediate life-threatening conditions
and simultaneously manage it in the following
sequence (discussed in detail in Chap. 8):
