Securing the airway and ensuring ventilation is the first thing required in emergency
management of maxillofacial trauma either in
prehospital or in hospital setting. Maintaining
an unobstructed airway is the most crucial part
of emergency management. Surgeries for facial
fractures can be performed later on a semi-elective basis [3].

Hutchinson has described the following
modes of airway compromise which may accompany maxillofacial injuries [4]:
• Posterior inferior displacement of fractured
maxilla blocking the nasal airway.
• Bilateral anterior mandibular or parasymphyseal fracture may cause the tongue to fall
back due to loss of its anterior insertion leading to oropharyngeal obstruction in supine
position.
• Teeth, bony fragments, vomitus, or other foreign bodies may obstruct the airway.
• Hemorrhage from open wounds or small vessels can cause obstruction.
• Soft tissue swelling and edema.
• Laryngeal or tracheal trauma resulting in
swelling or displacement of epiglottis, arytenoids, or vocal cords causing airway
obstruction.
Prompt identification and control of a
c­ompromised airway with cervical spine
stabilization is a must in life-threatening
emergencies.

7.3

Preanesthetic Evaluation
for Elective Maxillofacial
Trauma Surgeries

In trauma management, detailed preanesthetic
checkup (PAC) and classical perioperative optimization are not possible as hemodynamic
unstable severe polytrauma patients need urgent
surgeries.
In elective surgeries, optimization of the
patient condition before anesthesia and surgery
to improve the postoperative outcome is the
main aim of preanesthesia checkup (PAC), and
it emphasizes the role of the anesthesiologist as
the perioperative physician. It includes history

104

of present and past illnesses, allergies, addiction,
family history, and specifically any anesthesia-­
related adverse experiences in the past. Physical
examination can be divided into general examination, systemic examination, as well as examination of the airway and spine. Systemic physical
examination is focused on respiratory, cardiac,
neurological, vascular, hepatic, and renal organ
systems largely. Speciality consultation may
be required for specific diseases. Each patient
is then evaluated by a battery of tests targeted
toward their condition as assessed by history and
examination.
Based on the preoperative assessment, each
patient is graded according to ASA (American
Society of Anesthesiologists) physical status
classification where the patient is put in to one
of the six categories with an “E” being added
to their status if it is an emergency surgery. The
ASA defines an emergency as existing “when the
delay in treatment of the patient would lead to a
significant increase in the threat to life or body
part” [6].
This preoperative grading system does not
include the difficult airway issues, complexity
associated with the type of surgeries, and potential risk for adverse anesthesia-related outcomes.
However, it has been shown to be a fair predictor
of duration of postoperative hospitalization [7].
This important aspect of preoperative evaluation can be incorporated by using other specific
preoperative grading systems like the ACC/AHA
guidelines for preoperative evaluation for noncardiac surgeries. PAC also includes instructions for
preoperative fasting and preoperative medication
administration before surgery and also allows the
postoperative analgesia care plan to be discussed
with the patient.
Maxillofacial Surgeries may be categorized as
follows:
• Low risk—with very less physiologic stress
potential or risk toward the patient (independent of a patient’s medical condition); rarely

S. Sahu et al.

requires the need for blood transfusion, invasive monitoring, or ICU care; and includes
office-based surgery and minor surgery (routine dental extraction).
• Moderate risk—increased physiologic stress
and risk (such as fluid shifts), typically with
minimal blood loss, but the potential must be
appreciated, and includes full-mouth extractions secondary to teeth that have been
affected by extensive caries and/or periodontal disease.
• High risk—significant perioperative stress and
potential for added postoperative physiologic
stress; increased likelihood to require a blood
transfusion and/or larger amounts of fluids or
body fluid shifts, invasive monitoring, and
postoperative management in ICU setting; and
includes extensive maxillofacial surgery linked
to short-term stroke and heart attack risk or
maxillofacial surgery that deals with high-risk
medically compromising patients.

On the day of scheduled elective or planned

include cardiac (digitalis and ­

respiratory/asthma (e.g., metered dose inhalers

replaced with some other anticoagulants [8].

Airway Assessment

A maxillofacial trauma patient for elective surgery with a GCS (Glasgow Coma Scale) of more
than 10 would generally allow airway examination. The first step to which is assessment of
mouth opening and assessment of Mallampati

105

grade. A Mallampati score tells about the ease of
oral intubation as it assesses the size of the tongue
in relation to the other structures visible in the
oral cavity (Fig. 7.2). The size of the tongue is the
major factor causing obstruction of the airway in
an unconscious or anesthetized patient. The neck
movements, neck size (both length and girth), as
well as thyromental and thyrohyoid distances are
important for assessment of airway. The movement at the temporomandibular joint decides
the extent of mouth opening. The nares should
be checked for patency, deviation, or nasal spurs
which may be important in deciding the side for
nasal intubation. If not careful, bleeding from the
nose may obscure the airway and make airway
access more difficult [9].
Protocol for Airway Management in
Maxillofacial Trauma [9]
• Anticipate and recognize an airway obstruction based on signs and symptoms.
• Clear the airway by jaw-thrust maneuver and
suction.
• If still having airway obstruction, use artificial
airways (an oral airway is preferable over
nasal airway).
• Perform bag-valve-mask ventilation (preferably by “two-person technique”).

Fig. 7.2 Mallampati classification to predict difficult airway

106

S. Sahu et al.

• Orotracheal intubation is a choice.
• In unsuccessful orotracheal intubation or
“cannot ventilate, cannot intubate (CVCI) situation,” perform surgical airway or choose the
clinical algorithms given below.
Indications of Definitive Airway in
Maxillofacial Injuries [10]
• Airway or tracheolaryngeal injury or sign of
airway obstruction (partial or complete).
• High risk of aspiration.
• Absent or no spontaneous breathing.
• Comatose patient with GCS score < 9.
• Oxygen saturation < 90% (severe hypoxia)
and shock (SBP < 80 mmHg).
• Cannot intubate, cannot ventilate (CVCI)
situation.

7.6

Anesthetic Management
for Maxillofacial Surgery

Anesthesia management for elective surgery is quite
different from emergency management as paucity
of time is not an issue. A detailed airway management plan can be made with plan B as an alternative. There is availability of airway equipment and
anesthetists who are experts in airway management.
Nevertheless, management of airway can be quite
challenging in complex panfacial fractures [11].
The plan for airway management begins with
a detailed airway examination. Some important
points which are to be considered during assessment
are type of surgery, injuries involved, mouth opening, presence of edema, nasal patency, and features
of airway obstruction, status of mouth opening
after surgery, and whether prolonged postoperative
mechanical ventilation is required. Radiological
images (CT scans) should be reviewed to assess the
extent of injury, to assess the airway, and to exclude
head and spine injury [12].
Plan for securing the airway in maxillofacial
trauma and in difficult airway (Figs. 7.3, 7.4, and
7.5) by considering the following issues [13–16]:

1. Awake intubation after anesthetizing airway
vs intubation under anesthesia (RSI (rapid
sequence intubation)) or drug-assisted intubation (DAI) is used for medications to put
endotracheal tube (ETT) and to prevent
aspiration.
2. Orotracheal vs nasotracheal route: Orotracheal
intubation is choice in any trauma or faciomaxillary trauma patient.
3. Direct laryngoscopy/video laryngoscopy
(TRUVIEW™/GlideScope/McGRATH™,
etc.) vs fiberoptic-guided bronchoscopy
(Ambu A-Scope).
4. Front of neck access (FONA) either by emergency cricothyroidotomy or surgical airway
(tracheostomy) if required.
Awake intubation with topical airway anesthesia (Fig. 7.6a–c) is preferred in difficult airway
where difficult mask ventilation is anticipated
[17]. It preserves the spontaneous breathing of
the patient, thereby minimizing the risk of losing
the airway patency. It requires patient cooperation
and is not possible in uncooperative adults and
younger children who are unable to follow instructions. Nasotracheal intubation is required in cases
where mouth opening is not adequate and in maxillomandibular fixation (MMF) where orotracheal
intubation is avoided as tube comes into surgical
field. Nasotracheal route should be avoided in the
midface and base of skull fractures [18].
In cases where both oral and nasal routes are
not suitable for intubation, submental intubation and tracheostomy can be done to secure the
airway. It is prudent to have the difficult airway
cart ready even for elective maxillofacial surgeries. The cart must contain various equipments
for airway management in the form of different
types of laryngoscope blades (Fig. 7.7) and bougies (soft tip and stiff tip), various airways (OPA/
NPA use as shown in Fig. 7.8a and b to facilitate
bag-mask ventilation, methods to correct use of
BMV mask) (Fig. 7.9a, b), supraglottic airway
devices (SAD) like i-gel and LMAs (laryngeal

7.6.1.1 Types of Endotracheal Tube
In addition to standard endotracheal tube
(Fig. 7.13a), several modified endotracheal tubes
are used in maxillofacial surgeries. Ring-AdairElwyn (RAE) tubes are commonly used. They
have a preformed bent at the machine end which
can be cephalad (north) (Fig. 7.13b) or caudad
(south) facing (Fig. 7.13c). The preformed bend
in these tubes ensures that they are out of the
surgical field. For MMF surgeries, north-facing
nasal RAE tubes are used, while for zygomatic or
orbital fractures, south-facing RAE tube can be
used. Flexometallic or armored tubes (Fig. 7.13d)
may also be used, and they can be bent in any
direction without causing kinking [24].

laryngoscopy, it may lead to higher first-attempt
intubation success with lesser trauma and bleeding complications [26, 27].

7.6.3

Surgical Airway
(Cricothyroidotomy and
Tracheostomy)

Surgical airway is lifesaving and the last resort
in managing difficult airway cases in “cannot
intubate, cannot ventilate” (CICV) scenarios.
Cricothyroidotomy (Fig 7.17a) and tracheostomy are the available life saving techniques for
front of neck access, when patient can neither
be ventilated nor can be intubated after two or
more attempts [31]. Needle cricothyroidotomy
(Fig 7.17b) is a choice in pediatric patients less
than 14 years, and surgical or scalpel cricothyroidotomy (Fig. 7.17c) is a choice in adult
patients as per ATLS guidelines [1]. Surgical
cricothyroidotomy should always succeed as
ventilation is adequate that is often inadequate

through needle cricothyroidotomy and needed
transtracheal jet ventilation devices. It involves
incision on the cricothyroid membrane and passing 6.0 size endotracheal tube by railroading
over guidewire or GEB (Fig. 7.18a–e). This is
a safe and rapid technique as the membrane is
superficial, easily identifiable, and less vascular. Tracheostomy is not a preferable method in
emergency situations such as management of difficult airway in OT, as it’s a time-taking procedure and needs more expertise which is not often
available in emergency situation. Tracheostomy
is a choice in elective cases with difficult airway, where ENT surgeons first do it under local
anesthesia with spontaneous respiration and
then anesthesia is induced [32]. The recent DAS
giudelines recommend cricothyrotomy for emergency management and then conversion of such

Before attempting intubation, adequate preoxygenation should be done with bag and mask
ventilation. This implies giving 100% oxygen
to the patient for at least 3 min. It fills the functional residual capacity (FRC) of the lung with
oxygen prolonging the apnea time before the
patient desaturates providing the intubating personnel extra time for performing the intubation
­procedure. Bag and mask ventilation should preferably be performed by “two-person technique”
in which one person holds the mask with two
hands and the other person compresses as bag
mask ventilation may be difficult in these patients
due to distorted anatomy and presence of edema
in the upper airway [38].
After securing the airway, the tube and connections should be firmly secured as it is near the

operative field and will be covered under drapes.
Maintenance of anesthesia is achieved by muscle
relaxants and inhalational anesthetic agents in
oxygen, air, or nitrous oxide mixtures. One should
be vigilant about airway pressures and capnography as accidental dislodgement of tube and tube
compression can happen by surgical instruments.
Bradycardia can occur due to vagal stimulation
on manipulation of midface fracture which is
treated by anticholinergics like atropine or glycopyrrolate. The head should be kept slightly above
the height of body to minimize bleeding by prevention of venous engorgement in the head and
neck veins. Positioning the patient before surgery
is a very important step to optimize blood loss in
addition to helping the surgeon do surgery [39].
Besides securing airway, the hemorrhagic shock
assessment and simultaneous management (stop
the bleed) is also very important for successful
management of maxillofacial trauma as a part of
severe or polytrauma patient. Shock assessment

and management (arrangement of blood product
for massive blood transfusion protocols (PRBC,

had been discussed in details in Chap. 8 [1, 40].

7.8

Anesthesia Drugs in Brief

1. Neuromuscular blockers: These agents cause
muscle paralysis which is important in facilitating intubation and surgery. Based on their
mechanism of action on cholinergic receptors
in muscle, they are of two types:
(a) Depolarizing muscle relaxant: They block
the impulse by continuously activating the
acetylcholine receptor. Succinylcholine
(avoided in hyperkalemia, head injury,
burn patients). The dose is 1–2 mg/kg.
(b) Non-depolarizing muscle relaxant: They
block the acetylcholine receptors. Atracu
rium, cisatracurium, and rocuronium are
agents used with rocuronium being also
utilized in RSI due to its rapid onset.
2. Reversal agents: They are used to reverse the
neuromuscular blockade. Reversal agents are
acetylcholinesterase inhibitors which increase
concentration of acetylcholine. Neostigmine
supplemented with anticholinergic agent (glycopyrrolate) which counteracts its muscarinic
side effects is used.
3. Analgesic agents:
4. Opioids: They are the most powerful analgesics and routinely used for intubation and surgeries. Morphine and fentanyl are most
commonly used opioids for surgeries.
­Morphine is a long-acting agent and can cause
postoperative respiratory depression. Thus,
fentanyl is more suitable for dental procedures
as it’s short acting. Its adverse effects are nausea, vomiting, pruritus, and respiratory depression. The dose of fentanyl is 1–2 mg/kg.
5. Nonsteroidal
anti-inflammatory
agents
(NSAIDs): They provide analgesia to reduce
dose of opioids. Diclofenac and ketorolac
through IV route are commonly used.

If regional anesthesia blocks have been used
to anesthetize the airway, care should be taken
to extubate the patient only after their effect
has waned off and after full recovery of airway
reflexes. This will prevent inadvertent aspiration
of oral secretions in the postoperative period.
Regional anesthesia and blocks like US-guided
trigeminal, infraorbital, maxillary, and mandibular nerve blocks can be used for maxillofacial
trauma cases instead of general anesthesia or in
combination, as these are safe and efficient for
postoperative pain management [41].

7.9

Extubation
and Postoperative
Management

The main concern after completion of surgery is
safe extubation. As these surgeries involve the
airway, these patients are at high risk of developing complications during and after extubation.
The decision and plan to extubate depends on preoperative airway condition, surgery performed,
duration of surgery, airway edema, active bleeding, level of consciousness, and ability to protect
the airway [42]. Extubation should be performed
according to difficult extubation guidelines and
should be performed either when the patient is
fully awake or over an airway exchange catheter
[43]. Throat packs must be removed before extubation as they can be a source of airway obstruction if retained. It should be the responsibility of
the person who inserted the throat pack to remove
it, and all the OT personnel should be vigilant
about it. Those patients who cannot be extubated
should be shifted to postanesthesia recovery
area or ICU, and those who require prolonged
mechanical ventilation should get a tracheostomy
done. In patients in whom MMF is done, wire
cutters should be available at the bedside at all
times for emergency airway intervention.
These patients are prone to develop airway
edema in the postoperative period during the first
48 h. A single shot of dexamethasone (4–8 mg)
is helpful in preventing this complication [44].
Anesthesia should be maintained by short-­ They should be carefully monitored for signs
acting agents so that rapid awakening and return of any airway compromise. Hematoma formaof airway reflexes occur postoperatively.
tion may happen in early postoperative period,

7

Perioperative and Anesthetic Considerations in Maxillofacial Trauma

though it is uncommon. It warrants emergency
decompression to prevent airway obstruction
[45]. Postoperative nausea and vomiting can
frequently be observed in these patients due to
swallowed blood, oral secretions, and opioids.
Various antiemetics can be used like 5-HT3
antagonists, s­teroids, and prokinetics. Pain can
be severe in postoperative period and requires
multimodal analgesia consisting of paracetamol,
NSAIDs, and opioids and nerve and field blocks.
Short-­acting opioids like fentanyl should be used
for risk of airway obstruction. Patient-controlled
analgesia is a feasible option where patient
demands analgesic according to their demand
and risk of overdose is minimized [46].

7.10

Conclusion

Anesthetic management of oral and maxillofacial
trauma cases is challenging; it needs effective
team management with surgeon during prehospital transfer, resuscitation, and stabilization and
subsequent multiple damage control surgeries
and transfers as per ATLS guidelines. Securing
distorted airway is of prime importance to save
life from hypoxia and aspiration whether it is
isolated maxillofacial trauma or part of severe
polytrauma. No single method of airway management is best suitable; it all depends on the
type of trauma, anesthesiologist’s skill, and
availability of equipment and technology. For an
awake patient with an anesthetized airway, direct
or fiberoptic bronchoscopy is a choice. Surgical
or FONA should be sought early as per the discussed guidelines. General or regional anesthesia
or combination of both may be needed depending on the type or extent of facial trauma. Better
preoperative preparations including hemorrhage
control and blood product arrangements, intraoperative event management and monitoring, and
comprehensive postoperative care and rehabilitation can save most lives after trauma. But still as
per the World Health Organization (WHO), prevention is always better by following all safety
rules for zero road accidents or trauma.

8.1

Introduction

Among the myriad injuries seen in the emergency
department, maxillofacial trauma is one of the
most common entities that mandate special attention. Due to their close proximity and frequent
involvement, the vital structures in the head and
neck region must be evaluated thoroughly whenever the head and face are injured. Additionally,
the psychological impact of disfigurement associated with maxillofacial trauma can be devastating. Given the broad variety of facial injuries and

potential concomitant complications, management can be challenging even for the most experienced clinicians.
The incidence, epidemiological causes, and
pattern of maxillofacial trauma vary widely in
different regions of the world due to social,
economic, and cultural consequences, awareness of traffic regulations, and alcohol consumption. Various causes of facial fractures
mostly include those occurring by motor vehicle accidents, pedestrian collisions, and stumbling, sports, and industrial accidents, but the
leading cause shifts to road traffic accidents in
underdeveloped or developing areas of the
world followed by assaults and other reasons
including warfare.
Goals in the treatment of maxillofacial trauma
include a return of normal ocular, masticatory,
and nasal function, restoration of speech, rapid
bone healing, and an acceptable facial and dental
esthetic result. However, complex maxillofacial
fractures associated with head and/or spinal injuries, thoracic/abdominal injuries, or additional
other fractures in the body can result in significant morbidity or mortality.
Diagnosis and management of maxillofacial
trauma are a challenge particularly in the setting
of coexisting polytrauma in emergency department. The initial management of a trauma victim
is always focused on preserving the life first followed by preservation of function and esthetics
subsequently [1–3].

History

Following a tragedy that occurred in February
1976 in Nebraska cornfield, emergency management of trauma came into being. An orthopedic
surgeon, his three children, and his wife suffered
the plane crash in which his wife was killed
instantly and the rest were managed poorly even
after sustaining serious injuries. Following this, a
group of private practice surgeons and doctors in
Nebraska, the Lincoln Medical Education
Foundation, and the Lincoln Area Mobile Heart
Team Nurses, with the help of the University of
Nebraska Medical Center, the Nebraska State
Committee on Trauma (COT) of the American
College of Surgeons (ACS), and the Southeast
Nebraska Emergency Medical Services, collectively made an educational format for emergency
management of trauma currently known as ATLS
[4, 5].

8.3

Epidemiology

According to the latest information from the
WHO, more than nine people die every minute
from injuries or violence, and 5.8 million people
of all ages and economic group die every year
from unintentional injuries and violence. The

burden of injury is even more significant,
accounting for 12% of the world’s burden of
disease.
Road traffic accidents (RTA) alone cause more
than one million deaths annually and an estimated 20 million to 50 million significant injuries; they are leading causes of death due to injury
worldwide (Fig. 8.1). Improvements in injury
control efforts are having an impact in most
developed countries, where trauma remains the
leading cause of death in persons 1 through
44 years of age. Significantly, more than 90% of
motor vehicle crashes occur in the developing
world. Injury-related deaths are expected to rise
dramatically by 2020, with deaths due to motor
vehicle crashes projected to increase by 80%
from current rates in low- and middle-income
countries [4, 6].

8.3.1

 rimodal Death Distribution
T

First described in 1982, the trimodal distribution
of death implies that death due to injury occurs in
one of three periods or peaks (Fig. 8.2).
The first peak occurs within seconds to minutes of injury. Deaths during this period result
from apnea due to severe brain or high spinal

healthcare provider can have a positive impact on
morbidity and mortality to reduce the second

Pre-Hospital Management

A well-coordinated pre-hospital team can greatly
expedite treatment in the field. There has been a
great fall in mortality rates due to shift from a
primitive bystander trauma care to advance pre-­
hospital trauma care (Fig. 8.3a, b). Emphasis
should be placed on airway maintenance, control
of external bleeding and shock, immobilization
of the patient, and immediate support to the closest appropriate facility. Also, obtaining and
reporting information regarding time of injury,
events related to the injury, and patient history
constitutes an important aspect of this initial
phase. The mechanism of injury can suggest the
degree of injury as well as specific injuries for
which the patient must be evaluated.
All this information must be shared with
receiving hospital before personnel transports the
patient from the scene. This is beneficial as it
allows for mobilization of necessary personnel
and resources to the emergency department at the
time of patient’s arrival.
As soon as the patient reaches the hospital, a
resuscitation area should be available with all
team members wearing standard precaution
devices. Properly functioning airway equipment
(e.g., laryngoscopes and tubes) should be organized, tested, and strategically placed in the order
of their requirement. Availability of warmed
intravenous crystalloid solutions and appropriate
monitoring devices should be ensured (Fig. 8.4).

8.5

Triage

Triage involves the sorting of patients based on their
needs of treatment and the resources available to
provide that treatment [4]. It also includes the sorting of patients in the field so that a decision can be
made regarding the appropriate receiving medical
facility. One of the most common methods is to use
color tags for each triage category (Fig. 8.5):
1. Red (immediate)—life-threatening injuries
that require immediate intervention.
2. Yellow (delayed)—injury that may become
life−/limb-threatening if care is delayed
beyond several hours.
3. Green (minimal)—walking patients with
minor injuries.
4. Blue (expectant)—injury greater than life or
resources.
5. Black/gray—dead.
Triage is a continuous process and should be
repeated at each level and site: at scene, at outside the hospital, and at preoperative area.

Multiple and Mass Casualties

In multiple-casualty incidents, although there is
more than one patient, the number of patients and
the severity of their injuries do not exceed the
capability of the facility to render care. In such
situations, patients with life-threatening problems and those sustaining multiple system injuries are treated first [4].
In mass-casualty incidents, the number and
severity of their injuries exceed the capability of
the facility and staff. In such situations, the patients
having the greatest chance of survival and requiring the least expenditure of time, equipment, supplies, and personnel are treated first [4].

8.7

Rapid Assessment
of Severity of Injury

The sole aim of triage is to quickly and accurately
identify and sort the patients with serious lifethreatening injuries and to treat these patients
accordingly. Over a period of the past few decades,
various scoring systems have been developed to
assess the severity of injuries in trauma patients
and to predict the outcome as well.
(a) AVPU scale—It is the simplest and the quickest method of categorizing the severity of
injury.
A—awake.
V—response to verbal stimuli.

(b) Glasgow Coma Scale—This scale is very

Scale (GCS) was the first system to quantify

8.8

Primary Survey
and Resuscitation

Every trauma patient must be assessed quickly to
establish his/her treatment priorities based on his/
her injuries and vital signs. The management
consists of a rapid primary survey, resuscitation
of vital functions, a more detailed secondary survey, and finally initiation of definitive care.
The basic components of primary survey must
be assessed strictly in the following sequence:
• Airway maintenance with restriction of cervical spine motion.
• Breathing and ventilation.

130

M. Mishra et al.

• Circulation with hemorrhage control.
• Disability: neurologic status assessment.
• Exposure/environmental control.
Point to remember: In a trauma patient, A, B,
C, and D can be easily and quickly assessed,
within 10 s, by asking the patient his or her name
and asking what happened. An appropriate
answer reflects no major airway compromise (as
the patient can speak clearly), breathing is not
severely compromised (patient can generate air
movement to permit speech), and there is no
major decrease in the level of consciousness.

This is very critical especially in maxillofacial
trauma patients since a verbally communicating
patient ascertains no immediate jeopardy to the
airway. Patency of the airway should be ascertained by assessing the signs of airway obstruction like panic, agitation, cyanosis, hoarseness of
voice, wheezing, gasping, etc. The causes of
upper airway obstruction may be improper
tongue position, aspiration of blood clot, foreign
body or gastric contents, or maxillofacial/tracheal/laryngeal fractures.
Immediate suctioning of oral cavity and oropharynx should be done along with manually
cleaning the clot or any fractured loose bone
fragment/tooth or pieces of artificial denture. The
attending doctor must look for any remaining foreign bodies and assess for maxillofacial or tracheal/laryngeal fractures.
Point to remember: Agitation or aggression
shown by trauma patient may be a sign of hypoxia
and should not always be presumed as
intoxication.
Temporary interventions to establish patency
of airway include chin lift or jaw thrust maneuver while protecting the cervical spine, and if
the patient is unconscious and has no gag reflex,
the establishment of an oropharyngeal airway
can be helpful (Figs. 8.6 and 8.7), whereas
patients with severe head injuries who have an

altered level of consciousness or a Glasgow
Coma Scale (GCS) score of 8 or less and patients
with severe maxillofacial fractures, neck hematoma, and laryngeal and tracheal injuries usually require the placement of a definitive airway
(i.e., cuffed, secured tube in the trachea—orotracheal/nasotracheal intubation or cricothyroidotomy or tracheostomy).
Failure to secure orotracheal or nasotracheal
intubation necessitates a surgical airway, and
the fastest and safest method of securing a surgical airway is surgical cricothyroidotomy
(Fig. 8.8a–d). One may perform needle cricothyroidotomy to buy some time to arrange for a
definitive airway (Fig. 8.9). Needle cricothyroidotomy can provide temporary, adequate
supplemental oxygen for approximately
30–45 min. Tracheostomy is not recommended
as an emergency definitive surgical airway
option as it is relatively more time-consuming
and technically difficult.

B: Breathing and Ventilation

Not only a patent airway but each component
including adequate functioning of lungs, chest
wall, and diaphragm must be rapidly examined
and evaluated so as to ensure adequate
ventilation.
Immediate life-threatening injuries that
severely impair ventilation and require immediate attention during primary survey include tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, open
pneumothorax, and injuries to tracheobronchial
tree that require immediate thoracostomy.
Potentially life-threatening injuries include
simple pneumothorax, simple hemothorax, fractured ribs, flail chest, and pulmonary contusion.
Point to remember: In some instances, a simple pneumothorax can be converted to a tension
pneumothorax if the patient is intubated and
positive-­pressure ventilation is provided before
decompression of pneumothorax with a chest
tube and hence lies the importance of a sequential primary survey in terms of inspection, palpation, auscultation, and percussion.
The patient’s neck and chest should be
exposed to adequately assess jugular venous distention, position of the trachea, and chest wall
excursion. Auscultation should be performed to
ensure gas flow in both lungs. Visual inspection
and palpation can detect injuries to the chest wall
that may compromise ventilation, and percussion
of the thorax can be helpful in this scenario to
come to an accurate diagnosis.
Every injured patient should receive high-flow
supplemental oxygen at a rate of 6–8 l/min. Pulse
oximeter should be used to monitor the adequacy
of oxygen-hemoglobin saturation.
Point to remember: Pulse oximeter is an
adjunct to primary survey here.

(Fig. 8.11). This air pressure shifts the mediastinum to the opposite side, compressing the opposite lung and decreasing the venous return. The
shock thus developed is categorized under
obstructive shock. Positive-pressure ventilation
in a patient with visceral pleural injury (simple
pneumothorax) and a traumatic chest wall defect
when incorrectly covered with occlusive dressing
(constitutes a flap valve mechanism) may result
in tension pneumothorax.
Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis,
and clinician should not wait for radiographic
confirmation [4]. Classical signs and symptoms
are respiratory distress, tracheal deviation to the
opposite side, engorged neck veins, elevated
affected hemithorax without respiratory
movement, absence of breath sound on the
­
affected side, and hyperresonant note on
percussion.
A tension pneumothorax compromises the
ventilation and circulation dramatically and
acutely; chest decompression should be done
immediately when suspected by needle decompression in the fourth or fifth intercostal space
anterior to mid-axillary line, performed as a temporary measure while preparing for a tube thora-

costomy, i.e., placement of a chest drain (tube
thoracostomy) in the fourth or fifth intercostal
space anterior to mid-axillary line.
Open pneumothorax (sucking chest wound)—
A large traumatic defect in chest wall (approximately equal or greater than two third the
diameter of trachea) that allows air to pass preferentially through the chest wall defect with each
respiration (Fig. 8.12).
Initial management is done by prompt closure
of the defect with a sterile occlusive dressing
large enough to cover the defect edges, secured
with tapes on three sides to provide flutter-type
valve (Fig. 8.13). This type of valve closes during
inspiration and opens during expiration that
allows air to escape from pleural space. Securing
tape on all four sides would result in a tension
pneumothorax unless a chest tube is in place.
Flail chest and pulmonary contusion—This
condition results when two or more adjacent ribs
are fractured at two or more places. Children
have a more compliant rib cage and may suffer
pulmonary contusion without any overlying rib
fracture.
Classical paradoxical movement of chest wall
is seen during inspiration and expiration (flail
segment goes down during inspiration and goes
up during expiration, whereas the rest of the chest
wall moves in an opposite direction) (Fig. 8.14).
Pain, hypoxia, crepitations, and restricted chest
wall movement are other important features. If
the injury to the underlying lung is significant,
serious hypoxia may result.

secured and breathing has been established. The
cardiovascular system must be assessed, and control of baseline circulation to tissue must be
restored. The factors to be considered under this
are blood volume, cardiac output, and bleeding.

Hemorrhage is a predominant cause of preventable deaths after injury [4, 12]. Identifying and
stopping hemorrhage are therefore crucial steps
in the assessment and management of such
patients. Once tension pneumothorax has been
eliminated as a cause of shock, hypotension following injury must be considered to be hypovolemic in origin until proven otherwise [4, 13].
Thus, rapid and accurate assessment of an injured
patient’s hemodynamic status is essential, and
the elements for this assessment include level of
consciousness, skin color, and pulse.

8.11.2 Bleeding

Fig. 8.14 Flail chest—classical paradoxical chest wall
movement is seen during inspiration and expiration

The definitive management is to ensure adequate oxygenation, administer fluids, and provide
analgesia to improve ventilation.
Analgesia can be provided with intravenous
opioids or local anesthetic administration (intercostal nerve block, intrapleural/extrapleural, or
epidural anesthesia).

C: Circulation
with Hemorrhage Control

This is the third step in the emergency management of a trauma patient, and evaluation at this
step should start only when an adequate airway is

Bleeding can be categorized as external or internal. Identification and appropriate management
of hemorrhagic shock is done as the third step in
initial assessment and management (Table 8.2).
External hemorrhage is identified and controlled during the primary survey. Rapid, external
blood loss is managed by direct manual pressure
on the wound. One of the ways that has been
proven effective is the use of tourniquets for
extremities, but they carry a risk of ischemic
injury to that extremity and should only be used
when direct pressure is not effective, keeping in
mind that tourniquet deflation is necessary after
every 30–45 min and should never be put more
than 2 h straight [4, 12].
The major areas of internal hemorrhage are
the chest, abdomen, retroperitoneum, pelvis, and
long bones. Fractured tibia or humerus can be
associated with loss of approximately 750 ml
(1.5 units) of blood. About 1500 ml blood loss is
commonly associated with femur fracture,
whereas several liters of blood can accumulate in

8.11.3 Important Life-Threatening
Chest Injuries Affecting
Circulation
Massive hemothorax—This condition results
when there is a rapid accumulation of more than
1500 ml of blood or one third or more of total
blood volume in chest cavity (Fig. 8.15). It usually results from penetrating chest wound (medial
to the right and left nipple lines or between the
scapula) that damages the systemic or hilar
vessels.
Massive hemothorax is suspected when shock
is associated with absence of breath sound and
dullness note on percussion of affected thorax.
Neck veins are usually flat due to hypovolemia,
or they may be engorged if there is an associated
tension pneumothorax.
It is initially managed by fluid replacement
(rapid crystalloid infusion, and switch over to
type-specific blood transfusion as soon as possible) and decompression of the chest cavity.
Thoracotomy is indicated if 1500 ml blood is
immediately evacuated through chest tube, if
there is continuous bleeding noted through chest
tube (200 ml/h for 2–4 h) without any improvement, and if there is a persistent need for blood
transfusion.
Maneuvers that can be performed with a
resuscitative thoracotomy are evacuation of

136

Fig. 8.15 Massive hemothorax

blood in pericardial space causing cardiac tamponade, direct control of intrathoracic hemorrhage, open cardiac massage, and clamping the
descending aorta that would increase the perfusion to the heart and brain.
Cardiac tamponade—Cardiac tamponade
mostly results from penetrating injuries.
However, blunt injury can also cause bleeding in
pericardial sac. Even a small amount of blood in
pericardial sac can restrict the cardiac activity
and decreases the cardiac filling.
The diagnosis of cardiac tamponade is based
on classic Beck’s triad: increased venous pressure, decreased arterial pressure, and muffled
heart sound. Kussmaul’s sign (elevated venous
pressure with inspiration when breathing spontaneously) is another abnormality associated with
tamponade.
Pulseless electrical activity (PEA) on ECG
and elevated central venous pressure (CVP) may
be suggestive of cardiac tamponade. FAST
(focused assessment with sonography for trauma)
is a rapid and accurate method of imaging the
heart and pericardium with a 90–95% accuracy
for the presence of pericardial fluid.
In case of cardiac tamponade, a spinal needle
can be used for decompression (pericardiocentesis) as a temporizing maneuver, but it is best
managed by thoracotomy. Pericardiocentesis
may not be diagnostic or therapeutic when blood
in the pericardial sac has clotted.
Point to remember: ECG and urinary and gastric catheters are adjuncts to primary survey
here.

M. Mishra et al.

Patient monitoring and evaluation of fluid
resuscitation and end-organ perfusion are mandatory in a trauma patient. Urine output is a reasonably sensitive indicator of renal perfusion, and
placement of urinary catheter is essential in all
significant trauma patients. Transurethral bladder
catheterization is contraindicated in patients with
suspected urethral injury (blood at urethral
meatus, perineal ecchymosis, high-riding or nonpalpable prostate). Ideally, urinary catheter
should not be placed before rectal and genitalia
examination. Suprapubic catheterization is performed if transurethral bladder catheterization is
contraindicated.
Adequate resuscitation volume replacement
should produce a urinary output of approximately
0.5 ml/kg/h in adults, 1 ml/kg/h in children, and
2 ml/kg/h in infants.
A gastric catheter is mainly indicated to relieve
the gastric distension, and to decrease the risk of
spiration. Additionally, a healthcare provider can
also assess for upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage
in a truma patient. However, in severe maxillofacial injuries, the gastric tube is inserted orally to
prevent its intracranial passage.

8.12

 : Disability: Neurologic
D
Status

To establish the patient’s level of consciousness,
pupillary size and reaction, lateralizing signs, and
spinal cord injury level, neurologic evaluation is
necessary in the primary survey. The best tool for
this evaluation is GCS.
A decreased level of consciousness may indicate decreased cerebral perfusion/oxygenation or
may be caused by direct cerebral injury. An
altered level of consciousness indicates the need
for immediate reevaluation of the patient’s oxygenation, ventilation, and perfusion status.
Hypoglycemia, alcohol, or narcotics or other
drugs also alter patient’s consciousness level, and
these reasons must be ruled out.
Primary brain injury results from structural
damage to the brain due to trauma. Prevention of
secondary brain injury by maintaining adequate
oxygenation and perfusion is the main goal of
initial management.

8.12.1 Important Brain Injuries
Affecting Neurologic Status
Epidural hematoma—It is a relatively uncommon form of traumatic brain injury (TBI) which
accounts for 9% of patients with TBI. This usually results from tear in middle meningeal artery,
and other minor causes are disruption in major
venous sinuses or bleeding from a skull fracture.
The epidural hematoma is most often located in
temporal or temporoparietal region.
This hematoma typically appears as biconvex
or lenticular in shape on CT scan as it pushes the
dura away from the inner table of the skull
(Fig. 8.16). A lucid interval between the time of
injury and neurologic deterioration is the classic
presentation of an epidural hematoma.
Subdural hematoma—They are relatively
more common than epidural hematoma and
account for approximately 30% of patients with
TBI. They often develop from shearing of small
surface/bridging vessels. On CT scan, they
appear to conform the contours of the brain
(Fig. 8.17). The brain damage is more severe than
that associated with epidural hematoma.

Fig. 8.16 Epidural hematoma—biconvex or lenticular in
shape on CT scan

Fig. 8.17 Subdural hematoma—conform the contours of
the brain on CT scan

Contusion/intracerebral
hematoma—
Cerebral contusions are fairly common (25–30%
of total TBI). The majority of contusions occur in
frontal and temporal regions. Over a period of
hours or days, contusions may evolve to form an
intracerebral hematoma or a coalescent contusion
with enough mass effect that requires immediate
surgical evacuation (Fig. 8.18). For this reason,
patients with contusion generally undergo repeat
CT scan within 24 h of initial scan.
Diffuse brain injuries—These injuries range
from mild concussion to severe hypoxic-­ischemic
injuries. With a concussion, patient has a transient, nonfocal neurological disturbance that
often presents as loss of consciousness. Severe
diffuse injury results from prolonged hypoxic/
ischemic insult to the brain due to shock or apnea
occurring immediately after trauma.
In such cases, CT scan initially appears normal, or brain may appear diffusely swollen with
loss of normal gray-white distinction.
Another diffuse pattern referred to as diffuse
axonal injury results from high-velocity impact or
deceleration injuries (shearing injuries). There are
multiple punctate hemorrhages throughout the

8.13.2 Need for Patient Transfer
The transfer process may be initiated immediately by administrative personnel at the direction
of the examining doctor while additional evaluation and resuscitative measures are being performed. Once the decision to transfer the patient
has been made, communication between the
referring and receiving doctors is essential.
Therefore the transferring doctor is required to
share information such as event/mechanism of
injury, suspected/diagnosed injuries, treatment
provided, and current status of the patient.

injuries have a variable but often poor outcome.

8.13

E: Exposure/Environmental
Control

The patient should be completely undressed, to
facilitate a thorough examination and assessment. Following this, the patient should be covered with warm blankets or an external warming
device to prevent hypothermia in the trauma
receiving area. Intravenous fluids should be
warmed before being infused, and a warm environment should be maintained.

8.13.1 Adjuncts to Primary Survey
and Resuscitation
• Electrocardiographic monitoring.
• Urinary and gastric catheters.
• Ventilatory rate and arterial blood gas (ABG)
level monitors.
• Pulse oximetry.
• Blood pressure.

8.13.3 Secondary Survey
The secondary survey does not begin until the
primary survey is completed, the resuscitative
efforts are underway, and the normalization of
vital functions has been demonstrated. When
additional personnel are available, part of the secondary survey may be conducted, while the other
personnel attend to the primary survey.
The secondary survey is a head-to-toe evaluation of the trauma patient, that is, a complete history and physical examination, including
reassessment of all vital signs. Each region of the
body is completely examined.
During this survey, a complete neurologic examination is performed, including a repeat GCS score
determination. X-rays are also obtained, as indicated
by the examination. Such examinations can be interspersed into the secondary survey at appropriate
times. Special procedures, such as specific radiographic evaluations and laboratory studies, also are
performed at this time. Complete patient evaluation
requires repeated physical examinations.

8.13.5 Physical Examination
Head Visual acuity, pupillary size and response
to light, hemorrhage of the conjunctiva and/or
fundi, penetrating injury, contact lenses (remove
before edema occurs), dislocation of the lens, and
ocular entrapment.
Maxillofacial Structures Examination of the
face should include palpation of all bony structures, assessment of occlusion, intraoral examination, and assessment of soft tissues.
Maxillofacial trauma that is not associated with
airway obstruction or major bleeding should be
treated only after the patient is stabilized completely and life-threatening injuries have been
managed. Midface fracture patients may also
have suffered from fracture of cribriform plate,
and this necessitates gastric intubation via oral
route. Special attention must be paid toward
sight-threatening injuries (injuries affecting the
eyeball and surrounding regions) of the face.
Cervical Spine and Neck Patients with maxillofacial or head trauma should be presumed to
have an unstable cervical spine injury (fracture/
ligament injury), and the neck should be immobilized until all aspects of the cervical spine have
been adequately studied and an injury has been
excluded. The absence of neurologic deficit does
not exclude injury to the cervical spine. Various
radiological tools required for such injuries
include CT scans, angiography, and duplex ultrasonography (for major cervical vascular injury).
Chest Inspection of the anterior and posterior
chest along with palpation of the entire chest
cage, including the clavicles, ribs, and sternum,
should be carried out which can help us reveal

139

pain, dyspnea, and hypoxia. Along with this, auscultation of the chest high on the anterior chest
wall for pneumothorax and at the posterior bases
for hemothorax and a chest X-ray, so as to confirm the presence of hemothorax, simple thorax,
rib fractures, or aortic rupture, are required.
Abdomen Close observation and frequent
reevaluation along with palpation (pelvic fractures will elicit pain) should be done. Patients
with unexplained hypotension, neurologic injury,
impaired sensorium secondary to alcohol and/or
other drugs, and equivocal abdominal findings
should be considered candidates for peritoneal
lavage, FAST, or, if hemodynamic findings are
normal, CT of the abdomen.
Perineum, Rectum, and Vagina The perineum
should be examined for contusions, hematoma,
lacerations, and urethral bleeding. The rectum
should be assessed for the presence of blood
within the bowel lumen, a high-riding prostate,
the presence of pelvic fractures, the integrity of
rectal wall, and the quality of sphincter bone,
before placing a catheter. Vaginal examination
should be performed in patients who are at risk of
vaginal injury, including all women with a pelvic
fracture, and assessment of blood in the vaginal
vault and vaginal lacerations should be done.
Musculoskeletal System Inspection can help
rule out contusions and deformities, and palpation of tenderness in bones with abnormal movement can aid in identification of occult fractures.
Ecchymosis over the iliac wings, pubis, labia, or
scrotum can be seen in cases of pelvic fractures.
Because the manipulation can initiate unwanted
bleeding, it should be done only once and preferably by the orthopedic surgeon. Assessment of
peripheral pulses can identify vascular injury.
Significant extremity injury can exist without
fracture being evident on X-ray. Impaired sensation and/or loss of voluntary muscle contraction
strength can be caused by nerve injury or ischemia (compartment syndrome).
Musculoskeletal examination is not complete
without examination of patient’s back.

140

Neurologic System Along with the motor and
sensory evaluation of the extremities, reevaluation of the patient’s level of consciousness and
pupillary size and response should be done. Early
consultation with the neurosurgeon if necessary
should be carried out.

8.13.6 Adjuncts to the Secondary
Survey
So as to ensure the detection of all possible injuries, specific diagnostic aids can be used which
include X-ray examinations of the spine and
extremities; CT scans of the head, chest, abdomen, and spine; contrast urography and angiography; transesophageal ultrasound; bronchoscopy;
esophagoscopy; etc.

8.13.7 Importance of Team Work
A team that works well understands the strength
and weaknesses of the situation and acts accordingly to give out maximum benefits. As soon as
the patient arrives, the team leader supervises the
handover by EMS personnel, making certain that
no team member begins working on the patient
unless immediate life-threatening conditions are
obvious (“hands-off hand over”). This can be easily executed using the MIST acronym [2]:
•
•
•
•

Mechanism (and time) of injury.
Injuries found and suspected.
Symptoms and signs.
Treatment initiated.

An important aspect involved in efficient team
work is verbalizing each action and each finding
out loud without more than one member speaking at the same time.

8.13.8 Records and Legal
Consideration
This includes:
Records: Meticulous record keeping during
patient assessment and management, including

M. Mishra et al.

documenting the time for all events, is of utmost
importance since medicolegal problems arise frequently, and precise record keeping can prove to be
extremely helpful for all individuals concerned.
Consent for treatment: Consent is sought
before treatment, if possible. In life-threatening
emergencies, it is often not possible to obtain
such consent. In such cases, treatment should be
provided first with formal consent obtained later.
Forensic evidence: If a criminal activity is suspected in conjunction with patient’s injury, all
items such as clothing, bullets, etc. must be saved
by the personnel caring for the patient for the law
enforcement.

8.14

Conclusion

The correct sequence of management of patients
based on priority assessment starts with preparation in the pre-hospital phase. In a polytrauma
patient, this is followed by triage and primary survey and resuscitation in which a sequential
approach is taken to save the life of the patient by
first addressing the injury that will kill first. During
the primary survey, adjuncts provide a way to a better assessment and handling of patients. One should
consider for the need to transfer the patient while
continuously repeating primary survey and then
switching over to a detailed head-to-toe evaluation,
hereby known as secondary survey. To assist the
secondary survey, adjuncts can be utilized, and
finally a definitive care should be provided to the
patient once he/she is stabilized from danger to life.
It cannot be stressed enough that team work is one
of the most important keys to a successful management of a trauma patient in an emergency setting.

8.16.1 Airway and Breathing
• Look, listen, and feel to assess airway: Airway
is noisy, oral airway is inserted, and respirations are rapid and shallow. Pulse oximeter
and ECG can be placed at this time.
• Clean the airway: Chin lift/jaw thrust maneuver—Mandible is unstable; instability of airway (compromised airway).
• Bag-mask ventilation (100% supplemental
oxygen): All trauma patients must receive
100% supplemental oxygen.
• Removal of cervical collar: Tracheal deviation
to the right and distended neck veins.
• Secure an orotracheal tube as indicated by
compromised airway: Respiration improved
only slightly, and manual compression of bag
is difficult.
• Reposition the ET tube: SpO2 83%; respiratory efforts do not improve.
• Suspect left tension pneumothorax: Decreased
left hemithorax movement and subcutaneous
emphysema over the left chest wall, no breathing sound on auscultation, and hyperresonant
percussion note.
• Needle decompression followed by chest tube
placement (left-sided tube thoracostomy).
• Ventilatory parameters improved following left
thoracostomy: SpO2 = 93%, PaO2 = 78 mm
Hg (10.4 kPa), and PaCO2 = 44 mm Hg
(5.87 kPa).
• Chest X-ray: Multiple left rib fractures and a
chest tube in place with lung reexpanded.

Soft Tissue Injuries
Vibha Singh, Deepika Jain, and Shanthosh Kanna

9.1

Introduction

Soft tissue injury to the facial structures is commonly present in road traffic accident cases, and it
may be superficial or deep involving important
vital structures. It may be associated with facial
bone fractures, nerve injury, salivary glands and
their ducts and blood vessels. Nearly all the facial
trauma involves soft tissue injury. The general
injuries are greatly depending on the patient population, slips, trips and fall. Violence and motor
vehicle accidents are the predominant causes of
injury. Soft tissues include skin, mucosa, muscle,
tendon, nerve and ligament. Damage to any of
these structures can lead to pain, swelling and lack
of mobility of the specific area. In the absence of
craniofacial fracture, emergent airway stabilization is rarely indicated. Patient should always be
assessed for concomitant intracranial, craniofacial,
ophthalmological and cervical spine injuries. The
wound on the face should be handled carefully;
otherwise it can leave deformed scar in the most
beautiful part of the body.
It is often said that it is better to have an asymmetrical body than a symmetrical corpse. So the
first priority should be given to life-saving procedures in accordance with the ATLS (advanced
trauma life support) protocol such as establishV. Singh (*) · D. Jain · S. Kanna
Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery,
Faculty of Dental Sciences, King Georges Medical
University, Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh, India

ment and maintenance of patent airway, arrest of
haemorrhage, recognition of associated head
injury and shock and treatment of intraabdominal
or thoracic wounds. Facial injuries are important
and should be treated as soon as possible but after
life-saving procedures. When the general condition of the patient has stabilized, life is out of
danger, and then attention should be directed to
the soft tissue of the face.
The face is an aesthetically significant part of
the body which makes the management of facial
injuries more critical.

9.2

Aetiology

Automobile trauma, altercation, assault, animal
bite, human bite, burn, gunshot injury, infection,
sport accidents.

Closed Wound
(a) Contusion—It is more commonly called
bruise and indicates that some amount of tissue disruption has occurred within tissues
that resulted in subcutaneous or submucosal
haemorrhage without a break in soft tissue
surface. These are usually caused by blunt
object but are also frequently found with
concomitant dentoalveolar injuries or facial
bone fractures. The trauma to deeper tissue
has occurred from the disrupting effect of the
fractured bones. The diagnostic point of contusion is important because there are chances
of bone fracture. They generally do not
require surgical intervention. Once the
hydrostatic pressure within the soft tissue
equals the pressure within the blood vessels
(usually capillaries), bleeding ceases. If a
contusion is seen early, application of ice or
pressure dressing may help constrict blood
vessels and thereby decrease the amount of
haematoma that forms. If a contusion doesn’t
stop expanding, a haemorrhaging artery
within the wound is likely present.
(b) Haematoma—Haematoma is defined as a
collection of blood outside of a blood vessel.
The most common cause of haematoma is
injury or trauma to blood vessels. Even minimal damage to blood vessels can disrupt the
integrity of the blood vessel wall and can
result in a haematoma. Sometimes haematomas are named based on their location, like
sublingual haematoma and circumorbital
ecchymosis (Fig. 9.1). If uncontrolled, haematoma may require surgical exploration
and ligation of vessel.

(a) Abrasion—An abrasion is a wound caused
by friction between an object and the surface
of the soft tissue. This wound is usually

The lip, eyebrows, cheek and scalp are few of

(e) Amputation—It is the removal of extremity

(f) Gunshot/ballistic wound—Gunshot creates

can be of three types: penetrating, perforating and avulsive. The wound caused by carbon particles invades deeply below the

Such injuries vary greatly in character,
depending on the velocity, shape and striking
angle of the projectile. High-velocity bullets
usually cause small wound of entrance and
large ragged wound of exit when they strike
the bone or teeth which leads to fragmentation of these structures commonly producing
secondary missiles causing extensive internal trauma. Low-velocity projectiles often
become distorted on meeting resistance and
cause marked comminution and internal
destruction of the bone. Shrapnel and blasts
produce multiple penetrating wounds with
the projectile frequently becoming distorted

and scattered throughout the wound. Multiple
metallic bodies may retain in the soft tissue
which leads to gross contamination of all
these wounds. Fragments of clothes, dirt,
metal and other things when carried deep
into the wounds may result in infection
(Fig. 9.5).
(g) Burn—They are caused by contact of soft tissue of the face with flames, steam, acid, alkalies, electricity, sunlight, ultraviolet lights
and irritant gases. Burn injuries can be classified as first degree which causes erythema of
the skin, second degree which produces vesicle formation and third degree which causes
complete destruction of the dermis and epidermis extending into or beyond the subcutaneous tissues.
(h) Animal bite/human bite—It can be superficial or deep injury and is always contaminated. Management includes adequate
cleansing, conservative debridement and
proper observation and appropriate immunization (Fig. 9.6).
(i) Crush injury—It is an injury by an object
that causes compression of the body and
commonly occurs during natural disaster. It
may occur in road traffic accidents, building

For the repair of superficial wounds, the following guidelines should be followed:

Adequate Wound debridement & ensure clean tissue bed

Achieve proper haemostasis

Antibiotic & Tetanus prophylaxis

Skin margins must be relaxed without tension.
