150

The initial management of trauma patient
must include advanced trauma life support
(ATLS) protocol which includes establishment
of airway, control of haemorrhage, maintenance
of adequate circulation and evaluation of systemic injuries involving the major organ systems prior to evaluation of facial soft tissue
wound. Fractures of facial bones should be
excluded by careful clinical examination and
radiographs. Facial fractures should be reduced
and stabilized before final soft tissue repair.
During assessment period or management of
other injuries, wound should be kept moist with
sterile gauge.
If kept clean, simple wounds involving the
head (face and scalp) are unaffected by the interval between injury and repair.
When the trauma and wound are inflicted, at
least four major phenomena develop that may
threaten life unless measures are taken to control
and finally correct the condition. First the blood
is lost not only to the exterior but also in the damage tissues. Second the tissue is damaged with
derangement of the physiology of the tissues and
production of a suitable medium for bacterial
growth. Third the defence against bacteria is broken which allows the wound to become infected
by bacterial invasion of the tissues. Fourth
mechanical defect may develop. These defects
may be of major proportion like airway obstruction, haemothorax, pneumothorax, haemoperitoneum, cardiac tamponade and intracranial
haemorrhage leading to the raised intracranial
pressure. These four factors are not limited to the
area of origin alone but may provoke a response
in every system of the body. It is directly proportional to the severity of injury.
The nature has given an efficient and effective
healing response to these major phenomena. In
the initial phase following injury, immediate
vasoconstriction, retraction of vessels, haemostatic platelet plug formation and initiation of
coagulation cascade tend to arrest the haemorrhage. Damaged non-vital tissue becomes
necrotic and produces slough that tends to rid the
wound of damaged tissues. Wound contamination produces an antibody and leucocyte response
that combats the invasion of infectious organ-

V. Singh et al.

isms. Finally the tissue defect may be corrected
by proliferation of capillaries, fibroblasts and epithelium. These natural reparative procedures are
often sufficient to bring about healing of minor
wounds. In larger and complicated wounds, surgical procedures are required to assist healing
process. The surgeons’ aim is to aid to the body’s
healing response.
It is recommended that before final treatment
of the wound and after cleaning of the skin, photographic records should be obtained for legal
purposes and as well as for insurances too.
Follow-up photographs will aid in the assessment
of healing and scar maturation and for need of
scar revision.
Abrasion It is a superficial wound caused by
friction between the skin and rough surfaces like
road, ground, etc. They are painful because
removal of superficial epithelial surface leads to
the exposure of nerve endings present in the subcutaneous plane. Haemorrhage is not a problem
because it does not involve the major blood vessels; the involved capillaries retract and are
occluded by thrombi. Because the tissue damage
is superficial, it does not cause necrosis and
sloughing of the tissues. These wounds may get
infected, but local therapy is usually sufficient to
control infectious process. If the wound does not
extend below the level of rete pegs of the epithelium, healing without mechanical defect or scarring can be anticipated.
Soap does not harm skin surface as thick cornified layer of epidermis protects the underlying
tissue surface. But soap may enter in the wound
and causes cellular damage and necrosis. Toxic
material such as alcohol, hydrogen peroxide and
benzalkonium chloride and strong soap such as
hexachlorophene and povidone-iodine should not
have direct contact with open wound as these
materials kill cells on the contact. If these materials are around the wound, it should be thoroughly
cleaned by mechanical scrubbing and irrigation
with balanced salt solution. A rule regarding
application of antiseptic is to never put anything
in a wound that could not be comfortably tolerated in conjunctival sac.

9

Soft Tissue Injuries

Abrasions are often produced by traumatic
episode that causes dirt, glass particles and other
debris to enter into the tissue. It is very important
that these bodies be removed, particularly if they
are pigmented; otherwise, traumatic tattoo will
result that produces an unsightly defect. After the
mechanical cleaning, a wound resembling a second-degree burn is produced. It may left open but
frequently requires dressing. It should be covered
with good protective moist dressing like paraffin
gauze with impregnated antibiotic.
Contusion These are minor injuries that can be
treated conservatively. Haemorrhage is usually
self-limiting as the pressure of the extravasated
blood builds up within the tissues. The tissue is
usually viable, so necrosis and sloughing are
absent. Due to trauma by blunt object, the skin is
usually not broken, so contamination or infection
is rare. Because of the haemorrhage in deeper
structures, the contused area first turns into blue
and later yellow. In this type of wound, surgical
intervention is not required unless there is uncontrolled haemorrhage in the deeper tissues leading
to pressure phenomenon or evacuation of
haematoma.
Laceration It is the most common type of facial
injury that varies from superficial cut to a deep,
complex wound involvs the underlying structures. Whenever possible, these wounds should
be treated within few hours of injury. In a patient
who is severely injured, early closure of facial
laceration cannot be accomplished, even though
these wounds may get grossly contaminated. In
such conditions, primary closure within 24 h is
preferred. Debridement, irrigation with normal
saline and layered closure are steps in its
management.
Wound Debridement After proper local or
general anaesthesia, mechanical cleaning of the
wound is necessary. The skin around the wound
should be scrubbed, all areas should be
inspected, and foreign bodies should be
removed. After cleaning, debridement of
necrotic tissue should be done. The facial structures have a rich blood supply and possess good

151

resistance to infection which is seldom seen in
other regions. Necrotic and non-vital tissues
should be removed, and bleeding from a cut surface or contracture of a muscle when stimulated
is an evidence of viability. Rough, ragged, irregular margin should be excised to diminish the
ultimate amount of scar formation. It also
includes removal of bevelled wound margins for
perpendicular closure.
Haemostasis Control of haemorrhage in lacerated wound is essential; nature provides a degree
of haemostasis by vasoconstriction and thrombus
formation, but bleeding from larger surface must
be controlled. Either cauterization or ligation of
named vessels should be done. The cut end of
vessels should be grasped carefully avoiding
inclusion of excessive amount of subcutaneous
tissue so as to limit the amount of scar tissue formation. No primary closure is indicated until
complete haemostasis has been secured.
Closure of the Wound After debridement and
complete haemostasis, wound is ready for closure. The objective of closure is the accurate co-­
optation of the layers of tissue with the elimination
of dead space. Lacerations of the face that lie parallel to relaxed skin tension lines (RSTLs) may
be expected to heal with minimal skin closure. If
lacerations transect these lines at right angles,
immediate Z-plasty may be performed to prevent
scar contracture. Tissue handling should be gentle. If the wound involves mucosa, then it should
be approximated first to form water-tight closure
either by non-­resorbable or resorbable suture. If
at all possible, fracture of the facial bones should
be reduced before completing closure of soft tissue. If closure of soft tissue is done before fracture reduction, the manipulation of the bone will
cause disruption of the wound.
Deeper muscle and subcutaneous tissue layers
are closed by inverted buried interrupted sutures
with care being taken to eliminate all dead space;
resorbable suture material should be used for closure of deeper layers.
The final step is closure of subcutaneous tissues by the placement of subcuticular sutures

152

V. Singh et al.

just beneath the cutaneous surface, which should
accurately re-approximate the subcutaneous
plane and relieve all the tension at the skin margin. If any undue tension is encountered, undermining of the skin may be necessary prior to
placement of the subcuticular tissues.
Polyglycolic sutures are commonly used for
subcuticular region. Instead of subcuticular
sutures, interrupted sutures can also be used for
skin closure. Sutures should be placed at equal
distance and equal depth on either side of the
wound. They should be placed in such a manner
that slight eversion of the skin margin is
achieved. While suturing an extensive complicated laceration, it may be difficult to determine
the proper position of the tissues. In these cases,
it should start from a known point like the ala of
the nose, oral commissure and lateral canthal
regions.
Stellate Laceration If margins are bevelled or
ragged, they should be conservatively excised to
provide perpendicular skin edges to prevent scar
formation. Undermining of the tissue wound
margin will be helpful in suturing of the tissue
without excessive tension at the margins. But
extensive undermining leads to contracture of the
wound and scarring. Interrupted sutures should
be used to close the wound.
Flap-like Laceration It is a laceration with significant undermining of the soft tissue without
loss of tissues. Debris is commonly found in
deeper tissue planes under the flap. Pressure
dressing plays an important role in minimizing
dead space and limiting haematoma formation or
fluid collection within deep tissues. The use of a
drain may be helpful in achieving better cosmetic
results and proper healing.
Avulsion It is characterized by loss of segments of
soft tissue. This type of injury is relatively uncommon but commonly occurs due to gunshot wounds
or weapon injury or animal bite. Sometimes it
seems like soft tissue loss, but examination reveals
that soft tissue is retracted or rolled under the
wound margin. Small defects can be closed by
undermining soft tissue margin, but larger-sized
wounds can be closed by other options. These

Fig. 9.7 Clinical photograph showing degloving injury
of the right side face

include skin graft, local flaps, distant flaps or sometimes free flaps. Facial wounds should not be
allowed to heal by secondary intention because it
may lead to excessive scar formation.
Degloving injury is a type of avulsion in which
a large amount of the skin along with subcutaneous tissue is completely torn away from the
underlying tissue, leading to compromised vascularity (Fig. 9.7).

9.3.2

Animal and Human Bites

These are highly contaminated wounds and
have significant risk of infection. Animal bites
particularly from dog are more avulsive due to
pull-back response of the victim, whereas
human bites are usually on the lip, nose and ear.
Most of the wounds are irrigated with minimal
debridement, and primary closure is done, but
when the wound remains open for more than
24 h, the closure is controversial. Broadspectrum antibiotics along with tetanus and
rabies prophylaxis are necessary.

9

Soft Tissue Injuries

9.3.3

Delayed Primary Wound
Closure

Delayed primary closure is also indicated in
patients with extensive facial oedema or subcutaneous haematoma and when wound margins are
contused and tissues are devitalized. Primary closure in such damaged tissue is difficult. A programme of wound preparation should be instigated
and followed by a delayed primary closure when
conditions are suitable. Chips and associates have
outlined an excellent regimen for the preparation
of wound for secondary closure. It includes an initial examination and debridement at which time
all obvious devitalized and infected tissues are
removed. Associated fractures of facial bones
should be immobilized. Adequate drainage should
be maintained, and an effective antibiotic regimen
is employed to ­combat any infection that may be
present. Continuous moist dressing applied to the
injured tissues assists greatly in preparing the tissues for closure. The wound should be observed
daily, and when necrotic areas are discovered,
they should be removed by tissue forceps. Wound
involving oral cavity should be isolated, and oral
feeding is prohibited to eliminate contamination
and fermenting food debris from entering the
wound.
This regimen rapidly controls infection,
reduces oedema and indurations and renders the
wound amenable to delayed primary closure in
5–10 days.
Open wound treatment formerly universally
accepted for contaminated wound and bite injuries
is no longer practised for facial wounds except
abrasions. Wounds of the face and anterior cervical region should be mechanically debrided and
closed primarily. Open wound allowed to heal
with granulation tissues leaves a large unsightly
scar on the face. Delayed primary closure can be
done according to the status of wound.

9.3.4

Supportive Therapy

Successful treatment of wound requires consideration of several other factors such as the need for
drain, types of dressing and prevention or treatment of various infections.

153

Drains Superficial lacerations do not require
drainage. Deeper wounds particularly those
involving oral cavity should be drained properly.
This allows the escape of serum and tissue fluids
that prevents the collection of these substances
in deeper structures. Drain may be placed in
between the sutures or through a stab incision
approximating original wound. The ideal time of
removal of drains is when there is absence of
collection (<5 ml). Usually we secure drain for
5–7 days in facial space infections.
Dressings After suturing, some type of protective dressing is indicated. Larger wounds require
a secure pressure dressing. These dressings offer
tissue support and sufficient pressure on the tissue to prevent additional bleeding or collection of
fluid in the subcutaneous region.
Prevention of Infection Most of the lacerated
wounds are already infected or contaminated by
the time they are seen for treatment. This can be
minimized by strict adherence to sterile technique and adequate supportive care which
includes utilization of antibiotics.
Prophylaxis against tetanus should be done.
All the wounds of the face are contaminated and
are often produced by accidents that force dirt
and debris into the wound. Protection against
infection by the Clostridium tetani must be
provided.
Failure in Primary Closure The majority of
laceration heals by primary intention without any
complications, but some fails to heal properly.
There are six major factors responsible for
wound breakdown:
1. Tight closure of the wound without provision
for deep tissue damage.
2. Inadequate use of pressure dressing.
3. Failure to achieve water-tight closure of the
oral mucosa.
4. Secondary haemorrhage.
5. Secondary manipulation of the repaired
wound.
6. Inadequate antibiotic therapy leading to secondary infection.

154

Breakdown of small laceration can be corrected
by the conservative management consisting of
frequently changed saline dressing and healing
by secondary intention. In the wound in which
breakdown will lead to unsightly scar formation
and deformation of adjacent tissues, a secondary
aesthetic corrective surgical procedure should be
done only after complete healing and revascularization have occurred.
Punctured Type of Penetrating Wound
Isolated puncture wound in facial area is uncommon. When it occurs, entry point is narrow but
may penetrate deeply into the underlying tissues
involving the mouth, maxillary antrum, nasal
cavity or neck regions. This type of wound may
carry infection deep into the tissues. Treatment
should be conservative and must involve infection control primarily.
Firearm and Ballistic Injuries It creates large
defect in soft tissue and bones. It is of three types:
penetration, perforation and avulsion. Initially
these types of wounds were occasionally seen in
civilians, but now with changing pattern of incidents like assault and terrorist attack, they are
commonly seen nowadays. These wounds are
usually extensive; first attention should be given
to the general condition of the patient. The methods of treatment depend on the problem encountered in each individual case. Unfortunately not
all gunshots and missile wounds can be treated
early as many are seen with avulsion of soft tissues leading to gross contamination, oedema and
necrosis.
The treatment methods will depend on the problems encountered in each individual. Gunshot in
civilian practice usually receives definite treatment
within matter of hours, whereas definitive management of war wounds may be early or markedly
delayed. Regardless of which situation exists, when
certain fundamental principles are followed, satisfactory results may be obtained. Primary closure
should be done whenever possible. Associated
fractures should be reduced and immobilized followed by closure of the soft tissue wound. All gunshot or missile wounds cannot be closed by primary
or delayed primary suture. For the large avulsive-

V. Singh et al.

type wound in which it is not possible to restore the
normal facial contour, reconstructive surgery may
be required. Gunpowder wounds caused by carbon
particles invaded deeply below the dermis which
leads to burning and facial oedema.
Foreign Bodies Gunshot and missile type of
injuries are often complicated by foreign bodies
carried into the wound. These foreign bodies can
range from superficially located debris resulting
from explosion and deeply penetrating bullets or
metallic fragments. They include objects such as
pigmented debris, clothing, bullets, wood, glass,
stone and splinter of metals. Any foreign body
encountered during debridement of the wound
should be removed. Glass particles and metal
fragments are difficult to remove due to scattering throughout the deeper tissues that may
become a source of secondary infection. In evaluating metallic fragments in a wound, the possible
complication of these objects must be weighed
against the effect of surgical procedure necessary
for their removal. Many of them are sterile and
remain in the tissue indefinitely without injurious
effect. It is better to allow them to remain in the
tissue, and if any complication develops, removal
can be done as secondary procedures (Table 9.2).
Ballistic injuries and wound are notoriously contaminated, and special precautions are indicated to
prevent infection. Antibiotic therapy should be instituted as soon after injury as possible and continued
until primary healing is complete. Prophylaxis
against tetanus must be provided (Table 9.3).
Adequate debridement includes removal of
foreign bodies from the wound. Accurate localization before removal is essential. Search for
foreign bodies should be judicious to prevent
unnecessary trauma to the vital structures and
organs. Blind searching is time-consuming and
may produce further trauma.
Compartment or Crush Injury Syndrome It
can be described as prolonged severe compression
of one or several compartments of the body as a
consequence of multiple compartment involvement and extensive myonecrosis; there is excessive
formation of myoglobin and potassium which
enters into the systemic circulation and causes

from soft tissue [3]
1. Reactivity (thorns, woods, other vegetative

failure and death. The following clinical features
will be seen: sudden massive swelling, marked
oedema with variable degree of local haemorrhage,
paralysis of the involved limb and the peripheral
pulse which may be misleading as the main arterial
supply is damaged due to extensive involvement of
the muscle. Patient will have pale, cold and moist
skin while maintaining normal blood pressure. Due
to prolonged compression, there will be anoxia
which will increase capillary permeability and
massive transudation leading to extravasations of
plasma and electrolyte-­bearing fluid. This is the
first phase of shock which is compensated by
peripheral vasoconstriction; this compensatory
mechanism is capable to keep up with the fluid
loss, but once the blood pressure falls, then the second stage of shock will develop which is a life-

155

threatening situation. To prevent hypovolaemic
shock in patient with crush injury, intravenous
crystalloid solution is the most important.

9.4

Conclusion

Soft tissue injuries of the face are a very common
clinical entity with very wide presentation.
Proper wound management and meticulous layerwise closure are essential to obtain minimal
scarring and aesthetic outcome. Infectious and
burn wounds require long-term monitoring and
debridement to achieve pathogen-free stage.
Documentation and serial photographs of facial
soft tissue injuries are mandatory to provide valuable information for medicolegal purpose.

10.1

Introduction

Dentoalveolar injury (DAI) is common
among patients with maxillofacial fractures.
Dentoalveolar injury is injury related to tooth or
tooth-supporting structures (gingiva, periodontal
ligament (PDL), alveolar bone). Dentoalveolar
injuries may present in isolation or in association
with other fractures. Dental injuries and alveolar
bone fractures represent 5% of all dental trauma.
Isolated dentoalveolar trauma is generally a result
of low-velocity impacts. It is important for oral
surgeons to be aware of dentoalveolar injuries so
that they can treat them effectively.

10.2

Aetiology

Current literature suggests that paediatric population accounts for 5% of all facial fractures. Rezende
et al. reported a bimodal trend in the peak incidence
of dentoalveolar trauma in children aged 0–5 years
and 10–15 years [1]. Likewise, there was an overall
prevalence of 11–30% in the children with primary
dentition. Those with permanent or mixed dentition
ranged from 5% to 20%. Participation in contact
sports, such as hockey, soccer, football, basket-

A. Agrawal (*) · A. K. Tiwari
Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery,
Faculty of Dental Sciences, King Georges Medical
University, Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh, India

ball, boxing and wrestling, can predispose to facial
trauma. In adult patients, most of the dentoalveolar
injuries result from automobile accidents, fall from
height and physical assault. Dental trauma in older
age groups may result from assault and domestic
abuse, usually closely related to the abuse of drugs
or alcohol, or both [2].

10.3

Mechanism of Injury

It is important to know about the mechanism of
injury and the vector of forces since they may
give a clue to the diagnosis.
Direct Trauma
When an object directly hits the tooth, this is
more common in anterior teeth and in patients
with increased overjet and incompetent lips.
Indirect Trauma
When the mandible is forcefully closed against
the upper jaw as in the case of a blow on the
chin, this type of trauma favours fractures in the
premolar-­molar region.

10.4

Factors Determining
an Impact to Teeth or Jaws

1. Energy of the impact.
Low-velocity blows mostly damage supporting structures and tooth fractures are less.

© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2021
A. K. Singh, N. K. Sharma (eds.), Maxillofacial Trauma,
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-33-6338-0_10

159

160

A. Agrawal and A. K. Tiwari

High-velocity impacts cause tooth fractures
and are not usually associated with damage to
the supporting structures.
2. Resilience of the impacting object.
If labial soft tissue cushions the impact and
distributes it, then the chances for tooth fracture is reduced, on the contrary increasing the
chance of luxation and alveolar fractures in
such cases.
3. Shape of the impacting object.
Sharp objects cause clean crown fractures
with minimum displacement because the
energy is focused and effects over a limited
area. On the other hand, blunt object spreads
out the area of impact which resists, and thus
the impact traverses up to the apico-dento-­
gingival region resulting in either luxation or
root fracture.
4. Direction or vector of force.
Depending on the direction or angulation of
the impacting force, the type of fracture will
vary.

Dentoalveolar fractures are especially common in paediatric age groups as they are related
to tooth eruption, alveolar bone development,
occlusion and facial growth. There is relatively
low chance of other facial bone fractures in paediatric population because of the elasticity of
developing jaws, lack of sinus pneumatisation,
mixed dentition as well as retruded position of
developing mandible.

Patient’s name, age, address, phone number

The time elapse between injury and treatment
is very important in determining prognosis.
3. Location of incident to ascertain possibility of
microbial or chemical contamination. This
will help assess the need for antimicrobial
therapy and tetanus prophylaxis.

10.7.1 Extraoral Soft Tissues
Cuts, bruises and contusions are not uncommon with dentoalveolar injuries; they should be
documented meticulously, say if a cut injury is
present, the depth should be determined for the
considerations of layered primary closure or the
need of reconstruction in case of tissue loss.
Fig. 10.22 Fracture of the edentulous segment

10.7.2 Intraoral Soft Tissues

Fig. 10.23 Fracture of the dentulous segment with little
or no displacement

Thorough examination of oral cavity for any contaminated clots, lacerations and other areas of
blood ooze should be done. The contaminants have
to be flushed out by copious irrigation with saline
or Ringer’s lactate solution. Areas of blood ooze
usually respond to pressure gauze sponges. The
examination will also ascertain any foreign bodies
impinged in the soft tissue or socket. Also, sometimes part of the tooth like chipped enamel or part
of the crown or whole of the tooth may be found
in contiguous soft tissue areas. In some cases, the
maxillary incisors may be driven into the upper lip
and may lie completely within the soft tissue.

10.7.3 Alveolar Bone Fractures

detect any step deformities. However, because

be difficult. Mobility of a segment containing

Tooth fractures should be carefully examined,

10.7.5 Radiographic Examination
The radiographic examination should provide the
following information:
1. Presence of root fracture.
2. Extent or degree of intrusion or extrusion.
3. Any preexisting periapical pathology.
4. Length of root maturation.
5. Volume of pulp chambers and number of root
canals originating from it.
6. Associated jaw bone fractures.
7. Radio-opacities in soft tissues suggesting
tooth fragment and/or foreign bodies.
The most commonly used radiographic
modalities to assess dentoalveolar fractures are:
• Periapical radiographs with two different
angulations.
• Occlusal views.
• Orthopantomograms (OPG).
• CT/Cone-beam CT Scans can be used to detect
root fractures, especially for alveolar fractures.

10.7.6 Management
of Dentoalveolar Injuries
10.7.6.1 Emergency/Primary Care
Advance trauma life support (ATLS) protocols
and guidelines are followed in evaluation and
management. The first step is to secure airway.
A quick physical examination is carried out to
rule out chest, abdominal, head or spine trauma.
Blood sample is collected and sent for CBC,
viral markers and serum electrolytes. The aim
of this phase is to stabilise the patient and identify the injuries.
10.7.6.2 Treatment of Dental Injuries
The primary goal in the treatment of dental injuries is to re-establish the normal form, function
and aesthetics.

10.10 Most Commonly Employed
Method in Reduction
of Dentoalveolar Fractures
Splint is a device utilised to support, immobilise
and protect the dentition that has been luxated,
replanted, fractured or endodontically intervened. Various types of splint are used to stabilise
the dentoalveolar fracture [6, 7].
It is divided mainly based on the nature of
manufacturing material used for its fabrication. It
is divided into three types: rigid splint, semi-rigid
splint and flexible splint.
Rigid splint provides adequate immobilisation
of fracture fragment, but the major disadvantage
is that sometimes it causes pulp necrosis followed by external resorption of the teeth. On the
other hand, flexible splint allows physiologic

The Following Consideration Is Necessary
Before Splint Selection
• Number of teeth involved.
• Status of alveolar bone or process, simple or
comminuted.
• Type of alveolar fracture.
• Type of dentition—primary/permanent.
• Grading of tooth mobility.
• Status of adjacent intact teeth.
Ideal Properties of the Splint
1. It should allow reattachment of periodontal
ligament.
2. Be easily applied or removed without causing
any trauma to adjacent hard and soft tissue.
3. Maintain adequate immobilisation of fracture
fragment during splinting period.
4. Non-irritable and non-injurious to the adjacent soft tissue.
5. Allow some physiologic tooth movement, to
aid in healing of periodontal ligament of the
involved tooth/teeth.

• First-aid method; temporary splint.
• Indication—when technical facilities are

• Mainly used for subluxated teeth.

• Advantage—easiest and cheapest.

Stoma Adhesive Splint
• Temporary splint.
• To prevent pain at the site of fracture fragment, isolate from the adjacent soft tissue.

Arch Bar Fixation
• Rigid splinting method.
• Used for both alveolar fracture and subluxated
teeth.
• A 26-gauge wire for fixation of grade II
mobile teeth.
• Disadvantage—causes more external resorption, eventually leading to early loss of teeth.
Figure-of-8 Wiring
• Uses 0.35 mm soft stainless steel wire around
the abutment teeth and subluxated teeth.
• Disadvantage—tightening the wire causes it
to slide apically and extrusion of tooth occurs.

10.13 Case Discussion
Chief Complaint A 33-year-old female patient
reported a chief complaint of pain and loose
teeth.

Diagnosis According to Ellis and Dewey classification, it was a Type VI injury, whereas
according to William D. Clark, it was a Class 3
dentoalveolar fracture.
Treatment The patient was administered local
anaesthesia to anaesthetise the concerned region.
Dentoalveolar fracture was reduced manually, and
the teeth were reduced to its anatomic position.
After checking the occlusion, Erich’s arch bar
application was done only in the maxillary teeth,
to act as a splint, including at least two teeth on
either side of the fracture (Fig. 10.27). The arch
bar was removed after 4 weeks once the fractured
segment and the teeth were completely stable.

11.1

Introduction

A. K. Singh (*)
Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery Unit,
Faculty of Dental Sciences, Institute
of Medical Sciences, Banaras Hindu University,
Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh, India
e-mail: aksingh.dent@bhu.ac.in

parts—symphysis, parasymphysis, and body
region. The vertical part consists of the angle,
ramus, condylar, and coronoid process [1].
The blood supply of the mandible is from the
inferior alveolar artery and also from the direct
muscular attachments. The inferior alveolar nerve
enters from the medial aspect of mandible at the
mandibular foramen with the artery; it traverses
the medullary cavity near the lingual cortex
below the level of the tooth roots and then rises to
exit the mental foramen at about the second premolar region. This nerve provides sensory supply
to mandibular teeth and the skin and mucosa over
the lower lip. The two main groups of muscles
insert and act upon the mandible: the muscles of
mastication and the suprahyoid muscles.
Displacement of fracture segments commonly
occurs as a result of the differing forces of these
muscles acting upon the mandible. In general, the
muscles of mastication tend to displace the posterior segments medially and superiorly, while the
suprahyoid muscles pull the anterior segments
inferiorly (Figs. 11.1 and 11.2). In addition, the
lateral pterygoid muscles tend to pull the condylar head anteromedially in cases of high condyle
fractures.

D. Samal
Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery, Poole
Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, Poole, Dorset, UK

11.1.2 Embryology

The mandible is the largest and strongest bone of
the facial skeleton. It is the only movable bone of
the skull. The word mandible is derived from the
Latin word “mandibula” that means instrument to
chew. It plays a vital role in speech, mastication, and
deglutition and maintains the lower facial height.

11.1.1 Anatomy
The mandible is a V-shaped bone that articulates
with the glenoid fossa of temporal bone and constitutes temporomandibular joint (TMJ). It has
a vertical portion and a horizontal portion. The
horizontal portion of mandible has two main
structures, the basal and alveolar (tooth-bearing) bones. The basal bone is divided into three

Department of Dentistry, Oral and Maxillofacial
Surgery, All India Institute of Medical Sciences,
Patna, Bihar, India

The mandible ossifies as the second bone after
the clavicle, and on the lateral aspect of Meckel’s

grows backward and upward to form the condylar process [2].
In the neonatal period, the mandible is formed
from two halves, which further unites in the midline and forms symphysis and ossifies in the 1st
year of life. The mylohyoid sulcus is the remnant
of the groove, where Meckel’s cartilage existed.
The fibrous sheath framing the cartilage helps in
the development of sphenomandibular ligament.

Incidence and Etiology

The mandible is the most frequently injured facial
bone accounts for one third of all facial fractures.
Most of the studies suggest higher male predilection (70–80%) with age range 21–30 years.
Mandible fractures have many different etiologies such as interpersonal violence, motor vehicle accidents (MVAs), gunshot wounds, sport
accidents, work accidents, and falls [3]. The etiology of mandibular fractures varies from time to
time, technological advancement, and dynamic
culture. Studies in different periods demonstrate
changes in etiology based on age, demographic
pattern of countries, environmental conditions,
and socioeconomic and cultural configurations.
In developed countries, vehicle and sport accidents are the main causes of mandibular fractures, whereas in developing countries and rural
areas, interpersonal violence, gunshot wounds,
and falls are the main etiological factors [4–6].
Physical altercations mostly result in a higher
incidence of angle fractures due to a lateral blow
to the mandible, whereas MVAs are more commonly associated with body, parasymphyseal,
symphyseal, and condylar fractures [7–8].
Controversies exist regarding the common site
of involvement of the mandibular fracture. Lee
et al. reported angle region (36.75%) as the most
commonly involved site followed by symphysis/
parasymphysis (24.7%) and condyle (16.9%)
[4], whereas Murray reported condyle (36%) as
most common site followed by the body (21%),
angle (20%), and symphysis (14%) [9]. In Indian
scenario, parasymphysis region (33–41.1%) is
the most common affected site followed by the

11

Introduction to Mandibular Fractures

179

condyle (20–29.2%) and MVAs (68.8–80.31%)
among the most common etiology [10, 11].

Classification

1. Dingman and Natvig (1964)—most widely

(a) According to the direction of the fracture:
• Horizontally favourable—Fracture line

downward and anterior direction leading

pterygomasseteric pull (Fig. 11.3).
• Horizontally unfavorable—Fracture

downward and posterior direction
leading to superior displacement due
to pterygomasseteric pull (Fig. 11.4).
• Vertically favorable—Fracture line
runs from the outer buccal cortical
plate obliquely backward and lingually
leading to restriction of medial pull by
medial pterygoid (Fig. 11.5).
• Vertically unfavorable—Fracture line
runs from the inner lingual cortical
plate obliquely backward and buccally
leading to unrestricted medial pull by
medial pterygoid (Fig. 11.6).

11.4

Clinical Examination

11.4.1 Initial Assessment
Initial assessment of patients should be done
according to the Advanced Trauma Life Support
(ATLS) protocol. Recognition and treatment
of any life-threatening injuries should be done
accordingly. Most studies show an incidence of
C-spine injuries between 2% and 10%. Thus,
a careful evaluation of the C-spine is required
before proceeding with any operative management. In patients presenting with facial fractures,
it may be as high as 20% in patients with panfacial injuries. A published study showed that 15
combined facial fracture patterns, involving two
or more facial bones and unilateral mandibular injuries, account for the greatest number of
C-spine injuries [17, 18].

183

intubation and tracheostomy may be required
to maintain oxygen saturation.
2. Deformity—Clinically, external deformity is
very difficult to rule out due to swelling.
Intraoral examination may reveal displacement creating a step deformity, open bite
deformity, and malocclusion (Fig. 11.10).
Many patients can have significant preexisting
malocclusion which must be documented in
history of patient and considered during treatment planning. In order to assess that, preoperative impression should be made and study
model analysis should be done.
3. Crepitus—The sound produced by the grating
of the rough surfaces, when the bony ends
come into contact with each other.
4. Tenderness—Fracture sites are tender on palpation and compression.
Compression test—Placing the palm of both
hands over the angle region and bilateral compression will elicit severe pain. Positive compression test is suggestive of mandibular fracture.
TMJ pain which occurs under compression may
identify a fractured condyle or a contused and
inflamed joint.
1. Tooth and bone fragment hypermobility—
Hypermobility of the tooth and bone fragments are the signs of mandibular fracture. In
unconscious patients, airway obstruction can

11.4.2 Clinical Features
Symptoms (subjective)—Pain; swelling; bleeding; subjective malocclusion; lower lip numbness; difficulty in speech, swallowing, and mouth
opening (trismus); loosened/fractured tooth; and
airway embarrassment
Signs (objective):
1. Bleeding, hematoma, and swelling—Tearing of
the periosteum and muscles attached to the
mandible can cause severe bleeding, producing
visible hemorrhage, sublingual hematoma
(Coleman’s sign), swelling, and life-­threatening
airway obstruction. In this situation, emergency

Fig. 11.10 Intraoral photograph showing fracture involving the right side body region of mandible with step deformity, anterior open bite, and malocclusion

184

A. K. Singh et al.

occur with either posterior tongue displacement in bilateral mandibular fractures producing “flail mandible” or with traumatic avulsion
of tongue muscle.
2. Restricted function—It includes lateral deviation on opening to the side of fracture, inability to chew, lockjaw due to muscle spasm,
trismus, joint dysfunction, or impingement by
zygomatic fractures.
3. Sensory disturbances—The inferior alveolar
nerve (V3) courses through the mandibular
body and angle. Fractures through the bony
mandibular canal can cause temporary or permanent anesthesia of the lip, teeth, and gingiva. The lingual nerve lies close to the lingual
cortex near the mandibular third molar. Injury
may cause temporary or permanent anesthesia
to the ipsilateral tongue.

11.5

Radiological Evaluation

1. Mandible series—Three films are used for
isolated fracture of mandible:
(a) Posteroanterior (PA) view is used to analyze
the fracture involving the entire mandible. It
shows displacement in symphysis, body,
angle, and ramus fractures (Fig. 11.11).
(b) Reverse Towne view shows medial/lateral
displacement of condylar head and subcondylar fractures.
(c) Lateral oblique view for angle and body
fractures (Fig. 11.12).
2. Orthopantomogram (OPG)—It is a panoramic scan which shows the entire mandible,
including condyles on only one film. It is an
excellent diagnostic tool for the patient who is
able to stand or sit upright without motion. It
offers low dose of radiation, low cost, and
excellent detail. It is valuable for follow-up
evaluation (Fig. 11.13).
Demerits—inability to perform in:
• Unconscious and uncooperative patients
• Suspected C-spine fracture
• Pediatric patients less than 3 feet height

Fig. 11.12 Radiograph showing lateral oblique view of

3. Occlusal view—They are indicated to evaluate medial and lateral displacement of symphysis and body fractures. They are less
commonly practiced in the present era.
4. Periapical radiographs—Periapical radiographs show fractures of dental roots next to
mandible and alveolar fractures.
5. Computed tomography (CT) scan—CT scan is
a gold standard and most preferred method of
imaging for multiple mandibular fractures. It
has the ability to view the condition in multiple
planes like axial, coronal, and saggital view
(Fig. 11.14). Three-dimensional CT scan is
helpful for the diagnosis and treatment plan-

ning of complex facial fractures (Fig. 11.15).
Additionally, DICOM CT images help to provide 3D models for reconstruction, and they are
essential for proper approximations of fracture
fragments with prebended titanium plates.
Nowadays, the use of cone beam computed
tomography (CBCT) in maxillofacial surgery
has been providing less radiation and an accurate imaging tool, alternative to conventional
CT.
Keynote: The use of conventional or
advanced imaging modalities to diagnose
mandibular fractures should be decided after
considering:
• Severity of the injury
• Soft tissue imaging requirements
• Superimposition of structures
• Need for 3D views
• Restricted functions
• Cost-effectiveness
• Availability
6. MRI scan—It is better for evaluating soft tissue findings such as complications of trauma
and hematoma.

11.6

A. K. Singh et al.

Surgical Approaches
to the Mandible

The mandible can be approached for open reduction and fixation of fractures through either intraoral or extraoral means. Due to esthetic reasons,
intraoral approaches have become more popular.
While deciding which approach is best, a number
of factors such as location and type of the fracture, access, the position of the vital structures,
and natural relaxed skin tension lines on the face
are considered.
The common approaches include intraoral,
submandibular, retromandibular, preauricular,
endaural, postauricular, and through existing laceration. Recently, endoscopic approach is getting
popularized for condylar fractures.

11.6.1 Approaches Through Existing
Laceration
Lacerations are common, especially in the
anterior mandibular region. Wherever possible, lacerations may be utilized to access the
mandible. Lacerations can be extended parallel to the skin creases or Langer lines to better
visualize the mandible. The relevant anatomy
to be aware of are the facial and submental
vessels and the marginal mandibular nerve as
described above.

11.6.2 IntraOral Approach
The vestibular approach is the preferred approach
for addressing fractures of mandible in contemporary times. It has the advantage of an invisible
scar, which remains hidden in the oral cavity. It
provides good access for symphysis, body, and
external oblique ridge in angle region of the
mandible. The lower border in the angle region
is less accessible intraorally for direct placement
of plates and screws, but a trocar can be used to
circumvent that.
The vital structures of importance in this
approach include the mental nerves and vessels,

which exit the mental foramen in the region of
the first and second premolar. The nerve has three
main branches, supplying the chin, lower lip, and
gingiva. The facial vessels are closely related to the
lower border of mandible in the junction of angle
and body of mandible. However, it is unusual to
come across those when approaching intraorally.
The artery curves upward from the medial aspect
of the body of mandible to lie superficially in the
skin, in the antegonial notch, where it lies close to
the lower border of mandible.
The paired mentalis muscles arise from anterior mandible and insert into the skin of the chin.
For fractures of symphysis and parasymphysis,
this muscle must be elevated off the bone. In
the anterior region, from canine to canine, the
incision is curvilinear. The mucosa is incised
halfway between the depth of vestibule and
mucocutaneous junction, leaving approximately
10 to 15 mm mucosa attached to gingiva. The
mentalis muscle should be incised obliquely
so that enough muscle remains attached to the
bone to facilitate closure. The periosteum is then
incised and dissection proceeds subperiosteally
toward the fracture. In the body region, the incision should be placed 5 mm below the mucogingival junction. For exposure of angle fractures,
the incision may be extended over the external
oblique ridge. Periosteum should be incised in a
perpendicular fashion, and dissection should be
subperiosteal to avoid facial vessels which are
just superficial to the periosteum (Fig. 11.16).

11.6.3 Submandibular Approach
It is commonly used for fractures of symphysis,
parasymphysis, body, and angle of mandible. An
incision is placed directly at the region of the
fracture, about 1.5–2 cm below and parallel to
the lower border of mandible to avoid the marginal mandibular branch of facial nerve which
crosses/lies within 1–1.5 cm of the inferior border, in 19% of cases (Fig. 11.17) [19]. Incision
may also be placed along a neck skin crease, to
be less conspicuous, but the advantage of direct
approach to the mandibular border is then lost.

11.6.4 Retromandibular Approach

Fig. 11.17 Schematic diagram showing course of marginal mandibular nerve and position of the submandibular
incision

Dissection should be upward and in a sub-platysmal plane till the lower border is identified. The
marginal mandibular nerve can be seen beneath
the platysma, over the submandibular gland passing through a layer of fat.
Other structures of importance encountered
in the submandibular approach are the facial
vessels. The facial artery can be palpated just

This approach is advantageous in that it gives
a more direct access to the mandibular ramus
than the submandibular approach. It is also useful for fractures of condylar head and neck. The
structures of relevance in this approach include
the main trunk of facial nerve, its five branches,
and the retromandibular vein. The facial nerve
trunk lies at least 2 cm deep to the skin surface
behind the parotid gland. As it courses anteriorly
and laterally, it crosses superficial to the retromandibular vein and external carotid artery. The
peripheral branches of the nerve lie more superficially in the gland. The nerve bifurcates into its
temporo-­facial and cervicofacial divisions within
1.5–2.8 cm below the lowest concavity of bony
external auditory canal [20].

188

The retromandibular vein descends from its
origin behind the neck of the mandible in the
substance of the parotid gland, lateral to the
external carotid artery. At the apex of the gland,
it divides into anterior and posterior branches
which unite with facial vein and posterior auricular vein, respectively. The traditional retromandibular approach involves an incision of the
skin 2 cm behind the ramus. The parotid gland
is then dissected off the sternocleidomastoid
muscle and retracted anteriorly. The facial nerve
and the vessels are contained in the glandular
issue avoiding injury. A more direct, modern
approach was described by Hinds [21]. An incision is placed directly below the ear lobe. The
platysma and Superficial musculo-aponeurotic
system (SMAS) are incised to reach the parotid
gland. The dissection proceeds through the gland
anteriorly and medially toward the posterior border of ramus. The ramus of the mandible can be
approached safely through a gap between the
buccal and marginal mandibular branches. The
latter crosses the ramus in the lower third and
can be traced using a nerve stimulator. It can be
dissected off its surroundings and retracted superiorly or inferiorly. The final step is to divide the
pterygomasseteric sling to expose the underlying
bone (Fig. 11.19).

A. K. Singh et al.

11.6.5 Preauricular Approach
The preauricular approach is useful for fractures of mandibular condyle and ramus of mandible. Incision is made in the preauricular fold,
from the root of helix of the ear inferiorly to
the attachment of the ear lobule. It should not
be extended further down to avoid branches
of facial nerve. The length of the incision is
approximately 3–3.5 cm. The depth of the incision is at a plane just superficial to the cartilage, and dissection proceeds anteriorly till the
deep temporal fascia is visualized and attached
to the zygomatic arch. The plane of dissection
lies beneath the SMAS, and important structures such as superficial temporal vessels and
branches of facial nerve and auriculotemporal nerve lie superficial to this plane and are
included in the flap raised. The temporal branch
of facial nerve crosses the zygomatic arch on
an average of 2 cm (range 0.8–3.5 cm) in front
of the anterior concavity of external auditory
meatus. The anterior limit of dissection should
not cross that. The periosteum over the arch is
incised about 2 cm anterior to the skin incision,
and dissection is carried out subperiosteally to
expose the condyle. If access to the condylar
head is required, the lateral capsule must be
incised in addition.

11.6.6 Endaural Approach
The incision for this approach begins at the fold
between the helix and preauricular skin, similar to the preauricular approach. But instead
of descending straight downward, the incision
moves along the curvature of the tragal cartilage.
The tragal cartilage is released, and the dissection
then proceeds in a manner similar to the preauricular approach. This approach has a cosmetic
advantage over the preauricular approach.

11.6.7 Posterior Auricular Approach
Fig. 11.19 Schematic diagram showing the retromandibular approach and its relation with branches of facial
nerve

It is also known as the retro-auricular, trans-­
meatal approach. It is indicated for fractures of

11

Introduction to Mandibular Fractures

condylar head. It is used uncommonly and has
the advantage of avoiding the facial and auriculotemporal nerves. Scar is hidden behind the ear.
An incision about 2.5–3 cm long is placed
approximately 5 mm medial to the posterior
auricular fold. It should start about 5 mm from
the root of helix and terminate about 5 mm above
the attachment of the ear lobule. Dissection is
then done through the skin, subcutaneous tissue,
and muscle to the mastoid fascia till the ear concha can be visualized. The flap is then retracted
anteriorly, and an incision is made first through
the posterior aspect of the cartilaginous meatus
and then the anterior aspect, thus transecting the
external auditory meatus. The retromandibular
space can now be seen, with the retromandibular
vein coursing above downward. The vein is then
ligated and divided to provide access. Parotid
tissues are dissected bluntly till mandible is
reached, whereupon the periosteum is incised to
expose the fracture [22].
Common complications in this approach
include the stenosis of the ear canal, perichondritis, and formation of salivary fistula and sialocoele. Meticulous closure of the parotid capsule
with horizontal mattress sutures can prevent
salivary complications. The cartilage must be
sutured with slowly resorbing sutures such as
Polydioxanone suture (PDS) to avoid stenosis.

11.6.8 Endoscopic Approach
The endoscopic approach is useful for high subcondylar or ramus fractures of mandible. The
incision used is either transoral or submandibular. It precludes the need for extensive incisions
like preauricular or retromandibular, which are
quite conspicuous, while providing better visualization. It also prevents injury of facial nerve.
A 30-degree 4-mm endoscope is generally used.
Angled instruments are used for drilling. The
major disadvantage of using an endoscope is
that it is time-consuming and requires a learning
curve. The armamentarium required is also quite
extensive and may not be available in all settings.
Complications include myofascial pain and
resorption of the condylar head.

189

11.7

Conclusion

Mandibular fractures are among the common
fractures of the maxillofacial skeleton. The
bone dynamics makes it very important for various functions. Displaced mandibular fractures
require early attention; failing to that may lead to
airway obstruction. Untreated fractures may lead
to various complications such as malocclusion,
malunion, nonunion, temporomandibular joint
ankylosis, and facial deformity and asymmetry.
Thus, timing of intervention is important for better results and adequate function.

12.1

Introduction

The mandible occupies the lowest position of the
face. Being the largest and the strongest bone of
the face, it undergoes significant trauma, when
the lower face is hit by upward or obliquely
directed high impacts. The mandible comprises
of various regions such as symphysis, parasymphysis, body, ramus, angle, condylar and coronoid processes. Out of the entire facial fracture,
nearly 19–40% constitute mandibular fracture.
The main aetiology is road traffic accident involving automobiles, followed by interpersonal violence and sports-related injuries. Energy required
to fracture a mandible is about 44.6–77.4 kg/m2.
Symphysis is the region of bony union of the two
halves of mandible during first year of life. Due
to presence of mental foramen and canine roots,
parasymphysis region becomes weakened and
gets more prone to fracture [1]. The superior border of mandible is mainly composed of organic
component and the inferior border is of inorganic
component. Collagen fibres at the superior border
are responsible for taking over the tensile forces
over the bone, whereas the mineral phase absorbs
the compressive forces. Bones fracture mainly at
the regions of tensile strain. The interplay
between the mechanism of injury and the inherS. K. Mukul · A. Singh (*)
Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery, All
India Institute of Medical Sciences,
Patna, Bihar, India

ent anatomy and structure of defined subunits of
mandible predicts the fracture pattern. However,
it is true only in case of angle and body fractures
of the mandible, but the situation is opposite in
case of parasymphyseal and symphyseal fractures. Because of the presence of torsional forces,
a single behaviour of biomechanical form can be
predicted for the latter overall [2].
The therapeutic goals in treatment of these
fractures are reduction of the bone fragments to
their natural anatomical position and restoration
of function with least morbidity [3]. Various
impairments are caused by mandibular fractures
like TMJ (temporomandibular joint) disorders,
poor mastication, malocclusion, OSA (obstructive sleep apnoea) and chronic pain. In children,
facial development gets deteriorated by mandibular fractures resulting in disfiguring. Nowadays,
various types of internal rigid fixation which
evolved from splinting, extraoral pins, trans-­
osseous wiring and circum-mandibular wiring
are used for the management of mandibular fractures. AO/ASIF (Arbeitsgemeinschaft für
Osteosynthesefragen/Association for the Study
of Internal Fixation) promoted the rigid fixation
technique widely. More recently, the idea of
‘functionally stable’ semi-rigid fixation with
miniplates has been popularized by Champy
et al. to improve surgical treatment outcomes;
various researches are continued which are focusing on the size, shape, number and biomechanics
of screw/plate systems [4].

Classification

12.2.1 Symphysis/Parasymphysis
Region

Level 2 image-based AOCMF classification
system for mandible fractures describes and
classifies fractures based on their topographical
distribution. In this, the mandible is divided
into nine different regions which are identified
by letters:
• The symphysis/parasymphysis region (S)
anteriorly (single central unit)
• Two body (B) regions on each lateral side
• Combined angle and ascending ramus
regions (A)
• Condylar process (P)
• Coronoid process (C)
However, for the current chapter, we’ll consider only the symphysis/parasymphysis region
and two body regions. Based on the diagnosis
of CT scan imaging or X-rays, this classification system allows to classify the fracture
according to its topography within the defined
regions [5].

The parasymphysis/symphysis region forms the
single central unit of the mandibular arch. The
roots of the mandibular canine determine the lateral boundary on each side. There are two anterior transitional zones present as vertical strips on
each side along the contours of the canine roots.
In case of edentulous mandible, it is located at
5 mm (1/4 width of a premolar) in front of the
mental foramen (Fig. 12.1).

12.2.2 Mandibular Body Region
The body of the mandible lies between the canine
and the angle region. In the dentate mandible, the
anterior edge of the mandibular body goes
towards the root of the lower canines. Along the
outlines of the third molar roots, two posterior
transitional zones are defined. In an edentulous
mandible, the posterior transitional zone incorporates the retromolar area entirely.

The posterior transitional zones are considered within the area between the body and the

12.3

Clinical Features

12.3.1 General Signs and Symptoms
• Swelling
• Pain and tenderness
• Step deformity and mobility of the fractured
bone
• Lacerations and haemorrhage
• Restricted mouth opening
• Sublingual haematoma (ecchymosis of the
floor of the mouth is a diagnostic sign of fracture—Coleman’s sign).
• Abnormal bite (malocclusion)
• Fractured, subluxated or luxated teeth
• Anaesthesia or paraesthesia of the lip
• Airway obstruction due to loss of tongue control (in B/L parasymphysis/body and comminuted symphysis fractures)

12.3.2 Clinical Examination
Before performing clinical examination, the
detailed history is important. The mode of injury
is important in determining the magnitude and
direction of force delivered to the region. The
chronological order of events after trauma such
as loss of consciousness, vomiting, seizures and
bleeding from the ear and nose and oral cavity
should be recorded. The initial management
details and documentation of the findings should
be done properly in medicolegal cases. The clinical examination begins with inspection and palpation of the face and oral cavity.

12.3.2.1 Extraoral Examination
At first, the clinician should inspect the skin abrasion and lacerations over the face and scalp
region. Check for the bruises and haematoma.

193

Diffuse swelling and severe tenderness over the
lower face are indicative of the mandibular fracture. A bilateral parasymphyseal fracture could
result in loss of anteroposterior projection of the
chin. A flattened appearance of the lateral aspect
of the face is suggestive of body fracture. Perioral
numbness is also indicative of injury to inferior
alveolar nerve due to the mandibular fracture. On
palpation of the mandible, compression test is
done to confirm the presence of the fracture.

12.3.2.2 Intraoral Examination
On intraoral inspection, sublingual haematoma
and step deformity in anterior region are indicative of symphysis and parasymphysis fractures.
Both hands are used for the manipulation of mandible, with the thumb placed over the occlusal
surface of the teeth and other fingers placed on the
inferior border of the mandible, on both the sides.
By moving the both hands in opposite directions
(above and below) very carefully and precisely,
mobility can be detected in the fracture.

12.3.3 Radiographic Examination
Imaging plays a very important role in the management of mandibular trauma. Radiological
examination should contain at least two different
projections perpendicular to each other to confirm the fracture. They often include:

The orthopantomogram is the most commonly
used radiograph for the screening purpose; it
shows the entire mandible. For more detailed
information regarding the pattern of fractures and
the displacement, computed tomographic scans
are indicated. The three-dimensional images of
CT scan provides better details of the site of fracture and displacement; it is commonly used in
treatment planning.

12.4

S. K. Mukul and A. Singh

Management

The primary aim of the treatment is to achieve
proper anatomic reduction of the fractured bone
and restore the original form and function.
Various treatment methods have been explained
in the literature for the management of mandibular fractures. The choice of treatment may vary
depending upon the location of the fracture,
severity, displacement, status of the dentition,
patient’s demographics, associated comorbidities, etc. Undisplaced fractures which do not
exhibit any occlusal changes can be managed by
nonsurgical methods, whereas the displaced fractures require open methods for reduction and
fixation (ORIF).
According to the biomechanics of the mandible, it shows Class III lever which is joined in the
midline with the fulcrum at the crest of each condyle, and the muscular forces are delivered distal
to the fulcrum, whereas the occlusal forces are
applied distal to the muscle force. When planning
the treatment, a proper understanding of the muscle attachments and forces applied on the mandible is beneficial. Various linear and angular
forces are applied on the mandible such as tension and compression, torsion, shear and bending
[6] (Fig. 12.2a, b).
On the basis of these biomechanical principles,
Champy and his colleagues postulated the ideal
lines of osteosynthesis. They described the concept of zone of tension and compression.
According to this, the superior aspect of the mana

dible, i.e. alveolar region, is designated as zone of
tension and the inferior border of mandible as
zone of compression. Due to the complex behaviour of the mandible, these tension and compression zone can vary depending on the application
of force whether applied anteriorly or posteriorly.
This information allowed the development of the
idea of ideal lines of osteosynthesis for internal
fixation of mandible along the physiological tension lines.

12.4.1 Treatment Methods
They are broadly classified into two categories,
i.e. closed vs open reduction techniques. The
closed methods involve reduction of bone fragments without the need of surgery, whereas in
open method, the bone fragments are reduced
and fixed by various means under direct vision by
surgical exploration.

12.4.2 Closed Reduction Methods
• Direct interdental wiring (discussed in
Chap. 4)
• Arch bar fixation followed by intermaxillary
fixation/maxillomandibular fixation
• IMF screws
• Hybrid arch bar
• Circum-mandibular wiring with acrylic cap
splints

 rch Bar Fixation Followed
by Intermaxillary Fixation
(IMF)/Maxillomandibular
Fixation (MMF)
It is the minimally invasive and one of the
most commonly used methods in the management of mandibular fractures. The technique
involves fixation of Erich’s arch bar on the
individual teeth using circumdental wiring
followed by immobilization for 4–6 weeks
with the help of intermaxillary elastics. It
restores the preinjury occlusion by closed
reduction and stabilization of the fractured
bone (Fig. 12.3a, b) [7].

195

12.4.5 Contraindications
• Severely displaced fractures requiring open
methods for reduction
• Medically compromised patients like epilepsy, Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
(COPD), pregnancy or mental retardation
• Edentulous patients
• Paediatric patients with poor compliance

12.4.6 Advantages of MMF
• Minimally invasive and closed reduction
method can be performed under local
anaesthesia.
• Ease of application.
• Maintains the integrity of periosteum.
• Cost-effective.

12.4.7 Disadvantages

• Undisplaced or minimally displaced fractures
• Comminuted fractures
• Adequate dentition present to achieve normal
occlusion
• Patient not willing for open reduction

• Non-rigid fixation.
• Improper reduction due to poor control on
bone fragments.
• Unable to take oral diet.
• Poor oral hygiene maintenance.

• Post MMF trismus.

12.4.8 IMF Screw
The screw is applied into the periapical bone of the
anterior and posterior labio-buccal vestibule to
anchor the intermaxillary wires or elastics. It is easier to apply and less time taking and maintains better
oral hygiene. The major disadvantages are damage
to the tooth roots, screw head that gets embedded
under the soft tissue and screw loosening.

12.4.9 External Fixation
The external fixation devices were much popular
during the World War era. With the advent of bone
plate and screws, now it is rarely used. The main
indications are chronic infected bone fragments as
observed in osteomyelitis and osteoradionecrosis.

12.4.10 Open Reduction Method
It is the most popular method which involves
reduction and fixation of the fractured bone under
direct visualization. It is invasive approach and
requires general anaesthesia most of the time. It
requires minimal immobilization and allows
early restoration of functions.
The Arbeitsgemeinschaft für Osteosynthesefragen/Association for the Study of Internal
Fixation (AO/ASIF) had postulated four
principles for open reduction [8]:
1. Anatomical reduction
2. Functionally stable fixation
3. Atraumatic surgical technique
4. Immediate active function

12.4.11 Internal Fixation/
Osteosynthesis
Osteosynthesis is the reduction and fixation of a
bone fracture with implantable devices. Various
techniques can be used in the internal fixation of

S. K. Mukul and A. Singh

the symphysis and body region of the mandible.
The commonly used method is fixation with
miniplate and screws. Other available options are
transosseous wiring, lag screws and reconstruction plates.

12.4.11.1

Transosseous Wire
Osteosynthesis
This method involves reduction and fixation of
the fractured bone segments with the help of pre-­
stretched stainless steel wires. The wires can be
applied by either intraoral or extraoral approach.
The wires are inserted perpendicular to the bone
and in the fashion of figure of eight. A figure-of-­
eight wire can produce higher strength over the
straight wire when used at the superior or inferior
border of the mandible. It is a type of non-rigid
fixation and is rarely used [9].
12.4.11.2 Plate Osteosynthesis
Depending on the severity of fracture displacement, fixation of plate can be rigid or semi-rigid.
Luhr and Spiessl advocated the application of
dynamic compression plates (DCP) in the inferior border of mandible for displaced fractures.
It’s main disadvantage was difficult to fix due to
its bulkier size and causing distraction at the tension zone. Later on, eccentrically dynamic compression plates were introduced to overcome the
demerits of DCP. But due to technical difficulties, it was not popularized. The concept of semi-­
rigid fixation with miniplates (functionally
stable) was introduced by Michelet, and its biomechanical basis and line of osteosynthesis was
explained by Champy et al.

12.4.12 Symphysis/Parasymphysis
Fractures
According to Champy and colleagues, two miniplates are placed at the distance of 4–5 mm to
compensate the torsional forces. The first miniplate is fixed over the inferior border of the mandible and the other one 4–5 above the first plate.
It is important to place the screws at least 5 mm
below the root apices to prevent their injury [10].
For mildly displaced fracture segment, arch
bar with one miniplate at compression zone is

12

Symphysis, Parasymphysis and Body Fractures

also favourable. Single DCP at the inferior border
along with arch bar at the tension zone can be
used as a rigid fixation. Two lag screws also provide rigid fixation in transverse/oblique fractures
at symphysis/parasymphysis region. In case of
comminuted fractures at symphysis and parasymphysis region, single reconstruction plate
with at least three screws on either side of fracture is recommended. A retrospective study on
682 patients comparing the outcomes of using
two miniplates or one stronger plate suggested no
statistically difference in terms of occlusal as
well as osseous healing. Few complications like
wound dehiscence, tooth root damage and plate
exposure and need for plate removal were found
in group comprising two miniplate systems [11].

12.4.16 Paediatric Considerations

Previously it was considered that tooth in the line
of fracture acts as a potential source of infection
which may affect the healing. In contrary to it,
few studies suggested that presence of tooth at
the fracture site does not affect healing of the
bone and has a neutral effect on the fracture [13].
It has been observed that preserving the tooth at
fracture site facilitates reduction of fracture segment in some cases and makes it more precise
and accurate.

The incidence of maxillofacial fractures is around
5% in paediatric population [28]. The commonest fracture sites are condyle followed by the
angle and body of mandible [29]. Management of
the growing mandible is different as compared to
the adult patients. The most important consideration is the status of developing dentition.
Orthopantomogram is an essential tool for
screening purpose. Among the closed reduction
methods, circum-mandibular wiring around the

been reported [30]. Maxillomandibular fixation
is contraindicated due to the presence of short
roots of the primary dentition. Usually immobilization for 2 weeks is sufficient in young paediatric patients and 3–4 weeks is indicated in young
adolescents [31]. Open reduction is indicated in
severely displaced fractures, not amenable for
closed reduction. Bioresorbable plates and screws
have gained popularity in the management of

12.4.17 Recent Advances

12.4.17.2 Bioresorbable Plates
Bioresorbable plates are developed from materials like polydioxanone (PDS), polyglycolic acid
(PGA) and poly-l-lactic acid (PLLA). They are
metabolized by hydrolysis and eliminated
through respiration as carbon dioxide. The use of
these plates is indicated for minimally loading
region. Inflammation and foreign-body-type
reactions are the complications associated with
these plates [34].

12.5

Conclusion

The mandible is a dynamic bone of the facial
skeleton. The biomechanics of symphysis,
parasymphysis and body region is unique, and
its understanding is very important to manage
these fractures properly. To achieve good
results, one needs to understand the basics of
osteosynthesis and their application in proper
manner. Various treatment approaches have
been discussed in literature, but every case is
different and the management should be customized in special conditions.

13.1

Incidence by Decade of Life

Introduction

Mandibular angle is a region rather than a location designated as a triangular area. The anatomic
structures that are involved are the anterior border
of the masseter muscle forming the anterior border and the posterior border of the triangle which
is formed by an oblique line extending from
the third molar region to the posterior superior
attachment of the masseter muscle. The angle is
divided into central angle, peripheral angle and
marginal angle according to Spiessl [1]. If the
third molar is absent, the fracture line extends
from either the distal root of the second molar
or posterior to the second molar. The mandibular angle is considered as lever area, the point
from which the mandibular body ascends off
and forms ramus. It is one of the most frequent
sites of fracture of the lower jaw usually by side
impact. Approximately 19–40% of all facial fractures are fractures of the mandible, and 12–30%
of all mandibular fractures are fractures of the
mandibular angle [2]. According to the majority
of the studies, most of the mandibular angle fracture occurs at 21–30 years age group (Fig. 13.1),
the left side being predominantly involved, isolated angle fractures are approximately 51.5%

13.1.1 Anatomical Considerations
A sound knowledge of anatomy is essential for a
swift, sure and minimal traumatic exposure of the
fracture site that preserves functionally important
structures. However, a thorough anatomical understanding of the angle region is important to fathom
the biomechanical aspects of the fractures.
Six anatomical features should be considered
most important during management of angle
ramus fracture.
1. Retromolar space
2. Perimeter of the cross-section just proximal to
the second molar
3. Breadth of the cross-section of the ramus
4. OT: oblique ridge thickness
5. Transgonial angle
6. Location of the ipsilateral mental foramen
In cadaveric models, it is seen that majority of
the angle fracture lines pass directly through the
third molar or its socket. The presence of an overall thin oblique ridge in fractured jaws suggests
that the retromolar space does act as an important
stress concentrator.
Further, mental foramen closer to the angle
region (and perhaps therefore a mandibular canal
coursing closer to the buccal surface) would act
as another stress concentrator disrupting cortical
bone integrity.
In the studies, it was seen that the population
with fractured angle of mandible consistently

possessed ramal and bodily cross-sections that
were stronger in bending, and a stronger ramus
and body could increase fracture risk by concentrating stress in the comparatively weaker angle
region between them, whereas the stress would
be more evenly distributed across the entire lateral jaw in the healthy population. A larger transgonial angle was associated with fracture which
corresponds to the gonial angle rather than concentration of stress by reducing the radius of curvature. The antegonial notch is simply too small
a feature to influence the overall classification of
angle fractures. Also the effect of ramus and body
length on the maximum moment during impact is
negligible [3].

13.2

Classification

13.2.1 Comprehensive AOCMF
Mandibular Fracture
Classification System
(Cornelius et al. [4])
13.2.1.1 Angle/Ramus Region
The angle region and the ramus region excluding the condylar and the coronoid processes
are merged into a single region. An irregular
pentagonal region extending distal to the third
molar and superiorly bounded by a gableshaped configuration with two straight lines
diverging from the centre of the mandibular
notch. The antero-­inferior line joins mandibular notch to the subcoronoid indentation. The
postero-inferior line joins mandibular notch to
the masseteric tuberosity notch. The important
landmark differentiating the body from angle/
ramus region is posterior transition zone (PTZ).
It is a vertical strip of the bone along the outlines of the third molar roots equivalent to the
width of the third molar crown. They are also
present bilaterally (right and left). In edentulous
mandible, PTZ is located in approximation with
the retromolar area.
The anterior boundary of the angle/ramus
region is congruent with the posterior transitional
zone; hence, the retromolar area is included
within the angle/ramus region (Fig. 13.4). A frac-

Spiessl Classification
Central Angle Fracture The “three screw
rule”, which implies placement of three screws
on the either side of the fracture line, helps us to
define the area between the inner and outer angle
of the centre region of the angle of mandible,
which aids in plate selection and the classification of fracture. The apex of the mandibular angle
marks the junction of the body and vertical
ramus. The average apical distance between the
outer and inner angle is constant even in the
edentulous jaw. Fractures located within these
boundaries are by definition central angle fractures. This region includes the alveolus of the
third molar, which forms a site of predilection for
the mandibular fractures.
Peripheral Angle Fracture (Angle-Body and
Angle-Ramus Fractures) A post-canine fracture that extends back into the angle region or a

U. S. Pal and R. Ganguly

Clinical Angle It is the junction between the
alveolar bone and the ramus at the origin of the
internal oblique line.
Surgical Angle It is the junction of the body of
the mandible and ramus at the origin of external
oblique line.

Fig. 13.8 Peripheral angle fracture

Angular Margin Fractures) Due to the immediate proximity of the angle and the lack of a
clear definition, a fracture at the level of the second molar is included in the category of angle
fractures. But from the standpoint of plate selection, it is helpful to use specific terms like preangular and supra-angular margin fracture. The
preangular margin fracture offers at least enough
space to accommodate a three-hole DCP or
EDCP length on each side of the fracture line.
Many supra-angular margin fractures are amenable to fixation with a tension band. Usually there
is sufficient space for a two-hole or four-hole
plate. Occasionally a six-hole plate may be
applied to the basal side. Plate selection is aided
by the orthopantomograph which can also be
used to identify preangular and supra-angular
zones.

1. Diffuse oedema along with ecchymosis.
2. Mucosal laceration.
3. Bleeding in the posterior buccal and lingual
vestibules.
4. Biangular fractures present with swelling and
trismus, tenderness at the mandibular angle,
palpation bilaterally and post-traumatic malocclusion (left posterior pre-contact) (Fig. 13.9).
5. Sometimes tooth fracture and mobility of the
third molar are also evident.

13.4

Management

Treatment of angle fracture depends on various
factors such as the nature of the fracture, amount
of bony buttress in the region, presence of concomitant fracture, etc.
Treatment of angle fracture is often challenging
as it has highest post-surgical complication rate in
all types of mandible fracture. Various treatment
methods from a simple maxillo mandibular fixation (MMF) to rigid fixation using plates or lag
screws, changed and modified from a traditional
to contemporary practice leading to better outcomes and fewer complication rates (Table 13.1).

in 19–53% of the time. The nerve can run as far as
1.2 cm below the inferior border of the mandible,
so to prevent it being injured, the planned incision
should be at least 2 cm below the inferior border of
the mandible [6].
