of Angle Fracture

13.6.1 Closed Reduction/MMF
In the contemporary practice, clinicians show less
interest towards MMF, but in undisplaced types
of fracture, it is still considered a suitable option.
They are mainly used in favourable angle fractures
as there is a minimal chance that the elevator mus-

Open methods are used to treat the majority of
angle fracture cases. There is a large amount
of variation in methods of open reduction and
internal fixation (ORIF) in terms of surgical
approaches and the method of fixation. As surgical approaches have been already discussed in
previous sections, now we will focus on different
fixation methods at angle region.

13.6.2.1

Various Fixation Methods

Single Plate at Superior Border
It is mainly according to Champy’s principle
using 2.0 mm non-compression plate at the
superior border over the external oblique ridge
or along the lateral aspect of the mandible to
act as a tension band. It serves as a method of
functionally stable or semi-rigid fixation. These
techniques show fewer complications and a less
invasive surgical approach to provide adequate
stability for satisfactory healing. The plates used
in this technique are easily adaptable that can be
fixed with the help of intraoral approach, causing a lower rate of infection and dehiscence, and
result in shorter operating time.
Two-Plate Technique
In this technique, two plates are used one at the
superior border which acts as a tension band and
one plate at the lower border which acts as a
compression band. When compared with singleplate technique, it provides more stability and
less stress at the fracture site. Screws placed at
the superior border are monocortical and at the
inferior border are bicortical screws. Various

210

studies showed that both one-plate and two-plate
technique yield similar result in terms of malocclusion, infection and wound dehiscence which
suggests the use of inferior plate insignificant [7].
The major drawback with inferior border plating is that it requires a more invasive extraoral
approach which can lead to the increased risk of
facial nerve injury, scarring and fibrosis.
Single-Plate at Inferior Border
Inferior border plating using extraoral approach
requires an extraoral approach. To stabilize
angle fracture by placing plate at the only inferior border often requires placement of 2.3 mm
plate or reconstruction plate. With the improved
outcome with superior border plating, the use of
single plate at the inferior border is less prevalent
in contemporary practice, but it is still useful in
cases where there is inadequate bone buttressing
or in cases of comminuted fracture, pathological
fracture or hardware failure.
Fixation with Lag Screws
It provides rigid fixation. The major debate in
favour of lag screw is that it provides a higher
degree of compression at the fracture site
with increased stability of fracture segments,
decreased treatment cost and minimized operating time. The main drawback of lag screw at
angle region is that its placement is technique
sensitive and shows a steep learning curve that
causes its decreased popularity.
Fixation with the Reconstruction Plate
AO reconstruction bone plate is a thicker and
stronger variety as compared to the standard AO/
ASIF compression plate. It comes in various sizes
and is three-dimensionally bendable, allowing it
to attain proper and accurate contouring to the
surface of the mandible. Three screws are used
on either side of the fracture line that provide
adequate neutralization of functional forces even
in the absence of compression [8]. It serves as a
method of rigid fixation and load-bearing osteosynthesis that provide adequate stability with
fewer complications. It is mainly used in the case

U. S. Pal and R. Ganguly

of patients who do not have adequate bone buttressing like edentulous patients or patient with
comminuted multiple bony segments. The main
drawback is the use of extraoral approach with
more exposure which can put facial nerve at risk.
Fixation with DCP and EDCP
Fixation technique mainly varies based on the
location of angle fracture such as central angle
fracture (within the defined region of the mandibular angle) is stabilized with reconstruction plate
with six or more holes or lag screw. Peripheral
angle fracture (starting outside the angle and terminating at the base of the angle region) is stabilized with a pre-shaped reconstruction plate with
six or more holes or with a basal plate and alveolar tension band or with an EDCP. The marginal
angle fracture is stabilized with a DCP or EDCP
with six or more holes in a preangular margin
fracture and a tension-band plate with two or
more holes (preferably applied through the intraoral route in a supra-angular margin fracture).
EDCP and DCP are c­ ompression plating system
which is rarely preferred in contemporary maxillofacial practice as compression osteosynthesis
may cause bond end pressure necrosis that can
lead to hardware failure.
Fixation with 3D Plates
They are square or rectangular plates recently
introduced in contemporary maxillofacial practice. These plates are fixed on the lateral aspect of
the angle of mandible with the help of monocortical screws (Fig. 13.15). As compared to 2.0 mm
miniplates, they show superior resistance to torsional forces or out-of-the-plane movements [9].
Various studies showed favourable outcome with
low complication rates with 3D plates, and also
there is barely any report of malunion or non-­
union [10, 11].
Fixation with Bioresorbable Plates
Bioresorbable plates are rarely preferred in the
treatment of mandibular angle fracture as angle
region has a very large amount of muscular pull
which cannot be controlled with low-strength

13

Angle and Ramus Fractures

bioresorbable plates. However, in paediatric
angle fracture, it is a considerable option.

13.7

Consideration of Tooth
in the Line of Angle Fracture

Previously, the third molar tooth which is present in
the line of an angle fracture is believed to promote
infection as intraoral communication may allow
ingress of bacteria-laden saliva or other oral fluids [12]. However, in contemporary practice, protocols for managing tooth in line of fracture have
been modified. Here are the absolute indications
for extraction of the third molar tooth present in the
fracture line: (1) damaged tooth which are nonrestorable, (2) tooth having grade II or III mobility,
(3) presence of periapical pathology and (4) tooth
interfering with reduction of fracture segments [13].

13.8

Paediatric Considerations

Fractures at angle proximal to tooth-bearing area
are not sufficiently immobilized with splint alone
so closed reduction and intermaxillary fixation for
3 weeks are required. When tightening splints, sawing of wire through the mandible has to be avoided.
When a mandibular angle fracture occurs in
the presence of a condyle fracture, the combined
forces may be significant enough to cause displacement unless open reduction and internal fixation
(ORIF) at the angle fracture is carried out. Plating
at the tension-band zone is not recommended in
the mixed dentition (Fig. 13.16). In open reduction
for less than 5 years, it is possible to injure tooth
buds near angle when placing intraosseous wire or
screws which require caution.
Decreased height of the mandibular ramus and
body and alveolus may occur after fracture of hori-

212

U. S. Pal and R. Ganguly

zontal ramus of the mandible, if teeth are lost due
to injury or hardware through tooth buds. Earlier
most of the paediatric cases were treated with conservative measures or closed reduction techniques.
Only recently have the distinct advantages of
accurate primary repair and the stable fixation of
facial fractures been applied to the rehabilitation
of injuries in children too [14]. With the advent
of better investigative facilities like CT scan and
3D reconstruction and newer airway management
techniques with reliable anaesthesia techniques
and specifically introduction of mini- and microplates, open reduction and fixation of paediatric
facial fractures is getting commoner.
Also, resorbable materials have been made
available as a fixation option for paediatric craniomaxillofacial fracture management. According
to Peterson with the exception of mandibular
condyle fractures, judicious use of ORIF is preferable to the closed reduction and immobilization
techniques with splints when treating fractures in
the deciduous and mixed dentition.

13.9

Geriatric Considerations

Maxillomandibular fixation (MMF) becomes
a difficult task in cases with sparse or absent
dentition, and the complexity increases in geriatric patients. Decreased blood supply, atrophy
of ridges, reduced healing potential and lack
of definitive occlusal surfaces to capitalize on
for fracture reduction and MMF are the most
notable limitations in such cases. The difficulty
further increases in the presence of an underlying systemic bone condition like osteoporo-

sis. The treatment plan must be individualized
depending on the bone available, degree of
comminution, availability of dentures, medical
comorbidities including smoking and patient
preferences.
The solutions to overcome problems in an
edentulous mandible are to create an occlusal
guidance by either existing dentures or by fabricating intraoral splints to guide in reduction of
jaws in correct alignment. Cortical screw technique is not new, however; according to some
authors, it is rarely applied. A modification of
the cortical screws is to use MMF screws. These
screws are not completely inserted, and 4–5 mm
of these screws is left outside the bone level to
allow tie wires to pass around them. Some of
the authors recommend a minimum bone height
of 10 mm and do not recommend it in the maxilla and mandible. Bruce and Ellis concluded
that the optimal treatment for this kind of fractures is open reduction accompanied by stable
fixation with large osteosynthesis plates [15].
Periosteum removal in order to place the osteosynthesis material seems not to be a problem as
far as the plate is strong enough to support mandibular biomechanical forces. However, when
periosteum is detached, it is performed on the
vestibular cortical bone only, without injuring
the lingual periosteum. Interestingly, edentulous
mandibles have the advantage that they do not
require a strict anatomical alignment of the fracture fragments. Bone grafting is recommended
in situations where there is great loss of bony
tissue caused by comminution or debridement
of infected tissue or when treating nonconsolidated fractures (Fig. 13.17) [16].

13.10 Conclusion
Fractures of the angle of mandible are one of the
common facial fractures. However, managing
angle fractures is one of the challenging tasks and
its management is also a matter of debate. The
main controversy exists in terms of anatomical
aspects and also due to the complex biomechanics
of angle fracture. There are a number of methods
of fixation that exist in contemporary practice,
but choosing the most suitable one is still a matter
of debate. However, the most acceptable option is
single miniplate at the superior border which is
according to Champy’s principle, but when associated with other fractures, the other site should
be fixed with rigid fixation. The decision to use
antibiotics and extraction of tooth in the line of
fracture should be done according to individual
cases.

13.11 Case Discussion
Chief Complaint A 25-year-old male patient
reported with a chief complaint of pain and
inability to chew since 1 day from then.

History of Presenting Illness The patient gave
history of road traffic accident the previous day.
The patient was well oriented to time, place and
person and did not have any history of loss of
consciousness, vomiting, ENT bleeding, seizures
or any associated injury.
Past Medical History No history of any chronic
illness such as diabetes mellitus, hypertension,
asthma, etc.
Clinical Examination Extraoral examination
revealed facial swelling on the right angle of
mandible region and multiple abrasions over the
face. Intraoral examination revealed mobility of
the mandible, with step at the parasymphysis
region, along with occlusal derangement.
Investigation CT face with 3D reconstruction
was advised, which showed fracture of the right
angle region along with fracture at the left parasymphysis of mandible (Fig. 13.18).
Treatment The patient was intubated nasally
and put under general anaesthesia. Both the fracture sites were exposed intraorally and reduced
anatomically. It was decided to fix the mandibular

Condylar Fractures
Vidya Rattan

14.1

Introduction

Mandibular condyle is fractured in 25–30% cases
following trauma to the face. Aetiology, pattern
and prevalence of condylar fractures may vary
with geographical location. Condylar fracture
may involve only the condyle or can be associated with other fractures of mandible and facial
region. Historically, these have been managed
with closed management techniques because of
the risk of injury to facial nerve with open surgical techniques. The results with conservative
management techniques have been satisfactory.
Over the last two decades, there have been
advancements in the form of better understanding of biomechanics, newer surgical techniques
for getting access to condyle, newer geometric
plates for fixation, use of navigation-­guided surgery and virtual surgical planning. Therefore,
there is increasing trend to manage these fractures with open surgery.
Even with the newer advancement, managing
these fractures is challenging because of difficulty in accurate reduction and fixation due to
difficult access and availability of less stock of
bone. Managing these fractures in children needs

V. Rattan (*)
Unit of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery, Oral Health
Sciences Centre, Postgraduate Institute of Medical
Education and Research, Chandigarh, India

special consideration because of growth considerations and risk of ankylosis of the temporomandibular joint.
This chapter would formulate a rational
approach for managing these fractures and discuss newer developments in this field.

14.2

Surgical Anatomy
of the Condyle

The condylar process of mandible articulates with
the glenoid fossa at the skull base to form temporomandibular joint (TMJ) (Fig. 14.1).
Biconcave articular disc divides the joint into
upper and lower joint space. Disc acts as cushion
and aids in smooth movements of joint.
Masticatory muscles move both the joints in synchronous fashion and are responsible for mouth
opening and closing and lateral and protrusive
excursions. Condylar process consists of condylar
head, neck and base. Mediolateral dimension of
condylar head is double (15–20 mm) as compared
to anteroposterior dimension (8–10 mm). This
makes it more vulnerable to sagittal fractures.
Condylar base is quite thin mediolaterally making
it prone to fractures (Fig. 14.2). This provides protection to the brain by avoiding transmission of
forces towards the glenoid fossa. The screws used
for fixation of fractures in this region should not
be longer than 4–6 mm; otherwise, structures
lying on the medial side may get injured.

V. Rattan

TMJ capsule is lined with synovial tissues and
is thickened on medial and lateral side to form
lateral and medial capsular ligaments. Synovial
fluid is responsible for providing nutrition to disc
and articular surfaces. Sphenomandibular and
stylomandibular ligaments also check excessive
movements of joint. Lateral pterygoid muscle has
got a superior head and an inferior head. Superior
head is attached to TMJ disc and the inferior head
is attached at pterygoid fovea. Pull of the lateral
pterygoid muscle is responsible for anteromedial
displacement of the fractured segment. Masseter
and medial pterygoid muscle envelope the ramus
of mandible on the lateral and medial side.
Undisplaced fractures of ramus can heal very
well even without fixation because of this
envelope.
Vascular supply to TMJ is by the branches of
superficial temporal artery and maxillary artery
(Fig. 14.3). Attachment of muscles, capsule and
ligaments is a primary source of blood supply to
the condylar head. Condylar process apart from
periosteal perforators is primarily supplied by
medullary branch of inferior alveolar artery
which runs in superior direction intraosseously
towards the head. The small fractured fragments
of condyle after detachment from muscles often
undergo resorption and avascular necrosis due to
loss of blood supply. Similarly, removal of condylar process for extraarticular fixation may lead
to resorption of condyle.
Maxillary artery lies on the medial side of the
condylar neck. One should be careful while using
drill for making holes for screws in this region.
The drill should not pass too deep. The foramen
spinosum, carotid canal and jugular foramen are
in close relationship to the head on the medial
side (Fig. 14.4). Blunt shearing trauma may cause
damage to the vessels passing through these
foramina. One should be careful and not overlook injury to these structures while examining
patients with condylar fractures.
Facial nerve and its branches lie within the
parotid gland over the lateral surface of ramus of
mandible. During surgical approaches to expose

14.3

Aetiology

Road traffic accidents, falls and interpersonal
violence are the leading cause for condylar fractures. Causes for the condylar fracture may vary
due to geographical location, age and gender.
Children are more prone to fractures from falland sports-related injury, whereas in the adults, it
could be road traffic accidents. In a large study
involving over 12,700 cases of facial fracture in
children, 21% involved condyle [1]. Fracture site
and mechanism of injury varied based on gender
and age. Male-to-female ratio varied from 4:1.
Direct trauma to the chin results in transmission
of forces towards condylar process. Depending
on vector and impact of force, fracture of condylar process occurs at the weakest point. It is not
uncommon to see laceration over chin region and

facial widening which is difficult to correct
secondarily.

condyle may be pushed into intracranial fossa.
Anterior bony wall of external auditory canal
may get fractured and pushed posteriorly leading
to stenosis of the canal. There may be hypoacusia
due to obstruction caused by blood clot or stenosis of canal.
The patients with facial fractures are prone to
sudden head rotation and hyperextension of the
neck during impact. Condylar fractures and combined midfacial fractures are independent risk
factors for blunt cerebrovascular injuries. In highvelocity trauma, there may be injury to branches
of internal carotid artery and vertebral artery in its
extracranial and intracranial course. Blunt cerebrovascular injuries may present as late bleeding
and stroke even after a few days after the injury.
There may be associated injury to the cervical
spine and its structures. If injuries to these vital
structures are not diagnosed and managed early,
there can be potentially life-­threatening consequences and permanent disability.

Diagnostic Aids

The goal of any diagnostic evaluation of the
patient is to establish a definitive diagnosis and
provide the most appropriate and evidencebased treatment approach. The following diagnostic aids can be used to formulate a definitive
diagnosis.
Plain Radiographs Historically, plain radiographs such as posteroanterior view and lateral
obliques have been used to see the condylar process. There is difficulty in visualising fracture of
condyle due to overlapping of the structures.
Transcranial, transpharyngeal and plain tomograms
have been attempted to delineate the structures.
Reverse Towne’s view is a good radiograph for the
purpose of initial screening, and it can show mediolateral deviation of condylar process (Fig. 14.8).

Computerised Tomography
Scan (CT) and Cone Beam
Computerised Tomography
(CBCT)

CT scan is a gold standard and method of choice
for evaluating bony injuries. It gives exact location of bony fragments in all the three planes.
Three-dimensional reconstruction is possible to
visualise the structures (Fig. 14.10). CBCT is
gaining popularity for evaluating bony injuries of
maxillofacial area because of less radiation exposure. The main drawback of CT and CBCT is that
it does not show injury to soft tissue component
of temporomandibular joint. Portable CT and
CBCT machines are also available which can be
used intraoperatively to assess reduction and
fixation.

tissue components of temporomandibular joint
(Fig. 14.11a, b). Static and dynamic imaging protocols can be used to see joint effusion, haemar-

radiologist or clinician is required to delineate

14.8

Computerised Tomographic
Angiography (CTA)

Patients with thoracic injuries, cervical injuries,
intracranial haemorrhage and high-energy trauma
should have high suspicion for blunt cerebrovascular
injury (BCVI). These patients should be subjected to
CTA so that diagnosis of BCVI may not be missed.

14.9

Diagnostic
Temporomandibular Joint
(TMJ) Arthroscopy

TMJ arthroscopy is used for diagnosing internal
derangement of TMJ. TMJ arthroscopy has got
limited role in acute trauma setting in diagnosing
disc injury or displacement. Oedema, joint effusion and haemarthrosis make arthroscopy more
difficult. There are more chances of complications
and iatrogenic damage to joint structures even by
an experienced operator in acute trauma setting.

14.10 Classification of Condylar
Fracture
Condylar fractures have been classified by various researchers such as Wassmund (1934),
McLennan (1952), Rowe and Killey (1955),

Dingman and Natvig (1966) and Spiessl and
Schroll (1977) based on fracture location, displacement, deviation, dislocation and ramus
shortening [2]. Lindahl (1977) gave most comprehensive classification system based on all the
above-mentioned four factors. Ellis et al. in 1999
and Loukota et al. in 2005 also attempted to classify condylar fractures based on location and displacement [3]. AO Foundation comprehensive
system in 2010 divided the condylar fractures into
head, neck and base fractures. Bhagol et al. in
2011 classified subcondylar fractures based on
ramus shortening and displacement [4]. The comprehensive AOCMF classification by Neff et al.
(2014) though accurate is too complex for clinical
applications [5]. Therefore, most of the classifications are complex and difficult to remember.
There has also been confusion in terminologies
because of language differences in native Englishspeaking and other countries. The purpose of this
chapter is not to give a review of available classification systems, but attempt has been made to
standardise terminology and formulate a clinical
oriented classification, which is easy to communicate and helps in treatment decisions.
The first step is to define the location of fracture by drawing various lines as shown in
Fig. 14.12. The second step is to define the relation of fractured segments to each other and glenoid fossa in the form of deviation, displacement

14

Condylar Fractures

225

condylar neck. This can be further divided into
two equal halves: high neck and low neck.
Relation of Fractured Segments Defining relation of fractured segments is an important step
because it helps in decision-making whether the
given fracture should be managed with closed or
open treatment. Fracture segments can be deviated, displaced or dislocated.

Fig. 14.12 Lateral view of ramus of mandible showing

Location of Fracture Based on location, condylar fractures can be divided into four types: condylar base, condylar head, condylar low neck and
condylar high neck. Defining location of fracture
is an important step as it helps in communication
and determining whether enough bone is available
for applying osteosynthesis material.
Condylar Base Fracture To determine the location of fracture, an imaginary line is drawn parallel to posterior border of ramus. Loukota suggested
drawing a perpendicular line to this line passing
through the deepest point at the sigmoid notch.
Fractures running below Loukota line are labelled
as condylar base fracture (Fig. 14.12).
Condylar head is defined by two parallel lines,
one at the top and one at the inferior border of
condylar head.
Condylar Neck Fractures The area between
condylar head and condylar base is known as

Deviation Condylar fracture is deviated when
two fractured ends remain in contact with each
other. Degree of deviation is determined on coronal plane. Imaginary lines are drawn along the
long axis of ramus and long axis of fractured condylar process. Angle formed between these two
lines determines the deviation of fractured condylar process (Fig. 14.13a–c):
1. 0–15°
2. 15–45°
3. More than 45°
Displacement When there is loss of contact
between two fractured ends, the fracture is considered as displaced. Displacement of condyle
can be on the medial side or lateral side
(Fig. 14.14). Evaluation of displacement helps in
determining difficulty of reduction and selection
of approach for exposure of condyle. Medially
displaced fractures are difficult to reduce because
of difficult access.
Dislocation Dislocation defines relation of
condylar process with glenoid fossa. When fractured condylar process is out of glenoid fossa, it
is labelled as dislocated fracture (Fig. 14.15).
Most common dislocation is in anteromedial
direction because of pull of lateral pterygoid
muscle. But other types of dislocations such as
lateral, superolateral and posterior dislocation
do happen.
Ramus Shortening Other important factor in
clinical decision-making regarding closed vs
open management is to determine the amount of
ramus shortening. The height of ramus can be
measured and compared on orthopantomogram
(OPG), CT or plain posteroanterior (PA) radio-

14.12 Biomechanics of Fractured
Condyle
Forces of mastication during jaw movement lead
to compressive and tensile forces on the mandible. Due to fracture of the condyle, there are neuromuscular, skeletal and dental adaptations to
compensate these forces. There is increased masseter activity on the non-fracture side and
decrease in activity on fractured side during mastication to transfer the load away from injured
site [7]. These adaptations and dental compensations can be reduced by open reduction and internal fixation with suitable osteosynthesis.
Meyers et al. did experimental studies on photoelastic analysis of bone deformation in the
region of mandibular condyle during mastication
[8]. They consistently found compressive stress
pattern along the posterior border of the ramus
and tensile stress pattern along the anterior border
of the ramus and in zone situated below the sigmoid notch (Fig. 14.18). These results are consistent with poor clinical experience of fixation of
fractures of condylar process with single plate at
the posterior border. Therefore, they recommended the need of osteosynthesis plates in the

Fig. 14.18 Drawing showing direction of tensile strain
on the lateral surface of mandible during mastication

14

Condylar Fractures

region close to tensile strain and designed a trapezoidal plate in the year 2007 for fixation of condylar base and neck fractures. Since then, many
geometrical shapes of plates have been designed
for the fixation of base and neck fractures. Two
individual plates are gold standard, but fixation of
two plates in the condylar neck area can be very
demanding and is not always possible. Delta
plate, trapezoidal plate, shaped plate, lambda
plate and tripartite design-shaped plates can serve
the purpose. These plates are easy to fix because
of limited footprint and ease of handling. One disadvantage of small footprint plates is that screws
are placed in thin bone of condylar neck and base
area. The screw may traverse through the fracture
line due to obliquity of fracture line or may not
hold because of thin bone. At least two or more
than two screws are a must in each fracture segment to gain sufficient fixation.

14.14 Closed Treatment
Condylar fractures heal very well even without
fixation and non-union is rarely seen. The closed
treatment concept is based on adaptation capability of TMJ and neuromuscular system. Malposition
of disc does not affect occlusion; with appropriate
physical therapy, good function and mobility of
joint can be achieved. Indications for closed treatment are:

1. Minimally deviated/undisplaced condylar
fracture (less than 15°)
2. Ramus shortening less than 5 mm

Functional Treatment The patients who have
deranged occlusion and need guidance to close in
normal occlusion can be best treated with functional treatment. Occlusion is achieved with the
help of elastics placed onto the arch bars
(Fig. 14.19). Guiding elastics help in adapting
remodelling tissues with functional load without
the deleterious effects of maxillomandibular fixation. Patient can open the mouth and can have

soft diet. The direction of elastics is such that it
brings retruded mandible forwards. The duration
of guiding elastics may vary from few weeks to
months depending upon neuromuscular adaptation capacity of individual. The patient is weaned
off elastics slowly. When the patient can occlude
normally without guidance, elastics should be
taken off during day and are used only during
night. Slowly the patient is also weaned off from
use of elastics at night. Once the patient is able to
occlude normally and able to open without deviation, the arch bars can be removed. Functional
treatment can achieve promising results and
avoids the risk of surgery and discomfort of
MMF (Fig. 14.20).

Closed Management with Maxillomandibular
Fixation (MMF) Maxillomandibular fixation
offers no advantage over functional treatment for
management of condylar fractures, and it should
be avoided because of its deleterious effects. It
causes degenerative changes in the fibrocartilage
of joint and delays return to pre-traumatic function. Condylar head fractures with loss of vertical
height and displacement of disc have increased
risk of developing TMJ ankylosis following
MMF. TMJ ankylosis as a complication of condylar base and neck fractures is less frequent.
Children with severe crush injuries with extensive damage to capsule and disc have very high
chances of developing ankylosis (Fig. 14.35).
Therefore, the period of immobilisation should
be minimised to 7–10 days, and prolonged MMF
should be avoided.

14.15 Open Surgical Reduction
and Fixation
Over the years, various position papers, systematic reviews and consensus conferences have
tried to solve the controversy of closed vs open
management of condylar fractures [10–12]. It has
been concluded that surgical treatment can provide faster recovery and better functional and
morphological outcome because of exact anatomical reduction and rigid internal fixation.
Therefore, it is becoming a preferred choice for
managing condylar fractures.
Surgical management of condylar injuries is
challenging and difficult as compared to other
mandible fractures. Reasons for these challenges
are because of proximity of facial nerve and maxillary artery, limited access for surgery, failure to

14.16 Indications for Open
Reduction
1. Condylar fractures accompanied with major
deviation, displacement and dislocation
2. When there is associated shortening of ramus
more than 5 mm
3. When the occlusion cannot be guided
because of interference by the fracture or if
there is dropping back of mandible because
of lack of a posterior stop

The main aim of any surgical approach is to give
good access with minimal morbidity and complications. Surgical incision to be used depends upon
the location of fracture, comfort level and experience of operator. Low condylar neck and basal
fractures can be approached through retromandibular, submandibular, periangular or intra-­oral
incisions. The condylar head and upper neck fractures can be approached through preauricular,
endaural or retroauricular incisions (Fig. 14.21).
Submandibular Approach This approach
gives good access to angle and low basal fractures of condyle. The 4–5-cm-long incision is
given 1.5–2 cm below the inferior border of mandible. Undermining is done in subcutaneous
plane to expose platysma muscle. Platysma is
incised with dissecting scissors to expose the
superficial layer of deep cervical fascia over the
submandibular gland. The marginal mandibular
nerve should be looked in this plane, and careful
dissection is done to identify it and retract it
superiorly. Other useful method to protect the
nerve is Hayes-Martin manoeuvre in which after

Retromandibular Approaches A 3–4 cm skin
incision is started 5 mm below the pinna in retromandibular crease parallel to the posterior border
of mandible. Other shape of skin incisions can be
a combination of auricular and retromandibular
or in the form of rhytidectomy incision (incision
lines 3 and 4 in Fig. 14.21). Further dissection
planes can be different depending upon the handling of parotid gland.
Transparotid approach utilises the area
between the buccal and zygomatic branch of
facial nerve. After dissecting the parotid fascia,
blunt dissection is done parallel to facial nerve
branches through the parotid tissues and masseter

233

muscle to expose the bone. This way, direct
access can be gained to condylar base and neck
fractures (Fig. 14.22a–d). In a study by Ellis
et al., of the 93 patients operated on through a
retromandibular approach, 17.2% developed
temporary atony of the facial nerve, and they all
recovered within 6 months [13].
Other approach is retroparotid approach in
which parotid gland is retracted superiorly without transgressing it. The rest of dissection is like
submandibular approach. This approach gives
limited access to neck area. Reduction of fracture
and placement of superior screws are challenging. A trocar can be used to place superior screws.
The advantage with retroparotid approach is that
there are fewer chances of facial nerve injury and
parotid fistula formation.
In transmasseteric anterior parotid approach,
dissection is done superficial to parotid fascia
in anterior direction till the anterior border of
the parotid. Parotid gland is retracted posteriorly to expose masseter muscle, and then the
muscle and periosteum over the condyle are
incised to expose the bone. If any branch of
facial nerve is seen, it can be carefully dissected
and retracted superiorly (Fig. 14.22e, f). This
approach gives good access to the upper neck
and base of condyle.
Preauricular Approach This approach gives
good access to condylar head and upper neck.
The skin incision is given at the junction of
auricular and facial skin crease in front of the
pinna. Extension of skin incision over temple
region in a question mark shape can be done to
achieve wide exposure. Avascular plane of dissection just anterior to auricular cartilage is utilised to deepen the dissection till deep temporal
fascia. The flap is raised anteriorly in the plane
of loose areolar tissue. Zygomatic and temporal
branches of facial nerve cross the zygomatic
arch 0.8–3.5 cm anterior to external auditory
meatus. Dissection plane deep to deep temporal
fascia prevents damage to facial nerve branches.
Incision over root of zygoma is given to expose
the bone. The whole of the flap in subperiosteal
plane is retracted anteriorly to expose the zygomatic bone. TMJ capsule is identified and

Endoscopic-Assisted Intra-Oral Approach The
condyle is approached through intra-oral incision
over ascending ramus. Basal and low-neck fractures can be accessed through this approach.
Special set of endoscopic instruments are required
to visualise the lateral surface of condyle
(Figs. 14.24 and 14.25). This approach is best
suited for laterally displaced condylar fractures.
Right-angled screwdriver is required to insert the
screws (Fig. 14.26). Alternatively, screws can be
fixed through the trocar of transbuccal set. This
approach has the advantage of leaving no extra
oral scar, and there is no risk to facial nerve
branches. This technique requires specialised
training to use endoscopic instruments and has a
steep learning curve for achieving hand-eye coordination. It may take more time to reduce and fix
fractures as compared to other direct techniques.
The fractures which are dislocated or medially displaced are difficult to manage with this technique.

There are many options to fix the condylar process fractures. It varies from wire osteosynthesis,
lag screw fixation, use of K wire, titanium plates
and screw and resorbable plates and pins.
Currently, titanium plates and screws are the
method of choice.
Single Plate Fixation Single plate along the
posterior border has been used traditionally for

b

Fig. 14.25 Endoscopic view of the condylar process. (a) Laterally displaced fracture exposed through endoscopic-­
assisted intra-oral approach. (b) Fracture fixed with the help of geometric plate

Fig. 14.26 Right-angled screwdriver for insertion of

the fixation of condylar fractures. The posterior
border of condyle is biomechanically disadvantageous site as there are compressive forces in this
region. According to biomechanical principles of
osteosynthesis, plate for fixation should be placed
in tensile zone. The bone at sigmoid notch area is
quite thin and does not hold screws very well.
Single plate does not counteract torsional forces.
When single plate is used for fixation, there can
be fracture of plate, screw loosening, malpositioning of segments and infection. Whenever
single plate is used for fixation, one should use
2.0 or 2.4 mm system plate with bicortical screws
with at least two screws on each side (Fig. 14.27).
At the end of procedure for fixation, stability of
fractured segments should be checked clinically.
If there is any discrepancy in fixation, one may
resort to MMF for a period of 7–10 days.
Two-Plate Fixation Fixation with two plates is
the best strategy for managing condylar fractures.
Two plates can counteract tensile forces, compressive forces and torsional forces acting on the
condyle. For best results, each plate should have
minimum of two screws on each side of the fracture. Bicortical screws of appropriate length
should be used, and these should not project too
far on medial side of the ramus. The only disadvantage while using two plates is that wide exposure is needed and large area is required to place
two plates, which may not be available in certain
configuration of fractures.

Fig. 14.27 Low-neck fracture fixed with the help of
2.0 mm single plate. Note that screws are of appropriate
length, engaging both the cortices but not penetrating too
far medially

Geometrical Plates Over the past two decades,
plates in various geometric shapes have been
designed by companies which have small footprint and have biomechanical advantage of countering tensile and torsional forces. These shapes
vary from delta, trapezoidal, A-shaped, lambda,
tripartite design and strut plates (Figs. 14.28 and
14.29). These plates have been found to resist
mechanical forces in various finite element analysis studies and have satisfactory results in clinical studies [14]. The advantage of these shapes is
that these are easy to handle through small exposure and require only two to three screws for fixation in condylar neck area as compared to four
screws in two-plate technique. Geometric plates
are a preferred choice for fixation while using
endoscopic-assisted techniques because of ease
of handling.

V. Rattan

condylar base. (b) Fixation done with a delta plate

Fig. 14.29 Photograph showing various geometric plate
designs for fixation of condylar process fractures

Resorbable Plates and Screws These plates
have advantage that second surgery is not required
for their removal. Resorbable mesh fixed with the
help of ultrasonic-activated pins (SonicWeld, KLS
Martin, Germany) has been used successfully to
treat condylar fractures (Fig. 14.31). Their use is
not widely accepted, and these plates and screws
have not been found suitable to resist mechanical
forces in experimental studies. Their use warrants
further clinical studies.
Extracorporeal Fixation Sometimes when
there is difficulty in reduction and fixation due
to gross displacement and small size, the sur-

geon in frustration may remove the condyle and
fix the plate on the proximal segment extracorporeally. Such procedure needs to be discouraged because there is complete loss of
vascularity and condyle may undergo partial or
complete resorption.

14.19 Management of Condylar
Head Fractures
Management of condylar head fractures needs
special considerations. Intracapsular fractures traditionally have been managed with closed treatment methods. Over the last decade, there have
been reports of fixing these fractures with the help
of long titanium screws or with resorbable screws
and pins. Open treatment has the advantage of
anatomical reduction favouring early recovery
and better function. There are no comparative
studies with long-term follow-up to prove the
superiority of one method over the other.

14.20 Management of Condylar
Fractures in Children
Condylar fractures in children are not uncommon.
Children below the age of 3 years have short condylar neck. Therefore, they have more tendencies
to suffer from fractures of condylar head. Children
have growing skeleton, and due to growth concerns, it is imperative that condylar fractures in
children need to be managed accurately to avoid
potential long-term complications.
Children below the age of 12 years have good
regenerating and bone remodelling capability, and
conservative management has shown very good
results. Even severely displaced fractures do
undergo remodelling, and on a long-term follow­up, normal condylar anatomy is observed. Severe
impact can lead to crushing of condylar head,
leading to comminution. Severe impact also causes
damage to TMJ disc and capsule. The disc can be
crushed, perforated or displaced. Condylar head
fractures with medial displacement of fractured
segment and lateral displacement/dislocation of
distal segment can result in ramus shortening.
Such type of injury is the leading cause of TMJ
ankylosis (Fig. 14.35). In these cases, MMF should
not be done, rather patient is encouraged to do
active physiotherapy to decrease the chances of
TMJ ankylosis (Fig. 14.34). Any occlusal derangement and deviation on opening can be corrected
with the help of guiding elastics. Arch bars can be
easily placed even in primary dentition for this
purpose. Minor occlusal discrepancies in primary
or mixed dentition are acceptable as these get corrected by itself due to developing occlusion.
As the child enters teenage years, remodelling
capability of the condyle decreases. The decision
for open treatment is based on the same algorithm as for adults. Wherever possible, closed
treatment should be preferred over open treatment in growing skeleton. The children should be
followed up periodically to monitor growth and
signs of development of TMJ ankylosis. If any
problem occurs, it needs to be identified and
managed early.

Fig. 14.34 Active jaw physiotherapy with the help of
Therabite appliance to decrease the chances of ankylosis.
Active jaw physiotherapy can be started after a few weeks
of injury

Fig. 14.35 Extensive damage to TMJ disc and capsule
during condylar injury has led to bilateral ankylosis

14.21 Associated Other Fractures
of Mandible and Face
When condylar fractures are accompanied by
other fractures of mandible such as symphysis,
body or angle region, these need special considerations for management. Accompanying frac-

244

tures need to be reduced and fixed rigidly to
achieve the desired goals (Fig. 14.28b). Now
question arises which fracture needs to be fixed
first. Fixation of concomitant mandibular fracture first may hinder in reduction of severely
medially displaced fracture. The logical sequence
to be followed is to expose both the fractures, and
attempt is made to reduce them. If reduction is
stable, any of the fractures can be fixed first. If
reduction is unstable, then it can be maintained at
one end with a temporary fixing device such as
wire or loosely fixed plate.
Bilateral condylar fractures with symphyseal
fractures usually have ramus shortening and
increase in bigonial width. If these fractures are
not managed properly, it can lead to permanent
deformity, which is very difficult to correct by
secondary corrective procedures. In these cases,
vertical height is restored by proper anatomic
reduction and rigid fixation of condyles. Gonial
width is controlled by applying medial pressure
on both angle regions while fixing the symphyseal fracture. A close watch is kept on lingual
side of the lower border to achieve perfect
reduction. Even minimal discrepancy in reduction on lingual cortex is magnified in angle
region.
All deviated/displaced condylar fractures as a
part of panfacial fractures should be accurately
reduced and rigidly fixed to achieve normal facial
vertical height, width and projection.

14.22 Avoidance of Complications
of Open Reduction

V. Rattan

facial approaches. Thorough knowledge of anatomy, identifying and preserving the nerve
branches, avoidance of use of monopolar diathermy near the branches and avoiding excessive
forces during retraction avoid injury to facial
nerve branches. Majority of time, the paresis of
facial nerve branches is temporary, and complete
recovery occurs over a period of weeks to months.
Sialocele and Parotid Fistula Transparotid
approaches to condyle may lead to post-operative
sialocele or parotid fistula formation. Meticulous
suturing of parotid fascia, tight pressure bandage
and use of anti-sialagogues in post-operative
period avoid these complications.
Infection Use of perioperative antibiotics,
maintenance of aseptic surgical technique and
rigid stable fixation avoid the chances of
infection.
Malocclusion Accurate reduction and stable
fixation should be achieved to avoid this complication. Guiding elastics can be used to settle
minor deviation and malocclusion. Major discrepancy can be treated with orthodontic treatment or orthognathic surgery.
Chronic Pain and Temporomandibular
Disorders (TMD) Chronic pain and TMD following fracture management usually improve
with passage of time. Conservative management
such as analgesics, physiotherapy, transcutaneous nerve stimulation and occlusal splints may be
used to relieve symptoms.

Ankylosis Severe trauma associated with extensive damage to disc and joint capsule may lead to
ankylosis of TMJ. It is more common in children
but can occur in adults as well. Early mobilisation
and jaw physiotherapy may decrease the chances
of its development (Figs. 14.34 and 14.35). In
children, it can lead to growth problems.
Damage to Facial Nerve Branches There is Therefore, it needs to be diagnosed and managed
inherent risk to facial nerve branches with trans-­ early to prevent severe facial deformity.
Scar Scars though well-hidden are essential part
of trans-facial approaches. Taking incision in
skin crease or parallel to skin creases makes the
scar less conspicuous. Use of intra-oral
endoscopic-­
assisted technique avoids external
scars on the face.

14

Condylar Fractures

Growth Disturbance Trauma to growing children can lead to undergrowth or overgrowth of
mandible. There should be frequent follow-up to
monitor growth. Early orthodontic intervention
should be sought if any discrepancy in growth is
identified.
Condylar Resorption Post-traumatic avascular
necrosis may lead to partial or complete resorption of condyle leading to facial asymmetry and
deviation on opening. In certain cases, total
autogenous or alloplastic reconstruction of joint
may be required.

245

Stenosis of External Auditory Canal (EAC)
Fractures of bony wall of the auditory canal when
posteriorly displaced can cause stenosis and partial hearing loss. Proper diagnosis on CT and
appropriate management with packing of canal
during primary management avoid this
complication.

Haemarthrosis and joint effusion after trauma to
the joint are universally present (Fig. 14.36).
These do not require any management and
self-­

resolve with passage of time. Increasing
attention is being given to disc position in traumatic injuries. Improved MRI protocols can pick
up these injuries. Based on MRI findings,
Tripathi and Sharma have classified the articular
soft tissue injuries into four types: Grade I (haemarthrosis only), Grade II (haemarthrosis and
disc displacement), Grade III (haemarthrosis,
disc displacement and capsular tear), and Grade
IV (disc perforation in association with Grade I,
II or III) [16].
In majority of cases, accurate reduction of
condylar head in relation to glenoid fossa automatically repositions the disc into correct anatomic relation. Joint can function normally even
without intervening the disc. In 30–40% of normal population, disc is found to be anteromedially displaced on MRI examination. Therefore, it
is difficult to make out whether the disc displacement is because of current trauma or it was
already displaced.
However, there is an attempt by many surgeons for concomitant repair of soft tissues by
suturing retrodiscal tissues and repositioning
the disc with the help of Mitek anchors. Until
now, the relation between soft tissue injuries

Fig. 14.37 Intraoperative CT scan being taken to confirm the accuracy of reduction on operation table

V. Rattan

and type of condylar trauma and their influence on clinical outcome has been insufficiently investigated. Before considering
reduction of soft tissues next to reduction of
the fracture, more research is needed into the
impact of soft tissue injuries on oral functioning [17, 18].

14.24 Advances in Condylar
Fracture Management
Use of Intraoperative Imaging Portable CT
scan or CBCT machine is ideal for intraoperative
imaging (Fig. 14.37). It gives accurate picture in
all the three dimensions. The use of intraoperative imaging for confirmation of accuracy of
reduction and fixation can avoid poor results.
Problems in reduction can be diagnosed before
the patient is extubated. This gives the surgeon
opportunity to correct the underlying problem
without subjecting the patient to second surgery
or live with the permanent deformity.
Virtual Surgical Planning and Navigation-­
Guided Surgery Virtual surgical planning can
be done on CT data with the help of software.
Mirror imaging from normal side can be used to
normalise the damaged structures. The length of
screws to be used for fixing condylar head fractures can be predecided by measuring dimensions of normal opposite condylar head. In
complex cases such as extensive injuries caused
by gunshot wounds, customised plates can be
designed and preprinted before taking the
patient to the operating table. This improves
surgical outcome and decreases operating time.
The virtual surgical plan can be used to form a
guiding template which aids in reduction of
condylar fracture. Stereolithic models can be
used for accurate bending of plates without
distortion.

14

Condylar Fractures

Navigation-based real-time 3D intraoperative
imaging is also possible which enables the surgeon to see accuracy of reduction.
Shakya et al. in 2019 summarised six key points
for the satisfactory management of condylar fractures. These are virtual evaluation of condylar fracture, suitable surgical approach, good reduction,
stable internal fixation, repair of the articular disc
and restoration of mandibular arch width [19].

14.25 Conclusion
Management of condylar fractures is challenging. The desired goals can be achieved by both
closed and open treatment methods. The choice
of treatment is governed by thorough understanding of risks and benefits associated with each
treatment method. It is the responsibility of the
treating surgeon to choose the best method for
each patient after considering all the factors
based on the current scientific evidence.

14.26 Case Discussion
14.26.1 Chief Complaints
A 32-year male patient reported with pain, swelling and inability to chew following trauma to the
face in a road traffic accident.

14.26.2 Clinical Examination
On examination, there was lacerated sutured
wound over the chin and oedema over the lower
face (Fig. 14.38a). The patient was unable to
close the mouth. Mandibular excursions were
restricted. There was deranged occlusion with
molar gagging on the right side and open bite

247

(Fig. 14.38b). On palpation, mobility and crepitus could be felt over the left angle region and
right preauricular region.

14.26.3 Radiological Investigations
A computerised tomographic scan was taken
which showed fracture at the left angle region
and right condylar process of mandible. The condylar fracture was located at condylar base with
deviation of more than 45°, ramus shortening of
8 mm and had lateral override (Fig. 14.38c).
Non-tooth-bearing segment at the left angle fracture site was displaced superiorly (Fig. 14.38d).
A final diagnosis of fracture of right condylar
base and left angle region of mandible was made.

14.26.4 Treatment
A plan was made to reduce and fix the condylar
base fracture by external facial approach and the
angle fracture by intra-oral approach under general anaesthesia. Maxillary and mandibular
Erich’s arch bars were applied. Right condylar
base fracture was exposed via skin incision over
preauricular and retroparotid region. Further dissection was done as in transmasseter anterior
parotid approach (Fig. 14.38e). Left angle fracture was exposed by crevicular gingival incision
from the first molar to the third molar with distal
extension over ascending ramus region. Both the
fractures were reduced by manipulation, and
intermaxillary fixation was done to maintain the
reduction. Left angle fracture was fixed first, with
2 mm miniplate system (Fig. 14.38f). The condylar base fracture was fixed with a 2 mm geometric
plate (Fig. 14.38g).
Post-operatively light elastics were used to
guide occlusion. The arch bars were removed once

15.1

Introduction

The midface represents a significant part of the
maxillofacial skeleton in terms of function as well
as aesthetics. It plays a key role in maintaining a
proper facial contour and also helps to perform
many daily life functions such as speech, ocular
stability, olfaction and ingestion of food. Thus, the
trauma to the midface is a major concern across
the world as it causes significant functional and
aesthetic morbidity and also raises economic concerns among the affected population [1–3]. With
the diversity of fracture patterns and its intimate
relation to vital structures of the face, fractures of
the midface generate a significant interest among
maxillofacial surgeons and trauma surgeons to formulate a standardised management strategy for
improving functional and aesthetic outcomes.

15.2

Applied Anatomy
of the Midface

The midface is the area of the facial skeleton
whose upper limit is a straight line drawn joining
the bilateral zygomaticofrontal suture crossing
the fronto-maxillary and frontonasal suture and
the lower limit is determined by the occlusal
plane of maxillary teeth or the upper alveolus in
the case patient being edentulous. Posterior
extension is established by sphenoethmoidal
junction, but it incorporates the free margin of
pterygoid laminae inferiorly [4] (Fig. 15.1).
Midface is comprised of the following facial bones
(Fig. 15.1) [5]

Paired bones

• Maxilla

• Palatine bone

in midfacial region)

The skeleton of the face is often described in
terms of its horizontal and vertical buttresses.
The midface comprised thin wafer-like segments
of bone surrounded and supported by a more
rigid bony reinforcement known as “buttresses”.
The midface is attached to the cranium through
these rigid buttresses.
The concept of horizontal and vertical buttresses
of the facial skeleton is one of the most critical

1. Helps in diagnosis and treatment planning of

function
Application of force to the facial skeleton is
countered, absorbed and transmitted across this
buttress system. Forces generated during the
process of mastication are primarily transmitted to the skull base via vertical buttresses of
the facial skeleton, which are further aided by
the supporting horizontal buttresses. Although
skull base is not regarded as a part of the buttress system, it provides a major horizontal support system to the facial skeleton. The buttress
system prevents fracture of facial skeleton until
a critical limit of force exceeds; after that, fracture occurs. The fracture mainly takes place at
the area of weakness or area where maximum
stress ­concentration occurs and they act like

These medial and nasal processes fuse to form the

The Nasolacrimal apparatus is formed by the
fusion of the lateral nasal process and maxillary
process. During the fusion of these two processes, a double layer of epithelium is trapped
between them. Initially, this cord of cells lies in a
horizontal position, but in later stages when maxillary processes develop and the size of the midface increases, it assumes a relative vertical
position. During birth or in the early neonatal
period, this solid cord of cells canalises and forms
the nasolacrimal duct.

15.5

Clinical Examination

15.5.1 Initial Assessment

The initial assessment and management of midface trauma should be concentrated on stabilising
the patient. The high-energy pattern of maxillofacial trauma often leads to involvement of multiple
systems, and, therefore, a thorough, systematic
evaluation of the patient according to advanced
trauma life support (ATLS) protocol should be
considered before the definitive management. The
most common associated injuries in patients with
severe midfacial trauma include injuries to the
head, abdomen, pelvis, extremities, cervical
spine, sternum or ribs and may also accompany
pneumothorax or pulmonary contusion.
Assessment of cervical spine, airway and
haemorrhage is significant in case of midface fractures. The cervical spine should be immobilised
until and unless cervical fractures are confirmed
by radiological or clinical examination [10].
Airway obstruction can lead to asphyxia and
death; therefore, airway patency should be evaluated in case of midface trauma. Haemorrhage,
fractured teeth, oral secretions, vomitus, foreign

15.5.1.1 Symptoms
Malocclusion, sensory changes and pain are
common symptoms in case of midface fracture.
The patient’s subjective sign of abnormal bite can
be one of the most sensitive indicators for the
presence of a maxillary fracture. Loss or altered
sensation of the upper lip, side of the nose and
gingiva suggests a fracture involving the infraorbital nerve and is common with maxillary and
orbital fractures. Trismus or difficulty in mouth
opening can be an indicator of zygomatic complex fracture.
15.5.1.2

Signs

Extraoral
• Soft tissue examination may reveal laceration,
oedema (panda facies) and ecchymosis.
• Asymmetries in midfacial height, width and
projection may be present.
• The intercanthal distance may be abnormal
(traumatic telecanthus).
• Epiphora and rhinorrhea are present.
• Visual acuity and extraocular movements may
be disturbed.
• Step deformity, mobility, crepitus and tenderness of midface may be present on palpation.
Note: Sequence of palpation
Frontal bone → Supraorbital rim → Lateral orbit
→ Zygomatic arch → Body of zygoma Infraorbital
rim → Medial orbital rim → Nasal bone
The maxilla is then examined, and its mobility
is checked by holding the maxilla around the

255

upper anterior teeth, with the thumb below anterior nasal spine and the forefinger at the depth of
the palatal vault.
Intraoral
• Soft tissue may reveal lacerations and
ecchymosis.
• Fractures, luxations and avulsions of teeth
may be present.
• Displacement and mobility of alveolus may be
present.
• Restriction in mouth opening may be
present.
• Deranged occlusion and changes in lateral
excursive movement and protrusive movement may be present.

15.7.3 Comprehensive AOCMF
Classification [13]
It divided the craniomaxillofacial skeleton classification system into three levels depending on
their increasing complexity. Level 1 differenti-

257

ates facial skeleton into four major units that are
the mandible (code 91), midface (code 92), skull
base (code 93) and cranial vault (code 94). Level
2 system discusses the anatomical extent of each
unit. Level 3 classification system discusses each
anatomical unit based on its severity, extent of
displacement and fragmentation in details.

15.7.4 Level 2 Midface and Orbital
Fracture Classification
(Fig. 15.5)
1. Le Fort I (LF I): Includes lower central midface (LCM) and pterygoid process
2. Le Fort II (LF II): Includes LCM, pterygoid
process, intermediate central midface (ICM)
and upper central midface (UCM)
3. Le Fort III (LF III): Includes LCM, UCM,
pterygoid process, zygoma, and lateral, medial
and inferior orbital walls
4. Zygomatic en bloc (ZEB): Includes zygoma
and lateral and inferior orbital walls
5. Naso-orbito-ethmoid (NOE): Includes bilateral medial orbital rims and UCM
Note: Le Fort I, II and III fracture patterns are
exclusive, and they can’t be used in combination,
whereas NOE and ZEB fracture patterns can be
used in combination. ZEB can be used with LF I
and LF II (with or without NOE), and NOE fracture pattern being central can be combined with
ZEB and LF I fracture patterns.

15.8

Management Protocol

According to the various recent reports of the World
Health Organization (WHO) and Centers for Disease
Control and Prevention (CDC), people of all age
groups and economic background die each year due
to unintentional injuries and violence. Road traffic
accident (RTA) individually leads to one million
deaths each year with 30–50 million considerable
injuries [14]. More than 90% of RTAs occurs in
developing countries. It has been estimated that
deaths due to trauma may rise dramatically in 2020,
and mortality related to RTAs will increase by 80%

258

N. K. Sharma et al.

Fig. 15.5 Anatomical subdivisions of the midface on the frontal, lateral and caudal aspect of the skull according to
AOCMF level 2 midface and orbital fracture classification

from the present scenario in countries with low and
middle socio-economic status. Thus, looking at
these statistics, trauma management whether it is
maxillofacial or any other trauma should be a standardised system. ATLS (advanced trauma life support) that was developed in 1976 provides a
standardised protocol to assess and manage any
trauma [15].
The midface, being a key part of the facial
skeleton, should be managed accordingly:
1. Primary assessment and resuscitation
2. Definitive treatment
3. Rehabilitation/reconstruction
4. Post-operative care

Since midface fractures comprised various
types of fractures such as nasal bone fractures,
zygomatic complex fractures (ZMC) fractures,
Le Fort fractures of the maxilla and nasoorbito-­ethmoid fractures (NOE) fractures, the
basic features and management of these fractures will be discussed in their respective chapters separately.

15.9

Surgical Approaches
to the Midface

General principles for approaches to facial skeleton [16]:

15

Introduction to Midface Fractures

• Adequate access and exposure of the fracture.
• Approach should be as direct as possible but
also
taking
facial
aesthetics
into
consideration.
• Incisions should preferably be placed in areas
that are not readily visible such as intraoral
vestibules, behind the hairline, below or
behind the mandible, etc.
• Incision in hair-bearing area: parallel to the
direction of hair roots so that minimum hair
follicles are transected.
• Incision in non-hair-bearing area: perpendicular to the skin surface.
• Avoid incision in the area where future balding is expected.
• A properly placed long incision with adequate
exposure heals better with less scarring than a
short incision that requires excessive
retraction.

259

• Incisions to be placed over the lines of minimal tension/relaxed skin tension lines/
Langer’s lines (Fig. 15.6).
• Aesthetic compromise should be as minimum
as possible.
• Muscles of facial expression must be taken
into consideration.
• Care must be taken to prevent any injury to the
nerve supply of the face.
• Incision should not alter the contour of any
structure.
• It should not hinder the vascularity or lymphatic drainage of any structure.
• Should be placed in areas where healing is
comparatively easy and there are less chances
of infection.

15.9.3.1

 emporal Branch of Facial
T
Nerve
It emerges from the parotid gland immediately
inferior to the zygomatic arch. General course is
from a point 0.5 cm below the tragus to a point
1.5 cm above the lateral eyebrow. The nerve
crosses superficial to the zygomatic arch −0.8 cm
to 3.5 cm anterior to the external auditory canal.
Along the lateral surface of the arch, the temporal
branch courses under temporoparietal fascia and
subgaleal fascia, while antero-superiorly towards
the frontalis muscle, the nerve lies under the temporoparietal fascia. It enters the frontalis muscle
not less than 2 cm above the level of the superior
orbital rim.
15.9.3.2 The Medial Orbit
The lacrimal fossa lies between the anterior
and posterior lacrimal crest. The anterior crest
is the continuation of the frontal process of the
maxilla, while the posterior lacrimal crest is
an extension of the lacrimal bone. The bone of
the lateral nasal wall contains the nasolacrimal
duct, which enters the nasal cavity through the
inferior meatus located beneath the inferior
turbinate. The only vascular structures of any
significance are the anterior and the posterior
ethmoidal arteries. The anterior ethmoid foramen is located approximately 24 mm posterior
to the anterior lacrimal crest. The posterior
ethmoid foramen/foramina are located approximately 36 mm posterior to the anterior lacrimal crest. The optic canal is located
approximately 42 mm posterior to the anterior
lacrimal crest. The distance between the posterior ethmoidal artery and the optic nerve is
equal to or more than 3 mm.

15.9.3.5 Surgical Technique [16]
The incision starts from the preauricular skin
crease at the level of the tragus and extended over
the scalp 3–4 cm behind the hairline and continued till the corresponding region of other side is
reached. While placing the preauricular incision,
care must be taken not to injure the superficial
temporal artery which runs just in front of the tragus. The incision is carried down to the loose
subgaleal plane. Dissection is continued in this
plane anteriorly until approximately 2 cm above
the supraorbital rims. At this point, a sharp incision is given over the periosteum, and the dissection is done further in the subperiosteal plane.
This protects the supraorbital neurovascular bundles. The supraorbital neurovascular bundle can
be released from its foramen by osteotomising a
small fragment. The dissection is proceeded subperiosteally over the supraorbital rims and the
medial and lateral orbital rims along with the
nasoethmoidal complex.
Laterally, the dissection is continued in the
subgaleal plane up to 2 cm above the zygo-

b

Fig. 15.10 Bicoronal approach. (a) Citation is cranial view, (b) citation is lateral view

262

N. K. Sharma et al.

matic arch, to protect the frontal branch of
facial nerve, which runs deep to the temporoparietal fascia as it crosses the zygomatic arch;
at this point the deep temporal fascia is incised
and dissection is continued through temporal
fat pad to the temporalis muscle. Complete
exposure of the lateral orbital wall can be
achieved by stripping the temporalis muscle
from the greater wing of the sphenoid. Care
should be taken not to injure the deep temporal
artery perforators to the temporalis as it might
result in temporal fossa hollowing from temporalis muscle wasting. The zygoma is exposed
starting from its root, subperiosteally. It is connected to the dissection near the lateral orbital
rim at least 3 cm away from the lateral border
of the eyebrow, to avoid any injury to the temporal branch of facial nerve.

15.9.3.6 Modifications
Munro and Fearon [17] introduced the “stealth
incision” which has a zigzag or W-pattern. It is
said to reduce scar visibility and also better camouflage of the resulting scar [18]. Another study
recommends that the incision should be placed at
least 8 cm posterior to the hairline and continued
in the post-auricular region or a small triangular
flap above the auricle. This modification ensures
a well-hidden scar and preservation of the superficial temporal artery [19].
15.9.3.7 Complications
• Temporary (10–15%) or permanent (2%)
frontalis nerve injury
• Scalp sensory loss or pain
• Temporal fossa hollowing
• Hair loss with a visible scar
• Hematoma

15.12.1.2 Lateral Canthal Tendon
The lateral canthal tendon is a fibrous extension of
the tarsal plates laterally towards the orbital rim.
The lateral tendon has a superficial and deep component. The thicker, stronger deep component of
the lateral canthal tendon inserts into the periosteum of the orbital tubercle of the zygoma, approximately 2–3 mm posterior to the orbital rim.
15.12.1.3 Medial Canthal Tendon
The medial canthal tendon also has superficial
and deep component that attaches to the anterior
and posterior lacrimal crests of the medial bony
orbit. The incision should be placed 3 mm medial
to the canthus to prevent any injury to the lacrimal canaliculi and sac.

There are three types of dissection options available for a surgeon to use after the skin incision
has been given.

Layers of the upper eyelid
• Skin
• Orbicularis oculi muscle

superioris aponeurosis below

1. Dissection between skin and muscle until

Disadvantages

Disadvantages
• Risk of breach through orbital septum and

3. Layered dissection: Subcutaneous dissection

Advantages

15.12.2 Infraorbital Incision [16]

15.12.3 Subciliary Incision [17]

15.12.2.1 Surgical Technique
The incision is placed over the skin crease
along the infraorbital ridge (Fig. 15.13). It is
extended from one canthus to the other and may
be extended laterally if required along the natural skin tension line over the zygoma. The incision should not be extended lateral to lateral
canthus to avoid interrupting the lymphatic
channels, as it might lead to post-operative
oedema. Dissection is not much required in this
incision since it gives an almost direct approach
to the inferior orbital rim. However, it is done to
some extent to facilitate retraction. Care should
be taken not to injure the infraorbital nerve.
Periosteum is incised at the lateral end of the
rim and then stripped with periosteum towards
the medial end in order to avoid injury to the
infraorbital nerve.

15.12.3.1 Surgical Technique
Tarsorrhaphy sutures are placed, and the lower
eyelid is retracted superiorly. The incision is
placed 2 mm inferior to the eyelashes on the
lower eyelid which is extended along the entire
length of the eyelid (Fig. 15.13). If required, it
can be extended laterally over the natural skin
tension line or latero-inferiorly. Dissection is
done by using any of the three methods described
above. The skin is separated from the pretarsal
portion of the orbicularis oculi muscle followed
by 4–6 mm of subcutaneous dissection.
Dissection is then proceeded through the orbicularis oculi muscle to reach the periosteum of the
lateral orbital rim. Supraperiosteal dissection is
done to reach the infraorbital rim. The muscle
remaining continuous above this dissection plane
is cut with scissors, and the periosteum is incised
2–3 mm below, along the inferior orbital margin.
The infraorbital nerve is approximately 5–7 mm
inferior to the orbital rim on the medial aspect;
care should be taken to avoid its injury when the
periosteal incision is made. The closure is recommended in a minimum of two layers.

• Indications
–– To expose the infraorbital ridge for fixation
of the zygomatic complex fracture, Le Fort
II fractures or isolated infraorbital fracture
or for exploring the orbital floor
• Complication
–– Chances of injury to infraorbital nerve
–– Scar mark be readily visible when compared to other lower eyelid approaches

15.12.3.2 Subtarsal Incision [17]
Subtarsal incision is placed midway between the
subciliary and infraorbital incision (Fig. 15.13).
It is placed over the lower eyelid just inferior to
the tarsal plate, i.e. 4–5 mm below the lower
eyelashes.
• Indications
–– Exposure of the infraorbital rim
–– Exposure of the orbital floor
• Complications
–– Chances of ectropion due to contracture
during healing

15.12.3.3 Transconjunctival [18]
Incision is placed 2–3 mm below the lower margin of the tarsus over the lower palpebral conjunctiva (Fig. 15.13). It is placed midway between
the inferior margin of the tarsus and the inferior
conjunctival fornix. Medially it can be extended
up to the lacrimal punctum. The lower eyelid is
everted with fine forceps, and two or three traction sutures are placed through the eyelid. These
should be placed straight through the eyelid,
from palpebral conjunctiva to skin, approximately 4–5 mm below the lid margin to ensure
that the tarsal plate is included in the suture.
Scissors are used to cut the conjunctiva and lower
lid retractors midway between the inferior margin of the tarsal plate and the inferior conjunctival fornix. Orbital contents are retracted, and
incision is given over the periosteum.
• Indications
–– For exposure of the infraorbital rim for
fixation of fracture passing through the
infraorbital rim

15.12.3.4 Transcaruncular [18]
It is commonly combined with transconjunctival
incision to gain a wide exposure. Incision is
placed on the caruncle, superiorly extending

265

12 mm above and inferiorly continuing with the
transconjunctival incision (Fig. 15.13). Incision
is placed along the medial aspect of the superior
and inferior conjunctival fornices.
• Indications
–– For exposure of the medial orbital wall
• Complications
–– Chances of injury to lacrimal punctum and
canaliculi

15.12.3.5 Lateral Canthotomy
It was described by Berke in 1954. The incision
is placed on the lateral canthus and extended laterally for several millimetres as per requirement
(Fig. 15.13). It is commonly used with other
lower eyelid incisions to improve the access. One
tip of a pointed scissor is placed inside the palpebral fissure, laterally up to the orbital rim, and the
entire thickness of tissue is cut. Traction sutures
are used to evert the lower eyelid.
• Indications
–– To expose the frontozygomatic sutures and

15.13 Endoscopic Approach
to Midface Trauma
Endoscopic approach is an innovative minimally invasive method of open reduction and
internal fixation of facial fractures. In the midface, its application in orbital floor fracture is
widely reported. The advantages of this
approach are minimal incision; reduced
chances of injury to the nerves, blood vessels
and other vital structures; and minimal fibrosis
and subsequent scar. In the midface region,
endoscopic approach has been advocated for
zygomatic arch repair through preauricular,
Keen or Gillies temporal approach, orbital
floor fracture repair through maxillary sinus
approach, medial orbital fracture through
transnasal or transcaruncular approach or both
and frontal sinus fracture through percutaneous approach. The setback of this approach is
that it is technically challenging and requires
very expensive instruments [20].

15.14 Conclusion
Restoring midfacial skeleton is of prime importance as it is in close proximity to the orbits, nasal
cavity and oral cavity and also acts as a bridge
between the cranium and the mandible. Apart
from having life-­threatening consequences, due
to its prominent position in the face, fractures of
the midface lead to severe aesthetic disfigurement which is highly challenging for the patient
and surgeon. Thus a systematic and timely
approach is required to correct the deformity and
prevent unfavourable outcomes.

16.1

Introduction

Midfacial fractures are also popularly known as
Le Fort fractures based on classification given by
Rene Le Fort in 1901 [1]. While classifying midfacial fractures, he mentioned them as low-energy
impact injuries; however, in today’s rapidly progressing world, high-energy impact injuries are
common; thus, comminution and mixed patterns
of Le Fort fractures are mostly encountered [2].
The classical Le Fort Fractures represent 10–20%
of all facial fractures. High-energy blunt force
trauma mainly causes maxillary fractures. RTAs,
assaults and falls are supposed to be the main
aetiology [3]. In the present scenario, it is very
difficult to find the classical line of Le Fort fractures due to the changing pattern of the impact of
injuries. Le Fort fractures are often associated
with palatal fracture with the incidence being
8–15% [4]. Palatal fracture splits the maxilla near
midline either in sagittal or parasagittal direction
and leads to rotation of unstable alveolus.

N. K. Sharma (*)
Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery Unit, Faculty of
Dental Sciences, Institute of Medical Sciences,
Banaras Hindu University,
Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh, India
N. Mishra
Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery, Department of
Dentistry, Kalpana Chawla Government Medical
College, Karnal, Haryana, India

Fracture line traversing the palate is usually
found between the central incisors or separating
the lateral incisor and canine tooth.

16.1.1 Surgical Anatomy
of the Midface
The maxilla represents a key bone in the midface
skeleton. It is a paired bone which connects the
cranium and frontoethmoid complex to the occlusal plane in supero-inferior direction.
Transversally it connects the bilateral zygomatic
and orbital bones.
The maxilla has four processes:
1. Frontal process—which is directed superiorly
and articulates with frontal, lacrimal and nasal
bone
2. Zygomatic process—which articulates with
the zygomatic bone
3. Alveolar process—which holds the maxillary
dentition
4. Palatine process that forms the most of hard
palate
The maxilla and associated bones of the midface counter the masticatory force with the help
of its horizontal and vertical buttresses that are
already discussed in the previous chapter. So, the
fixation should be done along these buttresses to
restore form and function.

© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2021
A. K. Singh, N. K. Sharma (eds.), Maxillofacial Trauma,
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-33-6338-0_16

271

272

N. K. Sharma and N. Mishra

Both the lateral pterygoid and medial pterygoid muscles exert forces in downward and backward direction on maxilla. Despite this fact, the
muscular pull is less influential in the case of
midface fractures as compared to the mandible.
The displacement of midfacial bones is more
dependent on the amount of force transferred
during the traumatic impact.
Various neurovascular structures associated
with the midfacial region are also vulnerable to
damage during trauma or the surgical repair of
fractures. Paraesthesia of the cheek and upper
alveolar region is often associated with injury of
the infraorbital nerve which traverses through
inferior orbital fissure and exits from the infraorbital foramen which is located around 6.1–
10.9 mm from the inferior orbital rim. Internal
maxillary artery which is a terminal branch of
external carotid artery serves as major vascular
supply of the midface. Injury to the maxillary
artery may cause a life-threatening condition in
case of extensive fractures due to excessive epistaxis and bleeding and sometimes warrant the
need for ligation. But even in the case of ligation,
vascularity of maxilla is not compromised due to
the presence of collateral supply by various
branches of the internal and external carotid
artery. Orbit and its contents such as a globe,
optic nerve, extra-ocular muscle and lacrimal
apparatus are also at risk in midfacial injuries.
