16.2

Classification

Midface fractures are classified by various surgeons into many categories, the most popular
being classification by Rene Le Fort in 1901.

16.2.1 Le Fort Classification (1901) [5]
1. Le Fort I fractures—This type of fracture pattern occurs mostly when the force is being
directed above the level of maxillary dentition
leading to the floating maxilla.
2. Le Fort II fractures—This fracture pattern is
observed when the force is directed at the
level of nasal bone resulting in mobility of
midfacial skeleton.
3. Le Fort III fractures—This fracture pattern is
a significant finding when force is being
delivered at the orbital level which leads to
detachment of the whole midface from the
skull base causing craniofacial disjunction
(Fig. 16.1).

16.2.2 Based on Fracture Level [6]
1. Low-level fracture/Le Fort I
2. Mid-level fracture/Le Fort II
3. High-level fracture/Le Fort III

Le Fort I Fracture

It is a low-level, sub-zygomatic fracture whose
fracture line starts from the lateral border of anterior nasal aperture and passes laterally above the
apices of maxillary teeth, then extends further
downwards to pass below the zygomaticomaxillary buttress and along the wall of the maxillary
sinus and reaches posteriorly crossing the pterygomaxillary fissure to fracture the pterygoid plate
from lower one-third. The fracture line also
extends backwards across the lateral wall of the
nose and meets the lateral fracture line behind the

16.4

Le Fort II Fracture

Fig. 16.7 3D section CT scan showing maxillary fracture at Le Fort II level

It is a sub-zygomatic fracture whose fracture line
starts from the thin middle area of nasal bone
passing through the frontal processes of the maxilla; then it proceeds inferolaterally through the
lacrimal bone anterior to the nasolacrimal foramen and inferior orbital floor and rim, either
medial to or through the infraorbital foramen
along the anterolateral wall of maxillary sinus
below the zygomaticomaxillary suture, crossing
the pterygomaxillary fissure to fracture the pterygoid plates at the middle. This results in a pyramidal fracture (Fig. 16.7) [5].

16.4.1 Clinical Features
• Gross facial oedema causing ballooning of the
face (moon face, panda facies). It usually
develops rapidly within a few hours (Fig. 16.8).
• Bilateral periorbital oedema may be present
(racoon eye).
• Mobility of the maxilla from the level of the
base of the nose (Fig. 16.9).
• Paraesthesia of the cheek and infraorbital
region may be present.

Fig. 16.8 Gross facial oedema causing ballooning of the
face (moon face, panda facies)

posterior molar gagging and open bite).
• Occlusion may be deranged.
• Step may or may not be palpable at infraorbital region.
• Difficulty in biting food and speech.

Le Fort III Fracture

It is a high-level, supra-zygomatic fracture whose
fracture line starts at the region of fronto-nasal
suture passes through the medial wall of orbit and
involving the full depth of ethmoid bone including cribriform plates, then runs around the optic
foramen without causing its fracture, downwards
laterally keeping medial from the inferior orbital
fissure up to its posterior limit. Then fracture
moves downwards along the posterior aspect of
maxillae at a higher level, crossing the pterygomaxillary fissure to fracture the roots of pterygoid plate. Another fracture line that starts from
the same area moves superolaterally crossing the
lateral wall of the orbit leading to separation at
the region of frontozygomatic suture causing
detachment of frontal bone from zygomatic bone.
Thus, this fracture leads to separation of the cranial base from the midface [5].

16.5.1 Clinical Features

Fig. 16.10 Subconjunctival haemorrhage

• Presence of subconjunctival haemorrhage
bilaterally mostly confined to the medial portion of the eye (Fig. 16.10).
• Presence of depressed nasal bridge.
• Unilateral or bilateral epistaxis may be
present.
• Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) rhinorrhea may be
present.
• Presence of dish-face deformity (elongation
of the face due to inferior and posterior dis-

• Gross facial oedema causing ballooning of the
face (moon face, panda facies). It usually
develops rapidly within 24–48 h.
• Presence of bilateral periorbital oedema
(racoon eye) and periorbital ecchymosis
(black eye) (Fig. 16.11).
• Instability of the midface at the region of the
frontozygomatic suture when checked for
mobility of the maxilla (Fig. 16.12).
• Presence of epiphora if there is injury to lacrimal apparatus.
• Airway may be compromised, due to impingement of the fractured segment on the dorsum
of the tongue.
• Presence of subconjunctival haemorrhage
bilaterally extending mostly to the entire
extent of the eye.

16.6.1.1 Plain Radiographs
• For midface or maxillary fractures, occipitomental view (OMV) 10° and 30° are mainly

They have been now replaced by computed

• Whenever there is doubt regarding the presence of Le Fort or midface fractures, CT scan
is considered mandatory.
• Panoramic radiographs (OPG) are only useful

CT scan provides a detailed view of any fracture.
2–3 mm of sections are preferable.

Fig. 16.12 Assessment of instability of the maxilla in the

• In the case of Le Fort fractures, 2D CT has a
better role in diagnosis, whereas 3D CT
(Fig. 16.14) serves as a means for planning the
treatment [10].
• Coronal sections give a detailed view of anterior wall of the maxilla, infraorbital rim, palate and floor of the orbit (Fig. 16.15).
• Axial sections are a useful option for analysing posterior wall of maxillary sinus, pterygoid plates, the hard palate, zygomatic arch,

16.6.2 Management
16.6.2.1

Consideration of Timing
of Repair
• Initial management is based on the ATLS protocol for stabilisation of the patient.
• Definitive treatment of maxillary/Le Fort fractures must be undertaken after gross facial
swelling subsides to get adequate visualisation and cause less intraoperative blood loss.
Treatment can be delayed by 5–10 days, but
delaying more than that may cause compromised outcome.

 ethods of Reduction of Le
M
Fort/Maxillary Fractures

• Manual reduction—Mobile maxillary segments most commonly reduced with the help

•

•

•

Fig. 16.17 Rowe’s disimpaction forceps

of hand without use of any specialised instruments. But with the presence of severe displacement and palatal split, this method may
not help, and specific instruments are required.
Rowe’s disimpaction forceps in association
with Hayton William forceps—Rowe’s disimpaction forceps (Fig. 16.17) mainly used for
the reduction of maxillary fracture. For the
application of this instrument, the operator
should stand behind the patient and insert one
blade in the nose and another blade on the
hard palate (Fig. 16.18). It is always used in
pairs in rocking and rotational fashion in both
vertical and horizontal axis to disimpact
­maxillae causing the segment to move forwards. But in cases associated with palatal
fracture, it often leads to increased displacement of the fracture, so its use is combined
with the Hayton William forceps (Fig. 16.19)
that are applied on the buccal aspect of alveolus over tuberosity causing medial compression leading to an approximation of fracture’s
two halves [11].
Intermaxillary fixation—Here occlusion is
regarded as a key factor to get a reduction. So,
the main focus is to get correct occlusion
causing reduction of displaced maxillary segments (Figs. 16.20 and 16.21).
Transpalatal wiring—It is a simple technique
used for the management of sagittal maxillary
fracture/palatal split. It is a highly preferred
technique due to its non-invasiveness and easy
approach. This technique can be carried out in
emergency or outpatient settings. In this technique, maxillary molar and premolar teeth are
preferred for wiring because they help to regulate palatal width posteriorly as the tendency
for fracture splaying is more in the posterior
area (Fig. 16.22).
Open reduction—This is the last resort; if
fractures are not reduced by any means, then
direct exposure of fracture sites is done to
achieve accurate reduction and then osteosynthesis performed with the help of interosseous
wire or bone plate.

Internal Fixation

Internal Skeletal Suspension (Less
Preferred in Contemporary Practice)
It was introduced by Adams et al. in 1942 to
manage the fractures of the midface. The main
principle behind this treatment modality is to

suspend mobile fractured segments against a
firm stable segment by utilising a subcutaneous wire. Traditionally with previously was
commonly used and considered to be comfortable to the patient and quick technique, accurate and reliable for surgeons. But, in today’s
scenario with the advent of various newer fixation techniques and bone plating system, it is
less preferred.
Types of Internal Skeletal Suspension [11]
• Frontal suspension—It can be lateral or central; both can be used in the case of Le Fort I,
Le Fort II and Le Fort III fracture.
• Circumzygomatic suspension—Used for Le
Fort I and II fracture.
• Zygomatic suspension—Used in case of Le
Fort I fracture.
• Infraorbital suspension—Used in case of Le
Fort I fracture.

Approach to Infraorbital
Region (IOR) (Fig. 16.25)
Infraorbital approach—This approach nowadays is obsolete as it gives aesthetically unacceptable scar.
Subciliary approach (lower blepharoplasty)
[13]—The incision in this approach is placed
2 mm inferior to lower eyelashes. Minimal
inconspicuous scar formation occurs but is
technique-sensitive.
Subtarsal approach—The incision is given in
natural crease line below the tarsal plate to
reach the bone, dissecting through orbicularis
oculi muscle and periosteum.
Transconjunctival approach—In contemporary practice, this method is favoured to gain
access to the IOR and orbital floor. It is an
easy method that has a benefit of rapid access
with minimal visible scar in the conjunctiva. It
can be retroseptal or preseptal [14]. Risk of
entropion is common in this approach [15].

16.8.3.4 Coronal Approach
This approach gives an outstanding exposure to
FZS, IOR and NOE complex. It is a little extensive
and technique-sensitive approach. In this approach,
a long skin incision is placed within the hairline.
The initial incision should reach the loose areolar
tissue. The initial dissection should be up to this
plane until 3 cm above the supraorbital rim, after
which incision is given through the periosteum to
reach the desired fracture site. It is an extensive,
technique-­sensitive approach with risk of facial
and supraorbital nerve injury (Fig. 16.26) [16].

Through the Existing
Laceration
Sometimes preferred as it avoids unnecessary
need of second surgically created wound, but it
carries the risk of infection and hardware failure.

16.9.2 Special Considerations
16.9.2.1 Paediatric Patients
Maxillary fractures are relatively rare in paediatric age groups. In Rowe’s 1968 case series of
1500 patients, only 1% paediatric age group is
affected by midface fractures out of which 20%
were Le Fort fractures [11]. In the case series by
Izuka in 1995, paediatric patient only above
5 years had Le Fort fractures [17]. The main reason for low incidence of midface fractures in the
paediatric population is the incomplete development of paranasal sinus and the presence of
unerupted maxillary tooth. Since the consistency
of maxillae in child is spongy, soft and elastic and
it is protected by a thick layer of adipose tissue,
this further adds to the decreased incidence of
fracture. High-energy impact injuries (RTAs) are
considered to be the most common aetiology of
this fracture, which may also lead to increased
risk of associated injuries. Injury due to fall is
more common in a child less than 6 years.
Le Fort classification is the same in paediatric
patient as in an adult. Clinical features are similar
to adult patients. Treatment strategy should
involve restoring occlusion and buttress of midface region and should be considered within a
week as in paediatric group healing is faster and
there are chances of callous formation.
Approaches are the same but extensive proce-

N. K. Sharma and N. Mishra

dures are mostly avoided. Bioresorbable plates
are mostly preferred to avoid long-term complications of titanium plate and provide adequate
stabilisation. They also lower the risk of foreign
body infection and avoid secondary surgery for
plate removal.

16.9.2.2 Geriatric Patients
Discussing considerations in geriatric patients
means discussing fracture patterns and management of edentulous maxilla. About 6% of cases
of maxillary fractures occur in geriatric patients/
edentulous maxilla [18]. Fractures of the maxilla
are less common initially but it increase with age,
and after 65 years of age, their incidence becomes
equal to that of the mandible fracture [19]. This is
because pneumatisation occurs with age that
causes a decrease in bone resilience and atrophy
of the alveolus. Comminution is a common finding in geriatric maxillary fractures [20].
Treatment strategy should focus on minimal
intervention; if the fracture is undisplaced or
minimally displaced, conservative management
with a soft diet and appropriate antibiotics and
analgesics suffice satisfactory healing. If surgical
intervention is warranted, the aim is to restore
form and function which is same as that of adult
edentulous patients. Augmentation and bone
grafting of vertical pillars may be necessary in
geriatric patients. In case of the edentulous
patients, denture and acrylic splint like gunning
splint is a considerable option to get a correct
maxillo-mandibular relationship intraoperatively
in all cases where ORIF is undertaken; thus, it
prevents malposition and overriding of fracture
segments and can also be used as means of closed
reduction when used with per alveolar wiring.

16.10 Recent Evidences
According to various recent meta-analyses and
reviews, it has been suggested that velocity of
trauma decides the type and severity of Le Fort
fractures. Low-velocity injuries due to fall, blunt
trauma and assault were associated with 56% of
Le Fort fractures, whereas high-velocity injuries
such as fall from height and RTAs were mostly

16 Le Fort Fractures

associated with Le Fort II and III fractures.
Severe Le Fort fractures were also accompanied
by other head and neck injuries such as skull
base fracture (40.7%) and head and cervical
spine injury (5.4% each) [21, 22]. One of the literatures suggests that fall from a height of 7.3
meters causes 43.9% Le Fort fractures [23].
According to many studies, drug and alcohol
abuse compounds the severity of maxillofacial
injuries. One of the studies had reported that
patients were positive for alcohol and drug intake
in 13.6% Le Fort I, 18.1% Le Fort II and 52.1%
Le Fort III fractures [24]. According to another
study, patients with drug and alcohol abuse have
shown more number of Le fort III Fractures
(52%) as compared to Le fort I and II fractures
(32%) [25].
One study showed that 84.5% of facial fractures required hospitalisation [26]. Another
study reported that 9.1% of Le Fort I, 27.3% of
Le Fort II and 26.1% of Le Fort III fractures
were directly shifted to the operation theatre.
Evidences from literatures suggest that tracheostomy was needed in 22.4% of Le Fort fracture
patients and 43.5% of Le Fort III patients [22].
One of the recent reviews suggested that ORIF
is required in 60% of the Le Fort fractures, 30%
of fractures only require conservative therapy
and 10% do not require any treatment [10].
Literature also suggests that long-term rigid
fixation often leads to poor skeletal development causing facial deformity. Pain, infection,
hardware failure and wound dehiscence are usually causes for around 12% of titanium plate
removal [10].
A recent review suggested that one of the
studies reported a mortality rate of 11.6% in
complex midfacial fractures as compared to 5.1%
in simple midfacial fractures. Mortality rate of
0%, 4.5% and 8.7% was associated with Le Fort
I, II and III, respectively. Significant complications are associated with Le Fort fractures such as
ophthalmic complications (47%), traumatic diplopia (21%), epiphora (37%), dyspnoea (31%)
and masticatory problems (40%). Patients with
complex comminuted Le Fort fractures suffered
significant morbidity. A recent review suggested
a satisfactory functional and aesthetic outcome

289

was achieved in 89.1% of the cases, while infection, temporomandibular joint problems or permanent facial deformity was found in 10.9% of
cases [27].

16.11 Conclusion
Midface/maxillary fractures are often encountered by maxillofacial surgeons in emergency
settings. Managing maxillary fractures is one of
the challenging tasks to maxillofacial surgeons
due to its complex anatomy and functional and
aesthetic importance. Maintaining airway and
controlling haemorrhage should be given utmost
importance before initiating any further diagnostic workup. Primary aim of managing maxillary
fractures is to restore functional occlusion and
aesthetics, so precise surgical approach and
reconstruction modality are important to achieve
promising results.

16.12 Case Discussion
Chief Complaint A 52-year-old male patient
reported with a complaint of pain in the upper
jaw and inability to chew food following injury
over the face due to road accident for the last
2 days.
History of Present Illness As stated by the
patient, he was asymptomatic 2 days back; then
he met a road accident, leading to injury over the
face for which he reported to the local hospital.
The patient had a history of bleeding from the
nose and oral cavity. No history of loss of consciousness, vomiting and seizures was reported.
He had difficulty in chewing and swallowing the
food properly. He also noticed nasal regurgitation
of food and water.
Past Medical History Not contributory.
Clinical Examination Extraoral examination
revealed diffuse oedema over the bilateral midface region with periorbital oedema and ecchymosis more pronounced over the right side

290

N. K. Sharma and N. Mishra

(Fig. 16.28). On palpation, tenderness was
present in bilateral infraorbital region and
zygomaticomaxillary suture region. Mild paraesthesia was also reported over bilateral cheek
region.
Intraoral examination revealed restricted mouth
opening and tenderness over bilateral maxilla with
mobility. Mild crepitus, step deformity at zygomaticomaxillary buttress region and deranged occlusion were observed. Mucosal tear was observed in
hard palate suggestive of parasagittal palatal split
which was confirmed on palpation.
Investigations Initially conventional X-rays
like PA view skull and PNS view were advised
that revealed fractured maxilla. Computed tomographic scan with three-dimensional reconstruction revealed the fracture at bilateral Le Fort I
level and parasagittal split of the palate. Bilateral
maxillary antrum was obliterated suggestive of
hemosinus (Fig. 16.29).
Fig. 16.28 Clinical picture showing diffuse oedema over
the bilateral midface region with periorbital oedema and
ecchymosis more pronounced over the right side

a

Diagnosis Bilateral Le Fort I fracture with parasagittal palatal split.

b

Fig. 16.29 (a) 3D CT face showing the fracture at Le Fort I level. (b) Coronal section showing parasagittal palatal split

16 Le Fort Fractures

291

a

b

c

d

Fig. 16.30 1.5 mm titanium plate fixation at (a) right ZMB, (b) right NMB, (c) left NMB, d) left ZMB

Treatment The procedure was performed under
general anaesthesia via nasoendotracheal intubation. As the patient had partially edentulous condition, the occlusion was restored with the
application of IMF screws. The mobile maxillary
segment was reduced in its original position, and
fixation was done with 1.5 mm titanium miniplates at bilateral nasomaxillary buttress (NMB)
and zygomaticomaxillary buttress (ZMB) with

the help of intraoral vestibular approach
(Fig. 16.30). The palatal segments were approximated, and a palatal splint was given for
3–4 weeks to prevent nasal regurgitation.
Adequate antibiotic and analgesic coverage was
given for 5 days. Post-operatively, the patient was
kept on a high-calorie, protein-rich, complete liquid diet for 6 weeks. Oral hygiene maintenance
was advised.

17.1

Introduction

Zygomatic maxillary complex fractures are very
commonly addressed in the emergency as well as
day care clinics by the maxillofacial surgeons
and may occur due to variable causes including
road traffic accidents, accidental falls, fist fights,
assaults, military injury, sport injury, domestic
violence and many more. These are also known
as the tripod fractures and comprise approximately 40–60% of all the facial fractures and are
the second most common fractures of the facial
bones after nasal bone fractures being the most
common [1].
Among these about 80% of these fractures
occur in the males and about 20% occur in the
females and specially in the age group between
20 and 45 years as suggested by various available
literatures. Zygoma forms the prominence of the
cheek which subsequently contributes to the high
frequency of the fractures [2].

17.3.1 Paraesthesia
• Incidence is 40–50% of cases with ZMC fracture involving infraorbital rim fracture [4].
• Numbness over the cheek of the affected side
and perinasal area, lower eyelid, lateral nasal
aspect and the upper lip.
• In some cases paraesthesia may occur if the
orbital floor and the anterior wall of the maxilla bone are fractured leading to tearing,
shearing and compression of infraorbital
nerve along the canal or foramen.
• Paraesthesia of the anterior and middle superior alveolar nerve affects anterior teeth and
maxillary gingiva and vestibular mucosa.

17.3.2 Epistaxis
• Rupture of the maxillary sinus wall membrane
and mucosa leads to bleeding in the internal
antrum and drains through the middle meatus.

17.3.3 Crepitation
• Fracture of the sinus walls and tearing of the
mucosa lead to escape of the air into fascial
spaces and soft tissues causing crepitation.

17 Zygomaticomaxillary Complex Fractures

17.3.4 Displacement of the Palpebral
Fissure
• Rupture of the lateral palpebral ligament
which is attached to the zygomatic portion of
the orbital rim and specifically to Whitnall’s
tubercle in the lateral wall of the orbit leads to
visual deformity.
• Due to the displacement of the orbital floor
and lateral orbital rim, displacement of
Tenon’s capsule and suspensory ligament
occurs which leads to depression of the globe,
and further diplopia may result.

17.3.5 Diplopia
• Monocular—One eye specifically on the
affected side will have blurred vision. Such
type should be managed immediately as it
indicates underlying hyphema, detached lens
or injury to the eye globe.
• Binocular—Incidence is about 10–40% cases
and is more common than monocular type.
During trauma there is entrapment of the periorbital soft tissues and the muscles (inferior
rectus mostly) or fat. It can also be associated
with exophthalmoses, globe ptosis, neuromuscular injury, intramuscular haematoma and
globe displacement.

17.3.6 Enophthalmos
• It includes deepening and accentuation of the
sulcus of the upper eyelid and narrowing of
the palpebral fissure leading to pseudoptosis
of upper eyelid.
• It may occur due to increase in the orbital volume with inferior and lateral displacement of
the zygoma or may occur due to decrease in
the soft tissue volume due to herniation of the
orbital soft tissues.

17.5

Management

1. There are some basic protocols that should be
followed while managing zygomatic maxillary fractures.
• First follow triage principle, and identify
the patients according to the need of urgent,
wait and watch and delayed treatment
categories.
• 
Objectives of management should be in
mind which include:

17 Zygomaticomaxillary Complex Fractures
Objectives
• Anatomic reduction and structural stability
• Aesthetically sustainable surgical approach leading
to least scarring
• Prevent injury to orbit, prevent blindness and
enophthalmos correction
• Symmetry and aesthetic balance
• Reduction of pain, swelling, trismus
• Occlusion balance and improvement of mouth
opening
• Prevention and treating nerve injury
• Preserve globe integrity and vision
• Prevent mal-union and non-union
• Prevent infection and fibrous union

17.5.1 Five Fundamental Principles
Adequate Exposure Using
Esthetically Favorable
Surgical Approach.

Anatomic Reduction of The
Fractured Segements

Semi Rigid or Rigid Fixation.

Adquate and Stable
Immobilization

Minimizing Immobilization

297

• Recent concepts and according to our experience rigid fixation of the fractured segments is
superior to the semi-rigid fixation.
• Fixation that follows the skeletal buttresses
results in more stable outcomes.

17.5.2 Incision Principles
• Direct access to the fracture site
• Aesthetically favourable incision
• Longer incisions better than the smaller
incisions
• Include infected tissue and the already existing lacerated margins of the wounds
• Layered dissection and preservation of the
facial nerve branches

17.5.3 Number of Points to be Fixed
for a Stabilised Fixation
According to the available vast number of the literature and our experience, minimum two-point
fixation is necessary, and that should be at frontozygomatic suture and zygomatic maxillary buttress region.
• It should be insured that the first plate is placed
at the zygomatic maxillary buttress region to
ensure the bizygomatic width of the face and
then at the frontozygomatic suture region to
ensure the vertical height of the face [5].
• In case of associated fractures like pan-facial
fractures, we must ensure the correct order of
the fixation following inside out or outside in
protocols.
• For comminuted fractures, reconstruction
plates along with bone grafts can be utilised
wherever necessary.
• Most important factor to be considered for
favourable outcomes is properly layered suturing or placement of the suction tube or drains
in order to ensure reduction of the dead space
and post-operative haematoma.

298

V. Singh et al.

17.5.4 Rationale
• AMPLE history should be recorded taken;
clinical examination and necessary consultations regarding ophthalmic, neurology, ENT,
etc., for e­nsuring related trauma-associated
functional injuries.
• Rule out orbital floor fracture, facial nerve
injury, eye injuries, head injuries and most
importantly spine injuries.
• Adequate assessment and correct diagnosis of
the fracture sites through necessary radiographs and computed tomography.
• While planning treatment we should consider
the intervention needed whether an immediate
or delayed treatment is to be followed which is
affected by the injury-associated oedema, pain
and swelling.
• A necessary preoperative treatment plan and an
alternative treatment plan must be incorporated
before undertaking the patient for the treatment.

17.5.5 Optimum Time
Optimum time for the intervention should be
delayed for upto 5 to 7 days post-trauma if we
anticipate any ophthalmic injury.
The added advantages we ensure are:
• Gross oedema of the face subsides.
• Diplopia assessment can be done.
• Haematoma of maxillary antrum subsides and
better assessment can be done.

17.5.6 Options for Management

2. Open reduction and internal fixation.
3. No treatment or conservative treatment only
for symptomatic relief and observations of the
patient through regular follow-ups.
According to the literature [6]:
• 
Albright and McFarland recommended
that intermaxillary fixation should be done
as a treatment of the fractures which are
stable and reduced properly in order to balance and counter the masseter muscle pull
on the reduced and repositioned fractures.
• Rowe and Williams indicate that the unstable reduced zygomatic maxillary fractures
that belong to category 2 must be treated by
means of direct fixation.

2. Carroll-Girard Screw Method
This technique uses a T-shaped bone screw

Incision is made in the mucobuccal fold beneath

bone hook, a large Killey’s haemostat or urethral

force to reduce the displaced bone segment.

17.7

Special Considerations

17.7.1 Zygomatic Complex Fractures
in Paediatric Patients
Fractures of the midface and zygomatic bone
are usually less common in children as
compared to adults because the zygoma
­
becomes more prominent as one ages, thereby
increasing risks of fracture. Due to unique anatomical configurations such as lack of pneumatisation and flexibility at suture lines, the facial
skeleton in children is more resilient to
fracture.
Treatment can range from observation to
closed treatment or open reduction with internal fixation based on individual case and fracture dynamics, to avoid any later growth
disturbances. Fractures in children are often
greenstick and hence may not often require
open reduction and fixation. In cases with concomitant orbital injury, however, exploration
may be necessary. Resorbable plates, screws
and meshes have also been used. Management
for paediatric zygoma fractures lacks level 1
evidence [9].

17.7.2 Zygomatic Complex Fractures
in Geriatric Patients
Fractures of zygomatic bone and orbit have been
reported to be common in the elderly population
which is more vulnerable to self falls with
advancing age. Treatment guidelines in these
patients depend on their general health status and
specific indications. Restoring function is more
important than aesthetics unless specifically indicated by patients.

17.8

Recent Advances

Accurate reconstruction of the zygomatic bone
anatomy and restoring its various bony articulations
is the key to restore facial width and projection.
However, this is easier said than done even for experienced surgeons. Most zygomatic fractures also
involve fractures through the orbital walls. Complex
and comminuted fractures pose a significant problem especially when the treatment is delayed
beyond a few weeks. Technology-­driven advances
in surgical techniques may aid in improved accuracy of reduction and better outcomes.
These advances include:
1. Intraoperative CT scan (C-arm) evaluation to
assess achieved reduction.
The availability of intraoperative scans can be a
very useful adjunct to ascertain if accurate repositioning has been attained before closure. It
reduces the need for resurgery as any corrections
can be implemented in the same operation.
2. Computer-assisted and navigation-guided
surgery.
DICOM data set helps in planning surgery for
complex midface fractures by helping in accurate preoperative diagnosis, making stereolithographic models and manufacturing of
patient-specific implants by mirroring the nonfractured side to restore ideal facial contours. It
is also used for making splints that are used in
infrared-based navigation-guided surgeries.

17 Zygomaticomaxillary Complex Fractures

303

3. Endoscopy-assisted orbital floor and zygomatic reduction.
Fractures involving orbital floor and zygomatic arch can benefit from endoscopic assistance wherein minimal access is needed but
fractures can be better visualised especially
the posterior aspect of the orbit.

17.11 Case Discussion 1

17.9

17.11.2 History of Present Illness

Evidence-Based Knowledge

Lacking high-level evidence from RCTs and
meta-analysis, most units treat zygomatic complex fractures based on their own experience of
outcomes and complications and available
advanced equipments. However, some of the
important studies are listed below:
In their meta-analysis, Jazayeri et al. reviewed 2 RCTs
and 11 case series and suggested that while the quality
of literature evidence on ZMC fracture treatment was
low, three-point fixation seemed to be superior to
two- or single-point fixation and provided better
fracture stability [10]
In their systematic review, Gadkari et al. also
concluded that three-point fixation had better
outcomes [11]
Ridgway et al. in their meta-analysis concluded that
the subtarsal approach was superior to subciliary in
approaching the ZMC fractures as there were lesser
chances of ectropion, while the transconjunctival
approach was preferred for access of isolated orbit
floor fractures [12]

17.11.1 Chief Complaint
A 35-year-old male patient reported with the
chief complaints of pain and swelling over right
side of the face and cheek region since 1 day.

The patient gave alleged history of road side
accident in which he was riding at around
70kmph on his motorcycle, without protective
headgear, lost his balance and collided with the
road divider. He fell hitting the right side of his
face on the gravelled road. He gave no history of
loss of consciousness, seizures, vomiting and
bleeding from the nose and ears. There was history of bleeding from cut on the right side of the
face and chin and also from the mouth. Patient
was then admitted to our ward for further investigations and treatment.

No significant contributory past medical and dental history.

for accessing the zygomatic buttress and anterior maxilla. Vestibular incisions were given to
access the mandibular fractures.

and 17.13).

18.4

Clinical Examination

18.4.1 Initial Evaluation
Every injured patient should be thoroughly evaluated. Any missed diagnosis has the potential to
develop into a late complication with high morbidity. The primary survey consists of
­airway-­breathing-­circulation (ABC). Involvement
of NOE complex may block the nasal passage for
breathing. This finding must be immediately
tackled with either clearing the airway or using
an artificial airway. Upper-third facial fractures
are commonly associated with head injury. Any
history of loss of consciousness, single or multiple episodes of vomiting or altered sensorium or
yellowish watery discharge from the nose or ears
may warn the clinician for a possible cranial
component of injury and to consult a neurosurgeon. Once the general survey is completed as
per the clinician’s satisfaction, one must proceed
to local oral and maxillofacial examination.

allow its movement when pulled in opposite
direction. This is called the bowstring test
(Fig. 18.8).

18.5.1 Inspection
Facial inspection related to upper-third facial
fractures comprises:

or swelling.

haemorrhage, periorbital ecchymosis, movement of eyeball and altered vision. In context
of NOE fractures, presence of telecanthus
should be noted.
3. Nasal examination related to pain, swelling,
deviation, discharge from nose and ability to
smell.
4. Ear examination for bleeding or discharge.

18.7

Management

18.7.1 Approaches to NOE Skeleton
In author’s experience, the most common approach
to NOE fractures has been through lacerations
(Fig. 18.9). Other small incisions are the extraoral
Lynch incision to reduce and fix the upper pole of
central segment and intraorally vestibular incision
to reduce and fix the lower pole (infero-lateral pyriform rim) (Fig. 18.10). The most extensive and
ideal exposure is through the bicoronal incision
that exposes the complete upper third of the face.
An added advantage is that one can harvest a calvarial graft though the same exposure (Fig. 18.11).

Fig. 18.11 Exposure of the NOE fracture through the

18.7.2 Closed Vs Open Reduction

Fig. 18.9 Exposure of the NOE fracture through the
laceration

Like every fracture in the craniofacial skeleton,
the option of conservative versus open reduction
also applies to NOE fractures. Typically, the aesthetic and the functional requirement should be
measured against the age, gender and associated
co-morbidities of the patient. If the patient is fit
for general anaesthesia with no added risk, a surgeon should prefer opening and reducing the
fractures under direct vision.

Complications Associated
with Upper-Third Facial
Fractures

1. Chronic headache due to persistent infection
of the frontal sinus.
2. CSF leak from ear/nose due to unrepaired
dural tear.
3. Disturbed vision (blurring, double or diminished vision) due to fractured medial orbital
wall or any neuronal compression.
4. Traumatic telecanthus due to displaced medial
canthal ligament.
5. Anosmia due to injury to the olfactory nerve
fibres.

18.9

 dvancement in Upper or
A
Complex Facial Fracture
Management

1. Intraoperative CT scanning has led to immediate and accurate assessment of fracture
reduction on the operation table.
2. Use of bioresorbable fixation system.
3. Use of self-drilling screws has improved the
fixation technique in these critical areas having thin bones.
4. Intraoperative navigational techniques have
led to immediate assessment of fracture fixation and implant placement.
5. Endoscopic reduction and fixation through the
maxillary sinus or nasal cavity has resulted in
successful treatment of skull base injuries and
pathologies with minimum morbidity.

benefit to the patient. Any life-threatening/compromising situation like altered sensorium, persistent CSF leak or altered vision should be
immediately managed. Proper reduction and
fixation should be planned in the first surgery
only. It is extremely difficult to treat residual
deformities of the upper-third face. Sometimes
the results are unpredictable after the first correction. Hence, the patient should be always
advised regarding the possibility of secondary
corrections.

Orbital Fractures
Venkatesh Anehosur and Anandhi Visweswaran

19.1

Introduction

Orbital anatomy is complex, and various vital
structures and highly specialised organs are bundled in a small space. Optimal management of
orbital fractures remains challenging and often
enigmatic.
From a retrospective analysis of 227 patients
with midface fractures reporting to our centre from
2016 to 2018, we analysed the most common aetiology to be road traffic accidents (75%), followed
by falls (17%), assaults (6%) and industrial injury
(1%). The higher incidence is noted in the age
group of 21–30 years (48.6%) followed by 17% in
patients in the 41–50 years age group, 15.95% in
patients between 31 and 40 years, and 10 (8.5%)
between below 20 years. The lowest incidence was
noted above 50 years of age which comprised
5.3% [1]. Isolated orbital fractures are encountered in 4–16% of all facial fractures, and orbital
fractures are composed of 30–55% of zygomatic
complex and naso-orbital-ethmoid fractures.
Even though in the initial management of a
poly-trauma patient, orbital trauma is not a priority in itself, the evaluation performed after hemodynamic compensation has been achieved should
V. Anehosur (*) · A. Visweswaran
Department Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery, SDM
Craniofacial Centre, S D M College of Dental
Sciences and Hospital, Shri Dharmasthala
Manjunatheshwara University,
Dharwad, Karnataka, India

include a comprehensive assessment of the risk
for orbital structure involvement (cranial cavity,
paranasal sinuses or nasal cavity).
For these patients, modern imaging analysis
offers a unique chance to quantitatively assess the
surgical result and stability over the time. The
careful assessment of the defect size should be
performed preoperatively with the CT scan.
Primary repair offers injured patients their best
chance at functional recovery (Table 19.1).

19.2

Osteology

Orbit is a pyramidal structure with apex pointing
posteriorly and the base situated anteriorly with
intrabony orbital volume of 35 ml. The bony

framework of the orbit is formed by seven facial
bones, namely, maxilla, zygoma, lacrimal, ethmoid, palatine, sphenoid and frontal bone
(Fig. 19.1).
The ethmoid, frontal and maxillary bones—
closely related to sinus pneumatisation—act as
shock absorbers for the eye globe. The orbital
floor, which forms the roof of the maxillary sinus,
slopes upwards towards the apex of the pyramid,
which lies roughly 44–50 mm posterior to the
orbital entrance. The surgeon must be aware of
safe subperiosteal dissection distances correlating the reliable bony landmarks to the vital structures. The measurements of internal bony orbit as
depicted in Fig. 19.2 are referenced from intact
adult orbital rims. This complicated anatomy
makes repair and reconstruction of orbital fracture difficult for a novice.

19.2.1 Inferior Orbital Fissure (IOF)
It is a cleft measuring 25–35 mm bounded superiorly by the greater wing of sphenoid, inferiorly
by the maxilla and orbital process of palatine
bone and laterally by the zygomatic bone. It communicates with the retromaxillary space and the

V. Anehosur and A. Visweswaran

Fig. 19.2 Internal orbit anatomy—measurements and
potential sites of visual impairment (a) globe rupture
(intraocular haemorrhage), (b) orbit (retrobulbar haematoma, blow-in fracture); (c) optic nerve (oedema, bleeding, vasospasm), (d) optic canal (shearing of nerve,
contusion, bone fragment injury), (e) intracranial (central
injuries, optic tract, occipital cortex)

anterior entrance to the infratemporal fossa.
Posteriorly, it joins with the superior orbital fissure. This zone is crucial for assessment of orbital
fractures of the floor extending posteriorly may
result in disruption of the fissure and the orbital
volume.

19.2.2 Intraorbital Buttress
It is a thin bony brace at the confluence of the
medial orbital wall and the floor running from the
anterior section through the midorbit and merging with the posterior ledge. It is crucial for
assessment of the severity of intraorbital injury.
Undisplaced it can be used as an important landmark for reconstruction, which distinctively
facilitates orbital repair.

19.2.3 Posterior Ledge
The posterior ledge, also called the palatine
orbital surface, is a solid shelf in the posterior
orbit medially from the IOF. If present it offers a
reliable and stable landmark for correct volumet-

19.3

Surgical Anatomy

19.3.1 M
 edial Canthal Ligament
(MCL)
Medial canthal ligament is a band of fibrous
tissue which acts as a tendon of insertion for
the orbicularis oculi muscle to the medial
orbital wall. It originates from anterior and
posterior lacrimal crest and frontal process of
the maxilla and surrounds the lacrimal sac and
diverges to become the pretarsal and preseptal
portion of orbicularis oculi muscle. It attaches
the tarsal plate to the medial orbital wall. The
anterior limb functionally pulls the medial
commissure of the eyelid forwards and downwards, whereas the posterior limb maintains
the eyelid position in relation to the globe
(Fig. 19.4).
Medial canthal ligament acts as a suspensory
sling for the globe—maintaining its support
along with the lateral canthal tendon.

325

Fig. 19.4 Parts of medial canthal ligament (a) posterior
limb, (b) superior limb, (c) anterior limb

19.3.2 Lateral Canthal Ligament
The lateral canthal ligament attaches the upper
and lower tarsal plates to Whitnall’s tubercle
inside the orbital rim deep to the septum. It is a
complex bifurcated structure of the orbital septum (septal band—anterior limb) and a ligament (tarsoligamentous band—posterior limb)
which in combination is called the lateral canthal band. In 90% of the cases, the ligament is
attached to Whitnall’s tubercle, which is
located approximately 4 mm posterior to the
lateral orbital rim and 27 mm above the intersection of the lateral and inferior margins; this
area is 9 mm below the zygomaticofrontal
suture.

19.3.3 Lacrimal Drainage Apparatus
The lacrimal gland is a bilobular, tubuloacinar
gland located in the lacrimal fossa of the frontal
bone. It contains multiple ducts that secrete the
aqueous portion of the tear film. The distance
between superior and inferior lacrimal punctum
is 2 mm, superior and inferior canaliculi measure approximately 8 mm forming common
canaliculi of 3–5 mm and the lacrimal sac measures 13 mm which continues as nasolacrimal
duct with interosseous course for 12 mm and

19.4

Etiopathogenesis

Fractures involving the orbit may affect the
internal orbit, the external orbital frame or both.
Many hypotheses have been proposed regarding the
pathogenesis of orbital fractures; however, only the
following three theories have been most widely
accepted.

19.4.1 Buckling Theory/Bone
Conduction Theory [8]
When there is a direct impact to rim, the anterior
force is transmitted through the rim back into the
weak orbital floor causing rippling effect leading
the floor to buckle and fracture (Fig. 19.7).

19

Orbital Fractures

a

327

b

c

Fig. 19.7 (a) Illustrates buckling/bone conduction theory, (b) illustrates hydraulic/retropulsion theory, (c) illustrates
globe to wall theory

19.4.2 Hydraulic/Retropulsion
Theory [9]
States when force is received by eyeball by
larger object, it gets transmitted outwards via
hydraulic forces resulting in increased intraorbital pressure and hence leads to fracture of the
floor of the orbit (Fig. 19.7b).

19.4.3 Globe to Wall Theory [10]
Erling and colleagues proposed this theory for
isolated medial wall fracture. This theory explains

that when there is a direct impact on globe to an
extent where it gets displaced to 2.5 cm from
orbital apex, the globe itself fractures the orbital
walls (Fig. 19.7c).
This theory states when force is applied
directly to the bone, often the zygomatic bone or
the infraorbital rim, or both, which produces an
orbital floor fracture through direct transmission
of energy from the orbital rim to the floor and
results in a compression-­type fracture. The orbital
floor may fracture alone (termed pure blowout),
or there may also be rim involvement (impure).
Once an internal orbital fracture occurs, the
orbital volume may expand or contract secondary

328

V. Anehosur and A. Visweswaran

to the direction of displacement of the orbital
fracture (i.e. blow-in or blowout).
Extraocular muscle imbalance and diplopia are
result of muscle contusion. Less commonly, however, they can be the result of incarceration of either
the extraocular muscle (e.g. inferior rectus muscle)
or the soft tissue adjacent to the muscles, cranial
neuropathy (third, fourth or fifth cranial nerves) or
deviation of the visual axes. True entrapment in adult
patients is very unusual. In children, however, blowout fractures may produce complete immobility of
the ocular globe with enophthalmos. Such significant restriction of ocular motility implies actual
muscle incarceration, which is an absolute indication for immediate orbital exploration with release
of the entrapped extraocular muscle system. It is
typically accompanied by pain on attempted rotation
of the globe, nausea and vomiting, all of which are
unusual in adult patients with blowout fractures.

19.7

Clinical Features
and Evaluation

A thorough systematic clinical evaluation of the
patient is mandatory for diagnosis and treatment
planning.
1. Periorbital tissues.
• Oedema (Fig. 19.10a).
• Circumorbital ecchymosis (Fig. 19.10b).
• Subconjunctival haemorrhage (Fig. 19.10b).
• Surgical emphysema.
• Hyphema.
2. Eyelids
• Abnormality of palpebral fissure—height/
width/inclination (Fig. 19.10c).
• Ptosis (Fig. 19.10d).
3. Ligaments
• Alteration in the canthal level—mongoloid
slant (Fig. 19.10e).
• Alteration in the ocular level (due to disruption of suspensory ligament).
• Telecanthus (Fig. 19.10f, g).
4. Nose.
• Reduced dorsal nasal projection, upturned
nasal tip (Fig. 19.10h).
• Accentuation of naso-frontal angle—‘pig
snout’ accentuated nasojugal fold—inward
telescoping medial wall into ethmoid
(Fig. 19.10h).
• CSF rhinorrhea.
5. Neurological deficits.
• Paraesthesia.
• Paresis of extraocular muscles (Fig. 19.10i).
• Paresis of facial nerve.
6. Eye.
• Limitation of ocular movements.
• Diplopia.
• Exophthalmos/enophthalmos (Fig. 19.10j).
• Pupillary reflexes.
• Ophthalmic injuries.
• Increased interpupillary distance.

7. Lacrimal apparatus.
• Epiphora (50%).
• Wounds involving the puncta.

19.8

Clinical Examination

1. Ocular motility—Putterman et al.’s method of
evaluating diplopia (Fig. 19.11).
2. Pupil response—Examine the size, shape and
symmetry.
The response of the pupil of the eye upon
which light falls is direct light reflex and
that of the opposite side is consensual light
reflex, which occurs due to bilateral innervation at Edinger-­
Westphal nucleus
(Table 19.3).
For example: If left oculomotor nerve is damaged—[same side both direct and consensual lost]
(a) Left direct reflex is lost.
(b) Right consensual reflex is intact.
(c) Right direct reflex is intact.
(d) Left consensual reflex is lost.
If left optic nerve is damaged—[same direct
lost, opposite consensual lost]
(e) Left direct reflex is lost.
(f) Right consensual reflex is lost.
(g) Right direct reflex is intact.
(h) Left consensual reflex is intact.
3. Forced duction test—It was described for evaluating Duane syndrome in the 1900s. It is indicated for evaluating muscle ­palsy/restriction.
Technique: A topical anaesthetic agent
0.5% tetracaine hydrochloride eye drops is
applied following which the tendon of the
inferior rectus muscle is grasped through the
conjunctiva of the inferior fornix and the globe
is manipulated through its entire range of
motion (Fig. 19.12).
Interpretation:
Limitation of motion—Not invariably an
indication of muscular entrapment but other
causes are:

19.10 Other Modalities
• CT axial, coronal and sagittal view
(1–1.5 mm)—gold standard.
• 3D reconstruction
• Ultrasonography (indicated for posterior segment evaluation, intraocular lesion, tissue
thickness measurement, intraocular foreign

• MRI.

19.11 Assessment of CT Scans
• Preoperative assessment of CT scans in axial,
coronal and sagittal sections of 1 mm cuts for
assessing the fracture pattern, extent of
involvement of the orbital walls and defect
size for planning optimal surgical technique
and reconstruction options.

19.11.1 1 cm Rule
• The implant should stay away around 1 cm
from the entrance of the bony optic canal. The
implant overcorrection away from the optic
canal leads to a more lazy S-shaped implant in
the posterior orbital third for the midsagittal
plane.
• The muscle entrapment can be assessed by
observing the change in the direction of rectus
muscle, the honeycomb appearance and how
well the capsule is defined.

• Reduction of the fractures.

The various indications for surgery in an
orbital fracture were described by Gassner et al.
as follows [18]:
1. Fractures involving one half or more of the
orbital floor and/or medial wall.
2. Computed tomography (CT) evidence of
orbital soft tissue entrapment.
3. Diplopia and ocular motility limitation within
30 degrees of primary position.
4. Enophthalmos of more than 2 mm.
5. Hypaesthesia of the infraorbital nerve
territory.
Algorithm for Orbital Fracture
Management [19]

• Absent—but if signs of orbital blow in
fracture are significant, urgent decompression should be done.
2. Enophthalmos >2 mm, restriction in ocular
motility, loss of ligamentous support:
• Present—repair orbital floor.
• Absent—wait and reassess after 10–14
days.

19.12.2.3 Contraindications
• Lacerated globe.
• Hyphema.
• No sight in the other eyes.
• Recent ophthalmologic surgery and those
with medical instability.
Ophthalmologic evaluation and clearance are
necessary in such cases prior to any manipulation
of the bony orbit or periorbital soft tissue
(Table 19.4).

regarding lid retraction.

19.13.1 Surgical Steps
• Step 1: Protect the globe—tarsorrhaphy
suture/scleral shell.
• Step 2: Marking of incision line for subciliary incision—2 mm below the eyelashes
only through the skin (Fig. 19.17a, b).
• Step 3: Vasoconstriction.
• Step 4: Skin incision deepened and dissection carried out in layers leaving pretarsal
portion of orbicularis muscle; dissection
4–6 mm inferiorly in this plane is adequate
(Fig. 19.17c).
• Step 5: Subcutaneous dissection—skin should
be separated from pretarsal portion of muscle
along entire length, 4–6 mm dissection
(Fig. 19.17d).
• Step 6: Sub-orbicularis dissection—supraperiosteal dissection between orbicularis
oculi and orbital septum; extend completely
till the orbital rim at the subcutaneous
plane.
• Step 7: Incision is placed between the pretarsal and preseptal portion of orbicularis oculi
muscle is done just inferior to the level of initial incision line.
• Step 8: Periosteal incision—incision
through the periosteum along the anterior
maxilla 3–4 mm inferior to the rim
(Fig. 19.17e).

• Note: Pretarsal muscle still remaining on the
inferior tarsus and the orbital septum which
restricts the orbital fat from entering the field
• Step 9: Subperiosteal dissection of anterior
maxilla and/or orbit floor (Fig. 19.17f).
Follow-up of up to 6 months showed aesthetically acceptable scar with blepharoplasty incision
with no added complications (Fig. 19.17g, h).

19.13.2 Treatment Algorithm
for Orbital Wall Fractures
1. Small-sized, low-complexity defects (class I):
Most materials are suitable; biological behaviour is most important and resorbable may be
used in these cases.
2. Medium-sized, medium-complexity defects
(class II): Apart from the biological behaviour
of an implant, the experience of the surgeon
with specific types of orbital implants will
benefit the outcome. Various materials can be
used, from autologous materials to alloplasts
(e.g. porous polyethylene or titanium).
3. Large-sized, high-complexity defects (classes
III–VI): Stability and contour become more
significant, and pre-bent or patient-specific
titanium mesh is the preferred reconstruction
material.

19.14 Graft Materials Used
for Orbital Floor
Reconstruction

Factors influencing decision for the choice of
the material include surgeon experience, severity
of fracture, individual characteristics and the cost.
Gellrich mentions two premises in reconstructive orbital surgery:

The first step in a choice for an implant is to focus
on its most important features in order to reduce
complication incidence.
Ideal properties:

1. ‘You have to prove that you have been there’.
2. ‘Make sure your reconstructed contour stays’.

• Lightweight.
• Porosity (the implant must allow vascular
orbital tissues to invade its structure).
• Biocompatibility (the implant has to be tolerated and accepted by the orbital tissues).
• Lower incidence of complications.
• Easy to insert.
• Cost-effective.

• Materials can be broadly divided as radiopaque and radiolucent (Table 19.6).

19.14.1 Autologous Bone Graft
Autologous bone grafts can be harvested from
calvarial bone (Fig. 19.18 a, b), maxillary anterior wall (Fig. 19.19 a–c), symphysis, ramus of

19

Orbital Fractures

a

343

b

Fig. 19.18 (a) and (b) Post-op CT coronal section showing calvarial bone graft used for reconstruction of right orbital
floor. Courtesy: SDMCFU

mandible, iliac crest and coronoid process of the
mandible.
In 2012, a paper by Zunz et al. concluded that
the construction of the orbital floor fractures
after trauma by using autologous bone grafts is
safe and associated with a low rate of complications [21].
As demonstrated by studies, there is a lack of
consensus in recognizing one material as the
optimal one for orbital reconstruction. The available products are the following:
1. Titanium mesh presents a series of advantages
(Fig. 19.20a–d). In 2009, Scolozzi revealed in
his paper a high rate of success with an acceptable rate of major clinical complications
(10%) and an anatomic restoration of the bony
orbital contour and volume that closely
approximated that of the contralateral uninjured orbit [22].
Comparison of Calvarial Bone and
Titanium Mesh as a Reconstructive Material
(Table 19.7).
• Gear et al. (2002) (Safety of Titanium Mesh
for Orbital Reconstruction—Annals of Plastic
Surgery) in their study on 55 cases with 67
orbital fractures involving defect size >2 cm
reported only 1 case with abscess as a postop-

erative complication. No other implant related
complications was observed over a period of
44-month follow-up [23].
• Sargent and Fulks et al. (1991) (Reconstruction
of Internal Orbital Fracture with Vitallium
Mesh)—46 cases, 57 orbits, no post-op infection, 9-month follow-up [24].
2. Porous Polyethylene Sheets (PPE).
In a study published by Lin, it was demonstrated that porous polyethylene implants in
the repair of orbital wall fractures had good
results with few complications [25].
The advantages are availability, contouring
(eased by the artificial sterile skull), smooth
edges and allows tissue ingrowth.
The disadvantages are they are not radiopaque (not visible on post-operative images)
and lack of rigidity when a very thin wafer of
PPE is used. When a thicker rigid wafer is
used, there is a risk of causing a dystopia and
less drainage from the orbit than with a titanium mesh.
3. Composite of Porous Polyethylene and
Titanium Mesh.
By combining titanium mesh with porous
polyethylene, the material becomes radiopaque and more rigid than the porous polyethylene of a similar thickness. Some surgeons

a

V. Anehosur and A. Visweswaran

also believe that there is less risk of having
retained sharp barbs, which can lead to an
entrapment of soft tissues during placement.
The advantages are availability, stability,
contouring (eased by the artificial sterile
skull), adequate in large three-wall fractures
(the pre-bent plate is limited to medial wall
and orbital wall fractures only), radio-opacity,
no donor site needed and tissue incorporation
may occur.
4. Resorbable Materials.
Thermoplastic and non-thermoplastic
materials. Thermoplastic blends of cornstarch
material with ethylene vinyl alcohol
copolymers reinforced with hydroxyapatite
­

were used based on their mechanical properties and their modulus closed to that of human
bone [25].
The advantages are availability, ability to
contour (only for thermoplastics), smooth surface and smooth edges.
The disadvantages are no radio-opacity,
degradation of material with possible contour
loss, sterile infection/inflammatory response,
difficult to shape according to patients’ anatomy (only for non-thermoplastics) and less
drainage from the orbit than with uncovered
titanium mesh (in case when non-perforated
material is used).
5. Preformed Orbital Implant.

Advantages:
1. Proper positioning by metric info and implementing clinically relevant vectors—like the

design (Fig. 19.21).

implant together with a periorbital implant

versus extension of the orbital implant to the
periorbital rim.
3. No impingement of orbital soft tissues possible, an overcorrected posterior ledge in an
‘inverted snow shovel design (ISSD)’.
4. Patient-specific in design.
5. Stable and non-deformable.

19.14.2 Post-Operative Assessment
Our publication on ‘Orbital observation chart:
significant in orbital fractures or not?’ [26], a retrospective study on 236 patients with orbital fractures who underwent surgical intervention in our
centre from 2011 to 2016 was conducted. The
parameters included orbital pain, visual acuity,
proptosis, pupillary size and response for prompt
detection for potential post-operative complications (Fig. 19.22).
We inferred that orbital chart monitoring
represents straightforward and effective
method to detect any complications after surgical management.

19.15 Complications
Complications related to the injury itself or to
repair are difficult to predict in the acute setting
and, once clinically manifested, are challenging
to repair because of intraconal or extraconal
fibrosis.

19.16 Paediatric Consideration
We have a very limited experience in the management of orbital fractures in paediatric age
group; however, the important considerations in
the diagnosis and management include:
• The orbital fracture is the third most common
of paediatric facial fractures, and it will be
“trapdoor” pattern as there will be increased
subcutaneous fat which provides cushioning
effect to facial bones.
• In the paediatric population, the bony elasticity allows the fracture to open and close
back into position, tightly trapping the peri-

•

•

•

•

orbital tissue or inferior rectus or oblique
muscle. This clinical presentation is referred
to as the white-eyed blowout fracture
(age < 18 years), which involves a history of
periorbital trauma, little ecchymosis or
oedema (lack of black eye), but marked
EOM restriction [31].
Orbital floor fracture with entrapment—trapdoor/white-eyed blowout fracture (WEBOF)
is a RELATIVE EMERGENCY.
Nausea, vomiting, pain, restriction in ocular
movement and bradycardia, absence of subconjunctival haemorrhage.
Binocular diplopia is slower to resolve and
more likely to be persistent in paediatric
patients.
The management in younger patients is often
more conservative because of potential growth
impairment. As the facial skeleton matures,

350

more conventional surgical approaches
become appropriate.
• With white-eyed blowout fracture, ischemia
can cause permanent damage to the involved
EOM with resultant Volkmann contracture of
extraocular muscles (VC-EOM). Because of
this, white-eyed blowout fracture is considered a surgical emergency and warrants operative intervention within 24 h of injury. In
addition, VC-EOM could also occur in orbital
compartment syndrome, in elderly patients
who are hypotensive and in those with small-­
fracture diplopia.
• Steps followed in indicated paediatric orbital
floor fracture.
–– Assessment with CT scan.
–– Transconjunctival approach.
–– Bioresorbable mesh/titanium.
Observe for globe changes with regular
follow-up.

19.17 Recent Advances
Over the last 30 years, changes in terms of diagnostics, surgical approaches, material for reconstruction,
intraoperative
evaluation
and
post-operative management of orbital fractures
have evolved drastically. The post-traumatic orbital
surgery was regarded as a ‘yes’ or ‘no’ decision.
3D imaging is regarded as a standard before taking
a patient to reconstructive orbital surgery. The current trends in accurate treatment planning and
diagnosis include stereolithographic models,
CAD-CAM-based
individualised
implants,
patient-specific implant (PSI) [32], intraoperative
navigation, intraoperative 3D CT imaging [30],
MRI and cone beam computed tomography
(CBCT). Endoscopic-assisted monitoring can be
used to provide intraoperative evidence to verify
the extent of dissection and position of the implant
at the posterior ledge and to clarify whether dissection meets the implant dimensions or not.
Fixation of the orbital implant is another controversy. Edward Ellis III always sees a danger to

V. Anehosur and A. Visweswaran

negative effects once the orbital implant is covering the inferior orbital rim and states that one
screw fixation should be enough—stable orbital
implant position. There is absolutely no reason to
exclude fixation ‘on’ or ‘over’ the bony inferior
orbital rim.

19.18 Conclusion
With evolution and advanced recent concepts in
technology taking an upper hand, the future generation of craniomaxillofacial surgeons should take
the challenge of developing our specialty further,
using the benefits of modern 3D imaging and take
the advantage of digital analysing, planning, engineering and manufacturing in a routine protocol to
the benefit of patient treatment and team education.
Patient specificity of treatment was and is always
an issue in fields like orthognathic surgery and definitely should become an issue in reconstructive
orbital surgery now and in the future.

19.19 Case Scenario
Chief Complaints A 39-year-old male presented with the chief complaint of constant pain
and persistent double vision in the left eye since
2 weeks.
History of Present Illness Past history revealed
that the patient had sustained injury to the left
side of his face due to fall from height 2 weeks
before and presence of persistent double vision
since the time of injury. He was referred by an
ophthalmologist for further evaluation and
management.
Past Medical History Not contributory.
Clinical Examination On examination, subconjunctival haemorrhage was noted in the left
eye. Mild tenderness was noted in left infraorbital rim without any step deformity. Eye movements were normal in all the gazes except in

19

Orbital Fractures

a

351

b

Fig. 19.25 (a) Facial profile view showing left subconjunctival haemorrhage and enophthalmos, (b) CT scan coronal
section showing prolapsed left orbital contents

superior gaze. Clinical evaluation revealed evidence of orbital dystopia and enophthalmos of
3 mm (Fig. 19.25a).
Radiological Examination Computed tomography (CT) scan of the orbit with 1 mm slices
revealed the fracture of left orbital floor with herniation of orbital contents into the maxillary
antrum along with entrapment of inferior rectus
muscle which is diagnosed as ‘pure blowout fracture of left orbital floor’ (Fig. 19.25b).
Treatment Patient was explained about the
need for surgery to repair the orbital defect, and
written consent was obtained. All routine haematological investigations like hemogram,
bleeding profile, PA chest and ECG were done
and were within the normal limit. The repair of
orbital floor was planned using endoscopicassisted combined subciliary and transantral
approach under general anaesthesia with nasal
endotracheal intubation [33].

19.19.1 Technique
The anterior sinus wall was exposed by an intraoral upper buccal vestibular incision. A small
bony window of 10 × 9 × 10 mm was created on
the anterior sinus wall keeping the periosteal con-

tinuity superiorly (Fig. 19.26a). 30-degree endoscope (Carl Zeiss) was introduced into the sinus,
and prolapsed orbital contents were visualised
(Fig. 19.26b). The herniated fat was pushed superiorly with blunt end of periosteal elevator.
Orbital septum was identified and sutured with
4-0 Vicryl (Fig. 19.26c). The orbital floor defect
was explored with subciliary approach to identify
the floor defect and reconstructed with titanium
orbital mesh (Fig. 19.26d). The correct position
of orbital mesh was verified with endoscope
assistance intraoperatively (Fig. 19.26e). Wound
closure of the subciliary incision was done in two
layers—the periosteum and skin sparing the muscle layer which can cause ectropion. The antrostomy defect was closed by placing the bone back
and securing it with Prolene sutures. Intraoral
wound closure was done with 3-0 Vicryl resorbable sutures.
Post-operatively, patient was instructed not to
blow his nose; decongestive nasal drops and prophylactic antibiotics were added. Patient was put
on soft diet for 2 weeks. Healing was uneventful
with excellent improvement in diplopia and
enophthalmos. Post-operative CT scans were
performed, which demonstrated good anatomic
reduction in orbital floor and repositioning of
prolapsed orbital contents (Fig. 19.27a). Patient
was followed up for 6 months with no evidence
of restriction in ocular movements (Fig. 19.27b).

Sujata Mohanty

20.1

Introduction

The frontal sinus has highly varying presentations in the craniofacial region. The frontal
sinuses are a set of two pyramidal, air-filled cavities of the frontal bone. The floor of the frontal
sinus consists of membranous bone and is the
thinnest of the sinus boundaries, forming the roof
of the orbit. The anterior table of the frontal sinus
is present just deep to the skin as well as subcutaneous tissue of the brow. The posterior table of
the frontal sinus is present adjacent to the dura of
the frontal lobe separating the sinus and anterior
cranial fossa [1]. The anterior table with a mean
thickness of 4–12 mm is significantly thicker
when compared to the posterior table which is
0.1–4.8 mm thick [2]. The typical size of a frontal
sinus is 24.3 mm (height) × 29 mm
(width) × 20.5 mm (depth) [3].
Although absent at birth, frontal sinus pneumatises through the expansion of the ethmoid air
cells into the frontal bone [4]. The frontal sinus

S. Mohanty (*)
Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery,
Maulana Azad Institute of Dental Sciences,
New Delhi, Delhi, India

becomes well developed by age 6, can be detected
on the radiograph at 7 years of age and attains its
full size by 12–16 years. It is divided into two
asymmetric compartments by the bony septum
creating left and right divisions. It is completely
absent in 4% of the population, and 11% have
unilateral frontal sinus [5].
The drainage of frontal sinus is variable. True
drainage via a frontonasal duct (FND) occurs in
only 15% of the population, ranging from a few
millimetres to 1 cm in length [6]. In the remaining 85%, the frontal sinus drains directly into
middle meatus along its anterosuperior portion
through an ostium without a true duct or occasionally by communicating through the ethmoids
via the ethmoidal infundibulum. The drainage
pattern of the frontal sinus has an hourglass shape
which includes the sinus infundibulum (located
posteromedially within the sinus), sinus ostium
and frontal recess (present in the middle meatus)
running in a superior to inferior direction [7].
Anterior ethmoidal branch of ophthalmic
artery is considered as main blood supply of the
frontal sinus. Some part is also supplied by supraorbital branch and supratrochlear branches.
Anterior portion of frontal sinus drains by the
diploic veins of Breschet, which further drains
into facial and superior ophthalmic veins.
Posteriorly, these diploic veins communicate
directly with dural sinuses as well as marrow of
the frontal bone via the foramen of Breschet.

Function

The sinus has been proposed to protect the ocular
globes and the frontal lobes while supplementing
its sinus function [8]. Although the presence of a
frontal sinus has been assumed to increase the
likelihood of frontal bone fracture, still it provides a shock-absorbing barrier for the intracranial contents. The epithelial lining of the frontal
sinus is composed of pseudostratified ciliated
columnar epithelium, which helps to remove the
mucus secretions produced by the goblet cells
interspersed within the epithelium. Cilia typically transport mucus in a circular fashion across
the frontal sinus, nasofrontal ducts and hiatus
semilunaris and finally draining into the nose [9].

20.3

Epidemiology/Mechanism
of Injury

The incidence of frontal sinus wall fractures is
approximately 5–15% of all maxillofacial fractures. Most of the time, it is associated with naso-­
orbito-­ethmoid complex fractures. Road traffic
accidents (52%) are among the most common
cause followed by physical assault (26%) and
industrial accidents (14%). It is commonly seen
in adult males between 20 and 30 years of age.
Anterior table fractures (43–61%) are more common as compared to the isolated posterior table
fractures (0.6–6%). More often both anterior and
posterior table (19–51%) are involved. Around
2.5–25% of all cases have reported nasofrontal
duct injury. Around 800–1600 N force is required
to fracture the anterior wall of the frontal sinus,
which is two to three times greater than that
required to fracture the zygomatic bone or mandible [10–16].

20.4

Classification

Various systems for classifying the frontal sinus
fractures are present in the literature [1, 2, 6, 15].
Luce divided frontal sinus fractures into anterior
fractures, anterobasilar fractures and frontal skull
fractures with extension into the sinus [17]. The

frontal sinus fractures into four types based on
the location (Table 20.1) [18].

20.5

Clinical Features

The clinical presentation of a frontal sinus wall
fracture differs depending on the severity of the
injury. Palpable or visible depression of the brow or
forehead should raise the suspicion of frontal sinus,
although it is not appreciable initially because of
swelling. Another important feature is frequent
frontal headache. Physical findings may include
paraesthesia especially numbness in suprabrow
region, epistaxis, forehead abrasions, diplopia, eyelid ecchymosis, lacerations and subconjunctival
haematoma. Careful inspection and firm palpation
of all the bony buttresses must be performed, even
through the often-oedematous soft tissues to identify any irregularities, mobility and crepitus.
Altered consciousness is indicative of intracranial
injury; hence, radiographic evaluation of the brain
is mandatory. When identified, lacerations must be
carefully explored to identify underlying open
bony injuries. Palpable bony crepitus in the nasofrontal region is highly suspicious of nasofrontal
duct injury. CSF leak in another important clinical
presentation is s­uggestive of dural tear due to the

20 Frontal Sinus Wall Fractures

fracture of cribriform plate or posterior table.
Ophthalmologic examination is mandatory in complex frontal or naso-­
orbito-­
ethmoidal fractures
(Table 20.2) [9, 17].

20.7.2 Posterior Table Fracture
20.7.2.1 Undisplaced or Mildly
Displaced Posterior Table
Fracture Without NFOT Injury
These types of fractures should be treated conservatively. The patient must be carefully observed
for any CSF leak or for any symptoms of NFOT
obstruction (frontal sinusitis).
20.7.2.2 Nasofrontal Outflow Tract
(NFOT) Injury Without
Significantly Displaced
Posterior Table Fracture
The nasofrontal duct is not typically damaged with
minimally displaced anterior table fractures; however, it is commonly associated with extensively
displaced frontal sinus fractures or associated NOE
and Le Fort fractures. For mild NFOT injury, various researchers have suggested either observation
or application of stent, although 30% of patients
have developed stent obstruction which further
requires intervention. If the nasofrontal outflow
tract is considerably damaged, the sinus must be
either obliterated or cranialised. The objectives of
obliteration are diligent elimination of the frontal
sinus mucosa, obstruction of the nasofrontal outflow tract and filling dead space with allogeneic,
alloplastic or autogenous graft [22].
20.7.2.3 Displaced Posterior Table
Fracture with NFOT Injury
Although solitary posterior table frontal sinus
fractures do occur, they are exceedingly rare.
Only if the posterior table is fractured without
any evidence of brain injury or dural tear, conservative management, including non-treatment, is
recommended. In case of lack of intracranial
injury, including dural tears, surgical intervention
will be dictated by displacement and the potential
for cosmetic deformity. As mentioned there will
be a concomitant anterior table fracture in
patients with posterior table fracture.
With significant posterior table fractures leading to brain injury or in patients with suspected or

Fig. 20.4 Management of frontal sinus fracture using
obliteration technique and cranialisation: (a) Firstly, the
sinus mucosal tissue is removed. (b) The intrasinus cortex is removed using a high-speed bur. (c) The nasofrontal duct is closed with a bone graft. (d) The cavity of
sinus is packed with autogenous/alloplastic graft. (e)
Cranialisation of a frontal sinus fracture includes elimination of the sinus mucosa, replacement or removal of
the posterior wall and reconstruction of the anterior wall,
and thereafter, the brain gradually expands to seal the
defect

established nasofrontal duct injury, supplementary surgical procedures are required. For cases
that involve anterior table fractures and nasofrontal duct injury, debridement of the mucosal membrane and obliteration of the sinus and ducts must
be performed (Fig. 20.4).
Special precaution is taken to remove the bone
segments of the anterior table to provide adequate
access to the contents of the sinus. At this stage,
confirmation of nasofrontal duct patency can be
established. The nasofrontal ducts, present along
the posteromedial part of the frontal sinus, may
be cannulated with an angiocatheter and methylene blue, sterile milk or fluorescein or even
saline injected [23]. This manoeuvre can clinically establish the patency of the nasofrontal
ducts. If the ducts are not patent, the sinus membrane must be thoroughly debrided. A curette is
used to remove the gross remnants of the sinus
membrane [24]. Once complete debridement has
been achieved, the next step involves the use of a
burr for curettage of the bony cavity of the frontal
sinus. The frontal sinus contains numerous canals

360

S. Mohanty

within the bone, termed the foramina of Breschet,
that represents invaginations of the sinus membrane. Any residual mucosal tissue left behind
may subsequently develop into a mucocele or
mucopyocele. The incidence of these complications is exceedingly low; however, when they do
occur, considerable morbidity results, including
brain abscess and even death. After the sinus has
been meticulously debrided, obliteration of the
sinus and the outflow tract is completed. There
are different materials that are available for frontal sinus obliteration. The choice of material is
chosen according to surgeon’s experience and
surgical convenience and includes pericranial
flap, temporalis muscle and, most commonly,
abdominal fat.
In addition to obliteration of the sinus, it is
also important to obliterate the nasofrontal
ducts to stop any nasal contaminants from
migrating and entering the frontal sinus area.
Similar to obliteration of the frontal sinus, a
variety of materials may be used for this purpose, including abdominal fat, temporalis
muscle and bone fragments [14]. The obliteration procedures are then followed by reconstruction of the anterior table. If the initial
fragments of the anterior table bone can be

used, they can be pieced together for reconstruction, and later the skin flap is closed. If
the fragments cannot be pieced together
because of severe comminution or avulsion,
the deficiency can be reconstructed with
autogenous bone or mesh [24, 25].

20.7.2.4 Displaced Posterior Table
Fracture with Dural Tear/
CSF Leak
When significant dural tear along with a persistent CSF leak or intracranial haemorrhage that
requires evacuation or brain contusion along with
cerebral oedema and elevated intracranial pressure is present, craniotomy will be required to
control the injury to the brain. To achieve this,
removal of the posterior table, obliteration of the
frontal sinus and obliteration of the nasofrontal
ducts are essential. Removal of the posterior table
permits the oedematous brain to expand inside
the frontal sinus, thereby decreasing intracranial
pressure and preventing further brain injury.
Once the cranialisation is completed, the frontal
sinus will be obliterated along with the nasofrontal ducts.

Complications of Frontal
Sinus Fractures

Frontal sinus fracture complications could be a
result of the trauma itself or the outcome of treatment. They can range from cosmetic or else functional in nature and, in few cases, produce fatal
manifestations [26]. The patients carry risk for
complications throughout their lifetime, and the
overall rate of complication is approximately
10–20% [27]. The early complications include
wound infection, meningitis, sinusitis, pneumocephalus, CSF or death. After 6 months of the
injury, late complications such as mucocele,
mucopyocele, cosmetic deformity, brain abscess
and osteomyelitis have been reported.

20.9

Conclusion

The frontal sinus is a significant part of the face,
which requires urgent intervention and definitive
management. Improper management may lead to
various complications, and sometimes it may be lifethreatening. It is useful to divide the fractures into
those that affect the anterior table, posterior table or
both, as well as the amount of displacement involving each segment. Evaluation of the nasofrontal duct
is additionally crucial. High-risk patients are those
that present with posterior table disruption, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leak and severe frontal recess
injury. Long-term follow-up is crucial in these
patients as devastating complications may develop
months and even years after the surgery.

of Injury

trauma scoring scales are available [6, 7].

It was put forth in 2006 by Zhang et al. [10].
The Maxillofacial Injury Severity Score
(MFISS) only evaluates the injuries to the
maxillofacial region. Injuries other than
maxillofacial ones are not included.
