4. Facial Fracture Severity Score (FFSS):
Catapano et al. [11] in 2010 proposed this
score in which the craniofacial region is
divided into 41 different anatomic sites and
each is graded from 0 to 3 individually. The
grading depends upon the following
parameters:
• Presence of fracture
• Degree of displacement
• Bone loss
The maximum score in FFSS can be 123.
This scale has its application in evaluation
of facial fractures systematically, epidemiological studies and analysis of cost benefits.
Colour coding again makes it easy to use
(Fig. 21.2).
5. ZS Model: Ahmad et al. [12] in 2012 proposed
this model which uses models of MFISS,
FISS, Cooter-David Score and FFSS to predict the severity and patterns of the maxillofacial injury. The scoring system is based on a
colour-coded skeletal map. It incorporates the
best features from previous systems. The
model is very simple to use. It has an app
which is an interactive modality allowing for
fast scoring. This model marks comminution
of the fracture as a multiplier of the initial
score and also includes damage to teeth, as all
these factors alter the overall prognosis in
such patients. However, it leaves out critical
soft tissue components, physiological parameters and a cranial component.

Patients with panfacial trauma have multiple
potential associated injuries as the degree of
trauma sustained by the patient is very high [2].

Every patient with such a degree of trauma must
undergo Advanced Trauma Life Support
(ATLS)-staged assessment. The order starts
with triage, followed by primary survey, resuscitation, adjunct to primary survey, secondary
survey, adjunct to secondary survey and definitive care. This rules out any life-threatening
injuries, and then the surgeons can focus solely
on the specific regions. Also, the CSF leaks
must be diagnosed promptly and managed
efficiently.

1. Soft tissue injuries: Patients with panfacial

21.5

Clinical Features

All the features and specific presentations of individual facial fractures will be present in panfacial
trauma. These are explained extensively in the
individual chapters. Along with these, specific
features are given below:
• Facial projection and height problems in panfacial fractures [1]:
–– Frontal bone—Supraorbital comminution
and flattening of the frontal region. CSF
leak may or may not be present.
–– Nasal-orbital-ethmoid—There will be
comminution because buttressing will be
lacking in this region.
–– Zygomatic arch—Arch will be laterally displaced/bowing of the arch will be present.
–– Zygomaticomaxillary buttress—Buttress
will be collapsed.
–– Maxilla/mandible—There will be malocclusion, especially anterior open bite. The reason

Radiological Features

Role of 2D imaging is getting reduced in diagnosing panfacial trauma. In this age of surgical
navigation and computer-assisted presurgical
planning, facial X-rays cannot be relied upon
solely. Computed tomography (CT) is the gold
standard now for diagnosis and planning in panfacial trauma (Fig. 21.4a, b).
Key for any imaging modality is:

Presence of any one of the five criteria confirms the need of facial CT. Wisconsin criteria
has sensitivity of 98%, specificity of 22.3%, negative predictive value of 87.8% and positive predictive value of 68.5% for presence of facial
fractures. These criteria reduce the need for facial
CT use by 9% [16].
Standard X-ray imaging useful in panfacial
trauma is:

• To detect both the hard and soft tissue injuries
• To characterize both the hard and soft tissue
injuries
• To help the surgeon in surgical planning for

21.7.3 Surgical Approaches [1, 4]
Approach to the facial skeleton in cases with panfacial fractures should be based on wide exposure, adequate visualisation and adequate
reduction. There are various approaches which
can be taken and are explained in detail in the
respective sections of the book. The type of surgical approach depends on the location of the fracture, severity of the facial injury, extent of the
exposure required and amount of comminution
present in the region. Common surgical
approaches required in the panfacial fractures are
as follows:

Maintenance of a secure airway is the most
important aspect of treating panfacial trauma.
When the patient has extensive head injuries
along with panfacial fractures, we prefer to
secure the airway by performing a tracheostomy.
Other indications of performing tracheostomy •
include extensive fractures of the naso-orbito-­
ethmoid region, patient requiring prolonged intubation and patient requiring multiple surgeries.
Naso-endotracheal intubation is generally not
preferred especially in cases with naso-orbito-­ •
ethmoid fractures, fractures of naso-maxillary
buttress and cribriform plate fracture. Oral intubation is favoured when multiple posterior teeth
are absent and when intermaxillary fixation is
contraindicated. Another option to secure an airway in such cases is submental intubation. But •
the submental intubation is contraindicated especially when an extra-oral approach is required for
managing multiple fractures of the mandible. An •
algorithm for airway management must be followed in such patients (Fig. 21.6).

Coronal approach: To access the frontal sinus,
naso-orbito-ethmoidal region, supraorbital
rim, roof of the orbit, lateral and medial walls
of the orbit, medial canthal ligament and zygomatic arch.
Subciliary and transconjunctival approach:
To access the medial and lateral orbital wall,
orbital floor and infraorbital rim. An extended
lateral canthotomy incision with the transconjunctival approach can be used to access the
frontozygomatic suture.
Upper eyelid crease incision: To access the
frontozygomatic suture and lateral and superior walls of the orbit.
Peri-nasal incisions: To access the medial
canthal tendon, nasolacrimal sac and the naso-­
orbito-­ethmoidal region.

21

Panfacial Trauma

375

• Maxillary vestibular incision: To access the
maxilla and zygomaticomaxillary buttress.
• Mandibular vestibular incision: To access the
non-comminuted fractures of the mandible
including the ramus, body, parasymphysis and
symphysis region.
• Cervical approach (Risdon, peri-angular,
Hinds): To access the entire mandible except
the high condylar region.
• Pre-auricular approach: Can be used together
with the coronal approach to access the high
condylar fractures.

21.7.4 Sequencing in Panfacial
Fractures
Many authors have put forth various sequencing methods in managing panfacial fractures.
Historically, the maxillofacial surgeons being
trained initially in dentistry were more comfortable in starting with occlusal units as the
starting point [1]. The two most common
approaches used nowadays are the “bottom-up
and inside-­out” or the “top-down and outsidein” [1, 4].

21.7.4.1

Bottom-Up and Inside-Out
Approach [4] (Fig. 21.7)
This approach dates to the time where rigid
internal fixation was not developed but still is
one of the most popular approaches amongst
the maxillofacial surgeons even nowadays. In
this approach the mandible is fixed first and
then used as base/stable point over which the
other fractures are reduced and fixed. The subcondylar fractures however need to be reduced
by an open approach and fixed by internal fixation. The patient’s occlusion is brought into
maxilla-mandibular fixation (MMF). But before
bringing the occlusion into MMF, the maxilla
should be properly positioned. The mandible is
then restored by starting first with the subcondyle and then the ramus/body/symphysis
region. Now, originally the next fixation must
be of the maxilla at the zygomaticomaxillary
buttress, but many authors suggest that doing

Fig. 21.7 Bottom-up and inside-out approach (ref:
https://aocmf3.aofoundation.org)

this step first makes the correction of facial
width in midface region difficult. Thus, a break
in the sequence is preferred by reducing and
­fixating the zygomaticomaxillary complex first
at the sphenozygomatic suture and then at the
zygomatic arch and the zygomaticomaxillary
suture. This establishes the facial width in the
midface. Then next fracture to be addressed is
the frontal sinus wall fracture followed by nasoorbito-­ethmoidal fracture which is reduced and
fixed. The final fixation should be done at the
maxilla at the zygomaticomaxillary buttress
(Le Fort I level).
If there are associated palatal fractures, they
must be addressed in the initial steps. The disadvantage of this approach is that the subcondylar
fractures need to be reduced and fixed via an
open approach in all the cases. But this approach
can be useful when there is significant comminution of the frontal bone, so it is better to start
caudally.

21.7.4.2 Top-Down and Outside-In
Approach [2, 4] (Fig. 21.8)
This approach starts by addressing first the frontal and the supraorbital rim fractures. Next in the
line is the zygomaticomaxillary complex which
is reduced and fixed to restore the facial width
and the projection. Then the naso-orbito-ethmoid
fractures are repaired. The maxilla is then fixed

376

A. Datarkar and A. Bhawalkar

21.7.5 Soft Tissue Suspension [1, 2, 4]
In panfacial trauma, because of the wide exposure required, there is a lot of soft tissue sagging.
This needs to be corrected by resuspending the
periosteum, fascia, muscles and the superficial
muscular aponeurotic system. This can be prevented a little by limiting the exposure and extent
of dissection. This can be corrected by reapproximating the periosteum or fascia to the facial skeleton by drilling holes and putting the soft tissues
back in their place. Following are important areas
at which deep closure and resuspension are a
must:
Fig. 21.8 Top-down and outside-in approach (ref: https://
aocmf3.aofoundation.org)

by using the guidance from the zygomaticomaxillary buttress and the pyriform rim. The patient
is then placed under the maxillomandibular fixation. Finally, the mandibular fractures are
addressed by fixing first the subcondyle and proceeding next to the other regions of the
mandible.
The advantage of this approach is that the
open reduction of the condyle is not necessary
unless there is a bilateral or a highly displaced
fracture. But if the condylar fractures are not
fixed, the patient needs to be put under prolonged periods of maxillomandibular fixation.
This might lead to patient discomfort and potential cause for temporomandibular joint
ankylosis.
Whichever approach is followed, the goal
must be to restore the facial height, width and
projection. The panfacial fractures must be
addressed by restoring the “known” and then proceeding to the “unknown”. There are certain key
landmarks which might help the surgeon in getting the facial skeleton in a proper position. These
are [1, 4]:

Mandible

21.7.6 Timing in Panfacial Trauma
Management
Timing of treating the panfacial fractures has
always been a topic of debate amongst many surgeons. Many patients with such a level of trauma
always have other concomitant injuries. Very
often such injuries are life-threatening for the
patients. These potentially life-threatening injuries include the intracranial injuries, abdominal
injuries, pneumothoracic injuries and cervical
spine injuries [17]. Amongst them the most common concomitant injury associated with panfacial fractures is the intracranial injury [18]. The
incidence given in the literature for intracranial
injuries in panfacial trauma ranges from 20 to
40% [17, 18]. Thus, in most of the trauma set-­
ups, such life-threatening injuries are addressed
first and when the patient is out of any danger, the
panfacial fractures are addressed.
This delay in treatment for panfacial trauma
can have long-term consequences on the overall
treatment outcome. There are many conflicting
views amongst the surgeons whether treatment
delay really affects the treatment outcome [17,

21

Panfacial Trauma

377

19]. Hurrell and Batstone [17] did a systematic
review in which 18 studies found no statistically
significant relationship between treatment delay
and treatment outcome, while 9 studies found a
statistically significant relationship between
treatment delay and worse treatment outcomes,
and 3 studies had conflicting results. The major
variables to assess the treatment outcome were
infection, malocclusion, dehiscence of the surgical wound, malunion and non-union [17].
Late corrections of such fractures become
very challenging, and a proper treatment plan has
to be followed to restore the form, function and
aesthetics of the patient. He et al. [19] did a retrospective study of 33 late-treated cases and devised
a treatment order. The first step is to free the mandibular angle and condyle (if involved) followed
by reconstruction of the mandibular arch and
restoring the height. The second step is to restore
the facial width and projection of the upper face
and midface. Finally, maxillary fixation at Le
Fort 1 level by doing Le Fort 1 osteotomy is the
last step. He et al. [19] had a success rate of 80%
by treating such cases in the above order.

bony contacts or the use of bone grafts if excessive hard tissue loss is present. Calvarial bone
grafts are usually preferred as the coronal incision is taken in most of the panfacial trauma
patients.

Complications [2]

2. Long-term complications:
• Plate exposure
• Hollowing of the temporal region
• Malocclusion
• Orbital dystopia
• Frontal sinus mucoceles
• Facial width discrepancy
• Facial projection alteration
• Facial length alteration
Plate exposure can be treated by removing the
exposed plates. Temporal hollowing can be
addressed by soft tissue augmentation procedures
such as micro-fat injections, alloplastic implants
and dermal grafts [2]. Post-operative persistent
malocclusion requires orthognathic corrections.
Residual deformities need to be corrected based
on the functional and aesthetic problems.

21.10 Case Discussion
21.10.1 Case 1

–– Enophthalmos along with medial gauge
restriction of the right eye.
• Paraesthesia over the right supraorbital
region.
• Loss of contour over the right frontal
region.
• Sutured lacerated wound over the upper lip.
2. On palpation of the swelling:
• Swelling was soft in consistency, non-­
reducible, compressible and tender on
palpation.
3. Forced duction test of the left eye revealed lateral rectus muscle entrapment.
4. Goldman visual field test revealed binocular
diplopia.

• Chief complaint: A 25-year-old male patient
reported with a chief complaint of pain and
swelling over the right side of the face along
with inability to chew the food.
• History of present illness: The patient was
apparently alright when he met with an
RTA. The cause of the RTA was due to slippage of the bike. There was history of head
injury, loss of consciousness, bleeding from
the nose and mouth and retrograde amnesia
when brought to a tertiary trauma centre.
There was no history of cerebrospinal leak.
The primary management including maintenance of airway, achieving the bleeding
control from the lacerated wound over the
upper lip by primary suturing, nasal bleeding control by pressure packing and cervical spine stabilisation for a suspected
cervical spine injury was done. After the
initial stabilisation, patient was admitted in
our unit and was posted for surgery

22.1

Animal Bite Injuries

Animal bites are the complex type of injuries
requiring application of traumatology as well as
reconstructive principals simultaneously, making it more challenging and often enigmatic
(Figs. 22.1 and 22.2). Humans and animals
share a strong mutual bond and dynamic relationship amongst them. Interferences while having food, feeling of threat to their babies and
startling them suddenly may change behaviour
of domestic animal provoking them to behave
aggressively. However, deforestation, increased
interference of humans in forest and close contact with their territory are some of the reasons
for wild animal attacks.
As such, animal attack is a less common cause
of injury to maxillofacial region with incidence
I. B. Kar (*)

ranging from 1.2 to 2.3% cases [1, 2]. But contradictorily, injury to the facial region is third most
common occurrence in animal attack following
upper and lower limb. The nose and lips are
amongst the most frequently affected region also
called as ‘central target area’ [3]. Though pets
like dog and cat contribute up to 80–90% of the
total animal attacks, domestic animals like horse,
camel and sheep share up to 3%, while the rest
6% includes wild animals like bear, lion, hyena,
elephant and many more [4]. In adults, only 10%
of animal attacks involve head and neck region;
crosswise head/face region of children is more
commonly affected with 76% involvement of lip,
nose or cheek area [3]. Domestic animals generally present with minor to intermediate type of
injury except large domestic animals, rarely
causing a severe form of injury both in children
and in adult. In contrast, wild animals having
larger jaw size and big paws with long nonretractable claws, tusks or horns inflict an injury
of higher magnitude. Sometimes, the animal
attack may lead to life-threatening injuries or
death of the victim due to compromised airway,
cranio-cerebral trauma and exsanguinations [3].
Humans being a social animal may contribute
up to 20% of all bite injuries [5]. Human bites
clinically can be of two different types: ‘Direct’
type is secondary to child abuse, sexual crimes/
activity or self-defence bites. The ‘Indirect’ type
is because of a blow with the fist on another person’s teeth. It is also called as ‘fight bite or clench

22.2

Classification

Rueff et al. (Table 22.1) and Lackmann et al.
(Table 22.2) have classified the wound inflicted
in animal attack according to the depth of anatomic structures involved and injury to vascular
structure or nerve, making it easy to understand
the severity of attack [6, 7]. However, in 2005,
Stefanopoulos et al. modified Lackmann’s classification and further subdivided it into II and III
stages (Table 22.3) [8]. Early grades or stages of
classification denote mild to moderate degree of
trauma, while advanced grades or stages represent victim with severe impact. These classifications are useful to access the immediate wound
status in terms of anatomical depth and tissue
damage and helpful in deciding the need of antibiotic prophylaxis as well as choice of anaesthesia to be used.
Fig. 22.2 Complex injury to face, head and neck region
due to bear attack

fist bite’. The own bite pattern is specific for indirect type; hence, the name ‘reverse bite injury’ is
also used. Direct type may present as oval or
semi-lunar-shaped injury, abrasion or haematomas or sometimes with tissue loss (Fig. 22.3).

22.3.1.1

22.3.1.2 Basic Wound Care
• Wound irrigation helps in washing out the
debris and any residual foreign bodies. At
least 200–250 mL of solution should be used
for irrigation. Preferably 30–60 mL-sized
syringe and 19–20-G gauze needle or plastic
catheter should be used, which generates
5–8 psi pressure sufficient for optimum wound
cleaning. Washing the wound with soap followed by use of 1–2% benzalkonium chloride
or 1% cetrimonium bromide or 1% povidone-­
iodine solution reduces viral load significantly
in grossly contaminated wound. Continuous
irrigation is as effective as pulsatile lavage, but
area with loose connective tissue should be
avoided [3].
• A meta-analysis by Cheng et al. [9] states that
primary closure of wound does not increase the
chances of wound infection in animal bite cases
[9]. While on the contrary, Cochrane Systematic
Review (2019) concluded that the potential
benefits and harms of primary ­closure versus
delayed or no closure in animal bite have
remained uncertain, and more well-­formulated
trials are required [10]. After going through
review of many studies on facial wound due to
animal attack, the author’s opinion goes in

I. B. Kar et al.

Fig. 22.5 Temporary stabilisation of the mandible and

Fig. 22.4 Tusk of elephant ruptured the orofacial complex with tongue hanging in submental area (Category I)

favour of primary closure. Primary closure or
stay sutures have an advantage of good aesthetic over no closure with risk of infection
remaining unaltered, except in punctured
wounds (cat bites). Special injuries like wound
over the hand and avulsion injury to cartilage
are more likely to get infected, so we should
take utmost precaution for the same [11].
• Temporary stabilisation of fractured segments
should be done to reduce the blood loss as well as
for maintaining airway patency. Fig. 22.4 shows
a case of an elephant attack where a blow by the
tusk of an elephant has ruptured the orofacial
complex. Immediate stabilization of tongue and
maxillo-mandibular complex was done in ER
which has protected him from developing respiratory distress (Fig. 22.5).

22.3.1.3 Prophylaxis
1. Tetanus immunisation has to be considered, if
not taken as per vaccination schedule as
described in Chap. 9.

2. Post-exposure anti-rabies therapy is required
to protect victim from a fatal rabies
condition.
• For adults, local infiltration of equine
immunoglobulin with 40 IU/kg dose is
given, and in paediatric population, 20 IU/
kg should be considered. If human immunoglobulin is used, then 20 IU/kg dose is
adequate for both population.
• Two-site intradermal (Verorab™, Imovax™
or Rabipur™) administration of vaccine
(0.1 mL per site) should be given at 0, 3, 7
and 28 days as per the protocol for both
adult and paediatric population, while in
immunocompromised
patients,
an
­intermediate dose on 14th day should be
considered (five-dose protocol) [4, 12].

22.3.1.4 Antibiotic Prophylaxis
Oral flora of every animal is different and hence
should be considered while deciding antibiotic
prophylaxis of the victim. Variety of animals has
been studied for their attacks on humans; the various studies conclude that Pasteurella species,
Staphylococcus and Streptococcus are the common aerobic microbes found in animal bite

animal bite, the overall infection rate is 10–20%
[5]. Specifically child wound infection rates are
variable according to the species of attack, with
human bite 10%, dog bite 20% and cat bite up
to 50% [19]. P. multocida, the most common
organism in animal bite, causes early infection
(within 24 h), so signs of wound infection
should be watched closely [3].
Osteomyelitis, tenosynovitis, tendinitis,
orbital cellulitis or brain abscesses can occur if
bite injury is deep enough to involve bone.
Clenched -fist injuries sustained by the patient
himself can commonly involve metacarpal
joints, which are at high risk for septic arthritis,
osteomyelitis, tenosynovitis, tendinitis, joint
stiffness or permanent limited range of motion,
prompting the need for immediate antibiotic
drug treatment in such cases [3, 5].
Though transfer of rabies is rare, prophylaxis
should be given post-exposure as fulminate
rabies is 100% fatal [4, 5]. Post-traumatic facial
disfigurement raises the significant psychosocial
problems to victims. Children are more prone to
develop post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
with increased risk in animal attack of severe
form [20]. Facial nerve injury, parotid duct or
nasolacrimal duct injury and parotid fistula are
associated complication of animal attack and
have to be dealt with accordingly as per protocol
described in literature.

22.6

Recent Advances

Stereolithographic models, 3D navigation systems and patient-specific implants are the valuable addition in the field of maxillofacial surgery.
High-velocity animal bite injury causes significant distortion of facial bony framework. Use of
stereolithographic models helps in achieving better aesthetics and symmetry. 3D navigation system assists in detecting foreign bodies and
increased precision resulting in minimal intraoperative complication. Patient-specific implants
help in achieving the best fit and adaptability on
tissue with long-term success and negligible
chance of failure. Altogether, wise use of recently
developed techniques improves the patient out-

395

come, minimising the risk and reducing intraoperative time in a cost-effective manner.

22.7

Prevention

• People should be made aware about training
of domestic animals, understanding animal
behaviour and moulding our self accordingly,
to avoid their aggressive provocation.
• Children should be taught how to behave
when they are with or around animals.
• Any tool-aided defence is much protective
against animal attack with good possibility of
avoiding injury or death of the victim [21].
• Keeping safe distance, maintaining their habitat and avoiding deforestation are the points to
be implemented to avoid these sad incidences
in future.

22.8

Case Discussion

A 60-year-old gentleman was brought to emergency room with a history of bear attack
(Fig. 22.11). Advanced Trauma Life Support
(ATLS) protocol was followed to stabilise the
patient. Patient was conscious, oriented and a bit
anxious with vitals suggestive of Class II
Haemorrhagic shock. The upper face was severly
damaged while lower face was spared which
resulted in stable patent airway. Resuscitation
was done for compensation of fluid loss, and
wound closure was done for haemostasis.
Following improvement in vitals and patient
overall condition, the evaluation was done suggesting impact of attack was severe in nature with
soft tissue and bony injury to the face and significant damage to right eye. Urgent referral was
given to ophthalmologist, who confirmed the
ominous injury to organ with complete vision
loss and no eyeball movement detected.
Eventually, radiographic imaging was suggestive of a right side zygomatico-maxillary complex
(ZMC) tripod fracture with significant lateral and
downward displacement only. There was approximately a 6 × 5 cm soft tissue loss in right periorbital and temple region (Fig. 22.12).

396

I. B. Kar et al.

Fig. 22.11 Case of bear attack presented in emergency
room

Subsequently after stable general condition and
necessary prophylaxis, fixation of ZMC fracture
with miniplates along with orbital enucleation was
planned. For soft tissue coverage, radial artery
forearm free flap (RAFFF) was selected as a
choice of reconstruction. Procedure was explained
to patient and attendant with proper consents
taken. Multidisciplinary team approch was taken.
The opthalmologist performed the right eye enucleation. Then the two teams of Oral and maxillofacial surgeons simultaneously performed fixation
of zygoma fracture (Fig. 22.13), RAFFF was harvesting, insetting and microvascular anastomosis
with superficial temporal artery and branch of
common facial vein (Figs. 22.14 and 22.15).
Hospital course was uneventful. Orbital rehabilitation was planned on later stage, but patient was not
willing for orbital prosthesis and wished to continue with the present reconstruction (Fig. 22.16).

Gunshot injuries have become the second most
common cause of injury-related deaths. A gunshot may not be lethal most of the times, but it

and adjacent neurovascular structures and can
severely jeopardise the musculoskeletal system. Demographic records have shown that suicides and assault cases supersede the

(86%) have been used more than the shotguns

been reported in the mandible and the orbit.

22.10 Ballistics
It is the study of the projectile motion, of the way
it behaves in flight and on its impact with an
object. It is divided into three stages.
1. Internal ballistics which describes the forces
that apply to a projectile from the time the
propellant is ignited to the time the projectile
leaves the barrel.
Barrel length here is of importance as it
dictates the projectile motion. Longer barrels
as seen in the rifles allow the force of the propellant to act longer on the projectile, thereby
generating higher velocities. It also serves to
stabilise the bullet which can travel longer
distances.
2. External ballistics refers to forces that act on
the bullet during the flight like the weight and
the shape.
3. Terminal ballistics is the study of the bullet
behaviour once it hits the target. The energy

The contact wounds may have the characteristic muzzle imprint or laceration of the skin due to
gaseous effect or soot on the outside of the skin.
Intermediate or close range wounds due to some
distance will not show the muzzle imprint and
laceration, but there may be a wide zone of powder stippling. The area of the stippling depends
upon the distance from the muzzle to the point of
entry. More distant wounds lack the typical powder stippling but exhibit a hole which will be of
the calibre of the fired projectile. Most of the
gunshot wounds are found with a residue either
on the skin or clothes or both (Table 22.6).
The estimated size of the bullet entrance hole
is directly related to the tissue elasticity. As the
bullet enters the skin, the tissue accelerates radially and displaces in a centrifugal pattern. For an
instance of time, the hole appears larger than the
cross section of the bullet. In the elastic skin, the
radial displacement is quite reversible, and the
entry point narrows much after the bullet has
passed. Due to this, the measured diameter of the
permanent skin defect is usually smaller than the
bullet calibre. The difference in size is more
marked in the wounds caused by bullets with a
round or pointed nose. A punched wound with
cutting effect is seen with bullets with a flat front

effect in flat nose bullets produces larger skin
defects and narrower abrasion rings compared to
the round nose bullets. In cases of target shootings, the greater area, size and sharp definition of
the entrance holes from wadcutter bullets are useful distinguishing features. As a result the
entrance holes tend to be the largest in the wounds
affected by the wadcutter bullets, medium-sized
in the truncated cone bullets and smallest in those
caused by the bullets with a round nose.
Bevelling or coning may be seen at the surface
of the bone, inward into bone at the entrance
wounds of the skull and outward away from the
weapon on the inner table of the skull. Thin areas
of the bone such as the temple may not show this
feature. These findings can determine the direction of fire. A small, dense projectile may ‘punch
out’ a rounded portion of cranium. A larger projectile may produce circumferential fractures that
radiate outward from the point of entrance. A bullet expends energy when it enters into a closed
cranial cavity resulting in fracture of the bone
caused by energy dissipation. The fracture pattern may be of both radiating and concentric
type. The pattern of fractures can help identify
the sequence and direction of the fire.

(<600 m/s) and cause tissue damage along the
bullet tract only. The handgun bullets thus have a
low impact velocity and cause penetrating wounds
characterised by a small point of entry with the
bullet remaining embedded in the tissue [23].
Shotguns are smooth bore weapons designed
to fire shells filled with lead shots of various
sizes. They fire at low velocity but can be devastating when fired at a close range. Multiple shotgun pellets which travel close to each other cause
severe avulsive or ablative injuries characterised
by significant loss of bone and soft tissues [24].
Rifles are classified by calibre which is nothing but the diameter of the muzzle bore which is
same as the diameter of the bullet. Rifles can fire
both at low and high velocity. High-velocity rifle
bullets produce massive exit wounds quite similar to avulsive or ablative wounds due to bullet
tumbling, bone fragmentation or both [25]. In the
latter case, it may also be considered as a perforating injury. Rifle bullets are capable of producing both perforative and avulsive injuries.
Cartridge or round is the outer case containing
the ignition system (primer), the propellant and
the projectile, i.e. the bullet.

22.11 Firearms

When an object is in motion, the energy delivered
by it will be given by the physical equation:

Handguns, shotguns and rifles have been collectively referred to as firearms.
These firearms are broadly classified according to the bullet calibre and the muzzle velocity as:
1. Low velocity (<350 m/s)
2. Medium velocity (350–600 m/s)
3. High velocity (>600 m/s)
However, a projectile travelling with a velocity of 50 m/s is just sufficient enough to penetrate
the skin, and a velocity of 65 m/s may fracture
the bone [22].
Handguns may further be referred to as pistols
and revolvers depending on their mechanical
action. Many of these are low or medium velocity

Here, V1 is the strike velocity and V2 is the

transferred to tissue by a missile mostly depends
upon the square of its velocity, the density of the
tissue and the presenting area of the missile.
Factors such as projectile deformity, fragmenta-

400

tion, deceleration and drag within the tissues can
result in a greater transfer of kinetic energy (KE),
thereby causing greater wound potential.
Missile wounds have also been classified as:
1. Low-Energy Transfer (LET) Wounds
These are created by bullets and isolated
fragments striking at velocities way below
that of speed of the sound in the air, i.e.
340 m/s. Typically, there will be simply cutting or lacerating type of wounds but not with
widespread damage.
2. High-Energy Transfer (HET) Wounds
For wounds to fall in this category, two
phenomena have to be observed, i.e. propagation of stress waves and cavitation.

22.12.1 Stress Wave
This precedes the cavitation phenomenon. It is
transmitted well through the fluid-filled structures. So maximum damage can be seen at interfaces of differing acoustic impedance.

I. B. Kar et al.

2. Temporary cavity: It is produced while the
projectile is travelling through the target tissue. Stretching of the elastic tissue is seen due
to transfer of the kinetic energy. Irrecoverable
damage may happen to the tissues.

22.12.3 Fragmentation
Fragmentation at times may not be present in a
gunshot wound. But if seen, it could also be the
secondary fragments like clothing or bone that
develops from being struck by the projectile.
High-velocity rifle rounds can cause devastating
fragmentation.
For a bullet to travel a long distance, it is
imparted a spin by using the spiral groove (inside
the barrel) just before it leaves the rifle barrel.
Though it seeks to stabilise the yaw (yaw refers
to the oscillation around the long axis of the bullet), it imparts its own motion known as precession or circular yawing around the centre of the
gravity, thereby creating a decreasing spiral and
nutation. Further, to improve the range and the
penetration, the bullets are made long and
pointed (Table 22.7).

22.12.2 Cavitation
Cavitation is a feature of the high-velocity missiles whose impact velocity is greater than the
speed of the sound in the air. It is an effect of the
energy transferred to the tissues by the missile. A
possible cause for this may be the acceleration of
the tissue ‘particles’ by the bullet away from the
path of the missile. The expansion and collapse
of the cavity wall causes laceration of the tissue
away from the track. The extent of damage occurring depends upon the amount of energy transferred and the resilience of the involved tissues.
For cavitation to take place, it requires a wound
track of some length.
1. Permanent cavity: It is the space that results
from direct tissue disruption and destruction
and is a function of the penetration and size of
the projectile and is considered the most
important factor in the wounding and stopping
power of a cartridge and bullet.

22.12.4 Shotgun Wounds
Shotgun wounds are classified based on the distance to the target. Shotgun pellets have aerodynamic resistance. This causes loss of much of

their kinetic energy during the flight itself. The
injuries so caused may be classified as:
1. Type I shotgun injuries (<5 m): Here the pellets strike the target as a single mass resulting
in massive kinetic energy transfer and tissue
avulsion with a high mortality rate approaching 85–90%. Most of the patients with suicidal attempts by these shotguns survive
because much damage is caused to the face
rather than the cranium due to fact that while
attempting to pull the trigger, the head remains
hyperextended.
2. Type II shotgun injuries (5–12 m): Here also
there is less tissue destruction. Due to increase
in the distance, the pellets are well dispersed
with significant loss of energy. Penetration at
times stays limited to the deep fascia. Fractures
are rare. Ocular injuries can be found with
overall mortality rate at 15–20%.
3. Type III shotgun injuries (>12 m): In this only
the skin is penetrated at times with mortality
rate of 0–5% only.
One drawback here is that shooting distance
remains non-specific.
To deal with this, another system was suggested. It was proposed that >25 cm of pellet
scatter be classified into Type I injuries, 10–25 cm
of scatter as Type II and <10 cm of scatter as
Type III injuries. Though this system was applied
to abdominal shotgun wounds in an attempt to
guide therapy, it becomes difficult to apply it to
other anatomic sites and weapon types [26].
Close range shotgun injuries generally involve
four different anatomical areas corresponding to
the level of the wound and its primary location
affecting the medial or lateral facial structures.
They are the central face, the lateral mandible,
the lateral midface and orbit and the lateral
cranio-­orbital region. The destructive capacity of
the shotguns is much greater than their muzzle
velocity as their shot mass is more. The pellets
also which are designed so (ballistically unfavourable) tend to remain in the wound causing
full dissipation of the energy in the tissue.
Shotgun injuries in the midface create a ‘cone’ of
tissue destruction which further converts to a

401

large defect without support after debridement.
Further, the zone of injury remains wider indicating its high-energy nature with increased incidence of infection.

22.12.5 Rifle Gun Injuries
Rifles because of their long barrels can project
either low- or high-calibre projectiles but at high
velocity, thereby transmitting high amount of
energy to the victims. In these injuries, entrance
wounds tend to be stellate with torn irregular
margins. Exit wounds look more avulsive due to
the soft tissue defects which are irregular in shape
and two to three times greater than the entrance
wounds. The temporary cavity so formed may be
almost eight times the diameter of the projectile
with associated avulsion of both muscle and skin.
These injuries generally cause gross distension of
large diameter nerves [27]. The myelin sheaths
look deformed and protruded from site. Blood
vessels remain crushed and displaced and are
found to be congested and thrombosed. Veins
exhibit diapedesis of red blood cells with demargination and pavementing of the neutrophils.
Bone fragmentation occurs with avulsion. Gross
communition of the bony fragments with severely
damaged soft tissue frequently becomes secondarily infected.

22.13 Clinical Features
In an urban setting, more number of reported
cases of gunshot injuries is a result of the interpersonal violence. Around 60% of the cases are
due to assault followed by 27% suicidal
attempts. A small 9% accounted for accidental
injuries [28].
Most of the maxillofacial injuries seen vary in
clinical picture depending upon the anatomical
structures involved. Breach in oral mucosa
accompanied with severe comminution of bone
further complicates the scenerio [29]. Avulsive
injuries can be seen in the tangential bullet trajectories [30]. Because of the soft cushioning
effect of the midface, communition is seen with

Rifle bullet injuries are often found to be

greater than what initially appears [32]. The
potential lethal effects depend more upon the
anatomical track of the missile and not its energy

actual site of entry and the estimated trajectory of
the projectile give an analysis of the structures
disrupted. One may also predict the plausible
complications which may threaten the life. A
drawback here is that due to the ricocheting
effects of bony surfaces, the paths of the bullets
may be less predictable. A classification based on
such features definitely reduces its diagnostic
value.

22.13.2 Lateral and Posterior
Mandible
Low-velocity bullets after hitting the mandible
get rapidly destabilised and may further remain
within the tissues. The ricocheting effect causes
extensive tissue trauma with simultaneous bone
and tooth fragments driven deep into the floor of
the mouth and tongue. These injuries cause
severe bleeding with attendant severe haematoma and swelling imposing a threat to the airway [35].
High-velocity bullets cause extensive comminution which will look like an explosive wound
with splinters from the shattered bone along with
teeth bursting outwards [36]. At times it may also
happen that a high-velocity bullet may completely pass through the soft tissues of the cheeks
through the open mouth without intervening hard
tissues causing a low-energy transfer [37].

22.13.3 Midface
Midfacial entry sites are more associated with
intracranial penetration if directed towards it.
But those with a tangential or sideway hits by
the bullet escape lethal injuries. High-velocity
military rifle bullets completely traverse the
facial skeleton maintaining a stable path except
when hitting from a longer distance where they
may be affected by the yaw. Classical Le Fort
fractures may be absent, but the upper alveolus,
palate and the maxillary sinuses may be hit. The
globe of the eye may be injured in the wounds
affecting the orbital region and the nasoethmoidal complex. Damage to the structures like
the facial nerve, lacrimal apparatus or the
parotid gland may have an unfavourable outcome and sequelae.

403

22.13.4 I ndirect Injuries Caused by
the Projectiles
The cavitational effects produced by the high-­
velocity missiles are much decreased in the maxillofacial region due to the numerous air cavities
surrounded by the delicate bony structures and
the absence of bulkier muscles. The posterior
region of the mouth forms a compact area with
associated surrounding bones and can effectively
accommodate the cavitational changes. A bullet
penetrating the posterior part of the mouth transfers large amounts of energy creating a longer
wound track due to increase in both the tissue
volume and the density. The vascular damage has
been demonstrated to extend beyond the wound
edges due to the blunt injury caused by the
expanding cavity [38]. The temporary cavity and
the stress waves produced by the high-velocity
projectiles extensively damage the endothelial
surface of the blood vessels both locally and at
some distance from the wound. The stripping of
the investing soft tissues around the wound
caused by these effects further devascularises the
underlying area of bone comminution [39].
Indirect brain injury also has been reported in
those afflicted with fast projectile wounds. These
projectiles cause a strong vibration of the head
due to the sustained momentary acceleration and
hence the cerebral damage. Severe pathological
changes in the basal regions of the brains are seen
as these areas are subjected to shearing forces by
the inside rough surfaces of the skull base [40].
The shock waves transmitting through the dense
bone of the mandible may cause indirect subgingival fractures at a distance from the impact site.

of airway, if not identified properly. A definitive wall [46].

22

Animal Bite, Firearm and Ballistic Injuries

The neck may be divided into three zones
originally described by Monson and colleagues
from the Cook and County hospital [47].
1. Zone I: Defined as the area from the clavicles
to the cricoid cartilage. It contains the inferior aspect of the trachea and oesophagus
along with the major vessels of the thoracic
inlet: the common carotid arteries, thyrocervical trunk, internal jugular veins, brachiocephalic trunk, subclavian arteries and veins,
thoracic duct, thyroid gland and spinal cord.
Risk of injury to the great vessels is common
in this area, and, consequently, injuries to
Zone I carry a high mortality rate (approximately 12%).
2. Zone II: Represents the area from the cricoid
cartilage to the angle of the mandible. It contains the common carotid arteries, internal and
external carotid arteries, IJV, larynx, hypopharynx and cranial nerves X, XI and XII. It is
the largest area and therefore the most commonly involved zone in penetrating neck
trauma.
3. Zone III: It spans the region from the skull
base to the angle of the mandible. It contains
the carotid arteries, the internal jugular veins
and the pharynx along with multiple cranial
nerves exiting the skull base. It should be
appreciated that gunshot wounds that involve
mandibular fractures are accompanied by
injuries to Zone I.
Penetrating neck injuries can be addressed
once the patient gains stability from the airway
and the hemodynamic status. Once stable, a complete survey, as done in ATLS, is carried out looking for the signs of tracheal injury like
subcutaneous emphysema, stridor, hoarseness,
dysphonia or haemoptysis which may require
urgent intervention. When done, the evaluating
surgeon must then look for hidden injuries.
High-energy weapons can cause significant
bleeding in the Zone I because of presence of
large vessels. In patients whose vitals are stabilised, a routine angiography with evaluation of
the oesophagus via oesophagoscopy or barium
swallow can be prescribed.

405

Zone II injuries are common and yield better to
surgical exploration if required. CT angiography
can be used to screen and assist in the cases requiring surgical exploration. It is faster and less invasive than angiography but is less specific. Hidden
injuries can often be missed here. In cases of mandible fractures, the neck can be explored while the
mandible fractures are exposed for fixation.
Zone III injuries may require imaging in the
stable patients. Angiography may help in diagnosis of vascular injuries at the skull base and can
also allow intervention if required. Surgical intervention may rarely yield any fruitful results in
Zone III injuries.
• Angiography remains the gold standard for
exploration of vascular injuries in the neck.
• Ultrasonography can be a rapid non-invasive
technique for the evaluation of traumatic injuries in the emergency department.
• Screening tools such as USG are quite important in selecting patients for non-operative
management.

22.16 Imaging
• ATLS protocol is to be followed to get the
C-spine and the chest radiographs.
• Conventional radiographs may help in visualising the bullet fragments and to some extent
the path of the bullet.
• Spiral CT combined with 3D reconstructions
can help to quantify the extent of skeletal
injury.
• Simultaneous clinical examination may lead
towards an accurate assessment.
• CT angiography can be useful in evaluating
the vascular damage in the penetrating neck
injuries.
• Using angiography allows the intervention with
embolisation of continuous bleeding vessels
which may be difficult to approach surgically.
• However, imaging should not be a priority if
the patient is not stable. Definitive repair can
be delayed if needful imaging has not been
carried out owing to patient’s deteriorating
health status.

406

22.17 Nutrition
• Nutritional status is an issue in patients whose
injuries preclude oral alimentation for an
extended period, i.e. >4–5 days.
• Nasogastric intubation meets the nutritional
requirement manifolds and also bypasses the
oral cavity, thereby maintaining hygiene at the
injured areas.
• For long-term bypass of the oral cavity, percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy may be
required to avoid nutritional deficit status.

22.18 Operative Procedure
Many surgeons advocate closed reduction and
division of care into early (first 10 days),
intermediate (10–60 days) and late (>60 days)
phases. Characterisation of the wound as low
or high energy can help in formulating the
operative plan. The four components introduced by Mason, namely, soft tissue injury,
bone injury, soft tissue loss (true avulsion)
and bone loss, should be considered while
evaluating a gunshot injury. After thorough
evaluation of the injury, a decision has to be
made regarding early definitive repair or to go
for delayed repair. Most of the gunshot wounds
in civilians resulting from assaults can be
managed with early definitive repair as in
these the soft tissues and the bone only are
injured without loss of the tissue. At times the
soft tissue injuries may look somewhat terrifying but may not be avulsive and can be closed
primarily. Extensive debridement of the soft
tissues is generally not advocated by many.
Loose wound debris should be removed, and
the wound is thoroughly irrigated with normal
saline. Mechanical agitation helps to remove
the debris much better. Devitalised and loose
teeth are removed. Fractures should be reduced
and fixed. Drains are helpful. Dead spaces are
avoided by giving pressure dressings. In clean
avulsive wounds, local flaps or skin grafts can
be given. Delayed closure or grafting may be
required in grossly contaminated wounds.

I. B. Kar et al.

Free tissue transfer should be delayed until the
initial phase of wound healing when its accompanying vascular spasm and hypercoagulable
state would have decreased much. Wounds
exhibiting extensive soft and hard tissue damage with true loss of tissue can be approached
using early stabilisation of bony fragments
along with conservative management of soft
tissues. Second debridements can be performed
24 to 48 hours after the initial surgery. This
helps in judging the borderline tissues which if
has become devitalised can be excised. Wound
re-exploration every 24–36 hours for a period
of few days to identify the progressing necrotic
tissues so that serial wound debridement can
be done has become the most treatment protocol before any next definitive management.
Skin grafts if needed can be given as permanent or temporary replacement for missing tissues, thereby reducing scar contracture and the
deformity. Once the soft tissues have stabilised, judgement can be taken regarding the
early replacement of the lost tissues either with
free flaps or delayed reconstruction. Early correct repair leads to improved outcomes with
less scar contracture and the resultant
deformity.

22.19 Documentation
The retrieved bullet along with its fragments is
potential evidence which requires a proper custody. A proper protocol has to be followed so as
not to lose the piece of evidence. For ease of
inference, this documentation must be kept
extremely simple, but it must not miss out important details. The information which must be
recorded are (a) date and time of injury (b), cause
of injury (type of firearm used with range), (c)
treatment given (fluids given/drugs administered)
and (d) description of the injury (simple line
diagrams).
Documentation of the events with proper photographic records may help in differentiating, for
example, an apparent suicidal case which could
actually be an assault case.

22.20 Case Discussion
A young male about 24 years old had reported to
the casualty department of a tertiary care medical
centre with a large open wound on his face. Initial
inquiry revealed that it was a suicidal attempt
with his own service rifle while he was discharging the night duty. The left side of the face was
totally disfigured with severe bleeding
(Fig. 22.18). Vitals were poor. The patient was
agitated. After his vitals were stabilised, on initial
clinical examination, it was found that the point
of entry of the bullet was at the submental region
with a punctured wound. The exit wound was in
the left eye through the malar region. The tongue
was almost bisected into two halves, with perforation of left maxilla and loss of dentoalveolar
segment, ruptured nasal floor mucosa and a
degloved left half of the midface. He was bleeding from the oral and nasal cavity and the left side
of his midface. The left eye had left its place. It

23.1

Introduction

Maxillofacial trauma complications trauma
may be defined as any undesirable consequences of the trauma, health condition, or
treatment which adversely affect the prognosis
or outcome. Complications may arise at the
time of injury, during transport to the hospital,
in the preoperative phase, during the treatment,
or in the post-­
operative phase. Knowledge
about complications in maxillofacial trauma
not only helps us in preventing them but also
allows us to be prepared to deal with them in a
better way.
Classification The maxillofacial trauma can be
broadly classified in two categories and further
subdivided in subheadings as depicted below
(Fig. 23.1).

23.2

General Complications

23.2.1 Immediate Resuscitative
Complications
Maxillofacial injuries irrespective of severity
constitute 10% of all severely injured patients.
The immediate resuscitative complications of
maxillofacial trauma include airway obstruction,
hypovolemia, hypoxia, hemorrhage, and electrolytic imbalance. In the post-trauma period, the
first 60 min is called the “golden hour,” where all
the required measures should be taken to maintain all the vital signs within normal limit. Six
hours post-trauma is the watershed time that any
active surgical procedures are avoided unless it is
life-threatening like intracranial hematoma,
intra-­abdominal hemorrhage, or peripheral limb
trauma jeopardizing circulation. This vital period
should be devoted to managing ventilatory failure or peripheral circulatory failure due to hemorrhage or any other reasons.

23.2.2 Airway Obstruction

o­ bliterating the nasopharyngeal airway, bilateral
fracture of anterior mandible causing the fractured segment to slide posteriorly along with the
tongue causing oropharyngeal obstruction especially in supine position, entry of bone fragments/
vomitus/exfoliated teeth/blood into the airway,
and soft tissue edema and trauma to the larynx
and trachea. It is important that if you can’t hear
the respiration, then patient’s airway is clear, or
the patient is dead. Maintaining a clear airway
with the help of semi-prone position and suction
if required during and after transport is vital for
patient survival. Manual traction on the chin forward can prevent the complication of airway
obstruction by falling tongue backward especially in bilateral mandibular fracture, and any
bleeding into airway should be cleared off by
suction. Loss of chin especially by gunshot or
crush injury causing asphyxia by falling back of
tongue can be prevented by posterior deep muscle tongue suture to pull the tongue forward out.
Supraglottic airways can be inserted blindly as a
temporary measure until a definitive airway is
achieved. Nasopharyngeal airway is preferable in
an unstable bi-mandibular fracture. Stable airway
can be created by well-lubricated two nasopharyngeal tubes passed on either side of nasal septum in preventing occlusion of airway by
downward and posterior displacement of the
maxilla and soft palate in middle third fracture of
the face. Frequent vigilance should be ensured
for checking the patency of airway. If the problem of patency of airway persists, it may be due
to soft tissue swelling, surgical emphysema, or
hematoma, and then endotracheal intubation is
the best choice. In a study, around 26% of patients
with LeFort fractures of the maxilla presented
with airway obstruction, compromised respiration, or both and required endotracheal intubation
or tracheostomy. Airway control is often required
in maxillomandibular fractures with laryngeal,
chest trauma, or head injury. In emergency, early
oral intubation is an easy and a better option
which can later be changed to submental or nasal
routes. However, standard endotracheal trauma is
not always feasible in maxillofacial trauma cases
due to various reasons such as facial lacerations
and fractures obscuring the airway, bleeding
from the walls of the airway, and presence of tra-

413

cheal transection. In such cases emergency tracheostomy or cricothyrotomy is indicated to
immediately restore the airway. The incidence of
blockage of tracheostomy tube is less as compared to endotracheal tube. It is the best option
for compound fractures of the mandible, posteriorly displaced middle third fractures, or depressed
compound frontal bone fracture. If treating physician is less experienced or it is high emergency,
then percutaneous laryngotomy incision of cricothyroid membrane is done to establish airway.
However, a definitive airway should be established within 15–30 min after a cricothyrotomy
procedure. The patient should be properly
assessed and resuscitated before doing any definitive maneuvers [1, 2].

23.2.3 Complications
of Tracheostomy
In a long-standing tracheostomy tube, there are
higher chances for tracheocutaneous fistula formation. Similarly, a tracheoinnominate fistula
might develop due to prolonged attrition of anterior tracheal wall by the tube tip. Factors such as
long use, infection, pressure of cuff, or steroid
therapy may cause tracheal stenosis due to healing by fibrosis. Use of tracheostomy tubes for
minimum short time with low-pressure cuffs
avoids the tracheal stenosis complication. One
may also encounter tracheostomy tube displacement into the peritracheal tissues and unaesthetic
scars as a result of tracheostomy [3].

23.2.4 Acute Hemorrhage,
Hypovolemia, and Hypoxia
Persistent bleeding from any major vessel may
result in hypovolemic shock if not controlled
promptly. However, life-threatening bleeding from
maxillofacial region is a rare phenomenon.
Bleeding from the head and neck region commonly
involves branches of external and internal carotid
arteries, the various anastomoses between them,
the external and the internal jugular veins, their
tributaries, and rupture of periosteum. Reportedly,
the main origin of bleeding in maxillofacial trauma

414

is from the internal maxillary artery, since the
course of the artery passes within the LeFort fracture line borders. In mandibular fractures, bleeding
commonly occurs from inferior alveolar artery.
Inferior alveolar and maxillary arterial bleeding
can be usually stopped by reduction of fractured
segments by interdental wiring, arch bar fixation,
bone wax application into site of bleeding, or a ribbon gauge pack into the wound until the definitive
reduction and fixation is done. Intraoperatively,
mortality by major vessel injury is least likely to
happen, unless the surgeon is novice.
Incidence of airway obstruction commonly
occurs due to uncontrolled hemorrhage from the
soft tissues around the mandible, floor of the
mouth, and muscles of the neck. Such cases are
often difficult to intubate, requiring tracheostomy
under local anesthesia. Once the patency of airway is ensured, the active bleeding should be controlled by early intervention while simultaneously
replacing blood and fluids as per requirement, to
ensure that the patient does not end up in hypoxia
or hypovolemic shock. Anterior and posterior
nasal packing are done with gauze/Foley’s catheter/Epistat. Following this, immediate reduction
of fractured segments should be done for controlling the bleeding from intraosseous vessels, and
they are fixed temporarily or definitively. If bleeding persists even after fracture reduction, ligation
of external carotid artery (ECA) is recommended.
If the bleeding is from the maxillary artery region
or higher up, then ECA ligation can be done at the
level of the lower border of the mandible, at the
retromandibular fossa. If the bleeding is suspected
to be from any other branches of ECA, then ligation is recommended at the level of its origin, a
few millimeters above the origin of superior thyroid artery. ECA ligation is preferred in any case
of uncontrolled hemorrhage in maxillofacial
trauma, owing to the complex course of the vessels and difficulty in finding the exact location of
bleeding. It is of utmost importance to diagnose
hypovolemia and hypoxia swiftly and render
immediate treatment, since it could lead to major
complications such as cardiac arrhythmias, cardiac arrest, irreversible damage to visceral organs,
and gangrene formation of the extremities [4].

S. Singh et al.

23.2.5 Electrolytic Imbalance
Electrolytic imbalance in a maxillofacial trauma
patient can occur preoperatively, intraoperatively,
and post-operatively. Among these, the post-­
operative patients are more prone to electrolytic
imbalance due to factors such as loss of blood and
body fluids pre- and intraoperatively, the stress
response to surgery, fasting before surgery, and
inability to take proper nutrition due to jaw surgery.
Hyponatremia
(serum
sodium
level < 135 mEq/L) is one of the common electrolytic abnormalities and also the most common
post-operative disorder due to surgical stress. The
symptoms are nausea, vomiting, confusion,
fatigue, muscle weakness, irritability, and seizures.
It has potentially dangerous complications such as
rapid cerebral edema causing coma and death. The
second common electrolytic imbalance is hypokalemia (serum potassium <3.6 mEq/L), manifesting
as leg cramps, weakness, paresis, constipation,
metabolic acidosis, kidney failure, respiratory failure, cardiac arrhythmias, and heart failure.
Hypomagnesemia (magnesium level < 1.8 mg/dL)
is a common co-­factor and can show symptoms of
neuromuscular, psychiatric, neurologic, and cardiac disorders. Hypocalcemia is another common
electrolytic imbalance, reported post-operatively
in healthy patients undergoing surgery and also in
massive blood transfusion cases. The classical
symptoms of hypocalcemia are paresthesia, muscle spasms, cramps, tetany, circumoral numbness,
and seizures. Severe hypocalcemia (serum calcium <1.9 mmol/L) might result in life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias and neurological
complications. Since unattended electrolytic
imbalance in a patient could lead to life-threatening complications, it is important to readily identify these situations and manage promptly [5].

23.2.7 Associated Cervical Spine
and Head Injury
The presence of cervical spine injury in a case of
maxillofacial trauma makes it even more complicated for two reasons. Firstly, it makes the airway management difficult, as it needs certain
modification, and secondly, the standard management of maxillofacial trauma may require
specific changes according to the method of cervical fracture management and the degree of
neurological deficit caused by spinal cord injury.
The presence of associated head injury also
influences the management of maxillofacial
injury at various levels. Head injury can produce
a very low GCS score, which necessitates intubation of the patient in most of the cases. The

23.3.1.2

Local Hemorrhage
and Hematoma
Soft tissue hematomas of the maxillofacial region
are mostly superficial. Hematomas of the skin
and soft tissue commonly resolve by themselves
in time or with rest and cold or hot compression.
Decompression may be required in actively
expanding hematomas followed by ligation of the
causative blood vessel. Hematomas within the
masticatory muscles are most commonly associated with trismus. In these cases use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and ultrasound
therapy have proven to be beneficial. Rarely
intramuscular hematomas might lead to fibrosis
and contracture [1].

Contracture often occurs in cases when there
is scarring after tissue loss or when the laceration
is in the direction of muscle pull or across flexures. Contractures are unaesthetic and could lead
to movement restriction. They are commonly
associated with burn injury. The treatment
options are releasing with Z-plasty or complete
scar excision with skin grafting.
Traumatic tattooing involves dirt, gunpowder,
or sand that can create permanent discoloration
of skin. The incidence of unsightly scars and their
complications are less if wound is taken care in a
proper way during initial management within
24 h after the injury. Proper debridement or
scrubbing and good normal saline irrigation of
wound during primary care are a must to prevent
tattooing by foreign particles. Treatment includes
dermabrasion and overgrafting.

23.3.1.6 Oral Incompetence
Although it is rare in trauma cases, certain cases
could result in oral incompetence due to various
reasons. It could result in cases which have
undergone an avulsive injury to a portion of the
lip or the commissure, in cases when the surgeon
removes a considerable amount of non-viable
segment of the lip and fails to reconstruct it with
a flap, or in cases where the vermillion border is
not aligned properly during suturing (Fig. 23.5a,
b). Loss of only vermillion border can be repaired
by local advancement flaps, whereas defect
involving a larger portion of lip can be restored
by Abbe flap, Karapandzic flap, lip mucosa
advancement flap, arterialized advancement vermilion flap, chin advancement flap, Gillies’ fan
flap, nasolabial flaps, tongue flap, and deltopectoral and pectoral major myocutaneous flap. Lip
defects involving the commissures are restored
commonly by Abbe-Estlander flap. During lip
suturing or revision, the prime goal must be oral
seal rather than aesthetics [1].

23.3.2 Ophthalmic Complications
23.3.2.1 Ectropion
Ectropion and entropion are the post-trauma late
complications of eyelid deformity due to post-­

b

Fig. 23.6 Severe scar causing ectropion of lower eyelid

Fig. 23.5 (a) Severe trauma leading to lip injury, (b) lip

operative scarring and contracture. Ectropion is
known as the abnormal eversion or outward turning of the eyelid (Fig. 23.6). There are various
causes for ectropion such as congenital, senile,
cicatricial, and neurogenic. Post-traumatic ectropion is commonly cicatricial in nature. It may
involve upper eyelid, lower eyelid, or both.
According to the direction of contracture, it might
be medial ectropion or lateral ectropion. Lower
eyelid lateral ectropion is a common iatrogenic
complication following intervention through the
subciliary approach. Ectropion might result in vertical shortening, horizontal shortening, epiphora,
corneal exposure, and other ocular complications.
Scar release is the recommended treatment for
any type of ectropion. For a medial ectropion,
C-shaped incision is placed over the upper eyelid,
lateral nose, and lower eyelid, and the resulting
defect needs to be covered with full-thickness

skin graft to minimize secondary contraction. In
order to allow for maximum release, the skin
over the nose beyond the release incision is
undermined, and the periosteum over the frontal
process of the maxilla is excised to allow adherence of the graft to the underlying periosteum. If
required, adjunctive medial canthoplasty can also
be performed. In cases of lateral ectropion,
Z-plasty is preferred. Through this method, the
retracted lower eyelid tissue is transposed superiorly and posteriorly, to achieve better adaptation
of the lid margin to the globe [3].
In a case of cicatricial ectropion of any eyelid
with vertical height shortening, subciliary or subconjunctival approach is done. The incision is
made within the limits of medial and lateral canthi, and the skin flaps are raised to allow approximation of the upper and lower eyelid margins. A
bone-anchored lateral canthopexy is performed
and skin grafting is done if required. The eyelid
separation can be done immediately or in a secondary surgery.

23 Complications in Maxillofacial Trauma

23.3.2.2 Entropion
Entropion refers to inward rolling of the eyelid
and lashes toward the globe. It is a common complication seen after any surgery, performed
through lower eyelid approach. Entropion could
lead to increased scleral show, ocular discomfort,
trichiasis, corneal abrasion, vision loss, etc. Post-­
trauma entropion is usually cicatricial in nature,
which can be reconstructed with a keratinized tissue graft from the hard palate. There is also
another technique, in which the lateral tarsal tip
is anchored to the orbital rim using a single stitch
lateral wedge technique [3].

23.3.3 Glandular and Ductal Injury
23.3.3.1

 arotid Gland and Duct
P
Injury
Any patient presenting with a laceration over the
parotid region should be examined for integrity
of the gland and the duct system. It is done by
pressing the gland of the lacerated side and
checking for salivary flow from the ductal opening, intraorally. If the status of the parotid duct is
not clear, cannulation of the duct is done intraorally, followed by saline or methylene blue
injection, to check the patency of the duct. If the
injected dye is not seen in the lacerated facial
region, it confirms that there is no injury to the
duct. In that case, the catheter must be left in
place for 1 week and external pressure dressing
must be applied for 48 h. Checking the facial
nerve status is also important, since there are high
chances of its injury. Radiological examinations
do not play a major role in the diagnosis.
23.3.3.2 Parotid Gland Injury
The sequence of parotid gland laceration is
inspection, cleaning, suturing, and pressure
dressing. The pressure dressing is recommended
for a minimum period of 48 h post-trauma or
post-operatively, to prevent the formation of
sialocele. If there is saliva accumulation, it is
aspirated, and the pressure dressing is reapplied.
This procedure is continued, until there is no
saliva accumulation. The treatment could be
accompanied with fasting combined with antisialogogues or antisialogogues alone [3].

419

23.3.3.3 Parotid Duct Injury
Parotid duct injuries have been classified by Van
Sickels and Alexander into those occurring in the
glandular region, over the masseter muscle, and
anterior to the masseter muscle. If the injury has
occurred over the duct of glandular region, it can
be treated by closure of the capsule. Injury of the
duct over the masseter region is treated by direct
duct repair, whereas those occurring anterior to
the masseter muscle are treated by direct repair of
the duct or by creation of an intraoral fistula.
Nylon (9-0 and 10-0) and silk (7-0 and 8-0) are
the commonly used suture materials for the purpose of repairing the duct. Since direct anastomosis is not possible when a defect is more than
1 cm, repair with autogenous graft should be considered in such cases. In case of extensive laceration to the parotid region and there is hardly any
possibility for ductal repair, clamping of the
remaining proximal portion of the duct is indicated to prevent the formation of a sialocele.
However, clamping of the duct could also lead to
atrophy of the gland [3].

23.3.4 Complications of Parotid
Gland and Duct Injuries
23.3.4.1 Sialocele
A sialocele refers to the facial swelling that is
caused by continuous salivary secretion without a
proper drainage. On clinical examination, sialocele presents as a soft and mobile swelling in the
parotid region, which is commonly misdiagnosed
as hematoma. On aspiration, sialocele gives
saliva which shows a high amylase level of more
than 10,000 units/L. CT scan shows a single or
multiple loculated lesion with a density that is
lesser than the surrounding tissues. In case of
immediate complication, if the origin is in the
parotid parenchyma, then it is cleaned and
sutured layer-wise. If the origin is ductal, then
attempt is made to identify both the ends and
suture them, or if it is severely damaged, the
proximal end must be clamped. Treatment
options of a late-formed sialocele are repeated
aspirations, external compression, antisialogogue
therapy, radiotherapy, parotidectomy, and botulinum toxin injection [3].

23.3.5.2 Debridement
The process of removing the dead and inflamed
tissues from the wound is known as debridement.
Instruments such as tweezers, curette and scalpel
are very helpful in doing this. An enzyme-based
gel also can be used to help in the debridement.
Since debridement is painful, it is commonly
done under local anesthesia.
23.3.5.3 Wound Dressing
Dressing of a wound helps in removal of excess
fluid from it and also protects it from inflammation. There are various types of dressings available such as films, gauze dressings, hydrogel
dressings, hydrocolloid dressings, silver or alginate dressings, and foam dressings.
Compression dressings such as compression
stockings and bandages are used in certain cases
when required.
23.3.5.4 Antibiotics
If there is delay in wound healing due to infection, antibiotics are started according to the
severity of infection.
23.3.5.5 Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy is given to the patient
who suffers delayed wound healing due to ischemia. Hyperbaric oxygen administration follows

23.3.5.6

Ultrasound
and Electromagnetic
Therapy
Ultrasound and electromagnetic therapy is
believed to make the tissue warmer and increase
the blood flow, accelerating the process of wound
healing.
23.3.5.7

Negative Pressure Wound
Therapy
In negative pressure wound therapy, the wound
is covered with an airtight dressing that is connected to a pump by a thin tube. The pump continuously sucks fluid out of the wound, creating
negative pressure across the surface of the
wound. The aim is to increase the flow of blood
to the wound and to keep the wound moist,
which could accelerate the healing process.
However, its use has been hardly reported in
maxillofacial trauma.
23.3.5.8 Skin Grafts
Skin grafts are considered as a treatment option
when there is delay in wound healing due to its
large surface area. They can be either autograft or
synthetic. The most preferred donor site for skin
graft is the thigh region.

23.4.2 Immediate Complications
23.4.2.1

 erebrospinal Fluid Leak
C
and Meningitis
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leak can occur in fractures involving the floor of the anterior cranial
fossa, especially the cribriform plate, the posterior
wall of frontal sinus, and the ethmoidal and sphenoidal sinuses. Early leak can be accompanied by
blood; therefore, it is bloodstained but later turns
out to be a clear, watery discharge from the ear,
nose, or any associated lacerations. The typical
“tramline” effect is seen in CSF rhinorrhea and
epistaxis. CSF leak may be confirmed by determination of the glucose content and beta-transferrin
test. Localization of the leak may be done by
intrathecal fluorescein, but only when the ICP is
not raised, or by contrast CT cisternography.
Commonly it ceases spontaneously with no intervention; however, if it is persistent for more than
3 weeks, it should be repaired surgically. CSF
leakage significantly increases the risk of meningitis. Therefore, any high-level fracture with a
suspicion of CSF leak should be immediately
started with antibiotic prophylaxis [1].

23.4.2.2 Raised Intracranial Pressure
Raised intracranial pressure is a serious complication that could occur at any time following a
head injury. Etiology includes intracranial hematoma, contusion, edema, etc. The clinical signs
are headache, vomiting, loss of consciousness,
restlessness, bradycardia, raised blood pressure,
photophobia, slow breathing, papilledema, and
deranged pupillary responses. Failing to treat
immediately could result in midbrain distortion,
cerebral compression, and infarction, ultimately
leading to grave morbidity and death [1].

23.4.3 Carotid-Related Injuries
Carotid Cavernous Sinus (CCS) Fistula Due
to rupture of the part of internal carotid artery that
traverses in the cavernous sinus. Pulsatile exophthalmos and bruit felt around the orbit are the distinguishing characteristic features of CCS fistula.

the artery followed by thrombus removal.

23.4.5 Late Complications
23.4.5.1 Post-Severe Head Injury
After a severe head injury, it takes many months
or even years for a patient to recover completely.
Patient can have permanent disabilities such as
loss of memory, poor concentration, cranial nerve
