23.4.8 Complications Related
to Nasal Region
23.4.8.1 Septal Hematoma
Septal hematoma usually occurs secondary to
nasal trauma and presents within the first
24–72 h after trauma. It is a rare but a serious
complication that requires immediate intervention. The patient will present with pain on palpation of the nasal tip and unilateral or bilateral
fluctuant swelling of the nasal septum. Septal
hematoma actually refers to the collection of
blood under the mucoperichondrium or mucoperiosteum of nasal septal cartilage or bone. It
may be unilateral or bilateral, with the latter
being more frequent in the setting of severe
trauma. It is usually diagnosed clinically. Septal
hematoma causes stripping of the septal cartilage of its blood supply and may lead to abscess
formation, followed by cartilage necrosis,
resulting in significant nasal deformity and sep-

23.4.8.2 Nasal Deformity
Gross comminution of the NOE complex which
is not corrected immediately leads to saddle nose
deformity (Fig. 23.11), which cannot be corrected by late osteotomy since the fractured bony
fragments are small and they heal as a whole
chunk of bone. Therefore, secondary correction
is done in such cases by removal of the bony
chunk and reconstructing the nasal bridge with
calvarial bone grafts.
23.4.8.3 Traumatic Telecanthus
Persistent traumatic telecanthus after the surgery
is a sign of mismanaged naso-orbito-ethmoidal
fracture (Fig. 23.12). There occurs unsatisfactory
positioning of medial canthus specially in cases
when the surgeon addresses only the zygomaticoorbital component and fails to address the naso-­
ethmoidal component. Management includes
accurate reduction and stabilization of the
canthus-­bearing medial orbital rim segment with
adequate soft tissue management of the medial
canthal area, which remains the key to successfully repairing and restoring pre-injury facial
appearance in primary stage. In most cases, the
canthus remains attached to a bony fragment of
medial orbital rim, where miniplate and screw
fixation usually suffice. If canthal ligament is
partially or completely stripped or the canthal-­
bearing segment is comminuted, then the canthus
should be reattached to a site posterior and superior to lacrimal fossa which is done after bone
reduction and fixation is complete. Transnasal
wire fixation of canthus is an accepted method of
repositioning and fixing the medial canthal tendon but ensuring the transnasal wire reduction
posterior and superior to lacrimal fossa so as to

23 Complications in Maxillofacial Trauma

427

Fig. 23.11 Saddle nose deformity

avoid splaying of posterior aspect of frontal process of the maxilla which can accentuate telecanthus. However, while managing the late cases,
correction should be better with use of two hole
plates. The upper hole of the plate is fixed to the
solid bone anteriorly, and the lower hole is utilized for fixing the canthal tissue using a stainless
steel wire, thus ensuring that the canthopexy is at
the level of lacrimal crest. In highly comminuted
naso-ethmoidal fractures, improvement of nasal
height and contour requires placement of bone
graft over reassembled nasal framework.
However, in late cases, extensive stripping is
required to free the bony fragments from scar tis-

sue to accomplish reduction. So dorsal nasal
bone grafts are invariably required in this subset
of patients for adequate nasal height and projection [3, 15].

23.4.9 Complications Related
to Orbital Region
23.4.9.1 Retrobulbar Hematoma
Retrobulbar hematoma is the most common
cause of blindness in midface fractures. Venous
hemorrhage when occurring resolves spontaneously without any adverse effect, but arterial

428

S. Singh et al.

Fig. 23.12 Traumatic telecanthus (pre- and post-operative)

hemorrhage due to rupture of the infraorbital
artery or the anterior or posterior ethmoidal arteries can be debilitating by compromising the optic
nerve function and central retinal artery obstruction. This most commonly occurs in young individuals, in whom the orbital septum is inelastic
and impermeable, which prevents spontaneous
decompression by anterior displacement of the
globe and thus leakage of blood into subcutaneous tissue.
The patients with retrobulbar hematoma present with severe aching pain in the affected eye
and progressive loss of vision (after complete
loss the pupils become dilated and fixed), proptosis, marked subconjunctival hemorrhage, gross
eyelid swelling, loss of direct pupillary light

reflex, diplopia, and ophthalmoplegia. The diagnostic methods include vision charting, light
reflex examination, and MRI scan.
In cases with spontaneous recovery, in the first
10–20 min, there are only initial signs of retrobulbar hematoma which improves on its own,
thus requiring no treatment. In cases where there
is no spontaneous recovery even after 20 min and
the intraocular pressure has considerably
increased more than 30–40 mmHg, immediate
therapeutic intervention is warranted. Medical
conservative management includes slow IV
injection of acetazolamide (adult dose—500 mg),
IV mannitol 20% 1–2 gm/kg over 30–60 min and
IV dexamethasone 3 mg/kg every 6 h, and timolol ophthalmic drops 0.5%, 1–2 drops topically

23 Complications in Maxillofacial Trauma

twice daily. Surgical management includes lateral canthotomy, in which the palpebral aperture
is widened, and lateral cantholysis, where the lateral canthal ligament is divided. This allows the
globe to move forward and causes escape of
blood from the orbit [16].

23.4.9.2 Diplopia
Management of diplopia is considered in detail in
the previous chapter on midface fracture management. Surgery hardly plays any role in delayed
cases where fibrosis makes it very complex to
approach. Recent studies have revealed that
untreated diplopia cases are seen to recover on
their own after a time period of 3–6 months.
23.4.9.3 Enophthalmos
Enophthalmos is caused by decrease in volume
of the orbital contents or increase in volume of
the bony orbit. It is less of a clinical problem and
more of an aesthetic problem (Fig. 23.13). This

Fig. 23.13 Enophthalmos

429

may not always be apparent at the time of surgery. Defects along the medial and lateral walls
of the orbit in the posterior part, when overlooked
during surgery, frequently cause delayed enophthalmos, which is very difficult to treat. Orbital
volume expansion of 1 cc produces enophthalmos of 0.8 mm.
There is sunken eye with narrowing of palpebral width with pseudoptosis of the upper
lid, having supratarsal hollowing. There is also
hooding of the eye with decreased anterior projection of the globe. In response retraction of
the other eyelid occurs. Paresthesia of the
infraorbital nerve territory may occur.
Enophthalmos of 2–4 mm is considered mild,
while more than 4 mm is considered severe.
There are orbital volume expansion in CT scan,
herniated orbital content in maxillary antrum,
more than 3 mm floor fracture, or medial wall
fracture of 3–5 mm range. An increase in
orbital volume of approximately 1.25 ml will
result in 1 mm enophthalmos. Ten percent
(2.5 ml) increase in volume would be expected
to result in clinically significant enophthalmos,
which is roughly equivalent to 3 mm inferior
displacement of the orbital floor. Medial orbital
wall displacement of even 1 mm causes 0.4 ml
rise in orbital volume. Also, inferior displacement of orbital floor by 1 mm causes 0.8 ml
increase in orbital volume.
Goals of the treatment are to restore anatomy,
restore orbital volume, preserve vision, improve
eye movements, and restore aesthetics. Defects
should always be overcorrected by a minimum of
2 mm. Orbital fractures should always be repaired
after zygoma correction. If muscle surgery is
required, then it should be done after bony surgery. It is important that in enophthalmos, graft
should be placed behind the equator of globe and
in hypoglobus, it should be placed below the
globe. Therefore, in secondary correction of
enophthalmos, it involves reconstruction of the
internal orbit and reducing the volume of the
bony orbit. Placement of a space-occupying
material behind the globe displacing it anteriorly

23.5.1 Zygomatic Arch Depression
A depressed zygomatic arch fracture that
impinges on the coronoid process, if left
untreated, might cause restriction in mouth opening (Fig. 23.14). If there is associated coronoid
fracture, it might result in ankylosis between
coronoid process and the zygomatic arch, gradu-

431

ally over months or years. The ankylosis could be
either fibrous or bony and is common in children.
Management is by means of coronoidectomy
with or without osteotomy of the zygomatic arch
followed by plating. Sometimes, a subperiosteal
implant (silicone or polyethylene) or a bone
transplant can be placed over the malar prominence to re-establish the facial contour [20].

Fig. 23.14 Depressed zygomatic arch fracture and restricted mouth opening

432

S. Singh et al.

23.5.2 Altered Sensation/Paresthesia
Injury to the infraorbital and other branches of
the maxillary division of trigeminal nerve is
common in zygomatic complex fractures,
whereas injury to temporal branch of facial
nerve is common in open reduction of zygomatic arch fractures through preauricular
approaches. In addition to these, zygomaticotemporal and zygomatico-­facial nerves can also
be injured. Due to the deep and complicated
course of the terminal branches of maxillary
nerve, their repair is not feasible; however,
ultrasound therapy can be of some help.
Infraorbital nerve can be explored and compressed, in case of dysesthesia [1].

23.5.3 Maxillary Sinus Infection.
Maxillary sinus becomes prone to infection in
penetrating injuries, contamination during surgery, and presence of oro-antral fistula and dur-

ing displacement of any foreign body into the
sinus. In any of the above cases, the sinus must be
checked for any foreign body followed by thorough irrigation with copious saline. A nasal
antrostomy can be performed in chronic cases. If
oro-antral fistula is present, its closure must be
done after the control of infection, using any one
of the various options such as closure with buccal
fat pad, buccal advancement flap, palatal flap,
tongue flap, nasolabial flap, or temporalis flap,
according to the requirement [1].

23.5.4 Occlusal Complications
Major occlusal discrepancy is related to untreated
or inaccurately reduced maxillary fracture, which
is dealt with in detail in the following text. Most
common occlusal discrepancy seen in zygomatic
complex fracture is the posterior gagging resulting in anterior open bite, which is easily managed
with proper reduction; however, failing to reduce
it could be problematic.

Airway obstruction is a serious life-threatening

and inferior displacement of the maxilla.
Hemorrhage in these cases can also turn out to

displaced maxilla or tracheostomy if reduction is
not feasible [1].

23.6.1.1

Problems with Reduction
and Fixation
Two parameters that are of prime importance in
reducing a displaced maxillary fracture are the
anteroposterior positioning and the facial height.
Accuracy of both the parameters is usually determined easily by achieving proper occlusion
against the intact mandible. Hence, difficulty
arises when there is concomitant fracture of the
mandible, especially bilateral sub-condylar fracture cases, where a fixed reference landmark is
lost. Achieving coinciding dental midlines with
the facial midline is as important as achieving the
molar occlusion. Achieving proper midline could
become challenging in case of missing anterior
teeth and concomitant mandibular fracture and
when there is oral intubation preventing occlusal
check or nasal intubation deviating the nasal tip.

Malunion, Nonunion,
and Occlusal Complications
Malunion can occur in displaced fractures which
are old and untreated and due to inadequate
rigidity of the fixation hardware, inaccurate
reduction before rigid fixation, or fixation hardware failure. Slight malunion is acceptable in
certain cases until it does not cause facial asymmetry and functional disability. Inaccurate
anteroposterior and vertical positioning might
occur when there is concomitant mandible fracture or panfacial fracture, which could result in
significant aesthetic and functional compromise.
Cases of nonunion might require re-surgery to
eliminate the cause. In case of malunion, mild
occlusal deformities may be managed by occlusal rehabilitation, whereas severe cases require
subsequent osteotomy and re-fixation in anatomic position [1, 20].

23.7

Complications of mandibular
fractures

23.7.1 Preoperative Complications
23.7.1.1 Upper Airway Obstruction
Loss of control over the upper airway is the most
serious early complication of an unstable mandibular fracture, especially bilateral anterior
mandibular fracture. The scenario makes it difficult to access the oral cavity for the probable
cause of airway obstruction, and it is also troublesome during orotracheal intubation. The management includes stabilization of the mandible with
dental bridal wiring or supportive bandages tied
around the head supporting the chin and oropharyngeal airway placement.

23.7.1.2

Hemorrhage
and Emphysema
Uncontrolled hemorrhage or emphysema
could result in airway obstruction. Since it is
difficult to perform endotracheal intubation in
these cases, as an emergency measure, trache-

ostomy is performed to restore the airway as
quickly as possible.

23.7.2 Intraoperative Complications
23.7.2.1

Problems with Reduction
and Fixation
Difficulties might occur in accurate reduction of
the fractured segments in cases where there is
gross comminution, bone loss, unfavorable fracture with excessive muscle pull (Fig. 23.15), soft
tissue interposition, concomitant unreduced maxillary fracture, and old malunited fractures. Gross
comminution may be managed by simplification
with miniplates initially, followed by definitive
fixation, while bone loss could be reconstructed
with various types of bone grafts. Treating the
patient under general anesthesia is a wise decision to overcome the problem of unfavorable
muscle pull. Stripping off the muscle from the
fractured bone fragment can also be done, as in
case of unfavorable angle fracture, where the
pterygomassetric sling can be divided and
stripped to reduce the posteromedial pull of the
medial fracture segment [1].

23 Complications in Maxillofacial Trauma

Fig. 23.15 Unfavorable mandibular fracture with excessive muscle pull

23.7.2.2

Problems with Edentulous
Atrophic Mandible
As far as undisplaced fractures are concerned,
edentulous atrophic mandible does not pose any
challenge in reduction; however, displaced fractures are relatively difficult to reduce due to the
thin nature of the atrophic mandible, especially
when it is an old fracture and the fracture ends are
rounded by resorption. Undisplaced fractures can
be satisfactorily treated with gunning splints,
whereas displaced fractures require open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF). Atrophic mandibles usually have poor blood supply, added to
which, periosteal stripping done in ORIF deprives
it of blood supply even more, which could delay
the healing process. Moreover, elderly patients
usually have comorbidities such as uncontrolled
diabetes mellitus and cardiovascular disorders
which could make them unfit for general anesthesia, due to which the treatment can be delayed
leading to added complications [1].

435

(Fig. 23.16). Slight malunion is acceptable in certain cases, such as unilateral condyle fracture and
fractures in edentulous and pediatric mandible.
However, if the malunion is causing any step deformity, facial asymmetry, or deranged occlusion,
effort must be taken to correct it.
Nonunion in the mandible usually occurs
when there is inadequate rigidity in fixation
(Fig. 23.17). It may also be due to various other
reasons such as removal of fixation hardware
before bony union, necrosis of bone on either
side of fracture due to poor blood supply or infection, persistent movements after fixation, inadequate reduction, soft tissue inter-positioning,
metabolic factors, and pre-existing local conditions. Unlike malunion, nonunion is not acceptable in any condition. Re-exposure of the fracture
site is recommended for treating the cause followed by proper fixation and post-operative maxillomandibular fixation according to the
requirement [1, 20].

Fig. 23.16 Malunion in an operated mandibular fracture

23.7.3 Post-Operative Complications
23.7.3.1 Malunion and Nonunion
Malunion can occur in displaced fractures which
are old and untreated and treated with nonrigid
fixation, due to inaccurate reduction before rigid
fixation, or due to fixation hardware failure

Fig. 23.17 Nonunion in an operated mandibular

436

23.7.3.2 Occlusal Complications
Post-operative deranged occlusion could result in
case of inadequate reduction, malunion, nonunion, and early release of maxilla-mandibular
fixation (MMF). Patient finds deranged occlusion
highly unacceptable since it can cause inability to
chew, inability to close the mouth in certain
cases, and pain in temporomandibular joint,
which can even radiate up to the head cranially
and neck caudally. Deranged occlusion is more
prone to occur in cases where closed reduction is
done and MMF is released earlier than indicated
or in cases where MMF is not done after open
reduction and internal fixation. If the patient is in
the healing phase and bony union has not taken
place, then MMF with guiding elastics to normal
occlusion will suffice. If bony union has taken
place and there is only a mild occlusal discrepancy, it can be managed satisfactorily by MMF
with guiding elastics or cuspal reduction and
occlusal alterations, whereas severe discrepancy
requires a secondary surgery which involves
osteotomy to refracture and achieve normal
occlusion.
23.7.3.3 Altered Sensation
Inferior alveolar nerve and mental nerve are the
frequently injured nerves during open reduction
of mandible fracture. They might be stretched,
compressed, or even severed during the surgery.
Mostly they do not require any treatment, since if
the canal is realigned, the nerve has the capacity
to regenerate and repair itself, irrespective of the
degree of injury. Branches of facial nerve such as
marginal mandibular and cervical nerves are also
prone to damage, which is considered in detail in
the following text.

23.8

Nerve Injury

23.8.1 Cranial Nerves I, II, III, IV,
and VI
Injury to the first six cranial nerves commonly
occurs due to traumatic brain injury and during
trauma to anterior cranial fossa. Injury to olfactory nerve rootlets might occur in LeFort III fracture due to the fracture of cribriform plate. Injury
to this nerve results in anosmia. Injury to optic
nerve is relatively rare in maxillofacial trauma,

since the LeFort III fracture line does not pass
through the optic foramen. However, it may get
compressed or injured by a fractured bone fragment and retrobulbar hematoma and in orbital
apex syndrome due to various reasons. Injury to
optic nerve could result in decreased visual acuity and visual field defects according to the
­severity of the injury. Injury to oculomotor nerve
can cause blepharoptosis, diplopia, mydriasis,
and impairment of the extraocular muscle movements, and the response to direct or consensual
light reflex may be sluggish or absent. The lon-

438

S. Singh et al.

gest intracranial course of the trochlear nerve
renders it highly prone to injury from blunt head
trauma and from changes in intracranial pressure.
Injury to this nerve could result in vertical,
oblique, or torsional diplopia and restriction in
ocular motility. Abducens nerve injury may cause
binocular horizontal diplopia when looking to the
side of the paretic eye. It is also accompanied by
strabismus and slight adduction when the patient
looks straight.

23.8.2 Trigeminal Nerve Injury
All three branches of the trigeminal could get
injured during maxillofacial trauma. A study has
shown that the prevalence of trigeminal nerve
injury in maxillofacial trauma cases is approximately 40%. There can be various causes for
nerve injury such as the line of fracture passing
through the foramen, bony fragment impinging
on the nerve, excessive soft tissue edema, secondary ischemia, secondary to dental anesthesia,
crush injury, and iatrogenic injury. Fractures
extending from the temporal bone to the clivus
may result in injury to the trigeminal root or ganglion. Facial fractures commonly affect the
peripheral branches of trigeminal nerve. The lingual nerve is the second most common nerve
damaged during dental procedures, whereas
injury to the buccal nerve and greater palatine
and nasopalatine nerves is insignificant. The inferior alveolar nerve is also at a high risk for injury
during oral and dental procedures. Therefore, the
sensory defects are mainly noticed in the regions
supplied by lingual nerve and inferior alveolar
nerve. Paresthesia of the infraorbital nerve is not
uncommon in fractures involving the infraorbital
rim/foramen. The sensory defect is also accompanied by pain in most of the cases [3].

23.8.3 Facial Nerve Injury
The branches of facial nerve are commonly
injured intraoperatively rather than during the
trauma. Surgeons readily encounter the terminal
branches of facial nerve during open reduction of

Fig. 23.20 Facial nerve palsy

zygomatic arch, mandibular condyle, and ramus
fractures. The marginal mandibular and cervical
branches of facial nerve are often encountered
during standard submandibular and retromandibular approaches to the mandibular condyle. Injury
to the marginal mandibular nerve results in asymmetry of the mouth during smiling and also the
patient will be unable to move the lower lip down
or laterally on the affected side, due to loss of
innervation to the depressor anguli oris and
depressor labii inferioris. The temporal and zygomatic branches of facial nerve are commonly
encountered during preauricular approach to the
zygomatic arch or the head of the condyle
(Fig. 23.20). The injury to temporal branch may
result in loss of function of frontalis and orbicularis oculi muscles. Injury to zygomatic branch
results in paralysis of levator anguli oris, levator
superioris, zygomaticus major, and zygomaticus
minor, whereas injury to the buccal branch results
in paralysis of buccinator and orbicularis oris
muscles of the affected side. The root of cervicofacial branches may also be encountered by the
preauricular approach [3].

23.9

Infections

23.9.1 Wound Infection
Wound infection can be either acute or chronic.
In any case of wound infection, the region must
be explored for any foreign body such as pieces

23 Complications in Maxillofacial Trauma

439

frontal sinuses, while the least commonly
involved are the sphenoidal sinuses. Probable etiologies include nasal instrumentation, craniofacial trauma, concomitant use of steroids, and
severe polytrauma injury. Paranasal sinusitis
must be checked for when a patient with these
features develops unexplained fever or other
signs and symptoms of sepsis. Management
includes removal of the nasal tubes, antral puncture for irrigation, aspiration for microbiologic
culture, nasal decongestants, systemic antibiotics, and surgical sinus drainage if indicated [1].
Fig. 23.21 Wound infection

23.9.3 Space Infections
of glass, metal, grit, etc. If the infection occurs
during the post-operative period, the surgical
wound must be reopened and carefully explored
for leftover gauze or cotton rolls, loosened or dislodged screws, wires, and implant materials
which get infected with time (Fig. 23.21). Plain
radiographs can be used to assist in this procedure; however, certain materials such as wood,
glass, and plastics are not visible in a radiograph.
An infected tooth within the fracture line could
also be a source of infection, which should be
removed immediately. In acute infections,
removal of the etiology, thorough irrigation, and
proper closure suffice. In chronic infections,
there is often an area of tender induration with
discharging sinus. The chronic infection is often
due to penicillin-resistant anaerobic strains, but
occasionally it can be caused by Actinomyces
infection too. However, frequently, no growth is
obtained in the microbiological culture, and
hence it is termed inappropriately as “sterile pus”
by the pathologists. Management of these chronic
wounds with sinus tract formation relies on antibiotics, thorough debridement, and obliteration
of sinus tract [1, 3].

23.9.2 Post-Traumatic Sinusitis
Post-traumatic sinusitis develops due to craniofacial injuries combined with infection and often
accompanied by brain injury and skull and orbital
fracture. The most commonly involved are the

In the modern era of medicine, post-trauma space
infection can be considered a rare entity due to
the concept of “antibiotic prophylaxis.” Therefore
it is important put the patient on antibiotics as
soon as possible post-trauma. It is proven that in
any trauma case with deep lacerations, the
chances of it getting infected are higher when the
antibiotic prophylaxis is not started within 12 h
post-trauma period. Post-trauma space infection
usually occurs after a direct injury to the superficial primary facial spaces such as buccal space,
submandibular space, sublingual space, and submental space. Infection from these primary
spaces is passed on to the deep secondary spaces
such as submasseteric, pterygomandibular, infratemporal, lateral pharyngeal, retropharyngeal,
prevertebral, and parotid space. Patient usually
presents in an advanced stage with a huge swelling, breathing difficulty, and restricted mouth
opening, in which case, the primary goal would
be airway maintenance followed by antibiotic
coverage and pus drainage. If the patient presents
at an early stage, then antibiotics suffice in most
of the cases; if not, pus drainage should be carried out under antibiotic cover [1].

23.9.4 Osteomyelitis
After the advent of antibiotics, post-trauma
osteomyelitis has become a rare phenomenon.
However, it is reported to have occurred in some

Dacryocystitis refers to the infection or inflammation of the lacrimal sac, commonly due to any
obstruction in the nasolacrimal duct. Topical
antibiotics are the mainstay of treatment which
could be accompanied by retrograde massage
over the inner canthus to help in drainage. Last

Fig. 23.22 Osteomyelitis

cases, especially in the mandible (Fig. 23.22).
Systemic diseases such as diabetes mellitus,
nutritional deficiency, peripheral vascular diseases, and immunocompromised state due to any
reason can be the predisposing factors. Local factors that contribute to this situation include previous radiotherapy, local ischemia, presence of
foreign bodies, and impairment of normal drainage in case of fractures involving paranasal
sinuses. Most commonly the infections are found
to be polymicrobial. Management includes
course of antibiotics according to sensitivity,
hyperbaric oxygen therapy, debridement, and

23.9.5 Dacryocystitis
In orbital trauma cases, it is not uncommon for
the components of the lacrimal system to get
injured. Injury to the lacrimal sac and duct usually heals by itself. In case of canalicular injury
of either one of the eyelids, the function is compensated by the unaffected canaliculi. However if
both the upper and lower canaliculi are injured,

Cavernous sinus thrombosis (CST) following a
maxillofacial trauma is a rare event; however, it
can occur due to any infected wound in the dangerous area of the face or indirectly through
space infections involving the primary and secondary spaces of the head and neck. Patient might
present with periorbital edema, ptosis, proptosis,
chemosis, restricted eye motility, photophobia,
diplopia, and partial or complete vision loss. CST
is a fatal disease which requires swift diagnosis
and immediate management.

23.9.7 Hardware-Related
Complications
The introduction and evolution of fixation hardware revolutionized the management of maxillofacial trauma to a great level. However, it also
comes along with a considerable number of possible complications such as screw loosening,
screw displacement, plate exposure (Fig. 23.23a,
b), plate fracture (Fig. 23.24), metal sensitivity,
and stress shielding effect. These complications
lead to failure of the implant which eventually
leads to nonunion, malunion, and infection. The
indications for salvage versus removal of the
implant are not well defined in literature. If the
complications occur after the bony union, the
hardware removal is preferred, and if it occurs
before the bony union, then salvage operation
such as hardware revision is performed. Most of
the abovementioned complications are usually
treated by removal of the hardware, as in screw

23 Complications in Maxillofacial Trauma

a

441

This could be treated by removal of the reconstruction plate and replacing it with miniplates, if
bony union is not complete. Most of the hardware-related complications come to notice only
when they had already led to infection. Hardware
infections are treated with culture-­directed antibiotics accompanied by debridement with/without
tooth extraction and reconstruction of hard and
soft tissue defects, if present [24–26].

23.10 Summary
b

Fig. 23.23 (a) Plate exposure, (b) OPG shows malpositioned plates leading to intraoral exposure

The management of post-traumatic secondary
facial asymmetries aesthetically and functionally
needs highly skilled operative procedures, by
highly trained oral maxillofacial or plastic surgeons who by default respect the surgical principles of tissue handling, stable fixation by latest
hardwares like biodegradable plating system, and
maintaining proper rehabilitation. The advent of
CT and MRI has brought about a great revolution
in the meticulous diagnosis of late trauma cases
and their management. Mismanaged late complex fractures often leave the patient with some
long-term cosmetic and functional deficits. It is a
complex and a very difficult task to restore these
patients to their pre-trauma status. Therefore, it is
the best option to nip the bud in primary surgery
itself by preventing the late complications.

23.11.1 C
 ase Study of a Patient
with Severe Post-Burn
Contracture
of Maxillofacial-Neck
Region.
Chief Complaints A 10-year-old girl reported
with severe post-thermal burn face and neck
contracture.
History of Presenting Illness The patient had
suffered a fire accident in the house, which she
survived with thermal burns over her face. She

442

was ill-treated in her village by local practitioner
which resulted in severe post-burn contracture of
facio-cervicosternal region. She had difficulty in
eating and speech, and appearance was anxious
and slightly depressed due to lack of social
acceptance.
Past Medical History Not contributory.
Clinical Examination Severe contracture of
grade 3 with broad contracture scar causing flexion deformity of the neck as neck extension was
restricted. On trying to extend the neck, the lower
lip is pulled down with tongue getting projected
out and was accompanied by drooling of saliva as
a consequence (Fig. 23.25).
Extraoral Examination Revealed gross scarring over the lower face and neck region leading
to fixed neck contracture without much movement of the neck. The lower lip also appeared
stretched inferiorly leading to severe incompetent lips.
Intraoral Examination Nothing substantial
was found.

Fig. 23.25 Post-burn contracture over the face and neck
region

S. Singh et al.

Treatment Under local anesthesia and mild
sedation, the release of contracture and excision
of scar till deep fascia were done, and the neck
was extended fully and fish tailing at corners was
done. Split skin graft was taken from the thigh
and applied horizontally and fixed. Over the skin
graft, dressing with sofratulle was done and covered by saline-soaked cotton pads. Bandaging
was done and tie-over stitching done to prevent
graft movement. Then extension neck splinting
was done with plaster of paris. First dressing was
done after 7 days, and there was hundred percent
graft uptake. Dressings were repeated every fifth
day till 3 weeks, and then cervical collar along
with pressure garments was applied for 6 months
(Fig. 23.26).
Result The result was excellent with good
mobility and extension of the neck. The cervicomental angle achieved was satisfactory, and secondary contracture on the face has subsided due
to treatment of primary contracture of neck
region. However patient did not come for regular
follow-up due to expenses for travelling. As the
child grows further, corrective surgery is required
due to failure of growth of grafted skin as body
grows. This could have been avoided if flap was
tried in form of free tissue transfer but has its own
aesthetic problems to address later. The patient
reported 10 years later with healed scars over the
face and neck region and was living happily with
her family (Fig. 23.27a, b).

24.1

Introduction

Maxillofacial rehabilitation aims to achieve truly
what the word “Rehabilitation” means which is
the action of restoring someone to health or normal life through training and therapy after imprisonment, addiction or illness. The word
“maxillofacial” as in Merriam-Webster dictionary refers to “of, relating to, or treating the maxilla and the face”; term “craniofacial” refers to
“of, relating to, or involving both the cranium and
the face”; and “face” refers to “the front part of
the head that in humans extends from the forehead to the chin and includes the mouth, nose,
cheeks, and eyes”.
The Global Burden of Disease Study (GBD)
defines facial fractures as fractures to the nasal
bones, orbits, mandible, maxilla, and other facial
bones, as coded in ICD9 code 802 and ICD10
codes S02.2, S02.3, S02.4, S02.5, S02.6 and

Cuttack, Odisha, India
H. Gupta

Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh, India

S02.7. A study documenting till 2017 has added
that falls are the leading cause of facial fractures
globally and are most concentrated in Central
Europe and that there were an estimated 7.5 million new cases of facial fractures with 1.8 million
individuals living with disability from a facial
fracture [1]. As per a systematic review published
in 2016, road traffic accidents were the major
reason for maxillofacial trauma in India with the
mandible being the most affected [2].
Maxillofacial injuries can be simple as Ellis
Class I fracture and/or complex involving a
phased treatment with various specialities. The
management of such maxillofacial trauma
requires a multidisciplinary approach involving a
team of maxillofacial surgeons, plastic surgeon,
ENT surgeon and maxillofacial prosthodontist,
psychologist, speech therapist, nursing staff and
technicians.
The contribution of a prosthodontist starts
from the beginning of the phased treatment planning as the management of a panfacial trauma
starts with management of occlusion first along
with fractured split palate before plating and
reconstruction of the midface and frontal bones
[3], and the role continues as a part of maintenance phase.
The role of a prosthodontist is to communicate
with the surgeon regarding the extent of reconstruction, precise surgical technique, anticipated
postoperative defects and healing time so as to
ascertain the prosthodontics aspect. While

f­ormulating the treatment plan, recommendations can be made for the preservation of tissues

is to provide a natural, life-like, integrated, aesthetically pleasing, anatomically correct prosthesis, which blends with the body specially the
surrounding structures [4].
Rehabilitation goals focus on the restorative,
supportive and functional aspects of treatment,
restoration of speech deficit and control of oral
secretions, mastication and swallowing, and a
large percentage would require restoration of
mutilated facial parts like the eye, nose, ear and
midface for aesthetics. Restoration of such
defects is a combination of science and creativity.
It is not just the knowledge of materials and technique but involves empathy and patience as well.

24.2

 urgical or Prosthetic
S
Rehabilitation

Facial defects can be restored either surgically or
prosthetically depending on the location and size
of the defect, availability of tissues, ease of grafting, mobility of tissues, patient’s willingness to
accept a removable prosthesis and the age of the
patient. There are no absolute indications or contraindications to the surgical or prosthetic rehabilitation as each scenario is to be treated
individually while following basic guidelines.
Some of the factors to be considered for surgical/prosthodontics rehabilitation are as follows:
location and size of defect; amount of remaining
supportive tissue; limitations with grafting and
the available tissue; mobility of the tissue; number, position and condition of the remaining
teeth; risk to benefit ratio in old age; associated
co-morbidities, i.e. medical condition of the
patient; pathologic findings; projected outcomes
of the treatment plan; patient preferences regarding surgical versus prosthetic reconstructions;
technical skills of the reconstructive surgeon and
prosthodontist; economics, psychological status
and manual dexterity of the patient to deal with
maxillofacial prosthesis; and availability of ade-

quate supportive care in case the patient is not
able to take care of the prosthesis. However, plastic (or autoplastic) surgery is generally preferred
over alloplastic (or artificial) reconstruction,
wherever applicable [5, 6]. But in the absence of
manual dexterity of the patient and poor vision,
the prostheses are poor choices for prosthetic
rehabilitation. At times surgical correction fails
to achieve the necessary results or is unsuccessful; then prosthetic rehabilitation becomes a viable option for rehabilitating patients.
Prosthetic replacement of missing facial tissues offers several advantages over surgical
reconstruction. It is less complicated and has a
shorter process, lesser hospital visits with no
overnight stay, relatively inexpensive, less stressful with better aesthetics, has provisions for
incorporating ageing feature like wrinkles, folds,
etc., has better benefit to risk ratio in old age, for
paediatric patients, allows for periodic evaluation
and cleaning of the site, alternative to unsuitable
a patients. Disadvantages include possible irritation of the tissue site; for periodic remake, problems with retention; and daily removal of the
prosthesis. The prosthodontist is limited by materials available for facial restoration, movable tissue bed, too little tissue available and patient’s
willingness to accept a removable prosthesis.

24.3

Classification of Maxillofacial
Defects

Due to the varying degrees of maxillofacial
trauma and complex nature of the face, it is difficult to formulate a universally acceptable classification involving the whole face. Instead,
classifications for various areas of this region
have been separately proposed so as to enable
interaction between the surgeon and rehabilitating interdisciplinary team:

24.3.1 For the Maxilla
The popular Aramany classification was based
upon the relationship of the defect with the abutment teeth [7]. Liverpool classification proposed

24

Rehabilitation

447

by Brown et al. in 2000 classified surgical defects
separately according to the vertical and horizontal
components of the defect [8]. Cordeiro et al. in
2000 classified maxillectomy defects to provide a
reconstruction algorithm for these defects as well
[9]. Okay et al. in 2001 classified palatomaxillary
defects to organise and define the complex nature
of the restorative decision-making process [10].
Durrani et al. in 2013 proposed a classification
which should act as a guide for the clinician regarding reconstructive and rehabilitation options [11].

2. Based in terms of reconstruction, they are
classified under four types [9]:
• Type I defects: Limited maxillectomy.
• Type II defects: Subtotal maxillectomy.
• Type III defects: Total maxillectomy.
–– Type IIIa: Although the orbital floor is
removed, the orbital contents are
preserved.
–– Type IIIb: The orbital contents are also
resected along with total maxillectomy.
• Type IV defects: Orbitomaxillectomy.

24.3.2 For the Mandible

24.4

Most relevant classification systems for mandibular defects are by Cantor and Curtis in 1971, by
Urken et al. which is based on functional considerations caused by detachment of different muscle groups and difficulties with cosmetic
restoration and by Jewer et al. in 1989 that
included the complexity of mandibular reconstruction [12–14].

24.3.3 For Midfacial Defect
Midfacial defects are defined as those confined to
the middle third of the face in the horizontal
plane and that communicate with intraoral maxillary defects. They are complex three-dimensional
defects [15].
Several classification systems have been proposed, mostly related to the extension, location
and tissue involvement of the defect.
1. Based on sagittal plane, they are classified as
follows [15]:
• Midline midfacial defects include complete or partial involvement of the nose
and/or upper lip and communication with
an intraoral maxillary defect.
• Lateral midfacial defects include complete
or partial involvement of the cheek and
orbital contents and communication with
an intraoral maxillary defect.
• A combination of the above two is frequently seen in the cases of trauma.

Classification of Maxillofacial
Prosthesis

Ackerman in 1953 defined maxillofacial prostheses as the phase of dentistry that repairs and artificially replaces parts of the face after injuries or
surgical intervention [16]. This definition excludes
defects due to congenital craniofacial deformities.
Maxillofacial reconstruction involves restoring
intraoral and extraoral structures such as the eyes,
ears, nose, maxilla, mandible, oesophagus, cranial
bones and palate [17].
Maxillofacial prosthetics is defined by the
current Glossary of Prosthodontic terms (GPT
9) “as the branch of Prosthodontics concerned
with the restoration and/or replacement of the
stomatognathic (jaws) and craniofacial (facial)
structures with prostheses that may or may not
be removed on a regular or elective basis”
[18]. Craniofacial prostheses, also known as
epistheses, are artificial substitutes for facial
defects.

24.5.2 Based on Its Function
1. Restorative or primary: Extraoral and intraoral prosthesis to substitute for bone loss or
repair deformities of facial contour.
2. Complementary or secondary: Facial moulages which help with facial plastic surgery, in
the pre-, trans-, or post-operative period, surgical obturator after maxillectomy, flange
prosthesis, fluoride trays, mandibular exercisers [19].

24.5.3 Based on the Anatomical
Areas
1. Extraoral prosthesis: Orbital/ocular prosthesis, and facial prostheses which can be
classified as nasal, lip, oculopalpebral,
auricular, skullcap and traqueostomal.
These are generally for extensive facial
reconstruction and aim at improving appearance and quality of life [19].
2. Intraoral prosthesis: Dento-alveolar prosthesis, maxillary prosthesis including maxillary
obturator, palatal lift prosthesis, mandibular
prosthesis including mandibular exercisers,
guide flange prosthesis, tongue prosthesis.
3. Composite prosthesis: Combination of the
intraoral and extraoral prosthesis.

24.5.5 Based on the Type
of Fabrication
1. Conventional technique: The conventional
protocol involves making impressions, obtaining diagnostic models that accurately represent the defect and wax pattern, fabricating
the prosthesis by packing silicone into the
moulds, fitting the definitive prosthesis and
performing subjective evaluation.
2. Digital manufacturing: This computerassisted designing which is converted using
3D printing. This precludes making of physical impressions of the defect, wax pattern,
moulds and silicone processing and instead
directly prints the prosthesis through CAD
designing and printing.

24.6

Materials Used
for Maxillofacial Prosthesis

The origin of maxillofacial prostheses is not
clear. The only recorded case of maxillofacial
reconstruction between 200 AD and 1000 AD is
related to the Byzantine Emperor Justinian II
who had a golden nose manufactured while he
was crowned [20]. Ambroise Pare’ was the first
one to document the use of maxillofacial prostheses during the sixteenth century. He mentioned the use of the artificial eyes, ears and
noses and described the manufacturing of an
obturator prosthesis [20]. Since then experimentation with materials like gold, silver, paper,

24.6.1 For Fabrication
The properties like nontoxic/nonallergenic materials with high edge strength and colour stability
are the deciding features when choosing a maxillofacial prosthetic material/technique [22].
Modern materials used for maxillofacial prostheses are divided into methacrylates, polyurethane
elastomers and silicone elastomers. Silicones and
acrylic resins are the most used materials for
maxillofacial reconstruction as the advantages
outweigh the benefits of other materials.
The material of choice for fabrication of
intraoral prostheses is generally a combination

449

of silicone polymers which are of two types:
room-temperature vulcanising silicone (RTV)
and high-temperature vulcanising silicone, resins, tissue conditioners and soft liners. A survey published in 2010 observes the worldwide
preference for RTV silicones, pigments and
colourants in the quest to provide the best possible facial prosthetic service [22]. The advantages of RTV silicones are chemical inertness,
low toxicity, good aesthetics, ease of colouring, easy manipulation, margins can be thinned
and stretched till they become transparent and
adhesive compatibility. The disadvantages are
colour degradation over time, technique sensitivity, lack of reparability, extrinsic colours
peel/fade and lack of longevity which is compounded by exposure to ultraviolet rays, air
pollution, temperature variation and humidity.
Tissue liners are plasticiser-rich resins or silicones which are used when the prosthesis-­bearing
area is healing or the fit needs to be improved, but
this needs to be replaced every 3–5 days and soft
liner is more applicable for definitive prosthesis,
and their cushion-like effect lasts for few months
to a couple of years. Both are used to engage
available soft and hard tissue undercuts in the
defect area.
Colours The prosthesis may be stained
intrinsically (colour within the material) or
extrinsically (stain on the material). Dry earth
pigments, rayon flocking fibres (most commonly
used), artist’s oil pigments or a combination of
these materials for intrinsic tinting. The mostused extrinsic ­
colouring method was Medical
Adhesive Type A mixed with xylene as a retarder/
thinner tinted with dry earth pigments or artist’s
oil pigments applied to the surface of the prosthesis in a thin layer.

24.6.2 Retention of Maxillofacial
Prosthesis
The prognosis of retention of a maxillofacial
prosthesis is directly related to the type of retentive element used which indirectly relies on factors such as extent of trauma, design of the
prosthesis, availability of the material and experience of the operator.

Retention for maxillofacial prosthesis can be
derived from various factors divided as follows
(Table 24.3):
1. Are of four types [23]:
• Anatomically: by using body cavities/
defect area and/or teeth.
• Mechanically: by use of eye frames, wires,
magnets, snap buttons, studs, clips, headbands, straps.
• Adhesively: by use of adhesives, tapes.
• Surgically: by implants [24, 25].
2. Are of two types:
• Primary or anatomical support: defect/
body cavities, skin pockets, teeth.
• Secondary or mechanical support or extraneous means:
–– Osseointegrated retentive elements, i.e.
implants.
–– Non-osseointegrated retentive elements
such as adhesives, tapes, eye frames,
wires, magnets, snap buttons, studs,
clips, headbands, straps which help in
improving the prognosis.
Adhesives available for extraoral prosthesis
are in two common forms: liquid (silicone or
acrylic based) or double-sided medical grade
tape. They are easier to use, and medical adhesives often lose their bone strength as the adhesive naturally weakens, requiring reapplication
every 4–8 h, or sooner. Water-based adhesives are
milder to the skin but are not moisture resistant
and do not adhere as long as silicone-based adhesives [26].
There are limitations to adhesive retention
method as movement of the skin around the prosthesis, high humidity, oily skin or profuse sweating loosens the marginal seal and border
adaptation of the prosthesis. They are poor choice

for retention in patients with active outdoor
lifestyle.
Craniofacial/maxillofacial implants: Since the
introduction of extraoral implants in 1979 for
retaining a bone-anchored prosthesis, the positive
outcome of facial prosthesis has improved to a
great extent [27]. However, it is not just the retentive element, but the case selection by the operator, prosthesis fabrication by the prosthodontist
and the hygiene by the patient decide the longevity of the treatment. One should remember that
implants are not the end of all non-retentive
problems.
These implants are placed for osseointegrated
prosthesis [23]:
1. When
reconstructive
surgery
is
contraindicated.
2. As an interim prosthesis during individual
stages in plastic reconstructive surgery.
3. Following failed reconstructive procedures.
4. Due to patient’s unwillingness for reconstructive surgery.
5. If prosthetic reconstruction would produce
better results aesthetically.
Implants used for retention of maxillofacial
prosthesis can be divided into:
1. Based on the site of placement:
(a) Conventional intraoral implants: These
are placed in maxillary and mandibular
bone.
(b) Craniofacial or extraoral implants: These
are smaller than the conventional
implants.
2. Based on the amount of available bone at the
pre-decided site [28]:
(a) Alpha sites: Zygoma, anterior maxilla and
mandible are the alpha sites in craniofacial region where the amount of available
bone is from 6 mm or greater. Conventional
implant fixtures with greater lengths are
used for retaining complex facial prosthesis or dental prosthesis.
(b) Beta sites: Periorbital, temporal, zygomatic and anterior nasal fossa locations

24

Rehabilitation

where shorter implant fixtures (5 mm) or
phalanged fixtures (4 mm) are indicated.
(c) Delta sites: Buttress, pyriform, zygomatic
arch, medial orbit, temporal and frontal
bones and zygomatico-frontal process
where implant fixtures used that are 3 mm
or less are indicated.
Extraoral implant systems: These can be
divided into [23]:
1. Solitary implant system: Single screw implant,
e.g. Brånemark, ITI, IMZ.
The craniofacial implants are 3–4 mm in
length as the availability of bone is limited.
The implant has a perforated flange for
increasing the bone to implant contact area
which helps in enhancing the initial mechanical stability of implant and prevent intracranial pressure and later on prevents tilting of
the implant under the action of lateral forces
and moments [29].
2. Grouped implants system: Subperiosteal
frame implants use grid or plate systems
which are secured by several screws, and they
may contain multiple percutaneous abutments, e.g. Epitec and Epiplating systems.
The size of implant increases to 7–10 mm
when it supports both intraoral and extraoral
prosthesis. Such implants are called bifunctional implants [30].

24.6.4 Complications
The most common complication is peri-­
implantitis which is generally due to poor hygiene
around the implants. Peri-implantitis can be
avoided by having adequate distance between the
implants and by counselling the patient about the
maintenance phase.
Besides the use of above-discussed methods,
retention can be improved by:
1. Maximum extension for prosthesis dislodgement prevention
2. Judicious use of favourable undercuts in the
defect area
3. Lightweight prosthesis
4. Hollow bulb

452

S. Gupta et al.

Face is what a person is recognised socially for
it provides an identity to the person. All faces
are beautiful but once mutilated become
socially unacceptable. Facial disfigurement
whether congenital or acquired has the potential to cause cognitive defects and psychosocial
dysfunction [32].
Orbital/ocular, auricular, nasal or combination
including midfacial prosthesis is prosthesis
restoring facial defect(s).
For optimum prosthetic outcome, the surgeons
should keep in mind:
The prognosis of prosthesis is considerably
improved if the surgeon is careful while addressing the defect area(s).

2. Unsupported soft tissues should be removed
as these mobile tissues hamper with the process of impression making, make the prosthesis unstable and may be a disadvantage when
merging with the borders of the defect, so aesthetics is compromised.
3. The defect should be limitedly filled with flap or
graft as some negative space of the defect helps
in retention, provides space for attachments,
substructure for prosthesis, profile is improved.
But, too thin a layer is also not desirable.
4. Graft is to be placed where primary closure is
not possible. A split-thickness skin graft has
several advantages. The split-thickness skin
graft allows the defect margins and adjacent
skin areas to be less movable yet compressible and stable during facial movements,
reduces scar contracture and is a good adheophilic base due to absence of hair and glands.
It is more resistant to abrasive forces especially during insertion of removal of prosthesis [33].

1. The bony edges of/in the defect should be
rounded as the soft tissues or grafts may get
exposed over a certain time. Sharp edges are
more prone to trauma during insertion and
removal of prosthesis.

For a satisfactory prosthetic outcome, initial
tissue assessment, impression making, sculpting,
mould fabrication, familiarity with materials,
appreciation of colour, delivery of instructions
and patient education are important.

Nasal prosthesis helps in improving airflow and speech. This is the centre point of

453

• Preferred site for implant placement is the

attachment [41].
3. Eye prosthesis
Depending upon the impact of trauma,
three types of orbit and eyelid surgeries are
related to ocular prostheses: evisceration, the
partial removal of the eye bulb while preserving the sclera; enucleation, the complete
removal of eye bulb with only the capsule and
oculomotor muscles remaining; and exenteration, the removal of all contents of the orbital
cavity and surrounding tissues. Fabrication of
eye prosthesis has undergone a lot of change
from “glass eye” to “bionic eye” [5].
This can be of two types:

• Preservation of nasal bone helps in providing
retention, vertical support and blending of the
prosthesis with the surrounding skin.
• The cartilaginous septum should be reduced
in an anterior-posterior dimension as a concavity. This concavity allows the placement of
sub-framework.
• Maintaining the anterior nasal spine helps to
determine the final position of the lip.
• Few portions of the normal anatomy such as
the ala, anterior septum and columella may
need to be removed, to allow the prosthesis to
fit properly [36].

1. Ocular prosthesis
It is an artificial eye for it is an artificial
replacement for an eyeball. It maintains the
tonicity of the upper eyelid muscles, preserves
the tear duct whose secretions avoid eyelash
adherence and conjunctival dryness, prevents
eyelid atresia due to lack of function and protects
the cavity mucosa from debris and dust [42].
2. Orbital prosthesis (Figs. 24.1 and 24.2):
After 4–6 weeks of removal of the eye, the

mandibular defect which can be continuity

fabricated once healing is completed and for

of choice is guide flange prosthesis placing
either on the mandible or maxilla and inserted
immediately post-operatively.

3. Patient counselling/prosthetic rehab patient
preparation phase: The importance of this
phase can never be overemphasised. It
involves discussion about the prosthetic aspect
of treatment plan with the patient and related
people. Patients are to be educated about the
choice of prosthesis and retentive methods to
be used, removal and cleaning methods, the
limitations of the prosthesis and life span of
the prosthesis.
4. Initial/early healing phase: Post-operative
prosthesis is fabricated to assist in the healing
process or as an interim or provisional prosthesis till the next surgery is performed or definitive prosthesis is fabricated. Interim facial
prosthesis provides aesthetics and psychosocial support to the patient till the next phase of
rehabilitation. Interim/provisional obturator
provides aesthetics by addition of anterior
teeth, helps in obturating the communication
between the oral and nasal/antral cavities,

460

S. Gupta et al.

mum extension and stronger material like cast
metal, hollow bulb in case of obturator (e.g.
definitive obturator), cast metal framework
guide flange prosthesis (GFP), extraoral prosthesis, crowns/veneers, fixed partial dentures
and removable partial dentures. Implants are
osseointegrated to receive the super/substructure and the prosthesis.
6. Maintenance phase: This phase is crucial for it
involves active participation by the patient as
well without which the treatment plan may be
classified as a failure. It involves educating
and counselling (as the patient has to actually
wear the prosthesis) regarding maintaining
the hygiene of the prosthesis and aspects
about repair and refabrication of the prosthesis. Any reline/occlusion balancing are part of
this phase. Maintenance prosthesis includes
use of flexible mouth trays which cover the
teeth and are used to apply topical fluoride to
prevent the onset of tooth decay, continuous
use of jaw exercisers like Heister’s jaw opener/
exerciser and change of soft liner at periodic
intervals.

24.7.1 Paediatric Rehabilitation

Fig. 24.13 Surgical obturator in the mouth

minimises wound communication and helps in
speech and swallowing of liquids and food.
Interim eye prosthesis serves as a diagnostic
aid for predicting the patient’s compliance to
ocular prosthetic treatment [55].
5. Healed phase prosthesis: This phase starts
when epithelisation is completed, when the
graft has healed, when the defect area would
undergo negligible scar contracture and when
further surgery is not possible due to limitations of the defect, advanced age, poor health,
very large deformity or poor blood supply,
economic constraints or patient’s unwillingness. Such prosthesis is fabricated with maxi-

The incidence of facial fractures in paediatric
population increases with age. The rehabilitation
of a paediatric patient differs in the approach as
compared to adults. The prosthetics rehabilitation of a paediatric patient needs to consider factors like the age of the patient so as to maximise
growth and development, the anatomic site to
optimise form and function, the development
stage of the dentition, design and material for the
prosthesis to make it kid-friendly/acceptable, the
retentive mechanism as a child has an active life
and periodic refabrication to accommodate
growth developments with regular counselling
for motivation.

24.7.2 Maxillary Rehabilitation
Repeated fabrication of obturator is required to
accommodate for the growing bones. There is a

24

Rehabilitation

need to determine which teeth to clasp in patients
of mixed dentition. Innovative techniques like
brackets and light-cured retentive restorations
are required for retention of obturator. Since
such a resection would cause a disturbed occlusion, an orthodontic treatment should be made
part of the rehabilitation process. Special counselling of parents is required on need for physiotherapy to resist decrease in mouth opening
post-surgery, maintenance of oral hygiene and
care of prosthesis.
For surgeons to take note:
• Radiographs indicate tooth buds and erupting
teeth which would guide in placing the initial
incisions without damaging uninvolved tooth
buds.
• Attempts to preserve active growth centres are
important for preserving function, which have
a significant influence on future facial
development.
• Reconstructing the surgical defect can be considered after the patient’s facial growth is
completed.
• Restoring the infraorbital rim and zygomatic
complex can restore facial contours and provide future sites for placing dental implants to
stabilise and support a prosthesis.

24.7.3 Orbital Rehabilitation
Placement of successively larger orbital
implants/conformers/prosthesis during rapid
craniofacial development would stimulate a
more natural development of the orbital cavity
by distributing pressure equally along the
orbital wall, providing the tissue stimulus necessary for orbital growth for a potentially
improved symmetry between the healthy and
defective side [56].
• It is necessary to objectively determine a timetable of ocular prosthesis change along the
whole period of craniofacial growth in order to
minimise the possible discrepancy between the
compromised and the healthy sides, thus contributing to balance and harmony of the facial
development [57].

461

24.7.4 Implants in Paediatric
Patients
• An implantation should at best only be considered after puberty in adolescents although literature
recommends
bone-anchored
prostheses from the age of 10 years [58]. The
implants should be placed only after the threedimensional growth of the mandible and maxilla and other facial structures is completed.
Placing implants before the completion of
bone growth would result in submerged
implants, thus making rehabilitation difficult.

24.7.5 Geriatric Patient
• Facial fractures occurring in older patients
are usually associated with other significant
injuries, greater severity and death. The risk
to benefit ratio in older patients influences
operative decision-­making, often resulting
in a lower operative rate. Reconstruction
requires multiple surgeries, longer hospitalisation and increased cost, whereas prosthetic rehabilitation does not require
additional surgery, is safe and has a shorter
treatment time, making it a preferred option
for geriatric rehabilitation. Treatment plan
in a geriatric patient besides age is influenced by factors like dexterity of hands,
retention for the prosthesis, number of hospital visits, economics and treatment time.
In old age, the edentulous mandible and
maxilla are tricky to manage especially if
accompanied by smoking as they both contribute to poor prognosis. They cause
decreased osteogenesis and limited blood
supply. Atrophic mandible presents limited
space for plating due to reduced ridge
height, mental foramen and mandibular
canal. Dentures are used to function as gunning splint when conservative treatment is
desired; gunning splint is limited to fracture
of body and distal areas of the mandible.
Plating if done must be kept away from the
denture-­
bearing surfaces to avoid future
impingements [59].

462

S. Gupta et al.

24.7.5.1 Implants in Geriatric Patient
• The use of an adhesive-retained prosthesis can
be completely avoided for a non-dexterous,
geriatric patient by using craniofacial implants
to assist in prosthesis retention. Placement of
implants in geriatric patient is limited by
bisphosphonates, anti-coagulants and raised
blood sugar level to name a few limitations.
Atrophic mandible presents poor quality and
quantity for conventional implants.

24.8

Digitalisation
in Maxillofacial
Rehabilitation

Digitalisation is evolving the techniques for the
rehabilitation of a maxillofacial defect, starting
from initial diagnosis till the manufacturing of
the prosthesis. Four key elements form the digital
workflow for treatment of patients with maxillofacial defects: (1) visualisation for data acquisition, (2) design for manufacturing, (3) fabrication
for delivery and (4) evaluation. These key elements are computer-assisted or guided for
computer-­
assisted designing and machining
which have three functional components: (1) a
digitalisation tool/scanner that converts geometry
(digital imaging scans, 3D photographs) into digital data that can be processed by a computer, (2)
software (CAD software) which processes scanner data (DICOM) and produces a data set readable (STL files) by a fabrication machine and (3)
a manufacturing technology (rapid prototyping)
that takes the data set and transforms it into the
desired product by fabricating the restoration.
The digital workflow for rehabilitating a maxillofacial defect is as follows:
1. Digital visualisation: This is done using digital imaging techniques like magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography
(CT), 3D photogrammetry, cone beam computed tomography (CBCT), laser scanning or
ultrasound. This is a part of data acquisition
phase for designing and fabrication of prosthesis. A systematic review on digitisation of
facial defects published in 2019 mentions the

use of a combination of imaging techniques
instead of using only one for facial defects
data acquisition [60]. Besides the digital
scans, a 3D photographic image capture is
another option for capturing the data for fabricating an extraoral maxillofacial prosthesis
[61]. From preoperative scans, the surgeon
can preoperatively visualise and plan the
defect in consultation with the prosthodontist
for reconstruction/rehabilitation or create
patient-specific implants.
2. Digital design: The data obtained from digital
visualisation is processed to design the prosthesis. For designing, computer-assisted
design (CAD)-assisted mirroring techniques
can be used; in its absence digital library can
be accessed. In case of non-availability of
digital library, then impression of a matched
family member’s nose/ear can be scanned and
adjusted onto the patient’s defect digitally.
Once the prosthesis is designed in CAD software, the next stage towards fabrication of
prosthesis which is based on the type of 3D
printer available is completed.
3. Digital manufacture: Manufacturing is done
through 3D printing or rapid prototyping
(RP). As per GPT 9, the term “rapid prototyping”: a general term used for several additive
layer manufacturing techniques; stereolithography; comp, fused deposition modelling,
selective deposition modelling, selective laser
melting, selective laser sintering [18].
The design can be printed directly as prosthesis
or indirectly as a mould or template [62, 63]. A
directly printed prosthesis can be digitally colour
matched and printed as a final product which saves
on a lot of time and tedious shade matching process. A template is converted into a wax pattern
which is tried and adjusted on the patient’s defect
for refinement, which is later used for printing. A
mould needs to be manually packed with the
matching basic shade of silicone and extrinsic
stains done later [64]. Printing the prosthesis
directly eliminates the try-in phase and saves hospital visit but may lead to poor marginal adaptation, though the printed prosthesis is more resistant
to wear and tear than conventional ones [65].

It is advantageous to retain these digital scans,
designs and moulds for reprinting the prosthesis
later as silicone prostheses have limited life and
storing them does not require much physical
space.
Digital fabrication of auricular and nasal prosthesis is more popular as compared to orbital and
ocular prosthesis. Ocular prosthesis still remains
a challenge as the irregularity of the defect socket
is poorly captured in scans and also the 3D volume reconstruction of globe is still being worked
upon. Simply mirroring the healthy globe over
would lead to poor fit of the prosthesis due to the
irregularity of the defect socket, which is poorly
represented in scans [60]. A study showed that
39% of these technologies were used for intraoral
defects and 27% for extraoral defects, while 34%
involved no defect [66]. Colour matching of
facial prosthetic elastomers to skin colour with
portable spectrophotometer and computerised
colour formulation has been developed and has
achieved clinical success [67]. The salient features of CAD/CAM technique are listed in
Table 24.7.
The digitisation is still in its developmental
stage and has not been able to completely replace
the conventional techniques.

24.9

Upcoming Trends

1. Bionic eye, a visual prosthesis, is an experimental visual device intended to restore functional vision in those suffering from partial or
total blindness.
Bionic eye is a wide term for entire electronic system which is made up of the image

sensors, processors, radio transmitters and
receivers and the retinal chip clubbed together
in a single domain. It has the potential to
change people’s lives [68].
2. In an orbital prosthesis, exact mirroring of the
blood vessels and iris is possible by capturing
3D photographs of the healthy eye. This can
be printed or used with sublimation technique
to get perfect match [68].
3. Besides digital planning of extraoral implants,
robot-assisted placement of craniofacial
implants and placement of implants with
image guidance has undergone significant
changes [69].

24.10 Conclusion
The prognosis of maxillofacial prosthesis is dependent on the expertise of rehabilitating team, defect
factors like size and location of the defect, number
of remaining teeth, quantity of healthy tissue,
quality of the mucosa, type of prosthesis, contribution of the patient, the psychological status, peer/
family support and the patient’s ability to accept
the prosthetic treatment. Factors like large complex defect, fewer remaining teeth, non-dexterous
patient, medically compromised patient and poor
psychosocial status contribute to the poor prognosis. Rehabilitating maxillofacial defect is a challenging scenario for the working team and the
patient. With newer developments happening at
frequent intervals, the team needs a constant learning curve, and the patient has to have realistic
expectations for the rehabilitation to be
successful.
